chunks.heading: The EAA Is About to Point at WCAG 2.2: EN 301 549 v4.1.1 Explained
chunks.text:
The European standard behind the Accessibility Act is moving from WCAG 2.1 to WCAG 2.2. If your last audit stopped at 2.1, here is the gap you now have to close, and the parts of EN 301 549 that were never in WCAG at all.
AT

The Accessibility.build Team
August 12, 2026·7 min read

Most conversations about the European Accessibility Act reach for WCAG, but WCAG is not the standard the EAA actually points to. That role belongs to EN 301 549, the European standard for accessibility of ICT products and services. Under Article 15 of the Act, conforming to a harmonised standard whose reference is published in the Official Journal of the EU gives a business a presumption that it meets the accessibility requirements. And EN 301 549 has just moved: the edition built to carry that presumption for the EAA is built on WCAG 2.2, not WCAG 2.1.

chunks.heading: The EAA Is About to Point at WCAG 2.2: EN 301 549 v4.1.1 Explained
chunks.text: Update, 14 October 2026: ETSI published EN 301 549 v4.1.1 on 2 September 2026. It updates the web, document and software requirements to WCAG 2.2 Level AA, rewrites the real-time text clause, and adds an annex (Annex ZB) that maps the standard to the EAA. It has not yet been cited in the Official Journal; Ireland’s National Disability Authority expects that on 16 December 2026. Until then, note what is and is not cited today. The previous edition, v3.2.1 from March 2021 (WCAG 2.1 Level AA), is cited only under the Web Accessibility Directive for public-sector websites and apps. No edition is yet cited under the EAA, so no version currently gives the EAA presumption of conformity. When the v4.1.1 citation lands, the reference point for European accessibility becomes WCAG 2.2, and any programme still measuring itself against 2.1 has a defined gap to close.

chunks.heading: Why the standard, not the guidelines, is the thing to track
chunks.text:
EN 301 549 wraps WCAG rather than replacing it. Chapters 9, 10 and 11 pull the WCAG success criteria into web, non-web document and software contexts, so when EN 301 549 updates its WCAG baseline, the web criteria you are held to move with it. But the standard also covers a great deal that WCAG never addresses: hardware, two-way voice and video communication, real-time text, biometrics, and requirements for the documentation and support that ship with a product. Treating "EAA compliance" as "pass WCAG" quietly ignores those chapters.
The version number matters because the presumption of conformity is tied to the edition cited. A business audited against v3.2.1 was measured against WCAG 2.1. Once v4.1.1 is the cited standard, the benchmark is WCAG 2.2, and the delta between them is real work, not a rounding error.

chunks.heading: The WCAG 2.2 criteria your 2.1 audit never checked
chunks.text:
WCAG 2.2 kept everything in 2.1 and added new success criteria. At Level A and AA, the additions that a 2.1-era audit would have skipped are these:
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA: when an element receives keyboard focus, it must not be entirely hidden behind sticky headers, cookie bars or chat widgets. Fixed page furniture is the usual culprit.
2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA: anything you operate by dragging, sliders, reorderable lists, map panning, needs a single-pointer alternative that does not require a drag.
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA: interactive targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing around them. This is one of the most common new failures on dense mobile layouts.
3.2.6 Consistent Help, A: if you offer help such as contact details or a chat, it must appear in a consistent place across pages.
3.3.7 Redundant Entry, A: do not make people re-enter information they already gave you in the same process, unless it is essential.
3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA: log-in must not depend on a cognitive function test such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle, unless an alternative or a mechanism like a passkey is provided. This one quietly implicates a lot of checkout and account flows.

chunks.heading: The WCAG 2.2 criteria your 2.1 audit never checked
chunks.text: Two of these, target size and accessible authentication, tend to surface real defects on production sites rather than edge cases, so they are the ones worth checking first. WCAG 2.2 also removed the old 4.1.1 Parsing criterion, so a handful of legacy findings simply disappear.

chunks.heading: The parts of EN 301 549 that are not WCAG at all
chunks.text: If your product does anything beyond static web content, v4.1.1’s non-web chapters deserve attention. The real-time text updates matter for any service with live chat or voice and video calling, where text has to be transmitted character by character rather than message by message so that a deaf or hard of hearing user can follow a conversation as it happens. There are also functional performance statements, which describe outcomes for users with particular needs, and documentation requirements that mean your help content and support channels are in scope, not just the interface.

chunks.heading: What to do before the citation lands
chunks.text:
You do not need to wait for the Official Journal to act, and waiting is the wrong move. The safe posture is simple: treat WCAG 2.2 AA as your target now.
Re-run your audit against WCAG 2.2, not 2.1, and treat the six new A and AA criteria as first-class findings.
Prioritise target size and accessible authentication, which most often produce genuine defects.
If you build a mobile app, a kiosk, or anything with live communication, read EN 301 549’s non-web chapters rather than assuming WCAG covers you.
Check that your accessibility statement names the version of the standard you actually tested against, so it does not go stale the day v4.1.1 is cited.

None of this is speculative. WCAG 2.2 has been a finished W3C Recommendation for a while, the new criteria are stable, and the direction of the European standard is set. Auditing to 2.2 today is not getting ahead of the rules, it is meeting the ones that are about to be written down.
Work through every criterion, including the 2.2 additions, with the WCAG 2.2 checklist.
See exactly what changed between v3.2.1 and v4.1.1 in our EN 301 549 guide.
Track transposition across the 27 member states in our European Accessibility Act tracker.
Run a 2.2-level review end to end with the website accessibility audit guide.
Read any criterion in plain language in the WCAG reference.

chunks.heading: The European Accessibility Act at One Year: Enforcement Begins
chunks.text:
One year after the EAA became enforceable, the first actions have landed — formal notices, inspections, court orders, and daily penalties across the EU.

Khushwant PariharJuly 8, 2026·5 min read

The European Accessibility Act (EAA, Directive (EU) 2019/882) became enforceable on June 28, 2025. One year on, the first enforcement actions have arrived — though confirmed monetary fines under national EAA-implementing laws remained rare. Early enforcement has centered on complaints, inspections, formal notices, market surveillance, and corrective-action deadlines rather than immediate penalties. The pattern so far is notice, then investigation, then required fixes, with fines as a later step. Two developments stand out: a French court order against Carrefour, and daily penalties in Norway.

chunks.heading: What the EAA requires
chunks.text: The EAA sets accessibility requirements for a range of products and services sold in the EU, including e-commerce, banking, transport, and e-books. Its technical baseline is the harmonized standard EN 301 549, which incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA. There is a limited exemption for microenterprises providing services, but the reach is broad — and it is not confined to companies headquartered in Europe.

chunks.heading: France: formal notices, then a court order
chunks.text:
In November 2025, France’s DGCCRF — the consumer and competition authority — sent formal enforcement notices to four major retailers: Auchan, Carrefour, E.Leclerc, and Picard. Inspections had found systematic problems: keyboard-navigation failures, missing alternative text, and non-compliant checkout flows.
In June 2026, the Carrefour matter was heard, and a French court ordered Carrefour France to make both its e-commerce website and its mobile application fully accessible to people with disabilities within six months — under penalty of a fine for each day of delay. It has been described as an early EAA-era court ruling, and it underlines a key point: accessibility obligations extend beyond the website to the mobile app.

chunks.heading: Norway: daily penalties
chunks.text:
Norway’s equality and anti-discrimination authority imposed a daily penalty of NOK 50,000 — about EUR 4,500 per day — on the HelsaMi health portal operated by Norsk Helsenett, over persistent keyboard-accessibility failures. The case illustrates how the enforcement escalates: authorities generally issue a notice, investigate, and demand corrective action, with recurring daily penalties applied when problems persist.
The typical enforcement pattern is notice, then investigation, then corrective action — with fines as a later step, not a first resort.

chunks.heading: A recurring theme: keyboard access
chunks.text: Across the French inspections and the Norwegian penalty, keyboard-navigation failures appear again and again — alongside missing alternative text and broken checkout flows. These are foundational, well-understood barriers, and they map directly to WCAG success criteria. A structured WCAG checklist helps teams catch exactly these issues before an inspector does.

chunks.heading: What this means for you
chunks.text:
If you sell to consumers in the EU, the EAA can apply to you — even if your company is based in the United States or elsewhere outside Europe. That is the single most important takeaway for non-EU businesses. E-commerce is squarely in scope, and the early enforcement has landed heavily on online retail.
Confirm your exposure. If EU consumers can buy your products or use your services, assume the EAA is relevant and check whether the microenterprise exemption applies to you.
Test the whole journey. The Carrefour order covered both website and mobile app. Cover your full purchase flow — browsing, search, cart, and checkout — on both surfaces.
Fix keyboard access first. It is the most commonly cited failure and among the most straightforward to verify. Ensure every interactive element is reachable and operable by keyboard alone.
Measure against EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 AA. That is the standard authorities are applying, so it is the standard to build and test toward.

For deeper background, see our overview of the European Accessibility Act and our reference on accessibility laws worldwide.

chunks.heading: The bottom line
chunks.text:
A year in, EAA enforcement is real but still ramping. Big fines under national implementing laws remain uncommon, yet the machinery — inspections, formal notices, court orders, and daily penalties — is clearly in motion, and it is reaching household-name retailers. Organizations that treat WCAG 2.1 AA as the working standard, test both web and mobile, and start with keyboard access will be well ahead of the enforcement curve.
This article is general information, not legal advice.

chunks.heading: Focus Management: The Accessibility Skill Most Developers Skip
chunks.text:
Where keyboard focus goes after a click, a route change, or a closed dialog decides whether your app is usable. A practical guide to focus order, focus-visible, focus trapping, roving tabindex, and restoring focus — with copy-paste patterns.

Khushwant PariharJuly 11, 2026·12 min read

Most accessibility work is about what the user can see and read. Focus management is about something quieter: where the keyboard is right now. When someone navigates with the Tab key, a screen reader, a switch device, or voice control, the focused element is their cursor, their pointer, and their sense of place all at once. Move it carelessly — or lose track of it entirely — and the interface becomes a maze.
This guide covers the focus decisions that come up in real applications: styling the focus indicator, ordering focusable elements, sending focus into and out of dialogs, building composite widgets, and putting focus somewhere sensible after a single-page route change. Every pattern here is something you can apply the same afternoon.

chunks.heading: What "focus" actually is
chunks.text:
Exactly one element in a document holds keyboard focus at any time — you can read it in JavaScript as document.activeElement. Focus is what receives key events, what a screen reader announces as you move, and what a browser scrolls into view. Interactive HTML elements (links, buttons, inputs, selects, textareas) are focusable by default and appear in the tab order. Everything else is not, unless you opt in with tabindex.
The three rules of tabindex are short and rarely bent:
tabindex="0" adds an element to the natural tab order, in DOM position. Use it for custom interactive components built from non-interactive elements.
tabindex="-1" makes an element programmatically focusable — you can call .focus() on it — but keeps it out of the Tab sequence. This is the workhorse of focus management.
A positive tabindex ("1" or higher) forces an element earlier in the tab order than the DOM would suggest. It almost always creates surprises for other elements on the page. Treat it as an anti-pattern.

chunks.heading: Rule one: never delete the focus indicator
Rule two: keep the tab order logical
chunks.text:
SC 2.4.3 Focus Order requires that focus moves in an order that preserves meaning and operability. In practice, that means your DOM order should match your visual reading order. When you reposition content with CSS — flexbox order, grid placement, absolute positioning — the tab sequence still follows the DOM, so a visually top-right button might receive focus last.
Order elements in the DOM the way they should be read and operated, then style position with CSS.
Avoid the CSS order and grid-placement properties for anything interactive unless the visual and DOM order still agree.
Never use positive tabindex to patch a broken order — fix the DOM instead.
When new content appears (an expanded panel, an inserted row), make sure it lands in a sensible place in the sequence rather than at the end of the page.

chunks.heading: Skip links: the fastest win
chunks.text:
A keyboard user should not have to tab through fifty navigation links to reach the main content on every page. A skip link is the first focusable element on the page; it is visually hidden until focused, and it moves focus to the main region when activated. skip-link.htmlCopy Skip to main content
The tabindex="-1" on the target matters: without it, some browsers move the document position but not keyboard focus, so the next Tab press starts from the top again. Style the link to sit off-screen and animate into view on :focus so sighted keyboard users can see where they are jumping.

chunks.heading: Focus trapping in dialogs
Focus trapping in dialogs
chunks.text: Native <dialog> with showModal() gives you trapping, Escape handling, and an inert background for free, and is the recommended starting point today. If you build a custom dialog, follow the modal dialog pattern and pair it with the ARIA Authoring Practices dialog guidance rather than reinventing the keyboard behavior.

chunks.heading: Composite widgets: one tab stop, arrow keys inside
chunks.text: Menus, tabs, toolbars, radio groups, tree views, and grids should not put every child in the tab order. A toolbar with twelve buttons should be a single tab stop; the user reaches it once with Tab, then moves between the buttons with arrow keys. There are two accepted techniques for this.

chunks.heading: Roving tabindex
aria-activedescendant
chunks.text: The alternative keeps real DOM focus on a container (a listbox or combobox input) and points aria-activedescendant at the id of the "virtually" focused child. It suits large lists and comboboxes where moving real focus per item is awkward. Roving tabindex is the safer default for most menus, tabs, and toolbars; reach for aria-activedescendant when a text input must retain focus while a related list is navigated.

chunks.heading: Focus after single-page navigation
Common focus-management mistakes
chunks.text:
Removing outlines globally with outline: none and never adding a replacement.
Calling .focus() on a container that has no accessible name, so the screen reader announces nothing useful.
Setting focus on page load into a search box or ad, hijacking the user before they have oriented.

Triggering a context change purely because an element received focus, which fails SC 3.2.1 On Focus — focus should never, by itself, submit a form, open a new window, or move focus elsewhere.
Creating a keyboard trap where focus enters a widget and cannot leave with standard keys, which fails SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap. A dialog traps focus on purpose and releases it on close; an accidental trap has no exit.
Leaving focus on a button that gets removed or disabled after a click, dropping focus to the body.
Rendering off-screen or hidden content that is still in the tab order — hide it with display:none, the hidden attribute, or inert so it leaves the sequence.

chunks.heading: How to test focus management
chunks.text:
Focus problems are invisible in a static screenshot and often invisible to automated scanners, so test by driving the keyboard yourself.
Put the mouse away. Tab through the whole page from the top and confirm you can see the focus indicator on every stop.
Check that the order matches the visual reading order and that focus never jumps somewhere surprising.
Open every dialog, menu, and popover; confirm focus enters, cannot escape while open, closes on Escape, and returns to the trigger.
Operate composite widgets with arrow keys and verify they are a single tab stop.
Navigate between routes and confirm focus lands somewhere sensible each time.

Add a screen reader to the pass — NVDA, VoiceOver, or JAWS — because focus that looks fine visually can still announce the wrong thing. Then run the interaction through the WCAG 2.2 checklist alongside your broader keyboard accessibility review.

chunks.heading: Is it ever acceptable to use outline: none?
chunks.text: Yes — when you replace it with an equally visible indicator, such as a box-shadow ring or a border change with sufficient contrast. What fails WCAG is removing the indicator with nothing in its place. Scope removal to :focus:not(:focus-visible) so keyboard users still get a ring.

chunks.heading: What is the difference between :focus and :focus-visible?
chunks.text: :focus matches whenever an element is focused, including after a mouse click. :focus-visible matches only when the browser heuristically decides an indicator should be shown — typically keyboard and other non-pointer interactions. Use :focus-visible for the visible ring so mouse users are not distracted while keyboard users are supported.

chunks.heading: Should I move focus to the modal container or to a control inside it?
chunks.text: Move focus to a meaningful element: the first interactive control, the dialog heading, or the close button. Avoid focusing an empty wrapper. If you focus the dialog element itself, give it an accessible name with aria-labelledby so the screen reader announces its purpose.

chunks.heading: Do I still need focus management with a framework component library?
chunks.text: Mostly the library handles trapping and roving tabindex for you, but you still own the seams: restoring focus after your own custom flows, focusing after route changes, and not deleting the focus indicator in your global styles. Verify the behavior rather than assuming it.

chunks.heading: The bottom line
chunks.text: Focus management is a small set of habits: keep a visible indicator, keep the DOM order honest, trap focus in dialogs and give it back on close, make composite widgets a single tab stop, and land focus somewhere sensible after every navigation. None of it requires new tools — just tabbing through your own interface with the mouse set aside and fixing what you find.

chunks.heading: Hawaii Wants WCAG 2.1 AA From Private Businesses. Comments Close October 30.
chunks.text:
Hawaii Act 257 and the Civil Rights Commission’s draft rules would require places of public accommodation to make websites and apps meet WCAG 2.1 AA, with a private right of action. What the draft says, who it covers, and what to tell the Commission before October 30, 2026.
AT

The Accessibility.build Team
October 14, 2026·9 min read

Most US website accessibility law for private businesses still runs through courts interpreting a 1990 statute that never mentions the web. Hawaii is trying something different. On 14 July 2026 Governor Josh Green signed Act 257 (SB 2852), and on 18 September 2026 the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission published draft rules that would require places of public accommodation to make their websites and mobile apps conform to WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA. The Commission is taking public comment until 30 October 2026.
These are proposed rules, not final ones. No public hearing date has been set, the size threshold is explicitly open for comment, and the compliance clock does not start until a final rule takes effect. But the draft is specific enough to plan around, and businesses that will be covered have a short window to shape it.

chunks.heading: What Act 257 itself does
chunks.text: The Act amends Hawaii’s public accommodations law (chapter 489 of the Hawaii Revised Statutes). It makes it a discriminatory practice for a place of public accommodation to deny a person with a disability full and equal enjoyment of its goods and services by requiring the use of information and communication technology that is not accessible to them. It then directs the Civil Rights Commission to adopt rules consistent with the US Department of Justice’s Title II web accessibility framework, 28 CFR part 35, as it stood on 24 June 2024. That framework is the DOJ rule that set WCAG 2.1 AA for state and local governments, which is why the Hawaii draft looks so familiar.

chunks.heading: What the draft rules require
chunks.text:
Who is covered: any place of public accommodation as defined in section 489-2 of the Hawaii Revised Statutes. The draft does not change that definition, so how far it reaches businesses with no premises in Hawaii is a question the rules leave to the existing statute.
What is covered: web content and mobile apps the business provides directly or through contractual, licensing or other arrangements, plus self-service digital technology (including kiosks and QR codes that lead to an app) when that technology is the main way the public reaches the goods or services.
The standard: WCAG 2.1, Level A and AA success criteria and conformance requirements, incorporated by reference.
The timeline: businesses with 100 or more full-time and part-time employees would have 24 months from the effective date of the final rule; all other covered businesses would have 36 months. The Commission is asking whether 100 employees is the right threshold, or whether a revenue test should be used instead.
Self-service technology: a business that relies on self-service digital technology must also offer an alternative method of access, not only an accessible kiosk.

chunks.heading: The exceptions mirror the federal rule
chunks.text:
The draft exempts five categories, closely following the DOJ Title II rule:
Archived web content kept only for reference, research or recordkeeping, not changed after the compliance date, and stored in a dedicated archive area.
PDFs, word processing, presentation and spreadsheet files posted before the compliance date, unless they are still used to apply for, access or take part in the business’s services.
Content posted by third parties, unless the third party posts under a contract, licence or other arrangement with the business.
Individualised, password-protected documents about a specific person, their property or their account.
Social media posts made before the compliance date. New or updated posts after that date must be accessible.

chunks.heading: Defences, and the paperwork they require
chunks.text: A business can avoid full conformance only by showing that it would fundamentally alter its goods or services, or impose an undue financial and administrative burden. The burden of proof sits with the business. The determination must be made by a responsible official or senior officer after considering all available resources, written down with reasons, kept, and made available to the Commission. Even then, the business must still do whatever it can to give disabled customers substantially equivalent access. A conforming alternate version of a page is allowed only where making the original accessible is not possible for technical or legal reasons.

chunks.heading: Enforcement: the Commission and the courts
chunks.text:
Anyone who believes a business has violated the rules can file a complaint with the Civil Rights Commission. On a finding of a violation, the Commission can order the business to bring its web content and mobile apps into WCAG 2.1 AA conformance within a set time, award compensatory damages for actual injury, and order other relief available under chapter 489. The draft also provides a private right of action: an aggrieved individual can sue in Hawaii circuit court, within chapter 489’s limitations period, for the remedies available under section 489-7.5.
That combination is the part to take seriously. Federal ADA Title III suits over websites give private plaintiffs injunctions and attorney’s fees but no damages, and they rest on judicial interpretation rather than a written technical standard. Hawaii’s draft would give complainants both a named standard to measure against and a state-law route to a remedy.

chunks.heading: How this fits the wider picture
chunks.text: States are pulling in different directions. California’s AB 2190, which would have set a WCAG standard for business websites, died in the 2025-26 session. Missouri’s SB 907 went the other way, creating a cure period and penalties aimed at abusive website lawsuits. Hawaii is building an affirmative technical standard for private businesses, borrowed from the federal rule for governments. Note one detail: the Act ties the rules to the federal framework as it stood in June 2024, so the DOJ’s April 2026 extension of its own government deadlines does not carry over to Hawaii’s timeline.

chunks.heading: What to do now
chunks.text:
If you run a business in Hawaii, or a trade association representing them, comment before 30 October 2026. The Commission asks specifically about the size or revenue threshold and the 24 and 36 month timeline. Comments go to the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission by email or by mail to 830 Punchbowl Street, Room 411, Honolulu, HI 96813, with "Act 257, Comments on HCRC Proposed Rule Amendments" in the subject line.
Do not wait for the final rule to start. Audit against WCAG 2.2 AA, which includes every 2.1 requirement, so the work survives the next update of the federal and European baselines.
Check your contracts. Booking engines, ordering platforms and payment flows provided "through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements" are covered, so ask vendors for current conformance evidence now.
If customers reach you through kiosks or QR codes, plan an accessible alternative route as well as an accessible interface.
Inventory your PDFs. Documents posted before the compliance date are exempt only if nobody needs them to apply for or use your services.
Compare Hawaii with other jurisdictions in our accessibility laws tracker.
Work through every A and AA criterion with the WCAG 2.2 checklist.
Get a first automated read on a page with the free URL accessibility auditor, then test manually.
See how website litigation is trending in the lawsuit tracker.

chunks.heading: HHS Delays the Section 504 Healthcare Web Accessibility Deadline
chunks.text:
HHS extended the Section 504 web and mobile accessibility deadlines to 2027 and 2028 for funded providers, but the WCAG 2.1 AA standard and duties still apply.

Khushwant PariharMay 18, 2026·5 min read

On May 7, 2026, the HHS Office for Civil Rights issued an Interim Final Rule extending the Section 504 web and mobile accessibility compliance dates for recipients of HHS federal financial assistance. The original deadline of May 11, 2026 is replaced by two new dates: recipients with 15 or more employees have until May 11, 2027, and recipients with fewer than 15 employees have until May 10, 2028. The technical standard is unchanged at WCAG 2.1 Level AA, and the substantive obligations under Section 504 continue to apply in the meantime.

chunks.heading: What changed, and what did not
chunks.text:
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibits disability discrimination by recipients of federal financial assistance. The HHS rule applies that principle to digital services, requiring covered web content and mobile apps to conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA. The new Interim Final Rule moves only the compliance deadline; it does not alter the standard or the underlying duties.
Recipients with 15 or more employees: compliance now due May 11, 2027.
Recipients with fewer than 15 employees: compliance now due May 10, 2028.
Technical standard: unchanged at WCAG 2.1 Level AA.

The move closely mirrors the DOJ’s April 2026 extension of the ADA Title II web rule, and the parallel is spelled out in the Federal Register notice. Federal agencies are lining up their timelines, but not relaxing their standards.

chunks.heading: Who is covered
chunks.text:
The rule reaches a broad slice of the healthcare sector. Covered entities include hospitals both large and small, community health centers, and primary care providers that receive HHS funding. If your organization accepts HHS federal financial assistance, the deadline extension likely applies to you.
The scope of covered content is equally broad. The requirements apply to web content and mobile apps that a recipient provides directly or through third-party and contractual arrangements. That expressly includes patient portals and telehealth platforms, which are often built and operated by outside vendors. A recipient cannot outsource its way out of the obligation; if patients reach your services through a contracted platform, that platform is in scope.

chunks.heading: A pattern across federal agencies
chunks.text: The HHS action does not stand alone. It closely mirrors the DOJ’s April 2026 decision to extend the ADA Title II web rule for state and local governments, and both rules keep WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the benchmark while moving the compliance dates outward. For organizations that sit at the intersection of these regimes, such as public hospitals and government-run clinics, the aligned timelines are convenient for planning but should not be mistaken for a relaxation of expectations. The direction of federal policy is still toward accessible digital services; only the schedule has shifted.

chunks.heading: The duties still apply now
chunks.text: As with the DOJ extension, the delayed deadline does not create a pause on Section 504 obligations. Recipients must still make reasonable modifications to avoid discriminating against people with disabilities, and the extension does not relieve any other Section 504 duty. A patient who cannot book an appointment, read test results, or join a telehealth visit because of an inaccessible interface may still have a valid discrimination claim well before 2027 or 2028.

chunks.heading: What this means for you
chunks.text:
Healthcare providers should use the additional time to remediate systematically, not to defer. Digital health systems are complex, vendor relationships take time to renegotiate, and clinical content is constantly changing, so an early start is the only realistic path to conformance. Smaller practices with fewer than 15 employees receive the longest runway, until May 2028, but they also tend to have the least in-house accessibility expertise, which makes an early, well-paced program especially important for them.
Audit your patient-facing digital services against WCAG 2.1 AA now, using a WCAG checklist to track progress across portals, apps, and documents.
Ask your patient portal, telehealth, and scheduling vendors for conformance documentation and contractual accessibility commitments.
Prioritize the journeys patients depend on most: booking, intake, results, prescriptions, and billing.
Review our Section 504 deadline guide and Section 508 overview to see how the standards connect.

This article is general information, not legal advice.

chunks.heading: Inclusive Design Principles: Creating Digital Experiences That Serve Human Diversity
chunks.text:
Inclusive design transcends disability accommodation to embrace the full spectrum of human diversity. This exploration reveals how inclusive design principles create better experiences for everyone while challenging fundamental assumptions about user capabilities and interaction patterns.

Khushwant PariharJuly 7, 2025·13 min read

In 1990, the Americans with Disabilities Act mandated curb cuts at street intersections to accommodate wheelchair users. Today, those same curb cuts serve parents with strollers, delivery workers with hand trucks, travelers with rolling luggage, and countless others who benefit from accessible design without identifying as disabled. This phenomenon—solutions designed for specific needs that ultimately serve everyone—represents the core insight of inclusive design.
Inclusive design extends beyond accommodation to embrace human diversity as a design asset rather than a constraint. It recognizes that the traditional model of designing for an "average" user excludes vast populations and creates unnecessarily limiting experiences for everyone. By designing for the edges—the users with the most constraints and specific needs—inclusive design creates solutions that work better for all users.

chunks.heading: Understanding the Spectrum of Human Capability
chunks.text:
Traditional design approaches often assume a narrow range of human capabilities: perfect vision, precise motor control, consistent cognitive function, and stable environmental conditions. These assumptions create design solutions that work well under ideal conditions but fail when real-world complexity intrudes.
Inclusive design recognizes that human capabilities exist on continuums rather than binary categories. Vision ranges from complete blindness to various forms of low vision to temporary impairment from bright sunlight. Motor abilities span from fine motor control challenges to temporary limitations from injury or environmental factors. Cognitive function varies based on attention, stress, fatigue, and countless other factors that affect everyone differently at different times.

chunks.heading: Permanent, Temporary, and Situational Disabilities
chunks.text:
Microsoft's inclusive design framework introduces a crucial distinction between permanent, temporary, and situational disabilities that fundamentally reshapes how we think about user needs. A person might have a permanent visual impairment, a temporary eye injury, or be in a bright environment that makes screens difficult to read. Each scenario requires similar design solutions despite different underlying causes.
This framework reveals how inclusive design benefits extend far beyond traditional disability communities. Voice interfaces designed for users with motor disabilities also serve users driving cars or cooking in kitchens. High contrast modes created for users with visual impairments also help users in bright outdoor environments or using older displays.
Recognizing this spectrum challenges the notion that accessibility features are specialized accommodations. Instead, they become design solutions that address the reality of human diversity and environmental variability that everyone experiences.

chunks.heading: The Three Principles of Inclusive Design
chunks.text: Inclusive design operates on three foundational principles that guide decision-making throughout the design process: recognize exclusion, learn from diversity, and solve for one to extend to many. These principles provide a framework for creating solutions that serve human diversity rather than constraining it.

chunks.heading: Recognize Exclusion
chunks.text:
The first principle requires examining how design decisions create barriers and exclude potential users. This examination goes beyond obvious accessibility violations to subtle exclusions embedded in assumptions about user capabilities, cultural contexts, and interaction patterns.
Exclusion often emerges from unconscious bias rather than intentional discrimination. Designers who primarily use mouse and keyboard interactions might not consider touch-based navigation patterns. Teams working on high-speed internet connections might not account for users with limited bandwidth. These exclusions compound when multiple assumptions align to create systems that work well for designers but poorly for diverse user populations.
Recognizing exclusion requires systematic examination of design assumptions and their impact on different user groups. This includes considering how language choices affect non-native speakers, how interaction patterns affect users with different motor capabilities, and how information presentation affects users with various cognitive processing preferences.

chunks.heading: Learn from Diversity
chunks.text:
The second principle emphasizes learning from diverse user perspectives rather than designing for imagined user needs. This learning requires engaging with actual users who have different capabilities, backgrounds, and interaction preferences throughout the design process.
Learning from diversity reveals innovative solutions that wouldn't emerge from traditional user research approaches. Users with disabilities often develop creative interaction strategies that expose new possibilities for interface design. Users from different cultural backgrounds bring different mental models that challenge assumptions about information organization and task flow.
This learning process requires moving beyond consultation to genuine collaboration. Instead of asking diverse users to validate predetermined solutions, inclusive design involves them in problem definition and solution generation. This collaboration often reveals that the original problem framing was too narrow or that entirely different approaches might serve user needs better.

chunks.heading: Solve for One, Extend to Many
chunks.text:
The third principle recognizes that solutions designed for users with specific constraints often create better experiences for everyone. This principle challenges the assumption that accessibility features are specialized accommodations that add complexity for typical users.
Digital examples of this principle abound in everyday technology. Closed captions, originally created for deaf users, now serve language learners, users in noisy environments, and anyone who prefers visual text reinforcement. Voice interfaces, developed for users with motor disabilities, now serve users multitasking, driving, or interacting with devices hands-free.
The key insight is that constraints often drive innovation. When designers must create solutions that work without sound, they develop better visual communication. When interfaces must work without precise mouse control, they develop clearer touch targets and interaction patterns. These constraint-driven solutions often prove superior to unconstrained alternatives.

chunks.heading: Implementing Inclusive Design in Practice
chunks.text: Translating inclusive design principles into practical implementation requires systematic changes in design processes, team composition, and evaluation criteria. These changes affect every stage of product development from initial concept through ongoing maintenance.

chunks.heading: Inclusive Research and Discovery
chunks.text:
Inclusive design begins with research approaches that capture diverse user needs and contexts from the outset. This requires expanding beyond traditional user research demographics to include users with disabilities, different cultural backgrounds, varying technology access, and different usage contexts.
Effective inclusive research employs multiple methods that accommodate different communication preferences and capabilities. This might include written surveys, audio interviews, video calls with sign language interpretation, or in-person sessions with assistive technology. The research approach itself must be accessible to capture insights from diverse participants.
Research findings in inclusive design often reveal that user needs are more diverse and context-dependent than traditional personas suggest. Instead of creating average user profiles, inclusive research identifies the range of user capabilities and contexts that solutions must address.

chunks.heading: Flexible and Adaptive Interface Design
chunks.text:
Inclusive design principles lead to interface solutions that adapt to different user needs and preferences rather than assuming single optimal configurations. This flexibility enables users to customize experiences based on their capabilities, preferences, and contexts.
Adaptive design goes beyond simple accessibility options to fundamental flexibility in interaction patterns. Users should be able to accomplish tasks through multiple methods—keyboard shortcuts, voice commands, touch gestures, or traditional clicking. Information should be available in multiple formats—visual, auditory, and textual representations that serve different processing preferences.
This flexibility requires careful architecture that supports multiple interaction modes without creating complexity for users who don't need alternatives. The challenge is providing options without overwhelming users or creating maintenance burdens for development teams.

chunks.heading: Measuring Inclusive Design Success
chunks.text:
Evaluating inclusive design requires metrics that capture user experience quality across diverse user groups rather than just average performance measures. These metrics must address both quantitative outcomes and qualitative experience factors that determine long-term usage success.
Effective measurement includes task completion rates across different user groups, error recovery success for various interaction methods, and user satisfaction measures that account for different capabilities and preferences. These metrics reveal whether inclusive design solutions actually serve diverse users effectively or just meet technical requirements.
Long-term success metrics include user retention across different demographics, feature adoption patterns among diverse user groups, and qualitative feedback about empowerment and independence that inclusive design aims to provide.

chunks.heading: The Business Case for Inclusive Design
chunks.text:
Inclusive design creates business value that extends beyond compliance requirements or social responsibility initiatives. Organizations that embrace inclusive design often discover expanded market opportunities, improved user satisfaction, and enhanced innovation capabilities.
The global disability market represents over $15 trillion in annual disposable income, but this figure understates the business impact of inclusive design. When solutions serve diverse user needs effectively, they often capture broader market segments and create competitive advantages in user experience quality.
Inclusive design also drives innovation by forcing teams to solve problems under constraints that lead to breakthrough solutions. The creative problem-solving required for inclusive design often produces innovations that benefit all users while addressing specific needs.

chunks.heading: Building Inclusive Design Capabilities
chunks.text:
Implementing inclusive design requires building organizational capabilities that support diverse user research, flexible solution development, and ongoing evaluation with diverse user groups. These capabilities require investment in training, tools, and processes that enable inclusive design at scale.
Successful organizations develop inclusive design expertise across multiple roles rather than concentrating it in specialized positions. Designers, developers, product managers, and researchers all need understanding of inclusive design principles and practical skills for implementing them in their work.
The transformation to inclusive design represents a fundamental shift from designing for imagined average users to designing for real human diversity. This shift requires changes in mindset, process, and evaluation criteria, but the result is digital experiences that truly serve the full spectrum of human capabilities and contexts.
Inclusive design succeeds when it becomes invisible—when designing for diversity becomes so natural that it requires no special consideration. This transformation takes time, commitment, and ongoing learning, but it creates digital experiences that empower all users to accomplish their goals without barriers or compromises.

chunks.heading: Inclusive Design Principles for Accessible Experiences
chunks.text:
Learn inclusive design principles, universal design concepts, and practical strategies for creating digital experiences that work for users with diverse abilities and needs.

Khushwant PariharNovember 15, 2025·7 min read

chunks.heading: What is Inclusive Design?
chunks.text: Inclusive design is a methodology that creates products usable by as many people as possible, regardless of age, ability, or situation. It goes beyond accessibility compliance to consider the full spectrum of human diversity.

chunks.heading: 1. Equitable Use
chunks.text:
Design is useful to people with diverse abilities.
Example: Automatic doors benefit wheelchair users and people carrying packages
Web application: Voice input options help users with motor difficulties and multitasking users

chunks.heading: 2. Flexibility in Use
chunks.text:
Design accommodates preferences and abilities.
Example: Adjustable-height desks
Web application: Multiple navigation methods (mouse, keyboard, voice, touch)

chunks.heading: 3. Simple and Intuitive Use
chunks.text:
Design is easy to understand regardless of experience or language skills.
Example: Icons with text labels
Web application: Clear navigation with consistent patterns

chunks.heading: 4. Perceptible Information
chunks.text:
Design communicates information effectively to users.
Example: Traffic lights use color and position
Web application: Visual, auditory, and tactile feedback options

chunks.heading: 5. Tolerance for Error
chunks.text:
Design minimizes hazards of accidental actions.
Example: Undo functionality
Web application: Confirmation dialogs for destructive actions

chunks.heading: 6. Low Physical Effort
chunks.text:
Design can be used efficiently with minimal fatigue.
Example: Large touch targets
Web application: Single-click actions instead of complex gestures

chunks.heading: 7. Size and Space
chunks.text:
Appropriate size and space for approach and use.
Example: Wide doorways
Web application: Adequate spacing between interactive elements

chunks.heading: Consider the Full Spectrum
chunks.text:
Permanent disabilities: Blindness, deafness, paralysis
Temporary limitations: Broken arm, eye surgery recovery
Situational challenges: Bright sunlight, noisy environment, one-handed phone use

chunks.heading: Design for Extremes
chunks.text:
When you design for users with the most constraints, you often improve the experience for everyone:
Captions help in noisy environments
Large buttons benefit users with motor difficulties and small screens
Clear language helps non-native speakers and cognitive accessibility

chunks.heading: Visual Design
chunks.text:
Color: Don't rely solely on color to convey information
Contrast: Ensure sufficient contrast ratios
Typography: Use readable fonts and appropriate sizes
Layout: Create logical, scannable page structures

chunks.heading: Interaction Design
chunks.text:
Multiple input methods: Support mouse, keyboard, touch, voice
Timing: Allow users to control timing and animations
Feedback: Provide clear confirmation of actions
Error prevention: Use validation and clear instructions

chunks.heading: Content Strategy
chunks.text:
Plain language: Write clearly and simply
Structure: Use headings and lists for organization
Media: Provide alternatives for images, video, and audio
Context: Give users information about where they are and what to expect

chunks.heading: Research and Empathy
chunks.text:
User research: Include users with disabilities in research
Persona development: Create personas representing diverse abilities
Journey mapping: Consider accessibility challenges throughout user journeys
Empathy exercises: Use screen readers, navigate with keyboard only

chunks.heading: Design and Prototype
chunks.text:
Accessibility-first design: Consider accessibility from initial concepts
Multiple solutions: Design various ways to complete tasks
Progressive enhancement: Start with core functionality, add enhancements
Inclusive prototyping: Test with assistive technologies early

chunks.heading: Test and Iterate
chunks.text:
Diverse testing: Include users with various abilities
Assistive technology testing: Test with screen readers, voice control
Contextual testing: Test in different environments and situations
Continuous improvement: Regular accessibility reviews and updates

chunks.heading: 🎨 Design Inclusively
chunks.text: Use our Accessibility Audit Helper to evaluate your designs against inclusive design principles and get recommendations for improvement.

chunks.heading: Progressive Disclosure
chunks.text:
Present information in layers, allowing users to dive deeper as needed.
Reduces cognitive load
Helps users with attention difficulties
Benefits mobile users with limited screen space

chunks.heading: Redundant Encoding
chunks.text:
Provide information through multiple channels.
Color + text for status indicators
Icons + labels for navigation
Audio + visual feedback for interactions

chunks.heading: Flexible Layouts
chunks.text:
Design that adapts to different screen sizes and orientations.
Responsive design for various devices
Support for landscape and portrait orientations
Zoom-friendly layouts that don't break at 200% magnification

chunks.heading: Quantitative Metrics
chunks.text:
Accessibility compliance: WCAG conformance levels
Task completion rates: Success across different user groups
Error rates: Frequency of user errors
Time to completion: Efficiency for diverse users

chunks.heading: Qualitative Feedback
chunks.text:
User satisfaction: Experience ratings from diverse users
Usability insights: Observational research findings
Accessibility feedback: Input from disability community
Edge case discovery: Identification of overlooked scenarios

chunks.heading: Team Education
chunks.text:
Regular accessibility training
Disability awareness workshops
Inclusive design methodology training
Assistive technology demos

chunks.heading: Process Integration
chunks.text:
Include accessibility in design reviews
Add inclusive design checkpoints to workflows
Allocate time and budget for accessibility testing
Celebrate inclusive design wins

chunks.heading: The Business Case for Inclusive Design
chunks.text:
Market reach: 26% of US adults have disabilities
Purchase power: $490 billion in disposable income annually
Better UX: Inclusive design improves experience for everyone
Innovation driver: Constraints often lead to creative solutions
Legal protection: Reduces accessibility litigation risk
Brand value: Demonstrates commitment to social responsibility

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
Inclusive design is not about adding accessibility features as an afterthought—it's about designing for human diversity from the beginning. When we design for users with the most constraints, we create better experiences for everyone.
Start by including diverse perspectives in your design process, test with real users who have disabilities, and remember that small inclusive design decisions can have significant impact on user experience.

chunks.heading: Mastering Screen Reader Testing: Beyond the Basics of Assistive Technology
chunks.text:
Screen reader testing reveals the gap between technical compliance and real-world usability. This deep dive explores advanced testing methodologies, common pitfalls, and the nuanced differences between popular screen readers that every developer should understand.

Khushwant PariharJuly 10, 2025·13 min read

Marcus, a senior developer at a financial services company, thought he understood accessibility testing. His team ran automated scans, checked color contrast, and ensured all images had alt text. But when they brought in a blind user for testing, everything fell apart. The carefully crafted interface that passed every automated test was nearly unusable with a screen reader. Navigation was confusing, form interactions were unclear, and dynamic content updates went completely unnoticed.
This disconnect between technical compliance and real-world usability represents one of the most significant challenges in modern web accessibility. Screen readers don't just convert text to speech—they create entirely different interaction paradigms that require fundamental shifts in how we think about user interface design and testing.

chunks.heading: Understanding the Screen Reader Landscape
chunks.text:
The screen reader ecosystem is more complex and nuanced than many developers realize. While JAWS, NVDA, and VoiceOver dominate market share, each brings distinct interaction patterns, feature sets, and user preferences that significantly impact testing strategies.
JAWS, with its 40% market share, remains the gold standard for many professional environments, particularly in corporate settings. Its sophisticated navigation features and extensive customization options make it powerful but complex. JAWS users often develop highly personalized interaction patterns, using custom scripts and advanced navigation commands that can expose interface issues invisible to basic testing.
NVDA's open-source nature and growing 32% market share make it increasingly important for testing. Its more literal interpretation of web content sometimes reveals markup issues that other screen readers handle gracefully. NVDA's rapid development cycle means new features and behavior changes appear frequently, requiring ongoing attention to compatibility.
VoiceOver's tight integration with Apple's ecosystem creates unique interaction patterns, particularly on mobile devices. Its gesture-based navigation on iOS represents a fundamentally different paradigm from traditional keyboard-based screen reader interaction, requiring separate testing approaches and considerations.

chunks.heading: The Virtual Buffer Paradigm
chunks.text:
Understanding screen reader interaction requires grasping the concept of the virtual buffer—a linearized representation of web content that screen readers create for navigation. This buffer transforms the visual, two-dimensional layout into a sequential, hierarchical structure that users navigate through various commands and shortcuts.
The virtual buffer isn't just a technical implementation detail—it fundamentally changes how users perceive and interact with web content. Visual relationships that seem obvious—like a button positioned next to a form field—may not be apparent in the linearized buffer. Spatial proximity becomes irrelevant; semantic relationships become crucial.
This paradigm shift explains why many visually appealing interfaces fail screen reader testing. Complex layouts with multiple columns, floating elements, and absolute positioning can create confusing or illogical reading orders in the virtual buffer. Successful screen reader compatibility requires designing for linear navigation while maintaining visual appeal.

chunks.heading: Advanced Testing Methodologies
chunks.text: Effective screen reader testing extends far beyond basic functionality checks. It requires understanding user behavior patterns, testing across multiple usage scenarios, and evaluating the complete user experience rather than individual component compliance.

chunks.heading: Scenario-Based Testing Approaches
chunks.text:
Rather than testing individual elements in isolation, advanced screen reader testing focuses on complete user journeys. This means testing entire workflows—from landing on a page to completing a complex task—while paying attention to cognitive load, efficiency, and user satisfaction throughout the process.
Consider testing an e-commerce checkout process. Basic testing might verify that each form field has proper labels and error messages are announced. Advanced testing evaluates the entire purchase journey: Can users efficiently navigate the product catalog? Do they understand the current step in the checkout process? Are shipping options clearly differentiated? Does the confirmation page provide adequate detail for verification?
This scenario-based approach reveals usability issues that component-level testing misses. It exposes problems with information architecture, interaction flow, and cognitive load that significantly impact real-world usage but don't violate technical accessibility guidelines.

chunks.heading: Performance and Efficiency Metrics
chunks.text:
Screen reader testing should include quantitative measures of user efficiency and performance. Task completion time, error rates, and navigation efficiency provide objective measures of accessibility quality that complement subjective usability feedback.
Experienced screen reader users develop sophisticated mental models of web interfaces and employ advanced navigation strategies. They use heading navigation to quickly scan page structure, landmark navigation to jump between major sections, and form field navigation to efficiently complete data entry. Testing should evaluate how well interfaces support these advanced usage patterns.
Efficiency metrics also reveal interface complexity issues. If users require significantly more time to complete tasks compared to visual interfaces, it suggests that the interface design doesn't align with screen reader interaction patterns. This doesn't necessarily indicate technical violations, but it does suggest opportunities for optimization.

chunks.heading: Common Pitfalls and Advanced Solutions
chunks.text: Screen reader testing reveals categories of issues that rarely appear in automated testing or visual review. These problems often stem from misunderstandings about how screen readers interpret and present web content to users.

chunks.heading: Dynamic Content and Live Regions
chunks.text:
Modern web applications rely heavily on dynamic content updates, but screen readers handle these changes differently than visual interfaces. Content that appears or changes on screen may go completely unnoticed by screen reader users unless properly implemented with live regions and focus management.
The challenge extends beyond technical implementation to user experience design. How much dynamic content should be announced? When should announcements interrupt the user's current task? How should multiple simultaneous updates be prioritized? These questions require balancing information completeness with cognitive load and task flow.
Effective live region implementation requires understanding the different announcement priorities (polite, assertive, off) and their appropriate usage contexts. Status updates, error messages, and progress indicators each require different announcement strategies based on their urgency and relationship to the user's current task.

chunks.heading: Form Interaction Complexity
chunks.text:
Form interactions represent some of the most complex screen reader testing scenarios. Beyond basic label association, forms involve validation feedback, conditional field display, multi-step processes, and complex input types that each present unique challenges.
Consider a complex form with conditional logic—fields that appear or disappear based on previous selections. Screen reader users need clear indication when the form structure changes, guidance about new required fields, and context about how their selections affect subsequent options. This requires sophisticated ARIA implementation and careful attention to focus management.
Form validation presents particular challenges for screen reader compatibility. Visual validation cues—color changes, icon indicators, border modifications—don't translate to screen reader output. Effective validation requires text-based feedback, proper error association, and clear guidance about correction requirements.

chunks.heading: Mobile Screen Reader Testing
chunks.text:
Mobile screen reader testing introduces additional complexity layers that desktop testing doesn't address. Touch-based navigation, gesture controls, and different screen reader features create entirely different user experiences that require separate testing approaches.
VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android use gesture-based navigation that fundamentally differs from keyboard-based desktop screen reader interaction. Users swipe to navigate between elements, double-tap to activate, and use complex multi-finger gestures for advanced functions. These interaction patterns affect how content should be structured and labeled.
Mobile screen readers also handle responsive design changes differently than desktop versions. Content that reflows or reorganizes for mobile viewports can create navigation confusion if not properly managed. Testing must verify that responsive design changes maintain logical navigation order and clear content relationships.

chunks.heading: Cross-Platform Consistency Challenges
chunks.text:
Maintaining consistent screen reader experiences across platforms requires understanding the subtle differences in how various screen readers interpret and present identical markup. What works perfectly in NVDA might create confusion in VoiceOver, and mobile implementations might behave differently than desktop versions.
These differences aren't just technical quirks—they reflect different design philosophies and user expectations. JAWS users often prefer detailed, comprehensive information. VoiceOver users might prefer more concise announcements. NVDA users might expect more literal interpretation of markup. Successful implementations balance these preferences while maintaining core functionality across platforms.

chunks.heading: Building Screen Reader Testing Into Development Workflows
chunks.text:
Effective screen reader testing requires integration into development workflows rather than end-of-cycle validation. This means establishing testing protocols that developers can execute during feature development, not just during formal accessibility audits.
Successful integration starts with basic screen reader familiarity across development teams. Every developer should understand fundamental screen reader navigation, be able to execute basic testing scenarios, and recognize common accessibility anti-patterns during code review.
This doesn't require every developer to become a screen reader expert, but it does require basic competency that enables early issue detection and prevents major accessibility problems from reaching production. Regular training, testing checklists, and peer review processes help maintain this competency across growing teams.

chunks.heading: The Future of Screen Reader Testing
chunks.text:
Screen reader technology continues evolving, with artificial intelligence and machine learning beginning to enhance traditional text-to-speech functionality. These advances create new testing challenges as screen readers become more sophisticated in interpreting content context and user intent.
The emergence of voice-controlled interfaces and smart speakers also influences screen reader development, creating hybrid interaction models that combine traditional navigation with voice commands. Testing strategies must evolve to address these new interaction paradigms while maintaining compatibility with established patterns.
Perhaps most importantly, screen reader testing is becoming less about technical compliance and more about user experience optimization. As accessibility awareness grows and legal requirements strengthen, the focus shifts from meeting minimum standards to creating genuinely excellent experiences for screen reader users.
This evolution requires deeper understanding of user needs, more sophisticated testing methodologies, and closer collaboration between developers, designers, and users with disabilities. The goal isn't just functional compatibility—it's creating digital experiences that feel natural, efficient, and empowering for screen reader users.

chunks.heading: Missouri Built a Safe Harbor for Accessibility Lawsuits. It Does Not Lower the Bar.
chunks.text:
Missouri SB 907 takes effect on 28 August 2026. It rewards businesses that fix their sites within 90 days and punishes filers who sue anyway. What it changes, what it does not, and why it is not a reason to relax.
AT

The Accessibility.build Team
August 25, 2026·7 min read

On 28 August 2026, Missouri becomes the first state with a law written specifically to punish what it calls abusive website accessibility litigation. Senate Bill 907, the Act Against Abusive Website Access Litigation, passed the Missouri General Assembly on 21 April 2026 and applies to litigation pending on its effective date. If you sell to Missouri residents, or run on a platform like Shopify or Etsy that does, it is worth understanding exactly what the law rewards and, more importantly, what it leaves completely untouched.
The short version: SB 907 does not make your website any less obligated to be accessible. It changes who pays when a lawsuit looks less like an accessibility complaint and more like a business model. That is a meaningful shift in tone. It is not a shift in the standard.

chunks.heading: The mechanism: a 90-day cure, then the burden flips
chunks.text:
The heart of the law is a notice-and-cure window. When a business receives written notice of an alleged violation, it has 90 days to take substantial, good-faith steps to correct it. If it does, it earns a rebuttable presumption that any subsequent claim based on that same violation is abusive. Read that direction carefully, because it is the whole point: fixing the problem inside the window does not just resolve the complaint, it arms you with a presumption you can turn against a plaintiff who sues anyway.
The presumption is rebuttable, so a plaintiff can still argue the fix was cosmetic or the purpose was genuine. And if the business does not correct the issue within 90 days of notice or service, no presumption attaches at all. The law rewards remediation and only remediation. A defendant who ignores the notice for three months gets none of its protection.

chunks.heading: What counts as "abusive"
chunks.text:
SB 907 deliberately avoids a rigid checklist. A court decides, on the totality of the circumstances, whether the primary purpose of the original litigation was to obtain payment from the defendant because of the cost of defending the case rather than to secure an actual accessibility remedy. That is the line the whole statute draws: a suit aimed at a fix is legitimate, a suit aimed at a settlement cheque is not.
The Missouri Attorney General is given real teeth here. The AG can intervene in or bring an action on behalf of Missouri residents targeted by these suits, can pursue the parties, attorneys and firms that filed them, and can issue guidance identifying practices considered abusive. The statute is careful to say that guidance does not preclude legitimate enforcement, so the AG cannot use it to wave away real accessibility complaints.

chunks.heading: The penalties are designed to sting
chunks.text:
Fee-shifting: a court that finds litigation abusive may award attorney fees and costs to the party that had to defend against it.
Treble sanctions: on top of that, the court may award punitive damages or sanctions of up to three times the fees awarded. For a filer running a volume practice, that turns a routine cost of doing business into a genuine downside.

The economics of high-volume accessibility filing depend on defense being expensive and settlement being cheap. SB 907 attacks that math from both ends: it makes the fix a shield, and it makes a bad-faith continuation potentially cost the filer more than the settlement they were chasing.

chunks.heading: The three limits that matter more than the headline
chunks.text:
This is the part that gets lost when the law is reported as a win for merchants. There are three limitations, and each one should keep an accessibility program exactly where it was.
It does not change your obligation. The statute is explicit that it does not alter any merchant’s duty to build inclusive digital storefronts. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines still define accessible. A site that fails WCAG 2.2 AA is still inaccessible in Missouri on 29 August exactly as it was on 27 August. The only thing that changed is the cost calculus around one category of lawsuit.
It cannot rewrite federal law. The overwhelming majority of website accessibility suits are brought under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act, a federal statute, and many are filed in federal court. A Missouri state law can shape state-court litigation and the conduct of Missouri-registered entities, but it does not repeal the ADA and cannot bar a federal claim outright. Treat SB 907 as changing the terrain for one kind of filing, not as immunity.

chunks.heading: The three limits that matter more than the headline
chunks.text: It sunsets the moment the DOJ acts. The act is written to expire if the U.S. Department of Justice issues standards for website or web content accessibility under the ADA, at which point federal rules take over. Given how long a federal web rule has been discussed, that may be a distant trigger, but it means SB 907 is explicitly a stopgap, not a settled regime.

chunks.heading: What a business should actually do with this
chunks.text:
The uncomfortable irony of SB 907 is that the only businesses it protects are the ones that were already doing the right thing. The safe harbor is unlocked by fixing your site within 90 days of notice. A company with a clean, audited, WCAG 2.2 AA site has a short, cheap cure and a strong presumption to wield. A company with 60 unlabelled controls and no statement has three frantic months and, if it misses the window, no protection at all.
So the practical response is the same response as before the law existed, only now with a clearer payoff: know where your site actually stands, and be in a position to remediate fast. If you can close the common failures, missing alternative text, unlabelled form fields, low-contrast text, keyboard traps, before a demand letter ever arrives, the 90-day clock is a formality rather than an emergency. And if you cannot, no state safe harbor will save you from the federal claim underneath it.
Missouri has changed the price of suing a business that fixed its site. It has not changed the price of ignoring accessibility. That distinction is the entire law.

chunks.heading: The Overlay Reckoning: UserWay Class Action Advances in 2026
chunks.text:
A class action against UserWay cleared a key hurdle in 2026, and the data confirms it: accessibility overlays do not buy legal immunity.

Khushwant PariharMay 26, 2026·6 min read

Accessibility "overlay" widgets — the JavaScript add-ons that promise to auto-fix a website — spent 2026 under growing legal pressure. A class action against UserWay, brought by a small online flower business, cleared a significant procedural hurdle in February 2026 when a federal Magistrate Judge recommended that key portions of the case move forward. The lawsuit and the litigation data around it point to one conclusion: an overlay does not buy legal immunity, and it does not substitute for remediating the underlying code.

chunks.heading: What the Bloomsybox case alleges
chunks.text:
Bloomsybox, a small online flower-delivery business, filed a class action against UserWay. According to the complaint, Bloomsybox subscribed to UserWay’s overlay in 2023 and was served with an ADA website-accessibility lawsuit only about six months later. The overlay, the suit says, had not fixed core problems such as missing alternative text and broken keyboard navigation, and UserWay’s advertised "$1 million legal protection" did not shield the business from being sued.
The complaint brings four claims:
Breach of contract
Violation of the Delaware Consumer Fraud Act
Violation of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act
Negligent misrepresentation

In February 2026, after UserWay moved to dismiss, a federal Magistrate Judge recommended that key portions of the case proceed. That recommendation does not decide the merits, but it does mean the central theory — that an overlay marketed with legal protection failed to deliver either accessibility or protection — will be tested rather than thrown out at the pleadings stage.

chunks.heading: What the Bloomsybox case alleges
chunks.text: The sequence at the heart of the complaint is what makes it resonate. A small business adopts an overlay in good faith, in part to reduce legal exposure, and is nonetheless served with an ADA lawsuit roughly six months later — over the very barriers the overlay was supposed to have addressed. The advertised "$1 million legal protection," in Bloomsybox’s telling, did not prevent the suit or absorb its consequences. Framed as a class action, the case asks whether that experience was unique to one flower shop or a pattern many overlay subscribers share.

chunks.heading: The regulatory parallel: the FTC’s accessiBe order
chunks.text: The Bloomsybox suit does not stand alone. It parallels the Federal Trade Commission’s action against accessiBe, another overlay vendor. In April 2025 the FTC finalized a $1 million order and barred accessiBe from representing that its automated product can make any website WCAG compliant. The two matters arrive from different directions — one a private class action over contract and consumer-protection law, the other a federal enforcement order — yet they converge on the same objection: marketing that equates an automated widget with genuine conformance. When both a plaintiff’s bar and a regulator are pressing the same point, the market signal is hard to ignore.

chunks.heading: The data behind the pattern
chunks.text:
Litigation research from 2025 and 2026 shows that overlays are not keeping their users out of court:
AudioEye’s 2026 litigation report found that 38.5% of businesses sued for inaccessibility in 2025 already had some accessibility solution in place — usually an overlay.
Other analyses found that roughly 22–23% of web accessibility suits in the first half of 2025 targeted sites that already had an overlay installed.

In other words, a meaningful share of the businesses being sued had already paid for a tool sold, in part, on the promise of reducing legal risk. The numbers do not prove any single overlay caused any single lawsuit, but they undercut the core sales pitch: if a widget reliably prevented litigation, sued sites with an overlay installed would be rare rather than routine.

chunks.heading: What this means for you
chunks.text:
The through-line is simple: overlays do not provide legal immunity, and real conformance comes from remediating the underlying code — the HTML, ARIA, and interaction patterns that assistive technology actually reads. An overlay layered on top of unfixed markup leaves missing alt text missing and broken keyboard navigation broken; a screen-reader user still hits the same wall, and a plaintiff can still document the barrier.
That reframes the buying decision. The question is not "which overlay comes with the biggest legal-protection promise," but "how do we remove the barriers a tester or a user would actually encounter." A vendor guarantee is only as good as the accessibility underneath it, and the Bloomsybox case is, at its core, an argument that the guarantee was not enough.
