How selected allegations map to the standard

chunks.heading: Illustrative screen-reader output
chunks.text:
The three WCAG conformance levels as a stack. AAA is enhanced and rarely required in law. AA is the level regulators and contracts often name. A is the floor, and several allegations in this case map to criteria at that level. This is an editorial mapping, not a court finding.

The detail that decided the case
Domino's retained its own expert, a blind accessibility consultant, to assess the site. He found it was not fully accessible and said he could not place a future order using a screen reader. By the time of summary judgment in 2021 the court recorded that no expert had found the website fully accessible. Cannon had not tested the website before September 2020, so his findings did not concede each defect Robles said he encountered in 2015 through 2017. They did undermine the argument that Robles's older browser was the sole cause of the problem.

One further fact, which comes from outside the litigation, changes how the failure should be read. Blind users rated the Domino's iOS app highly in 2012 and early 2014, praising the pizza builder and its braille support, and then documented it breaking in October 2014. The company had built something that worked and then shipped releases that users reported had broken it. The record does not identify why the regression occurred, but it illustrates that accessibility can be lost as a product changes.

1 Sep 2016

chunks.heading: Complaint filed
chunks.text:
Four causes of action in the Central District of California, covering the website and the app. The complaint asks for a WCAG 2.0-based injunction, statutory damages of $4,000 per violation under California law, attorney's fees, expenses, interest and costs. It does not address whether ordinary telephone ordering was available.

Feb 2017

chunks.heading: A phone line appears
chunks.text:
After the suit is filed, the website begins displaying a number for screen-reader users. The district court notes callers may be placed on hold. Robles later testifies he called twice and waited more than forty-five minutes each time before giving up.

20 Mar 2017

chunks.heading: Domino's wins round one
chunks.text:
Judge S. James Otero agrees the ADA reaches the website and app, but dismisses all four claims without prejudice under the primary jurisdiction doctrine, holding that ordering compliance with WCAG in the absence of a federal rule flies in the face of due process. He calls on Congress and the Department of Justice to set standards.

12 Oct 2018

chunks.heading: Argued in the Ninth Circuit
chunks.text:
Fourteen disability organisations file in support of Robles. Business groups including the US Chamber of Commerce, the National Retail Federation and the Restaurant Law Center file in support of Domino's.

15 Jan 2019

chunks.heading: Reversed
chunks.text:
The Ninth Circuit holds the ADA applies, because the site and app connect customers to physical restaurants, a nexus Domino's did not contest. It rejects the due process argument and the primary jurisdiction dismissal, and returns the case for discovery.

13 Jun 2019

chunks.heading: Petition to the Supreme Court
chunks.text:
Domino's retains Lisa Blatt of Williams and Connolly as Supreme Court counsel. Five amicus briefs are filed in support of the petition. None are filed for Robles.

7 Oct 2019

chunks.heading: Certiorari denied
chunks.text:
The Supreme Court declines the case without comment. The Ninth Circuit decision stands. Litigation continues for another two years and eight months.

23 Jun 2021

chunks.heading: Judgment on the website
chunks.text:
Judge Jesus G. Bernal grants summary judgment for Robles on the website claims, orders conformance with WCAG 2.0 and awards $4,000. The claims about the app are not resolved; whether it was accessible by then remained a disputed fact.

Nov 2021

chunks.heading: The parties report a settlement
chunks.text:
The parties file a joint notice saying they have reached a settlement. The case does not end: in January 2022 they tell the court that they were unable to complete it and ask for a trial date.

21 Jan 2022

chunks.heading: The first settlement fails
chunks.text:
The parties notify the court that they have been unable to settle. The remaining app claims and related issues remain pending until a later agreement.

6 Jun 2022

chunks.heading: Settled
chunks.text:
A second notice of settlement is filed and the case is dismissed with prejudice on 21 June 2022. The agreement's terms are confidential. In a public joint statement, the parties said Domino's was committed to maintaining the accessibility of its website and apps through compliance with WCAG 2.0 Levels A and AA. The app claims are not resolved on the merits before dismissal.

Checked 2 Sep 2026

chunks.heading: Domino's publishes an accessibility policy
chunks.text: The company states that it strives to comply with ADA Title III and WCAG 2.0 Levels A and AA, assigns responsibility across its technology, customer care and legal teams, and runs a reporting line and an accessibility email address. The wording is careful: it claims effort rather than conformance, and names the version from the 2021 injunction rather than the current WCAG 2.2.

chunks.heading: How Domino's defended it
chunks.text:
The James R. Browning courthouse in San Francisco, home of the Ninth Circuit, where the appeal was argued on 12 October 2018 and decided three months later. Photo by Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, public domain
Five arguments, made across three courts. Understanding why four of them failed is the practical value of this case, because they recur in website-accessibility litigation and commentary.

Argument Where it was made Result
The website is not a place of public accommodation, so the ADA does not reach it District court, Ninth Circuit, cert petition Rejected. The statute covers services of a public accommodation, not only services in one.
Enforcing the ADA online without a federal technical rule violates due process District court, Ninth Circuit Won in 2017, reversed in 2019. Fair notice of a legal duty is required, not a blueprint for compliance.
Courts should defer to the Department of Justice District court, Ninth Circuit Won in 2017, reversed in 2019. The DOJ had withdrawn its rulemaking, so delay was not just likely but inevitable.
A telephone line is an adequate alternative District court, 2021 Rejected on the facts. Two calls, more than forty-five minutes on hold each time. The court did not need to decide every other feature comparison.

chunks.heading: How Domino's defended it
chunks.text:
Compliance is expensive and the litigation is opportunistic Cert petition Never tested. Presented as policy argument, not as a legal defence.

“The Constitution only requires that Domino's receive fair notice of its legal duties, not a blueprint for compliance with its statutory obligations.”
Ninth Circuit, 15 January 2019
The last row is often misunderstood. In its Supreme Court petition Domino's argued at length that accessibility is costly, citing a grocery chain's $250,000 estimate, bank estimates reaching $3 million per website and a publishers' floor of $100,000. But those were other companies' numbers, offered as a reason for the Court to take the case. At the Ninth Circuit stage, on its own website, Domino's did not argue that fixing it would be an undue burden or would fundamentally alter its business, which are the actual statutory defences. The court noted that absence expressly.

“No person who has ever waited on hold with customer service, or ever been hungry for a pizza, would find this to be an acceptable substitute for ordering from a website.”
District court, 23 June 2021, on the telephone alternative

chunks.heading: How Domino's defended it
chunks.text:
At the Supreme Court the argument shifted again. Rather than defend the website in isolation, Domino's proposed that Title III should be satisfied by the combined means of access a business offers, so that no single channel need be accessible on its own provided the whole adds up to equal enjoyment. Had it been accepted, a working phone line would have excused an unusable website. The Court did not take the case, so the theory was never tested.
In its statement on the day certiorari was denied, Domino's said it had already developed an accessible website and app and pressed for national rulemaking to eliminate what it called a tsunami of website accessibility litigation. That word was Domino's own, taken from its petition rather than from the business groups supporting it.

chunks.heading: How each argument fared
chunks.text:
One argument succeeded, once, and was reversed. Two were never tested at all, including the one about cost.
Each argument Domino's made, and its outcome at the district court in 2017, the Ninth Circuit in 2019, and finally
Argument District, 2017 Ninth Circuit, 2019 Final
The ADA does not reach a websiteRejected at every stage. The statute covers the services of a public accommodation. Failed Failed Failed
No federal technical rule, so enforcing it denies due processThe only argument that ever won, and it was reversed. Succeeded Failed Failed
Defer to the Department of Justice firstReversed once the DOJ withdrew its rulemaking, making delay indefinite. Succeeded Failed Failed
A telephone line is an adequate alternativeDecided on the facts in 2021: two calls, more than forty-five minutes on hold each. Not decided Not decided Failed
Compliance is too costly across the industryMade as policy in the cert petition. Never pleaded as undue burden for its own site. Not decided Not decided Not decided

chunks.heading: Practical lessons from the record
chunks.text:
Six points where a different operational or litigation choice could have shortened the dispute. The public record does not disclose what any alternative would have cost.

1

chunks.heading: Exit point 1. Address basic Level A failures before release
chunks.text:
Automated checks can identify some missing text alternatives and accessible names. Manual keyboard and screen-reader testing is still necessary to determine whether controls are understandable and whether a customer can complete an order.

Practical step: test accessible names, text alternatives and the ordering journey before release.

2

chunks.heading: Exit point 2. Give people a way to report a barrier, and answer it
chunks.text:
The record says Domino's began displaying a dedicated screen-reader assistance number after the suit was filed. It does not establish that no other telephone or contact route previously existed. A documented, monitored accessibility channel can nevertheless surface barriers before they become prolonged disputes.

Practical step: publish a monitored feedback channel with a named owner.

3

chunks.heading: Exit point 3. Settle and remediate on receipt of the complaint
chunks.text:
The complaint requested $4,000 per violation under California law, along with fees, expenses, interest and costs. The court ultimately awarded one $4,000 recovery, but that later award does not establish what early settlement exposure or remediation would have cost.

Record limitation: the settlement value, legal spend and remediation cost are not public.

4

chunks.heading: Exit point 4. Test the workaround before relying on it
chunks.text:
Domino's displayed a screen-reader assistance line after the suit began. Robles testified that he called twice and abandoned each call after waiting more than forty-five minutes. On that undisputed evidence, the court rejected the line as an acceptable substitute for website ordering.

Practical step: measure wait time, availability, privacy and price equivalence.

5

chunks.heading: Exit point 5. Fix it after losing the appeal
chunks.text:
In January 2019 the Ninth Circuit held that the ADA applied in this nexus context. Domino's petitioned the Supreme Court, which declined review, and the parties continued litigating through the 2021 judgment and 2022 dismissal.

Procedural fact: the case continued for about three and a half years after the Ninth Circuit decision.

6

chunks.heading: Exit point 6. Do what the company now does anyway
chunks.text:
Domino's today publishes an accessibility policy naming WCAG 2.0 Levels A and AA, assigns responsibility across its technology, customer care and legal teams, retains third-party accessibility consultants and runs a reporting line and email address. The policy says Domino's strives to comply; it does not itself prove conformance or disclose the confidential settlement terms.

Current policy, not proof of past or present conformance.

What the case did not decide
No accessibility overlay was at issue in the complaint, the Ninth Circuit opinion or the 2021 judgment. The case therefore does not establish whether an overlay can satisfy the ADA or WCAG, and the absence or presence of a widget would not by itself prove that the ordering experience is accessible. See our guide to accessibility overlays for why that distinction matters.

chunks.heading: What to do if you are on the receiving end
chunks.text:
The practical translation of the six exit points above, in the order you are likely to need them.
Before anyone complains+
Do: Run an automated scan on your main journeys and fix every Level A failure it finds. That is the class this case turned on.
Do: Publish an accessibility contact route with a named owner, and answer it.
Do: Put an automated check in the pipeline so a release cannot silently remove a label.
Avoid: Do not buy an overlay and treat the problem as closed. The defendant here did not, and the reason is that it does not work.

When a complaint arrives+
Do: Reproduce it on the device and software the complainant actually used.
Do: Fix what is reproducible before arguing about what is not.
Do: Get a written scope and a date for the rest.
Avoid: Do not offer a phone line as the remedy without measuring what happens when someone calls it.
Avoid: Do not rely on the absence of a federal technical rule. Courts have declined to wait for one since 2019.

If it becomes litigation+
Do: Decide early whether you are fighting the barrier or the duty. Fighting the duty is what cost six years here.
Do: Preserve the evidence: the build, the device, the dates.
Do: If you intend to argue undue burden, plead it, with your own numbers.
Avoid: Do not assume your own expert will help. Here, the defendant's expert could not place an order either.

chunks.heading: Public and professional reaction
chunks.text: The court record is only part of the story. A Hacker News discussion posted after the Supreme Court denial attracted extensive debate, and the public arguments were often different from Domino's due-process argument in court.

chunks.heading: Developers argued about whether the duty should exist at all
chunks.text:
Hacker News records 591 descendants for the discussion. That metadata includes deleted or unavailable items, so it should not be read as 591 surviving substantive comments. The observations below are qualitative, not a frequency analysis.

Participants repeatedly raised telephone ordering, the absence of a government technical regulation, implementation cost, litigation incentives and the practical limits of automated testing. Those comments show the range of public reaction; they do not establish how common any position was outside that discussion.
At least five surviving comments were posted by one participant who identified as blind. He described web accessibility worsening as frameworks proliferated, rejected separate accessible versions because they tend to fall out of sync, and described accessibility reports and a submitted code change being ignored. This is evidence of one participant's experience, not a representative survey of blind users.

chunks.heading: Blind users had already documented the app breaking
chunks.text:
A useful independent record of what Domino's was like to use was not made by either party. It sits on AppleVis, a community site run by and for blind Apple users, where the app has a page with comments running from 2012 to 2023.
In September and November 2012, and again in March 2014, blind users praised it. One described the pizza builder working properly, including putting a topping on one half of the pizza, the exact interaction the litigation was later about. Another praised its support for braille displays. In October 2014 the same community reported it breaking: payment fields could no longer be reached by swiping, the order tracker stopped working, and buttons lost their labels. By July 2023 other users reported it working again.
Robles filed in September 2016, after the reported regression. The AppleVis posts independently document that some blind users encountered app barriers before the lawsuit, but they do not test Robles's device, version or individual experience. The court later denied summary judgment on the app claims because its current accessibility remained a disputed fact.

chunks.heading: Disability organisations answered the no-standard argument
chunks.text:
Fourteen disability organisations had backed Robles at the Ninth Circuit. After the denial, the American Council of the Blind answered the no-standard argument on its merits rather than in general terms: accessibility guidelines have existed for decades, and the latitude they leave a business is a benefit to that business rather than a defect. That is the same answer the Ninth Circuit gave when it said flexibility in the standard was a feature rather than a bug.
Robles's own counsel called the certiorari denial the right call on every level, and framed the underlying proposition as one nobody actually disputes: that blind people need access to websites and apps to take part in ordinary life. That framing is worth noticing, because it is precisely the proposition large parts of the public discussion went on to dispute.

chunks.heading: Blind organisations backed the case and attacked the machinery around it
chunks.text:
This position is more nuanced than a simple choice between supporting all such litigation and opposing accessibility enforcement.
In the same month that certiorari was denied, the National Federation of the Blind published an article in its member magazine attacking high-volume accessibility litigation. Lawyers were picking a category of business and filing near-identical complaints in bulk, some of the resulting suits were close to meritless, and small businesses were settling for a few thousand dollars without fixing anything. It warned that bad cases make bad law, and told members to decline invitations to serve as named plaintiffs in such campaigns. A resolution adopted that year condemned mass filings and confidential cash settlements, and called for public settlement agreements with specific remediation commitments instead.
At that same convention, the disability rights lawyer Eve Hill, whose firm later helped take this very case to judgment, told an audience of blind people that some blind people and some lawyers treat inaccessible websites as a business opportunity rather than a civil rights problem. Her distinction is the one worth borrowing: the problem is not the number of lawsuits but their quality, and whether the lawyer bringing them can actually litigate. She defended the Domino's case in the same breath.

chunks.heading: Blind organisations backed the case and attacked the machinery around it
chunks.text: The documented position was therefore more specific than blanket support for or opposition to litigation: these organisations supported the Domino's case while criticising high-volume practices that could produce payments without remediation.

chunks.heading: Practitioners were harder on both sides than the coverage was
chunks.text:
The disability rights lawyer Lainey Feingold, who published a response to the public reaction a week after the denial, spent more of it deflating the result than celebrating it. She also addressed a recurring objection, and it is worth stating plainly because it is a matter of law rather than opinion. Title III of the ADA provides no damages to private plaintiffs at all. The remedy is an injunction, plus legal fees to a prevailing party, which is the ordinary enforcement mechanism across American civil rights statutes. The $4,000 in this case came from a Californian state statute, not the ADA.
Criticism of the plaintiffs' bar came from inside the profession too. Karl Groves, an accessibility consultant and court-qualified expert, has argued that mass demand-letter campaigns actively damage the cause: they crowd out collaboration, and they invite judges to treat genuine claims as opportunism. He has advocated collaborative approaches as an alternative. The Domino's record does not show that the parties used a structured-negotiation process before suit.

chunks.heading: A critique of the nexus approach
chunks.text:
Writing in 2019, developer Ben Myers mapped the disagreement between the circuits and warned that resting the duty on a physical connection could end up harming the accessible web rather than advancing it, because it leaves the business that exists only online with the weakest obligation. The pandemic sharpened the point: when venues close, the website is not an adjunct to the service, it is the service.

The Supreme Court declined the case on 7 October 2019 without comment. A denial of certiorari produces no opinion on the merits and creates no Supreme Court precedent. Photo by the Architect of the Capitol, Wikimedia Commons, public domain

chunks.heading: The later ruling received less attention
chunks.text:
Public discussion peaked around the Supreme Court's denial of review, even though that event did not decide the merits.
The October 2019 event was a denial of certiorari. It decided nothing. It produced no opinion, set no precedent, and did not even tell you which way the court leaned. The adjudication that resolved the website merits was the June 2021 summary judgment; the remaining app claims ended through settlement and dismissal in June 2022.
The sources reviewed for this article show substantially more public discussion of the 2019 denial than of the 2021 summary-judgment order. That helps explain why some later summaries incorrectly say the Supreme Court ruled on the merits, that Domino's was fined, or that the court specifically ordered Level AA.

chunks.heading: What the record says about the plaintiff
chunks.text: The sources reviewed for this article did not reveal a public interview with Robles; the public statements attributed to his side came from his lawyers. Domino's told the Supreme Court that he had filed at least fourteen similar lawsuits, a defence characterization rather than a finding made by the Court. In this case, the district court found the website was not fully accessible in 2021. Domino's 2020 expert did not concede every historical defect, while AppleVis posts separately documented an app regression before Robles filed.

chunks.heading: Correcting the record
chunks.text:
This case is described inaccurately in a great deal of published commentary, including by vendors selling accessibility products. The differences matter if you are relying on it to brief a board. Eleven claims circulate widely enough to be worth answering directly, each set here against what the filings and the judgment actually say.

Often said
The Supreme Court ruled against Domino's.

The record
The Court denied certiorari on 7 October 2019. A denial is not a ruling on the merits and sets no precedent. The binding decision is the Ninth Circuit's.

Often said
Domino's was ordered to meet WCAG 2.0 Level AA.

The record
The June 2021 order requires conformance with the WCAG 2.0 guidelines and specifies no level and no deadline. Level AA appears in Domino's own later policy, not in the order.

Often said
Domino's was fined.

The record
There was no fine. $4,000 in statutory damages was awarded under California's Unruh Act, treated as a single violation rather than $4,000 per visit.

Often said
The plaintiff was in it for the money.

The record

chunks.heading: Correcting the record
chunks.text:
The record does not establish Robles's subjective motive. His ADA claim offered injunctive relief rather than private damages, while his Unruh Act claims requested $4,000 per violation and the complaint also sought fees and costs. The court disregarded Domino's motive allegations when they failed to dispute the facts to which they were offered as objections.

Often said
Court documents showed fixing the site would have cost $38,000.

The record
The reviewed complaint, appellate filings, Supreme Court filings, Ninth Circuit opinion and 2021 judgment do not contain that figure. Its traceable public origin is an August 2019 tweet asserting that Domino's had disclosed it in court papers; the linked article did not state a remediation cost. The public record reviewed here does not establish Domino's remediation cost.

Often said
The case cost Domino's millions, against a cheap fix.

The record
The comparison cannot be verified from the public record. Domino's litigation spend, remediation cost, fee resolution and settlement amount are not disclosed. The publicly documented $4,000 figure is the Unruh Act amount awarded to Robles, not the total cost of the case.

Often said
The cert denial opened the floodgates to web accessibility lawsuits.

The record

chunks.heading: Correcting the record
chunks.text:
The cited federal series does not show a jump in 2019: it records 2,256 cases, two fewer than in 2018. The large annual increase occurred in 2018, when filings rose 177% from 814 to 2,258 after the Justice Department withdrew its web rulemaking. That timing alone does not prove what caused the increase.

Often said
The courts ruled the app inaccessible.

The record
They did not. Summary judgment was denied on both app claims because accessibility was a disputed fact, and the claims were never decided. Only the website was adjudicated.

Often said
The case established that accessibility overlays cannot substitute for accessible code.

The record
It established nothing about overlays. No overlay was at issue in the complaint, Ninth Circuit opinion or 2021 judgment. The presence or absence of a widget on Domino's current site would not change what the case decided.

Often said
Blind people and their organisations were united behind the litigation.

The record
Fourteen disability organisations supported Robles in the Ninth Circuit. Separately, the National Federation of the Blind criticised high-volume, near-identical accessibility cases and confidential cash settlements while continuing to support the Domino's case. Those records show a distinction between this case and criticism of some litigation practices.

Often said

chunks.heading: Correcting the record
chunks.text:
The case establishes that all websites are covered by the ADA.

The record
It does not. The Ninth Circuit relied on the nexus between the website and physical restaurants, and expressly declined to decide the position where no such nexus exists. Other circuits differ.

chunks.heading: What it means now
chunks.text:
Domino's told the Supreme Court that leaving the decision undisturbed would turn a flood of litigation into a tsunami. The filing record does not support the case being the cause. The largest year-over-year increase in the cited federal series occurred in 2018, after the Justice Department withdrew its web accessibility rulemaking in December 2017; that timing does not establish causation.

The series records a 177% increase in 2018, after the Justice Department withdrew its web rulemaking. Timing alone does not establish causation. In 2019, when the Supreme Court declined this case, the annual total was two cases lower than in 2018.

chunks.heading: What it means now
chunks.text:
Certiorari was denied in October 2019, and that year was flat against 2018. Counts that include state courts run considerably higher, so do not mix the two series. A separate EcomBack dataset, which includes federal and state cases, reported that in the first half of 2025 sixteen firms accounted for more than 90 percent of its matters and that the firm representing Robles had the largest count in that period. That concentration figure should not be combined with the federal-only chart. Our accessibility lawsuit tracker keeps the current numbers.
One part of Domino's complaint also turned out to be durable. There is still no federal technical regulation for private business. The rule the Justice Department published in 2024, adopting WCAG 2.1 Level AA, binds state and local government under Title II only.

chunks.heading: What has changed since the case closed
chunks.text:
Three developments since 2022 bear on the argument this case started, and two of them cut against the plaintiffs' bar rather than for it.
In February 2026 the Justice Department filed a statement of interest opposing a proposed class settlement in a website accessibility case, objecting that the injunctive relief set out no concrete steps, that monitoring was optional, and that $2.52 million in fees was disproportionate to what class members received. It recorded that the same counsel had filed substantially the same lawsuit more than 500 times between 2019 and 2023, mostly resolving in undisclosed individual settlements, and said it opposed using a civil claim principally to enrich class counsel on the backs of disabled people. That is the federal government making, in court, the criticism the National Federation of the Blind made in its member magazine in 2019.
Second, filings by people representing themselves rose sharply in 2025, which practitioners attribute to general-purpose AI tools making a complaint easy to draft. Third, Missouri has now responded: Missouri enacted a safe harbour operative from 28 August 2026. It creates a rebuttable presumption concerning allegedly abusive litigation when a defendant takes substantial good-faith steps to correct a noticed violation within ninety days; it does not replace the substantive federal accessibility duty.

chunks.heading: What has changed since the case closed
chunks.text: None of this disturbs the holding. It does mean the honest summary of 2026 is not that enforcement is uncontested, but that Robles's nexus holding remains binding in the Ninth Circuit while the machinery around it is under pressure from the courts, the regulator and disability organisations alike.

chunks.heading: Did any of it make websites better?
chunks.text:
WebAIM's 2021 survey of the top million home pages found the Food and Drink category improving from an average of 66.1 automatically detected errors in 2020 to 46.8 in 2021. Its authors said increased accessibility litigation may have contributed to the change.
This is an observational category-level comparison. It does not establish that litigation caused the decline, that Domino's was among the measured sites that improved, or that a blind customer could complete an order. Automated home-page error counts and end-to-end usability are different forms of evidence.

Evidence limit

chunks.heading: Did the website actually get fixed?
chunks.text:
The public record reviewed for this case study cannot answer that question conclusively. The 2021 order found that the website was not fully accessible at that time. Domino's policy, checked 2 September 2026, describes an accessibility program, but a policy is not proof of conformance.

Court finding
In June 2021, no expert had found the website fully accessible. The court ordered compliance with WCAG 2.0 without specifying a conformance level or deadline.

Policy checked 2 September 2026
Domino's says it strives to comply with WCAG 2.0 Levels A and AA and describes monitoring, training, consultants and feedback channels.

What remains unknown
This repository contains no reproducible, end-to-end test of the current ordering flow or app, so it cannot support a present-day conformance or usability conclusion.

Home-page markup counts cannot demonstrate that a customer can configure, purchase and schedule an order. A supportable current conclusion would require documented keyboard and screen-reader tests of the complete journey, with URLs, builds, devices, browsers, assistive technologies, dates and results preserved.

chunks.heading: What to take from it
chunks.text:
The nexus argument is settled in the Ninth Circuit. If your website connects customers to a physical location, expect it to be covered.
The absence of a federal technical rule did not erase the duty. The Ninth Circuit held that Domino's had fair notice of its ADA obligation and declined to wait for the Justice Department to issue a technical standard.
An alternative channel must be measured. The line failed on the facts here because Robles waited more than forty-five minutes on each of two calls. Comparable timing, privacy, independence and access to the same offers should be tested rather than assumed.
Several allegations mapped to Level A criteria. Missing text alternatives and accessible names can sometimes be detected automatically, but their quality and the usability of a complete journey require manual review.
Your own expert's findings may narrow a defence. Domino's expert completed ordinary website and app orders in 2020, but found the website was not fully accessible and could not schedule a future website order.
Accessibility is a maintenance property, not a project. Blind users praised the app in 2012 and reported an October 2014 version broken; the app was part of the complaint filed in 2016.

A closing note on statements

chunks.heading: What to take from it
chunks.text:
The policy Domino's published after all this is worth reading as an object lesson. It is undated. It does not say that conformance has been achieved; it says that the company strives to comply with WCAG 2.0 Levels A and AA, a standard that is now two revisions behind. It gives one telephone number, while the site footer gives a different one. None of that is unlawful, and the governance it describes is more than most companies publish. But it is a statement of intent rather than a statement of achieved conformance. If a statement is the artifact you show a regulator or a procurement team, this is a reminder that it is worth exactly what it commits to. Ours is checked with the accessibility statement checker.

chunks.heading: EAA Readiness Checklist
chunks.text:
Every obligation in the European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882, as a trackable row with its article or annex reference, the evidence to keep, a status, your notes and Excel export. 82 obligations in 15 sections, filtered by sector.

What is the EAA?Am I in scope?EN 301 549 Checklist

Sourced to the Directive (verified 19 October 2026): every row cites the article, annex, section and point of Directive (EU) 2019/882 it comes from, checked against the EUR-Lex text (CELEX 32019L0882). Obligations are plain-language paraphrases, not the normative text. Your duties sit in the national law transposing the Directive, which can add detail and sets the penalties.

Standards note: as of 19 October 2026 no edition of EN 301 549 is cited in the Official Journal under the EAA. v3.2.1 is cited under the Web Accessibility Directive only, so it gives no presumption of conformity under this Act. ETSI published v4.1.1, aligned to WCAG 2.2, on 2 September 2026; its citation under the EAA is expected in late November or December 2026. Until then, treat WCAG 2.2 AA and EN 301 549 results as evidence of meeting Annex I, not as a legal presumption.

chunks.heading: Scope, dates and exemptions
chunks.text:
Articles 2, 3, 4 and 31
Work out whether the Directive applies to you, which category you fall in, and which content and organisations it leaves out. 0 of 5 done; 5 shown.
Article 2(2)(a) to (f); Article 31(2)
Confirm which Article 2(2) service category you provide to consumers, and record when the service was first provided after 28 June 2025.
Applies to: Every service provider
Evidence to keep and notes
Evidence to keep: A written scope determination naming the category, the Member States served, and the consumer-facing channels (website, app, e-tickets, terminals) it covers.
Note: The six categories are electronic communications services, services providing access to audiovisual media services, listed elements of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport, consumer banking services, e-books and dedicated software, and e-commerce services. Article 3(30) defines e-commerce services as services provided at a distance, through websites and mobile device-based services, by electronic means and at the individual request of a consumer with a view to concluding a consumer contract, so any online consumer sales journey is in scope. Business-only services fall outside Article 2(2) because Article 3(22) limits 'consumer' to natural persons acting outside their trade, business, craft or profession.

Add your noteYour note for Article 2(2)(a) to (f); Article 31(2)

Confirm whether any product you manufacture, import or distribute is listed in Article 2(1) and was placed on the market after 28 June 2025.
Applies to: Manufacturers, importers and distributors
Evidence to keep and notes
Evidence to keep: Product register mapped to the Article 2(1) list with the date each product was placed on the market.
Note: Covered products: consumer general purpose computer hardware systems and their operating systems; payment terminals; automated teller machines, ticketing machines, check-in machines and interactive information terminals dedicated to covered services; consumer terminal equipment used for electronic communications services; consumer terminal equipment used for accessing audiovisual media services; and e-readers. Terminals installed as integrated parts of vehicles, aircraft, ships or rolling stock are excluded.

Article 3(23); Article 4(5)
Decide whether you qualify as a microenterprise and, if you rely on the service exemption, keep the headcount and turnover or balance sheet figures that prove it.
Applies to: Service providers with fewer than 10 staff
Evidence to keep and notes

chunks.heading: Scope, dates and exemptions
chunks.text:
Evidence to keep: Dated headcount and annual turnover or balance sheet total, re-checked each financial year, with a note of the national transposition provision relied on.
Note: Article 3(23): fewer than 10 persons employed and an annual turnover not exceeding EUR 2 million or an annual balance sheet total not exceeding EUR 2 million. Article 4(5) exempts microenterprises providing services from the Article 4(3) service requirements and any obligations relating to them. It does not exempt microenterprises dealing with products from the product requirements; Article 14(4) and Article 14(8) only relieve them of documenting and notifying an Article 14 assessment. Crossing either threshold ends the exemption. Article 4(6) obliges Member States to publish guidance and tools for microenterprises, which are worth checking in each country.

chunks.heading: Scope, dates and exemptions

Note: Excluded: pre-recorded time-based media published before 28 June 2025; office file formats published before 28 June 2025; online maps and mapping services where essential information for navigational maps is provided in an accessible digital manner; third-party content that is neither funded, developed by, nor under the control of the economic operator; and archives whose content is not updated or edited after 28 June 2025. Editing an archived page or re-publishing an old PDF removes the exclusion. Embedded payment or identity widgets that you pay for or configure are under your control and are not third-party content for this purpose.

chunks.heading: General requirements for all services
chunks.text:
Annex I, Section III
The requirements every in-scope service must meet: accessible websites and apps, accessible information about the service, accessible products used to deliver it, and support services that can talk about accessibility. 0 of 11 done; 11 shown.
Annex I, Section III, point (c)
Make every website, related online application and mobile device-based service, including mobile apps, used to provide the service accessible in a consistent and adequate way by making it perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
Applies to: All in-scope services except urban, suburban and regional transport services (Article 4(3))
Evidence to keep and notes
Evidence to keep: Accessibility audit reports for each site and app in the consumer journey against WCAG 2.2 Level AA or EN 301 549 clauses 9 and 11, with retest records and an open issues log.
Note: Perceivable, operable, understandable and robust are the four WCAG principles. The practical benchmark is EN 301 549, whose web and software clauses incorporate WCAG at Level AA: v3.2.1 uses WCAG 2.1 and v4.1.1, published by ETSI on 2 September 2026, uses WCAG 2.2. As of 19 October 2026 no edition of EN 301 549 is cited in the Official Journal under this Directive, so conformance is strong evidence rather than a legal presumption until that citation lands (see the harmonised standards section).

chunks.heading: How the Directive is organised
chunks.text:
The Act states outcomes, not techniques. The requirements themselves live in Annex I; the operating duties, exceptions and transition live in the articles. The checklist follows that structure so each row can be traced back to the text.
Annex I, Section III
General requirements for every in-scope service: accessible websites and apps, accessible information about the service, accessible products used to deliver it, and support services that can talk about accessibility.

Annex I, Section IV
Additional requirements by sector: electronic communications, access to audiovisual media, passenger transport, consumer banking, e-books and e-commerce.

Article 13 and Annex V
The service provider's operating duties: the published accessibility information, the procedures that keep the service compliant, corrective action, and notifying the authorities.

Article 14 and Annex VI
Fundamental alteration and disproportionate burden: the assessment criteria, the five-year documentation and renewal cycle, and the notification duty.

Article 32
The transition: products in use and contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 are protected to 28 June 2030, self-service terminals for up to 20 years. Websites and apps are not.

Articles 7 to 12, Annex I Sections I and II, Annex IV

chunks.heading: How to use it
chunks.text:
Pick your sector. The common sections (scope, general service requirements, service provider duties, disproportionate burden, transition, enforcement and standards) stay in every service scope; the sector section is added on top. Manufacturers, importers and distributors use the products scope.
Work through the scope section first. If you are an exempt microenterprise or a requirement genuinely does not apply, mark it not applicable; the progress bar then counts only what applies to you.
Open the evidence line on each row and record where that evidence lives in your note. Article 13(5) and Article 14(3) both turn on being able to hand documents to an authority on request.
Export to Excel to share with colleagues or an auditor. Statuses and notes stay in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
Does the European Accessibility Act apply to my website?▾
It applies if the website is part of a service listed in Article 2(2) and provided to consumers after 28 June 2025. The widest category is e-commerce services, defined in Article 3(30) as services provided at a distance, through websites and mobile device-based services, by electronic means and at the individual request of a consumer with a view to concluding a consumer contract. Any site where a consumer in the EU can buy something, subscribe or sign a contract online is in. A purely business-to-business site, or a brochure site with no consumer transaction, is not caught by that category. Use the sector buttons above the checklist to filter to your situation, or run the EAA scope checker first.

What is the microenterprise exemption and does it cover me?▾

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
Article 4(5) exempts microenterprises providing services from the service requirements. Article 3(23) defines a microenterprise as an enterprise that employs fewer than 10 persons and has an annual turnover not exceeding EUR 2 million or an annual balance sheet total not exceeding EUR 2 million. Both parts matter: an agency with 8 staff and EUR 3 million turnover is not a microenterprise. The exemption does not cover products. A microenterprise manufacturer still has to meet Annex I; it only escapes documenting its Article 14 assessment and the Article 14(8) notification. Keep the figures that prove your status on file and re-check them each financial year.

What information does the EAA require me to publish?▾

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
Article 13(2) requires every service provider to prepare the information described in Annex V, explaining how the service meets the applicable accessibility requirements, to make it available to the public in written and oral format in a manner accessible to persons with disabilities, and to keep it for as long as the service operates. Annex V says the information goes in the general terms and conditions or an equivalent document and must contain a general description of the service in accessible formats, the explanations needed to understand how the service operates, and a description of how the Annex I requirements are met. In practice this is an accessibility statement that your terms link to. Annex V, point 3 also asks for information showing that your delivery process and its monitoring keep the service compliant.

Is WCAG 2.2 AA conformance the same as EAA compliance?▾

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
No, but for a website or app it is most of the technical work. Annex I, Section III, point (c) requires websites and mobile apps to be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, which are the WCAG principles, and the technical route is EN 301 549, whose web chapter incorporates WCAG at Level AA. Article 15 gives a presumption of conformity only for harmonised standards cited in the Official Journal under this Directive, and as of 19 October 2026 no edition of EN 301 549 is cited under the EAA: v3.2.1 is cited under the Web Accessibility Directive only, and ETSI's v4.1.1 (WCAG 2.2) is expected to be cited in late November or December 2026. WCAG also says nothing about the rest of the Act: the published Annex V information, support services, electronic documents such as invoices and e-tickets, the sector requirements, the corrective action and notification duties, and the Article 14 paper trail. This checklist covers those.

Does the transitional period until 2030 mean my website can wait?▾

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
No. Article 32(1) lets service providers keep using products that were lawfully in use before 28 June 2025 until 28 June 2030, and lets service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 run unaltered until they expire, but no longer than five years from that date. Article 32(2) lets Member States allow self-service terminals in use before 28 June 2025 to continue until the end of their economically useful life, capped at 20 years from entry into use. None of that covers a website, an app or the service itself; those had to comply from 28 June 2025 under Article 31(2).

What is disproportionate burden and how do I claim it?▾

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
Article 14 says the accessibility requirements apply only to the extent that compliance does not fundamentally alter the basic nature of the product or service and does not impose a disproportionate burden. It is not a declaration you make. It is an assessment you carry out against the Annex VI criteria (the ratio of net compliance cost to overall cost, the costs and benefits set against the benefit to persons with disabilities, and the ratio of net compliance cost to net turnover), document, keep for five years, renew at least every five years or when the service changes, and notify to the authority of each Member State concerned under Article 14(8). You cannot rely on it at all if you received outside funding to improve accessibility (Article 14(6)), and it never covers the requirements you can meet, only the specific ones the assessment supports.

Who enforces the EAA and what are the penalties?▾

chunks.heading: EAA Checklist FAQ
chunks.text:
National authorities, not a European body. Article 23 requires each Member State to designate authorities that check services, follow up complaints and verify corrective action; Articles 19 to 22 do the same for market surveillance of products. Article 29 gives consumers the right to go to court or to an administrative body under national law, and lets organisations with a legitimate interest act on their behalf. Article 30 requires national penalties that are effective, proportionate and dissuasive, with remedial action, scaled to the seriousness of the breach and the number of people affected. The actual fines, and whether breaches are criminal offences, are set in each national transposition law, which is why the first section of the checklist asks you to list the national laws that apply to you.

Can I export this checklist to Excel, and where is my progress saved?▾
Yes, free and with no account. The Export Excel button writes every obligation in your selected scope with its source, who it applies to, the evidence to keep, the Directive notes, your status and your notes, plus a summary sheet with the date, scope and progress. Statuses and notes save to your browser's local storage on this device; nothing is sent to our servers. Use the export to share progress with colleagues or to hand an auditor a starting point.

chunks.heading: 4. Functional performance statements
chunks.text:
0 requirements shown
4.1 Meeting functional performance statements
Statement

Explains how the functional performance statements in clause 4.2 are used: they describe outcomes that let people locate, identify, and operate ICT functions regardless of physical, cognitive, or sensory ability, and Annex B maps every requirement to them.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.1 Usage without vision
Statement

Where ICT has visual modes of operation, at least one mode of operation should not require vision at all.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.2 Usage with limited vision
Statement

Where ICT has visual modes of operation, it should provide features (such as magnification or contrast adjustment) that let people with limited vision use it.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.3 Usage without perception of colour
Statement

Where ICT has visual modes of operation, at least one visual mode should not depend on the user perceiving colour.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.4 Usage without hearing
Statement

Where ICT has auditory modes of operation, at least one mode of operation should not require hearing.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.5 Usage with limited hearing
Statement

Where ICT has auditory modes of operation, it should provide enhanced audio features (such as clarity enhancement or volume boost) for people with limited hearing.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.6 Usage with no or limited vocal capability
Statement

chunks.heading: 4. Functional performance statements
chunks.text:
Where ICT requires vocal input, at least one mode of operation should not require the user to speak.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.7 Usage with limited manipulation or strength
Statement

Where ICT requires manual actions, it should offer alternatives that do not need fine manipulation, simultaneous actions, or hand strength.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.8 Usage with limited reach
Statement

Where ICT products are free-standing or installed, every element needed for operation should be within reach of all users, including wheelchair users.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.9 Minimize photosensitive seizure triggers
Statement

Where ICT has visual modes of operation, at least one mode should minimise the potential for triggering photosensitive seizures.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.10 Usage with limited cognition, language or learning
Statement

ICT should provide features and presentation that make it simpler to understand, operate, and use for people with limited cognition, language, or learning.
Applies to: All ICT

4.2.11 Privacy
Statement

Where ICT provides accessibility features, using them should not cost the user more privacy than other users get.
Applies to: All ICT

chunks.heading: 5. Generic requirements
chunks.text:
33 requirements shown
5.1.2.1 Closed functionality
ICT with closed functionality must meet the applicable requirements of clauses 5.2 to 13 for those closed functions.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.2.2 Assistive technology
Closed functionality must be operable without the user attaching, connecting, or installing assistive technology, and must meet clauses 5.1.3 to 5.1.6 instead of assuming AT support.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.1 Audio output of visual information
Where visual information is needed to use functions closed to screen readers, provide at least one non-visual mode of access (such as speech output) conveying the same information.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.2 Auditory output delivery including speech
Auditory output used as non-visual access must be delivered either by a mechanism included with the ICT or through a standard personal headset connection that can be used without vision.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.3 Auditory output correlationAdvisory

Advisory: where information is displayed on screen, auditory output should let the user correlate what they hear with what is on the screen.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.4 Speech output user control
Speech output must be interruptible and repeatable on request, where security requirements permit.

chunks.heading: 5. Generic requirements
chunks.text:
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.5 Speech output automatic interruption
The ICT must interrupt current speech output when a user action occurs and when new speech output begins.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.6 Speech output for non-text content
Alternatives for non-text content must be spoken aloud, unless the content is pure decoration or only visual formatting.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.7 Speech output for video information
Where pre-recorded video is needed to use closed functions, speech output must present equivalent information for the video content.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.8 Masked entry
Speech output must not read masked characters (such as PIN digits) aloud unless the user explicitly chooses audible unmasked entry.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.9 Private access to personal data
Auditory output containing private data must only be delivered through a private listening mechanism (such as a headset) or another user-chosen private means.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.10 Non-interfering audio output
The ICT must not automatically play interfering audio lasting longer than three seconds at the same time as the speech output.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.11 Private listening volume

chunks.heading: 5. Generic requirements
chunks.text:
Where auditory output is delivered through a private listening mechanism, at least one non-visual way to control the volume must exist.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.12 Speaker volume
Where auditory output is delivered through speakers, a non-visual incremental volume control with amplification up to at least 65 dBA must be provided.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.13 Volume reset
On shared-use ICT, a function must reset the volume to 65 dBA or less after every use.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.14 Spoken languages
Speech output must be in the same human language as the displayed content, with narrow exceptions such as proper names, technical terms, and languages the ICT cannot speak.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.15 Non-visual error identification
Where an input error is automatically detected, speech output must identify and describe the item in error.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.3.16 Receipts, tickets, and transactional outputs
Receipts, tickets, and other transaction outputs from self-service ICT must have their essential information available via speech output (printed copies themselves are exempt).
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.4 Functionality closed to text enlargement

chunks.heading: 5. Generic requirements
chunks.text:
Where functionality is closed to text-enlargement features, the ICT must itself provide a mode where text needed for all functionality is legible at distance-appropriate sizes.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.5 Visual output for auditory information
Where auditory information is needed to use closed functions, the ICT must provide equivalent visual information, such as captions.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.6.1 Closed functionality
Where functionality is closed to keyboards and keyboard interfaces, all of it must be operable without vision as required by clause 5.1.3.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.6.2 Input focus
Where input focus can be moved to an element, it must also be movable away from that element using the same mechanism, so focus cannot get trapped.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.1.7 Access without speech
Where speech is needed to operate closed functions, at least one alternative input mechanism that does not require speech must be provided.
Applies to: Closed functionality
Add note

5.2 Activation of accessibility features
Documented accessibility features must be activatable without relying on a method that the feature's target users cannot use.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.3 Biometrics

chunks.heading: 5. Generic requirements
chunks.text:
ICT using biometrics must not make one particular biological characteristic the only way to identify a user or control the ICT.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.4 Preservation of accessibility information during conversion
When ICT converts information, it must preserve all documented non-proprietary accessibility information the destination format can hold.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.5.1 Means of operation
Operable parts requiring grasping, pinching, or wrist-twisting must have an accessible alternative means of operation.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.5.2 Operable parts discernibility
Every operable part must be discernible without vision and without performing its action, for example through tactile marking.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.6.1 Tactile or auditory status
Where a locking or toggle control shows its status visually, at least one mode must expose the status by touch or sound as well.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.6.2 Visual status
Where a locking or toggle control exposes its status non-visually, at least one mode must make the status visually determinable too.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.7 Key repeat

chunks.heading: 5. Generic requirements
chunks.text:
A key-repeat function that cannot be turned off must allow a repeat delay of at least 2 seconds and a rate adjustable down to 1 character per 2 seconds.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.8 Double-strike key acceptance
On keyboards and keypads, the delay for rejecting an accidental identical second keystroke must be adjustable up to at least 0.5 seconds.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

5.9 Simultaneous user actions
Any operation requiring simultaneous user actions must have at least one mode of operation that does not.
Applies to: Generic ICT capabilities
Add note

chunks.heading: 6. Two-way voice communication
chunks.text:
17 requirements shown
6.1 Audio bandwidth for speech
Two-way voice communication must support speech encoding with an upper frequency limit of at least 7 000 Hz, for intelligible audio quality.
Applies to: Two-way voice communication
Add note

6.2.1.1 RTT communication
ICT providing two-way voice communication must also provide two-way real-time text (RTT), except where that would require adding input or output hardware.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.1.2 Concurrent voice and text
Where voice and RTT are both provided, the ICT must allow concurrent voice and text over a single connection.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.2.1 Visually distinguishable display
Displayed sent RTT text must be visually distinguishable from and separated from received text.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.2.2 Programmatically determinable send and receive direction
The send and receive direction of RTT text must be programmatically determinable, unless the RTT is closed functionality, so screen readers can voice who typed what.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.2.3 Speaker identification
Where speaker identification is available for voice, it must also be available for RTT participants.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.2.4 Visual indicator of Audio with RTT

chunks.heading: 6. Two-way voice communication
chunks.text:
Where voice and RTT are both active, a real-time visual indicator of audio activity must be shown on the display.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.3 Interoperability
ICT with RTT functionality must interoperate with other RTT ICT using the applicable standard mechanisms listed in the clause (such as ITU-T T.140 for IP telephony).
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.2.4 RTT responsiveness
RTT input must reach the network or platform within 500 ms of the smallest reliably composed unit of text being available, so text truly flows in real time.
Applies to: Real-time text (RTT)
Add note

6.3 Caller ID
Caller ID and similar functions must be available in text form and be programmatically determinable, unless the functionality is closed.
Applies to: Two-way voice communication
Add note

6.4 Alternatives to voice-based services
Where real-time voice services offer voicemail, auto-attendant, or interactive voice response, the same information and tasks must be achievable without hearing or speech.
Applies to: Two-way voice communication
Add note

6.5.2 Resolution
Real-time video used with voice communication must support at least QVGA resolution, and preferably VGA or better.
Applies to: Voice + real-time video
Add note

6.5.3 Frame rate
Real-time video used with voice communication must support at least 20 frames per second, and preferably 30 or more.

chunks.heading: 6. Two-way voice communication
chunks.text:
Applies to: Voice + real-time video
Add note

6.5.4 Synchronization between audio and video
The time difference between speech and video presented to the user must not exceed 100 ms, keeping lip-reading viable.
Applies to: Voice + real-time video
Add note

6.5.5 Visual indicator of audio with video
Where video is part of two-way voice communication, a real-time visual indicator of audio activity must be provided.
Applies to: Voice + real-time video
Add note

6.5.6 Speaker identification with video (sign language) communication
Where speaker identification exists for voice users, an equivalent means must identify who is currently signing in real-time video.
Applies to: Voice + real-time video
Add note

6.6 Alternatives to video-based servicesAdvisory

Advisory: where real-time video services offer answering machine, auto-attendant, or interactive response facilities, users should be able to access them through video as well.
Applies to: Two-way voice communication
Add note

chunks.heading: 7. ICT with video capabilities
chunks.text:
9 requirements shown
7.1.1 Captioning playback
ICT that displays video with synchronized audio must have a mode that displays available captions, including user-selectable closed captions.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.1.2 Captioning synchronization
Caption display must stay synchronized: within 100 ms of the caption timestamp for recorded material, and within 100 ms of caption availability for live captions.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.1.3 Preservation of captioning
ICT that transmits, converts, or records video must preserve caption data so captions can still be displayed correctly downstream.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.1.4 Captions characteristics
Users must be able to adapt caption display characteristics (such as size, colour, and background) except where captions are unmodifiable characters.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.1.5 Spoken subtitles
ICT displaying video with synchronized audio must offer spoken output of the available captions (spoken subtitles), where caption content is programmatically determinable.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.2.1 Audio description playback
A mechanism must exist to select and play available audio description to the default audio channel.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.2.2 Audio description synchronization

chunks.heading: 7. ICT with video capabilities
chunks.text:
Audio description playback must stay synchronized with the audio-visual content.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.2.3 Preservation of audio description
ICT that transmits, converts, or records video must preserve audio description data for downstream playback.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

7.3 User controls for captions and audio description
Controls to activate captions and audio description must sit at the same level of interaction as the primary media controls, not buried in deeper menus.
Applies to: ICT with video capabilities
Add note

chunks.heading: 8. Hardware
chunks.text:
31 requirements shown
8.1.1 Generic requirements
The generic requirements of clause 5 also apply to hardware.
Applies to: Hardware
Add note

8.1.2 Standard connections
Where hardware provides input or output connection points, at least one must use an industry-standard non-proprietary format, directly or via commercially available adapters.
Applies to: Hardware
Add note

8.1.3 Colour
Hardware must not use colour as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing an element.
Applies to: Hardware
Add note

8.2.1.1 Speech volume range
Hardware with speech output must allow speech volume adjustment over a range of at least 18 dB.
Applies to: Hardware with speech output
Add note

8.2.1.2 Incremental volume control
Where the volume control is incremental, at least one intermediate step of 12 dB gain above the lowest setting must exist.
Applies to: Hardware with speech output
Add note

8.2.2.1 Fixed-line devices
Fixed-line handsets held to the ear must provide magnetic coupling meeting ETSI ES 200 381-1, marked with the T symbol, for hearing-aid users.
Applies to: Hardware with speech output
Add note

8.2.2.2 Wireless communication devices
Wireless communication devices held to the ear must provide magnetic coupling to hearing technologies meeting ETSI ES 200 381-2.
Applies to: Hardware with speech output
Add note

chunks.heading: 8. Hardware
chunks.text:
8.3.1 Forward or side reach
Stationary ICT must meet either the forward-reach dimensions of clause 8.3.2 or the side-reach dimensions of clause 8.3.3.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.1 Unobstructed high forward reach
With unobstructed forward reach, at least one of each type of operable part must be no higher than 1 220 mm above the floor.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.2 Unobstructed low forward reach
With unobstructed forward reach, at least one of each type of operable part must be no lower than 380 mm above the floor.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.3.1 Clear space
Where an integral obstruction hinders access, clear space must extend beneath it at least as far as the obstruction's own depth.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.3.2 Obstructed (< 510 mm) forward reach
With an integral obstruction shallower than 510 mm, forward reach to at least one of each type of operable part must be no higher than 1 220 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.3.3 Obstructed (< 635 mm) forward reach
With an integral obstruction between 510 mm and 635 mm deep, forward reach must be no higher than 1 120 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.4 Knee and toe clearance width
Knee and toe clearance under an integral obstacle that forms part of the access space must be at least 760 mm wide.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

chunks.heading: 8. Hardware
chunks.text:
8.3.2.5 Toe clearance
Toe clearance (space under 230 mm above the floor) must extend no more than 635 mm under the whole obstacle and meet the clause's minimum depth and height dimensions.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.2.6 Knee clearance
Knee clearance (230 mm to 685 mm above the floor) must meet the clause's depth and height dimensions so a seated user can approach.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.3.1 Unobstructed high side reach
With unobstructed side reach (obstruction under 255 mm), at least one of each type of operable part must be within a high side reach of no more than 1 220 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.3.2 Unobstructed low side reach
With unobstructed side reach, at least one of each type of operable part must be no lower than a side reach of 380 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.3.3.1 Obstructed (≤ 255 mm) side reach
With an integral side obstruction up to 255 mm deep and under 865 mm high, the side reach must be no higher than 1 220 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.3.3.2 Obstructed (≤ 610 mm) side reach
With an integral side obstruction between 255 mm and 610 mm deep and under 865 mm high, the side reach must be no higher than 1 170 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.4.1 Change in level

chunks.heading: 8. Hardware
chunks.text:
Any change of floor level within or entering stationary ICT must be ramped at no steeper than 1:48, with small level changes excepted.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.4.2 Clear floor or ground space
An operating area within stationary ICT must provide clear floor space of at least 760 mm by 1 220 mm.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.4.3.2 Forward approach
Where a forward approach into an alcove deeper than 610 mm is necessary, the access space must be at least 915 mm wide.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.4.3.3 Parallel approach
Where a parallel approach to an alcove deeper than 380 mm is possible, the access space must be at least 1 525 mm wide.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.5 Visibility
At least one of each type of display screen must be legible from a point 1 015 mm above the centre of the clear floor space.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.3.6 Installation instructions
Installation instructions must be available and must cover installing the ICT so its operable parts and displays stay within accessible reach and sight ranges.
Applies to: Stationary ICT
Add note

8.4.1 Numeric keys
Physical numeric keypads laid out in a rectangle must have a tactilely distinct number five key.
Applies to: Mechanically operable parts
Add note

8.4.2.1 Means of operation of mechanical parts

chunks.heading: 8. Hardware
chunks.text:
Mechanical controls requiring grasping, pinching, or wrist-twisting must have an accessible alternative means of operation.
Applies to: Mechanically operable parts
Add note

8.4.2.2 Force of operation of mechanical parts
Mechanical controls requiring more than 22.2 N of force must have an alternative requiring less than 22.2 N.
Applies to: Mechanically operable parts
Add note

8.4.3 Keys, tickets and fare cards
Keys, tickets, and fare cards whose orientation matters for further use must have tactilely discernible orientation.
Applies to: Mechanically operable parts
Add note

8.5 Tactile indication of speech mode
Shared-use ICT with speech output must give a tactile indication (such as braille) of how to start the speech mode.
Applies to: Hardware
Add note

chunks.heading: How the chapters map to products
chunks.text:
Websites & web apps
Chapter 9 (WCAG 2.1 A/AA in v3.2.1; WCAG 2.2 A/AA plus user preferences in v4.1.1) and chapter 12. In v4.1.1 this is EAA Table A.1.

Documents
Chapter 10 applies adapted WCAG criteria to PDFs, Office files, and e-books. In v4.1.1 this is EAA Table A.2.

Software & apps
Chapter 11, including assistive-technology interoperability; authoring tools are 11.8 in v3.2.1 and 5.10 in v4.1.1. EAA Table A.3.

Hardware & terminals
Chapters 5 to 8: closed functionality, communication, video, and physical access. EAA Table A.4, with the generic clauses in Table A.5.

chunks.heading: Which versions of EN 301 549 does this checklist cover?
chunks.text: Both current editions, with a switch at the top. Version 3.2.1 (March 2021) is the edition cited in the Official Journal of the EU, and only for the Web Accessibility Directive (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/2048 as amended by Decision (EU) 2021/1339). Version 4.1.1 was published by ETSI, CEN and CENELEC on 2 September 2026: it aligns clauses 9 to 11 with WCAG 2.2, rewrites the real-time text and total conversation requirements, and adds Annex ZB and the clause A.2 conformance tables for the European Accessibility Act. V4.1.1 is not yet cited in the Official Journal; the citation is expected between late November and mid-December 2026. Each edition keeps its own progress, notes, and Excel export.

chunks.heading: How many requirements does EN 301 549 contain?
chunks.text: V3.2.1 has 285 testable requirements across chapters 5 to 13, of which 50 in chapter 9 are the WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria, plus 12 functional performance statements in chapter 4 that are descriptive rather than testable. V4.1.1 has 319 testable requirements, of which 55 in chapter 9 are the WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA criteria; its chapter 4 criteria are now written with "shall" and have their own Annex C tests, so they count as requirements. Both editions keep void slots so the clause numbering stays aligned with WCAG; those appear as information rows.

chunks.heading: What changed between v3.2.1 and v4.1.1?
chunks.text: Against the v3.2.1 dataset, v4.1.1 has 91 new rows, 93 changed rows, and 48 v3.2.1 clauses with no v4.1.1 row (merged, moved, dropped, or made informative). The headline changes are WCAG 2.2 in clauses 9 to 11 (six new criteria, Parsing removed), new user-preference clauses 9.7, 10.7 and 11.7, a rewritten clause 6 built around total conversation and real-time text, functional performance criteria written with "shall", a rewritten stationary-ICT clause 8.3, and the EAA mapping in Annex ZB. Switch to v4.1.1 and tick "Only rows that are new or changed" to see them, or read the clause-by-clause guide linked above the checklist.

chunks.heading: Which version should I audit against today?
chunks.text: Test against WCAG 2.2 AA now, whichever edition you cite. WCAG 2.2 is backwards-compatible with 2.1, so work done against 2.2 satisfies the WCAG 2.1 clauses of v3.2.1 and is already aligned with v4.1.1. For a Web Accessibility Directive statement, cite v3.2.1 until the Official Journal lists v4.1.1. For the European Accessibility Act there is no cited edition yet, so a conformance claim today is a statement of what you tested against, not a presumption of conformity; v4.1.1 is the edition built for the Act and the one to prepare for. Always name the exact edition in your conformance report.

chunks.heading: Do I need to check every chapter?
chunks.text: No. The chapters apply by product type: a website is assessed against chapter 9 plus chapter 12 (information about products and services); downloadable documents add chapter 10; native software and mobile apps use chapter 11 (and, in v4.1.1, the authoring-tool clauses now in 5.10); hardware and self-service terminals bring in chapters 5 to 8. Use the scope buttons above the checklist, or, in v4.1.1, pick one of the five EAA conformance tables from clause A.2 (web page, non-web document, software, hardware, all ICT), which are the sets the standard itself says to assess for the European Accessibility Act.

chunks.heading: Why do some clause numbers show as void?
chunks.text: EN 301 549 keeps its clause numbering aligned with WCAG so that, for example, clause 9.1.4.3 is always WCAG 1.4.3. Where a WCAG slot is Level AAA (such as 1.4.6), or a criterion does not apply in a context (such as Bypass Blocks for a single document), the standard marks the slot void rather than renumbering everything. V4.1.1 adds a void at 9.4.1.1 because WCAG 2.2 removed Parsing. This checklist shows void rows so auditors are not left wondering whether something is missing.

chunks.heading: Can I export this checklist to Excel?
chunks.text: Yes, free and with no account, for either edition. The export contains every clause in your selected scope with its type, applicability, WCAG mapping, advisory flag, your status and notes, and the plain-language summary, plus a summary sheet stating the edition and its legal status. The v4.1.1 export adds the change against v3.2.1, the previous clause number, and a third sheet listing the v3.2.1 clauses with no v4.1.1 row. Your checkmarks and notes also auto-save to your browser's local storage, separately for each edition.

chunks.heading: Is completing this checklist the same as EAA compliance?
chunks.text:
No checklist is. Once v4.1.1 is cited in the Official Journal under the European Accessibility Act, conformance with the clauses in its Tables A.1 to A.5 gives a presumption of conformity with the Act's accessibility requirements; before that, no edition does. Even then, the summaries here are plain-language explanations, not the normative text, and self-assessment against any checklist is only as good as the testing behind it. Use this to structure and track an assessment, verify findings against the published standard, and consider a professional audit for anything with legal exposure.
