Counts come from the two datasets behind the interactive checklist, generated from the ETSI PDFs by a committed script and reconciled against Annex C and the clause A.2 tables. “Changed” means the clause number or title differs from V3.2.1, or the clause moved; it deliberately ignores the editorial rewrite that turned every precondition into “Where ICT is, or includes, ...”, which touched almost every row without changing what is tested.

chunks.heading: The six WCAG 2.2 criteria now required
chunks.text:
Clause 9.1 to 9.4 is now a one-to-one list of the WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA success criteria, each clause saying that the web page “shall satisfy WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion” so-and-so. Clause 9.6 requires the five WCAG 2.2 conformance requirements at Level AA (conformance level, full pages, complete processes, only accessibility-supported ways of using technologies, non-interference), and clause 9.5 lists the 31 Level AAA criteria as informative. Six criteria are new against V3.2.1, and one slot is newly void: 9.4.1.1 Parsing, with a note explaining that WCAG 2.2 removed the criterion because the problems it prevented “either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria”.

WCAG 2.2 success criteria added in EN 301 549 V4.1.1 and their clause numbers
Criterion Level Web Documents Software How V4.1.1 applies it
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA 9.2.4.11 10.2.4.11 11.2.4.11 Clauses 10 and 11 apply it only where the document or software accepts keyboard input.
2.5.7 Dragging Movements AA 9.2.5.7 10.2.5.7 11.2.5.7 Adapted in Tables 10.12 and 11.12: dragging determined by the user agent or platform and not modified by the author is exempt.
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA 9.2.5.8 10.2.5.8 11.2.5.8 24 by 24 CSS pixels with the spacing, equivalent, inline, user-agent and essential exceptions carried over.

chunks.heading: The six WCAG 2.2 criteria now required
chunks.text:
3.2.6 Consistent Help A 9.3.2.6 10.3.2.6 11.3.2.6 (void) Applies to a document within a set of documents; void for software, which has no concept of a set of pages.
3.3.7 Redundant Entry A 9.3.3.7 10.3.3.7 11.3.3.7 Referenced directly from WCAG 2.2 in all three clauses.
3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA 9.3.3.8 10.3.3.8 11.3.3.8 Adapted in Tables 10.20 and 11.16 with the alternative, mechanism, object recognition and personal content exceptions.

Two subtleties are easy to miss. First, clauses 10 and 11 reference WCAG 2.2 directly for most criteria but restate 38 of them in tables (Table 10.1 to 10.20 and 11.1 to 11.16) where web wording does not fit; the table versions are where the exceptions for documents and software live, and each table's note names the WCAG criterion it is identical to. Second, the document and software equivalents of Consistent Help differ: 10.3.2.6 applies to a non-web document “within a set of non-web documents”, while 11.3.2.6 is void because software has no equivalent of a set of pages. The same logic voids 11.3.1.2 Language of parts and 11.3.2.3 Consistent navigation for software, as it did in V3.2.1.

chunks.heading: The six WCAG 2.2 criteria now required
chunks.text: Three slots that were void in V3.2.1 are now requirements: 10.3.2.3 Consistent navigation and 10.3.2.4 Consistent identification apply to a document within a set of documents, and 11.2.4.2 (software titled) now requires a title describing each window or screen on platforms that support one. If your document remediation process assumed those three slots were empty, it needs a line each.

chunks.heading: The user-preferences rework
chunks.text:
V3.2.1 had one user-preferences clause, 11.7, which asked software to follow a fixed list of platform settings: measurement units, colour, contrast, font type, font size and focus cursor. V4.1.1 replaces that list with a concept, “documented platform accessibility features”, and extends the duty from software to web pages and documents through three parallel clauses:
9.7 User preferences for web pages (new): a web page must not block the browser's modes of operation that present the page according to user preference settings, and must not explicitly override user preferences for documented platform accessibility features, unless that is essential to the page. The note names the CSS forced-color-adjust property as the kind of override the clause limits to essential cases.
10.7 User preferences for non-web documents (new): the same duty for documents, aimed at files that lock out the viewer's reflow, colour or text-size modes.

chunks.heading: The user-preferences rework
chunks.text:
11.7 User preferences (rewritten): software that is not designed to be isolated from its platform must follow the values of the user's preference settings for documented platform accessibility features unless not doing so is essential to the software's function. The notes list colour filters, contrast, text size, pointer size and text cursor as the kinds of feature meant, and say that a user agent (browser or document viewer) meets the clause by offering at least one mode that enforces the user's settings when rendering content.

The chain closes through two older clauses: 11.6.1 requires platform software to give users control over its documented accessibility features and 11.6.2 forbids software from disrupting them, while 12.3 requires product documentation to say what the accessibility features are and how to use them. In other words, the features a platform documents under 12.3 are the features that 9.7, 10.7 and 11.7 oblige content and apps to respect. For a web team the practical test is simple: with Windows high contrast, a larger system text size and a custom cursor switched on, does the page still honour them?

chunks.heading: Clause 6: total conversation and real-time text
chunks.text: V3.2.1's clause 6 was titled “ICT with two-way voice communication” and held 17 requirements. V4.1.1's is “ICT supporting real-time bidirectional communication” with 38, 20 of them new. The standard now describes a communication system end to end: clients, systems, interconnection, roaming, and emergency communications, each with a set of requirements that must hold in every scenario.

chunks.heading: 6.0 Operational scenarios
chunks.text: Eight new self-scoping clauses, 6.0.2 to 6.0.9, define the situations in which the rest of clause 6 must be met: a communication client, a communication system with its own clients, a system connecting to another system, a system serving a roaming visiting client, and the same four again for emergency communications with public safety answering points (PSAPs), including a client that is abroad and contacts the visited country's PSAP over an IP-based system that does not use roaming at call-control level. Annex C turns each scenario into test preconditions, so a product is tested in the configurations it will actually be used in.

chunks.heading: 6.1 Voice
chunks.text: 6.1.1 (new) requires ICT that connects to other ICT for voice to document how its voice interoperates, covering at least 100 Hz to 7 000 Hz, either by mutual agreement or by implementing ITU-T G.722. 6.1.2 keeps the 250 Hz to 7 000 Hz capture and presentation range from the old 6.1. 6.1.3 (attached listening devices down to 100 Hz) and 6.1.4 (subtitles for voice calls within 2 seconds) are recommendations.

chunks.heading: 6.2 Real-time text
chunks.text:
This is the rewrite the foreword flags. The headline change is in 6.2.1.1: where V3.2.1 excused ICT from providing RTT when that would require redesign, V4.1.1 simply requires that ICT providing real-time voice “shall provide functionality that allows real-time bidirectional RTT communication”, with notes that this implicitly covers interoperation and multi-party use. Clause 6.2 holds 16 requirements in all:
6.2.1.2 Concurrent voice and RTT and 6.2.1.3 Single user action (new): one action must act on all media when a session is started, answered, modified or ended.
6.2.2.1 to 6.2.2.5 Display of RTT: sources distinguished (a label such as Speaker 1 is enough), all active communicators indicated, a real-time indicator of non-local audio, text presented as blocks in relative time order (block ends at sentence punctuation plus space, a line separator, or 5 seconds of silence), and the ability to review the whole conversation during and, if recorded, after the session.
6.2.3 DTMF during RTT: touch-tone digits must be sendable by a method distinct from typing them as text.
6.2.4 Responsiveness: the 500 ms transmission limit from the smallest reliably composed unit of text is kept, with a note that 300 ms or less feels better.

chunks.heading: 6.2 Real-time text
chunks.text:
6.2.5 to 6.2.9 (new): erasing text from the current end without being blocked by earlier line breaks, 90 characters per second from 3 simultaneous sources in multi-party calls, a character set covering Latin-1, the regional scripts, platform emoji and U+FFFD, RTT input through every general text-input method, and RTT media that can be requested, answered or added mid-call regardless of settings.
6.2.10 RTT interoperability: the old 6.2.3, now a documentation requirement with ITU-T T.140 plus IETF RFC 4103 (updated by RFC 9071) as the fallback that always satisfies it.

chunks.heading: 6.3 to 6.7 Caller ID, alternatives, video, total conversation
chunks.text: 6.3 (caller identification in text and programmatically determinable) and 6.4 (voicemail, auto-attendant and IVR usable without hearing or speech) survive with rewritten preconditions. 6.5 keeps the video floor of QVGA, 20 frames per second and 100 ms audio-video synchronisation, and widens 6.5.6 from identifying who is signing to indicating all active participants. 6.6 (alternatives to video-based services) is now labelled a recommendation. 6.7 is new: 6.7.1 Total conversation provision requires any ICT that provides real-time voice and includes video to also provide RTT conforming to 6.2, so that voice, video and text are available together, and 6.7.2 requires documented video interoperability (ITU-T H.264 constrained baseline level 3 as the fallback, H.265 or VP8 where codecs are negotiated).

chunks.heading: Why 28 June 2027 is in this clause
chunks.text: The European Accessibility Act requires, in Article 4(8) and Annex I Section V, that emergency communications to the single European emergency number 112 be answered by the most appropriate PSAP using synchronised voice and text, including real-time text, and synchronised video where video is provided. Article 31(3) lets member states apply that requirement as late as 28 June 2027. The emergency scenarios in 6.0.6 to 6.0.9, the note in 6.2.10 that emergency communications are “an important case” of required interoperation, and the pointer in 13.3 to ETSI EN 303 919 (the detailed emergency-communications standard) are V4.1.1 giving the Act a testable definition of what an accessible 112 call is. For vendors of PSAP software, telecoms equipment and emergency apps, clause 6 is the part of the standard with a hard date attached.

chunks.heading: Annex ZB and the conformance tables
chunks.text:
A harmonised standard needs a formal map from the law's essential requirements to its own clauses. V3.2.1 had one such map, Annex A, for the Web Accessibility Directive. V4.1.1 has three Z annexes plus a working annex:
Annex ZA replaces the old Annex A: Table ZA.1 for web pages and documents and Table ZA.2 for mobile applications under Directive (EU) 2016/2102, drawing on clauses 9, 10 and 11 and parts of 5, 6, 7 and 12.
Annex ZB maps Directive (EU) 2019/882: ZB.1 provision of information on products, ZB.2 user interface and functionality of products plus support services, ZB.3 information about specific products, ZB.4 accessibility of services (the general service requirements of the Act's Annex I Section III), and ZB.5 functionality of specific services. Each row quotes the essential requirement and names the clauses that cover it.
Annex ZC covers the other directives that the Act's Annex I Section VI refers to, by pointing back at the ZB tables.

chunks.heading: Annex ZB and the conformance tables
chunks.text:
Clause A.2 is the working route. Its clause A.2.0 says, in a paragraph headed “Important”, that each of A.2.1 to A.2.5 is to be considered in order, that every requirement in a table whose condition applies must be assessed, and that Table A.5 applies to all ICT. The note in ZB.0 adds that a product can fall into several rows of several ZB tables, which “makes the tables in Annex ZB impractical for use in assessing whether a specific ICT product or service meets all the applicable requirements”, and sends assessors to A.2.

The five conformance tables in clause A.2 of EN 301 549 V4.1.1 and the number of clauses in each
Table Condition Clauses What it contains
Table A.1 Where the ICT is, or includes, a web page 57 55 WCAG 2.2 A and AA criteria plus 9.6 and 9.7.
Table A.2 Where the ICT is, or includes, a non-web document 54 Clause 10 criteria plus 10.7; the recommendations 10.5 and 10.6 are not listed.
Table A.3 Where the ICT is, or includes, non-web software that provides a user interface 68 Clause 11 criteria, the accessibility-services clauses 11.5.2.1 and 11.5.2.4 to 11.5.2.17, 11.6 and 11.7.
Table A.4 Where the ICT is, or includes, hardware 28 Clause 8 plus 5.5 (tactilely discernible operable parts).
Table A.5 All ICT 106 Clauses 4.2, 5 (including 5.10 authoring tools), 6, 7, 12 and 13.1, every one self-scoped by its own precondition.

chunks.heading: Annex ZB and the conformance tables
chunks.text:
Together the five tables list every testable requirement of the standard except the six recommendations; our build script asserts that equality against the extracted clause list. One erratum is worth knowing before you copy Table A.4 into a report: the published PDF misnumbers four stationary-ICT rows, printing 8.3.10.1 and 8.3.10.2 for the free-space clauses that the body numbers 8.3.11.1 and 8.3.11.2, and 8.3.11.2 and 8.3.11.3 for the obstructed side reach clauses 8.3.10.2 and 8.3.10.3. The row titles and the Annex C references make the intent clear; follow the clause numbers in the body of the standard.
The foreword and A.2.0 state the legal effect in one sentence: once the standard is cited in the Official Journal under the Act, conformance with the normative clauses in Tables A.1 to A.5 confers, within the scope of the standard, a presumption of conformity with the corresponding essential requirements, and that presumption “stays valid only as long as a reference to the present document is maintained in the list published in the Official Journal”. Note the word “corresponding”: the Act also has requirements the standard does not cover, such as the service-provider information duties in Annex V, which no clause of EN 301 549 discharges for you.

chunks.heading: What changed for documents (clause 10)
chunks.text:
WCAG 2.2: the six new criteria at 10.2.4.11, 10.2.5.7, 10.2.5.8, 10.3.2.6, 10.3.3.7 and 10.3.3.8, and 10.4.1.1 Parsing void. Focus Not Obscured applies only where the document accepts keyboard input (forms and interactive PDFs, not a flat report).
10.7 User preferences for non-web documents (new): the document must not block the viewer's preference-driven modes or override documented platform accessibility features unless essential.
Sets of documents: 10.3.2.3 Consistent navigation and 10.3.2.4 Consistent identification, void in V3.2.1, now apply to a document within a set of documents, alongside 10.3.2.6 Consistent Help. A multi-file manual or a series of statements is a set.
10.2.4.2 Non-web document titled is reworded to require a title where the format has a programmatically determinable title that common authoring tools can edit; the substance (a title describing name, topic or purpose) is unchanged.
10.5 Subtitle positioning and 10.6 Audio description timing are now explicitly labelled recommendations, as their Annex C entries always treated them.
Terminology: captions are subtitles throughout; the notes point out that WCAG's definition of captions covers both words.

chunks.heading: What changed for documents (clause 10)
chunks.text: PDF/UA: note 11 to clause 10.0 names ISO 14289-1:2014 (PDF/UA-1) and ISO 14289-2:2024 (PDF/UA-2) as the technical standards for accessible PDF that “would be useful in meeting EN 301 549”, the first time the 2024 edition is referenced; note 9 recommends Schema.org accessibility metadata for discoverability. See the PDF accessibility guide and the free PDF accessibility checker.

chunks.heading: What changed for software (clause 11)
chunks.text:
The open/closed split is gone. V3.2.1 numbered many software clauses as X.1 (open functionality) and X.2 (closed functionality, redirecting to clause 5.1). V4.1.1 has one clause per criterion whose precondition excludes functionality “closed to programmatic access of information by assistive technologies”; clause 5.1 covers closed functionality, and gains 5.1.8 Identify input purpose (closed functionality), which requires the purpose of user-data fields to be presented in audio. 17 v3 closed-functionality variants therefore disappear from clause 11, including the three not-applicable slots for Parsing, Name/role/value and Status messages.
WCAG 2.2: 11.2.4.11, 11.2.5.7, 11.2.5.8, 11.3.3.7 and 11.3.3.8 are new; 11.3.2.6 Consistent Help is void; 11.4.1.1 Parsing is void; 11.2.4.2 (software titled) is a requirement where it was void.
11.5 is now “Interoperability with keyboards and assistive technology”. 11.5.1 becomes informative, 11.5.2.2 is void because its content merged into 11.5.2.1 (platform software must provide documented accessibility services covering every concept in 11.5.2.5 to 11.5.2.17), and 11.5.2.3 Use of accessibility services is demoted from a requirement to a recommendation. The thirteen object-information, relationship, action and notification clauses (11.5.2.5 to 11.5.2.17) carry over.

chunks.heading: What changed for software (clause 11)
chunks.text:
11.6 is now “Documented accessibility features” and 11.7 User preferences is rewritten as described above.
Authoring tools moved to clause 5.10. The old 11.8.1 to 11.8.5 (content technology, accessible content creation, preservation in transformations, repair assistance, templates) are now generic requirements that apply to any ICT with authoring functionality, including web-based editors, and their targets now include clause 11 as well as 9 and 10. A CMS, a form builder or a design tool that outputs web content is in scope whether or not it is itself non-web software.

chunks.heading: Clause 4: statements become criteria
chunks.text: The “functional performance statements” are now “functional performance criteria”, and every one is written with “shall”: where ICT provides visual modes of operation, it “shall provide at least one mode of operation that does not require vision”, and so on. A new 4.2.11 Privacy requires that using accessibility features does not cost the user privacy. Annex C gives each criterion a two-check test: the ICT passes if it meets every requirement that Annex B marks as primary or secondary for that criterion, or if there is evidence of the outcome. The notes also add a measurable floor for the first time: best practice for the smallest text is an x-height of at least 8 CSS pixels, 1.2 mm at 400 mm.

chunks.heading: Clause 5: generic requirements
chunks.text: Every closed-functionality clause in 5.1 now starts “Where ICT includes closed functionality” and 5.1.3.3 Auditory output correlation is promoted from a recommendation to a requirement. The two operable-parts clauses 5.5.1 and 5.5.2 collapse into 5.5 Tactilely discernible operable parts, which lets a touchscreen edge, corner or tactile marker count as a discernible part. 5.10 is the relocated authoring-tool clause.

chunks.heading: Clause 7: video capabilities
chunks.text: Captions become subtitles; 7.1.2 keeps the 100 ms synchronisation to the subtitle timecode; 7.1.5 is reworded so a player must be able to play spoken subtitles that exist, not generate them; and 7.3 User control of audiovisual accessibility features now requires that subtitles, audio description or spoken subtitles can each be switched with a single operation at the same level as the volume control.

chunks.heading: Clause 8: hardware, and a rewritten 8.3
chunks.text: Standard connections, colour and contrast leave 8.1 to become 8.6, 8.7 and the new 8.8 (non-digital characters, symbols and unlabelled parts must contrast light-on-dark or dark-on-light; a Michelson contrast of 0.7 and 0.4 is the usual approach). 8.3 Stationary ICT is rebuilt around two sets of dimensions, Set 1 for designs with no functional or design restrictions and Set 2 for designs with them: display screens no lower than 800 mm (8.3.2), operating information no higher than 1 600 mm or 2 000 mm (8.3.3), one of each control between 800 mm and 1 100 mm or between 380 mm and 1 220 mm (8.3.5), all controls within a 900 mm horizontal span (8.3.6), reach depth of 300 mm or 510/610 mm (8.3.7), obstruction limits for forward and side reach (8.3.9, 8.3.10) and knee and toe clearance from Table 8.2 (8.3.11). The v3 clear-floor-space, change-in-level and alcove clauses are gone; access space is declared out of scope and left to the built-environment standards.

chunks.heading: Clause 12: information about products and services
chunks.text: 12.1 and 12.2 route digital information about a product or service, including support services, to clauses 9, 10 or 11 by format; 12.3 keeps the duty to document accessibility features and how to get support; 12.4 and 12.5 are new and require electronic programme guides to state, and let users check without playing the item, whether subtitles, audio description, spoken subtitles and sign language are available. The v3 “effective communication” clause for support services has no direct successor.

chunks.heading: Clause 13: relay services
chunks.text: The five per-service clauses (text, sign, lip-reading, captioned telephony, speech-to-speech) are replaced by 13.1.2 Relay service access (five invocation requirements: using the primary user's normal destination addresses, conveying caller ID, user-controlled invocation on outgoing and incoming calls, emergency invocation) and 13.1.3 Relay service requirements (relaying action for every modality, pass-through of unconverted media, conference participation, accepting PSAP-initiated invocations). 13.2 is void and 13.3 Access to emergency services is informative, deferring to clause 6 and EN 303 919.

chunks.heading: Migration list for teams on V3.2.1
chunks.text:
Re-baseline web, document and software testing on WCAG 2.2 AA. Add the six criteria above to your test plan, drop 4.1.1 Parsing from your findings, and keep the rest: every WCAG 2.1 A and AA criterion is still required in v4.1.1. If your audit tooling already runs WCAG 2.2, most of this step is renaming the column header.
Add the three user-preference checks. Clause 9.7 (web), 10.7 (documents) and 11.7 (software) are new or rewritten. For web, look for CSS that overrides forced colours, text size or cursor settings; for documents, viewers' reflow and colour modes; for software, whether the app honours the platform's contrast, text size, pointer and cursor settings.
Re-map chapter 11 clause numbers. Every open-functionality variant (11.x.x.x.1) is now the clause itself (11.x.x.x), and the closed-functionality variants (11.x.x.x.2) are gone; closed functionality is assessed under clause 5.1 instead, which gained 5.1.8 for input purpose. Authoring-tool requirements moved from 11.8 to 5.10 and now also cover web-based tools.

chunks.heading: Migration list for teams on V3.2.1
chunks.text:
Treat the functional performance criteria as requirements. Chapter 4 moved from 12 descriptive statements to 11 criteria written with "shall", each with an Annex C test and a new criterion 4.2.11 Privacy. Annex C accepts either evidence that the outcome is achieved or a pass on every requirement Annex B maps to the criterion, so a complete clause 5 to 13 assessment usually satisfies them, but your report should now state that.
Rescope anything with voice, video or chat. Clause 6 is now 38 requirements, 20 of them new. If your product offers real-time voice, it must offer real-time text with no "unless it would require redesign" exception, and if it offers video too it must offer total conversation. Contact centres, telehealth, conferencing, in-app support calls and messaging apps with calling are all in scope.
Re-measure self-service terminals and kiosks against the new clause 8.3. The reach, height and free-space rules were rewritten as two sets (15 requirements): Set 1 where nothing in the design prevents the preferred dimensions, Set 2 where functional or design restrictions apply. Old findings against 8.3.2 to 8.3.5 of v3.2.1 do not carry over; display screens must now sit no lower than 800 mm, and three hardware clauses (8.6 connections, 8.7 colour, 8.8 contrast) moved out of 8.1.

chunks.heading: Migration list for teams on V3.2.1
chunks.text:
Rename captions to subtitles in reports. Clauses 7, 9, 10 and 11 now say subtitles where v3.2.1 said captions; the underlying WCAG criteria (1.2.2 and 1.2.4) are unchanged. Clause 7 also gains 7.1.5 spoken subtitles and rewrites 7.3 so subtitles, audio description and spoken subtitles can each be toggled with one action at the same level as the volume control.
Restate documentation and support duties under clause 12. The old 12.1 (product documentation) and 12.2 (support services) became 12.1 to 12.5: information about products, information about services (which now includes support services), accessibility and compatibility features in the documentation, and two electronic programme guide clauses for media services.
Pick the right conformance table for the EAA. Clause A.2 has five tables: A.1 web pages, A.2 non-web documents, A.3 non-web software with a user interface, A.4 hardware, A.5 all ICT. Assess every table whose condition applies to the product, in order; the standard itself says the Annex ZB tables are impractical for assessing a specific product and points you to A.2.

chunks.heading: Migration list for teams on V3.2.1
chunks.text:
Update your statement and ACR template, but not the citation yet. Keep citing v3.2.1 for Web Accessibility Directive statements until the Official Journal lists v4.1.1, and say which edition you tested against in any EAA conformity documentation. Prepare the v4.1.1 wording now; the only thing you cannot do before citation day is claim a presumption of conformity through it.

Work the delta directly: open the interactive checklist in its v4.1.1 edition, tick “Only rows that are new or changed since v3.2.1”, pick the EAA conformance table that matches your product, and export the result to Excel with the change notes included.

chunks.heading: The legal-status trap
chunks.text:
V3.2.1 is cited in the Official Journal only under the Web Accessibility Directive, by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/2048 as amended by Decision (EU) 2021/1339. It has never been cited under the European Accessibility Act.
No edition of EN 301 549 is cited under the European Accessibility Act today. That means conforming to V3.2.1, or to V4.1.1, gives you no presumption of conformity with the Act. It is still the right technical benchmark, and market-surveillance authorities use it, but a statement that your service “complies with the EAA because it conforms to EN 301 549” is not true in law yet.
V4.1.1 is the edition built to be cited under the Act, and when it is, the presumption attaches to the clauses in Tables A.1 to A.5, within the scope of the standard, for as long as the reference stays in the Official Journal list. Until then, cite v3.2.1 for public-sector statements, test against WCAG 2.2 AA, document which edition you tested against, and do not write “presumption of conformity” anywhere.

chunks.heading: Get ahead of the citation
chunks.text:
Audit against WCAG 2.2 AA now, work the v4.1.1 delta in the checklist, and have the conformance documentation ready for the day the Official Journal lists the standard.
Open the v4.1.1 checklistProfessional EN 301 549 auditEAA compliance guide

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Is EN 301 549 V4.1.1 in force?▾
It is published but not yet cited. ETSI, CEN and CENELEC adopted V4.1.1 on 24 August 2026 and published it on 2 September 2026. Legal effect under EU law comes only from citation in the Official Journal of the European Union: until the Commission publishes a decision citing V4.1.1, V3.2.1 remains the edition cited for the Web Accessibility Directive, and no edition of EN 301 549 is cited under the European Accessibility Act at all. The citation is expected between late November and mid-December 2026; ETSI's own date of 30 November 2026 is the deadline for national standards bodies to announce the standard, not an Official Journal date.

Does EN 301 549 V4.1.1 require WCAG 2.2 AA?▾
Yes for web content, and the equivalent for documents and software. Clause 9 requires every WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA success criterion (55 of them) plus the five WCAG 2.2 conformance requirements at Level AA in clause 9.6, and clause 9.5 lists the Level AAA criteria as informative only. Clauses 10 and 11 apply the same criteria to non-web documents and non-web software, adapted where web wording does not fit, following the W3C's WCAG2ICT guidance.

Which WCAG 2.2 criteria did V4.1.1 add, and which did it remove?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
It added 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum). It removed 4.1.1 Parsing, which WCAG 2.2 deleted; clauses 9.4.1.1, 10.4.1.1 and 11.4.1.1 are now void. Every other WCAG 2.1 A and AA criterion carries over unchanged.

What is total conversation and why does the EAA care?▾
Total conversation is real-time voice, real-time text and video in one communication session, each meeting the quality rules of clause 6 and able to interoperate. V4.1.1 clause 6.7 requires it from any ICT that provides real-time voice and includes video, and clause 6.2 requires real-time text from any ICT that provides real-time voice. The European Accessibility Act requires that emergency communications to 112 be answered by the most appropriate public safety answering point using synchronised voice and text, including real-time text, and synchronised video where video is provided; member states must apply that from 28 June 2027 at the latest. Clause 6's emergency scenarios (6.0.6 to 6.0.9) and the reference to ETSI EN 303 919 are how the standard connects to that date.

What is Annex ZB?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Annex ZB is the informative annex that maps the essential requirements of the European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) to the clauses of EN 301 549, in five tables: ZB.1 information on products, ZB.2 user interface and functionality of products plus support services, ZB.3 information about specific products, ZB.4 accessibility of services, and ZB.5 functionality of specific services. It is what makes V4.1.1 a candidate harmonised standard for the Act. Annex ZA does the same job for the Web Accessibility Directive (replacing the old Annex A), and Annex ZC covers the other directives that the Act's Annex I Section VI points at. For assessing one product, use the tables in clause A.2 instead; Annex ZB itself says so.

Do I need to redo an audit done against V3.2.1?▾
Not from scratch. A V3.2.1 audit that tested WCAG 2.1 AA is still valid for every criterion it covered; add the six WCAG 2.2 criteria, the user-preference clauses 9.7, 10.7 and 11.7, and the renumbered chapter 11 references. Products with voice or video communication, self-service terminals and hardware need a fuller re-assessment because clauses 6 and 8.3 were rewritten. The interactive checklist's v4.1.1 edition flags every new or changed row so the delta can be worked through on its own.

What happens on the day V4.1.1 is cited in the Official Journal?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text: Conformance with the clauses in Tables A.1 to A.5 will confer a presumption of conformity with the corresponding essential requirements of the European Accessibility Act, within the scope of the standard, for as long as the reference stays in the published list. If the same decision also cites V4.1.1 for the Web Accessibility Directive, public-sector statements should move to it, usually with a transition period stated in the decision. Until the decision is published, nothing changes legally; this page and the checklist will be updated on that day.

chunks.heading: EN 301 549: The EU's ICT Accessibility Standard, Explained
chunks.text:
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated October 2026

EN 301 549 is the harmonized European standard that defines what “accessible” means for technology in EU law. It sits behind both the Web Accessibility Directive and the European Accessibility Act, incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA for web content, and extends comparable requirements to documents, software, hardware, and support services. If you sell into Europe, this is the standard your conformance claims map to.
Not legal advice. This guide is educational information about EN 301 549 and the EU laws that reference it, not legal advice. Which version of the standard applies, and how, depends on the law, the member state, and your product, so consult a qualified lawyer for compliance decisions.

chunks.heading: What EN 301 549 is
chunks.text:
Formally titled “Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services,” EN 301 549 is a European standard produced jointly by ETSI, CEN, and CENELEC, the three official European standardization organizations, under mandates from the European Commission. It began life as Europe's answer to the US Section 508 standards: a single technical yardstick that public buyers and regulators could reference instead of writing their own accessibility specifications.
Its legal significance comes from harmonization. When the European Commission cites a version of the standard in the Official Journal of the EU as a harmonized standard for a given law, conforming to it creates a presumption of conformity with that law's accessibility requirements. That makes EN 301 549 the safe, well-lit path to compliance with:
the Web Accessibility Directive (Directive (EU) 2016/2102), which covers EU public-sector websites and mobile apps, and
the European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882), which extends accessibility duties to private-sector products and services from June 28, 2025. No edition is cited under the EAA yet; V4.1.1 is expected to be the first, with an Official Journal citation anticipated in December 2026.

chunks.heading: How the standard is structured
chunks.text:
Chapter Topic What it covers
Ch. 4–5 Functional performance & generic requirements Usage without vision, with limited hearing, without speech, with limited manipulation or strength, and more; requirements that apply across all ICT
Ch. 6–7 Two-way voice & video capabilities Real-time text, audio quality, captioning and audio description capabilities for ICT that handles voice or video
Ch. 8 Hardware Physical ICT: self-service terminals, kiosks, devices with operable parts and displays
Ch. 9 Web Websites and web applications: incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria (WCAG 2.2 in v4.1.1)
Ch. 10 Non-web documents PDFs, Office documents, e-books and other non-web documents, via adapted WCAG criteria
Ch. 11 Software Native mobile and desktop apps and other non-web software, via adapted WCAG criteria plus assistive-technology interoperability
Ch. 12–13 Documentation, support & relay services Accessible product documentation, accessible support channels, and relay/emergency service access

Highlighted rows (chapters 9, 10, and 11) are the ones most digital product teams work with day to day.

chunks.heading: The WCAG connection
chunks.text:
For web content, EN 301 549 does not reinvent anything: chapter 9 incorporates the WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria. A website that conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA satisfies the web chapter outright. The standard's real added value is everywhere WCAG stops:
Chapter 10 applies adapted WCAG criteria to non-web documents: PDFs, Office files, e-books.
Chapter 11 applies adapted criteria to native software and mobile apps, and adds requirements such as interoperability with assistive technologies and preservation of platform accessibility features.
Functional performance statements (chapter 4) describe outcomes (usable without vision, without hearing, with limited manipulation) that act as a benchmark where specific technical provisions do not apply.
Chapters 6–8 and 12–13 reach voice and video communication, hardware such as kiosks and terminals, product documentation, and support services.

Since WCAG 2.2 is backwards-compatible with 2.1, auditing against the WCAG 2.2 AA checklist covers the EN 301 549 web baseline while future-proofing your conformance as the standard is revised to track newer WCAG versions.

chunks.heading: Versions of EN 301 549
chunks.text:
Version What changed
v1.1.2 (2015) First edition; aligned with WCAG 2.0 for web content
v2.1.2 (2018) First version harmonized for the Web Accessibility Directive; introduced WCAG 2.1 alignment
v3.1.1 (2019) Restructured and extended requirements across document and software chapters
v3.2.1 (2021) Current baseline cited for the Web Accessibility Directive; WCAG 2.1 A/AA for web, documents, and software
v4.1.1 (September 2026) Published by ETSI on 2 September 2026: aligns web, document, and software chapters with WCAG 2.2, adds Annex ZB mapping requirements to the EAA, and rewrites the real-time text clause. Not yet cited in the Official Journal (expected December 2026)

Version 3.2.1 (March 2021) is the established baseline. Version 4.1.1, produced under the European Commission's standardisation request M/587 and published on 2 September 2026, is the edition aligned to the European Accessibility Act. When citing the standard in contracts or conformance reports, always name the exact version and check the Official Journal for the version currently harmonised for the law you care about.

chunks.heading: EN 301 549 v4: exactly what is changing
chunks.text:
Status as of 14 October 2026: ETSI published EN 301 549 V4.1.1 (2026-09) on 2 September 2026, after the national vote on the V4.1.0 final draft. It has NOT yet been cited in the Official Journal; Ireland's National Disability Authority expects that on 16 December 2026. Until then, v3.2.1 remains the version cited for the Web Accessibility Directive, and no version is cited under the European Accessibility Act, so the EAA's presumption of conformity is not yet available through any edition. Test against WCAG 2.2 AA now, and cite the version you tested against.

These changes come from the standard itself, produced by ETSI under the Commission's standardisation request M/587, not from second-hand summaries. We read them first in the V4.1.0 final draft and re-checked them against the published V4.1.1:
WCAG 2.2 alignment. Clauses 9 (web), 10 (documents), and 11 (software) are updated to align with WCAG 2.2, referenced as the W3C Recommendation of 12 December 2024 and as ISO/IEC 40500:2025. WCAG 2.2 is now also an ISO standard, which matters for procurement language.

chunks.heading: EN 301 549 v4: exactly what is changing
chunks.text:
A dedicated EAA mapping. A new Annex ZB maps the standard's requirements to the European Accessibility Act across five tables covering products and services, and a new clause A.2 lets a specific product or service be evaluated for EAA conformance. Today's v3.2.1 was harmonized for the Web Accessibility Directive; v4 is built to serve the EAA directly.
Real-time text rewritten. Clause 6.2 on real-time text is significantly revised and extended to cover total conversation, which connects to the EAA's June 2027 date for accessible answering of 112 emergency communications.
Web Accessibility Directive mapping refreshed. A new Annex ZA replaces the old Annex A for the 2016/2102 Directive mapping.

That is the summary. The clause-level detail, including the six WCAG 2.2 criteria now required, the user-preferences rework, the total conversation and real-time text rewrite with its link to the EAA's 28 June 2027 date for 112 calls, Annex ZB and the clause A.2 conformance tables, and a migration list for teams on v3.2.1, is in our EN 301 549 V4.1.1 clause-by-clause guide.

chunks.heading: EN 301 549 v4: exactly what is changing
chunks.text: Practical takeaway: if you are remediating now, audit against the WCAG 2.2 AA checklist rather than 2.1. WCAG 2.2 is backwards-compatible with 2.1, so work done against 2.2 satisfies today's v3.2.1 and is already aligned with where v4 lands. To work through the standard itself, clause by clause, use our free interactive EN 301 549 checklist with both editions, 285 requirements in v3.2.1 and 319 in v4.1.1, every new or changed v4 row flagged, product-type and EAA conformance-table scopes, and Excel export.

chunks.heading: Who needs EN 301 549
chunks.text:
EU public-sector bodies: websites and mobile apps must meet the harmonized standard under the Web Accessibility Directive, with a published accessibility statement and a feedback mechanism, monitored by national authorities.
Businesses covered by the EAA: e-commerce, consumer banking, e-books, telecoms, transport services, and manufacturers of covered devices use EN 301 549 conformance as their technical benchmark, which becomes a formal presumption-of-conformity route once V4.1.1 is cited in the Official Journal. See the EAA compliance guide for scope and deadlines.
Vendors selling ICT to European public buyers: public procurement rules require accessible ICT, and buyers request conformance evidence against the standard, typically as an ACR on the VPAT EU edition (the EU counterpart to the US Section 508 VPAT).
Non-EU companies serving EU customers: the laws that reference the standard apply based on where the product or service is offered, not where the company sits.

chunks.heading: Conforming in practice
chunks.text: For a typical website or app, EN 301 549 conformance work is WCAG conformance work with a wider perimeter: audit web content against WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA, apply the adapted criteria to your mobile apps and customer-facing documents, verify assistive technology compatibility, and make sure support channels and documentation are accessible. Then document it (an accessibility statement for regulators and users, an ACR for procurement) and wire accessibility checks into your release process so conformance survives the next sprint. Litigation risk looks different in Europe than the US lawsuit wave (tracked in our lawsuit tracker), but regulator complaints and market-surveillance action follow the same trail of unfixed barriers.

chunks.heading: Map your product against EN 301 549
chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
What is EN 301 549 in plain terms?▾
EN 301 549, 'Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services,' is the European standard that defines what 'accessible' means for technology in EU law. It was developed jointly by the European standards organizations ETSI, CEN, and CENELEC under a mandate from the European Commission. Where US rules point to WCAG for web content, EU laws point to EN 301 549, which itself incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA for web content and extends similar requirements to documents, software, hardware, and support services. Conforming to it gives a legal presumption that you meet the accessibility requirements of the EU laws that reference it.

How does EN 301 549 relate to WCAG 2.1 AA?▾
Chapter 9 of EN 301 549 incorporates the WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria directly for web content: if your site conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA, you satisfy the web chapter. Chapters 10 (non-web documents) and 11 (software, including mobile apps) apply adapted versions of the same criteria to those contexts. So WCAG 2.1 AA is the core of EN 301 549 but not the whole of it: the standard also covers functional performance, hardware, two-way communication, video capabilities, and documentation and support services that WCAG never addressed.

What is the current version of EN 301 549?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Version 3.2.1, published in March 2021, is the established baseline and the version harmonized in the Official Journal of the EU for the Web Accessibility Directive. It aligns web, document, and software requirements with WCAG 2.1. ETSI published V4.1.1 on 2 September 2026: it aligns the standard with WCAG 2.2 and adds a dedicated mapping to the European Accessibility Act. V4.1.1 has not yet been cited in the Official Journal; Ireland's National Disability Authority expects the citation on 16 December 2026. Until then no version of EN 301 549 is cited under the EAA, and v3.2.1 remains the version cited for the Web Accessibility Directive. Conformance claims should always name the version they were tested against.

Who needs to conform to EN 301 549?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Three main groups. First, EU public-sector bodies: the Web Accessibility Directive requires their websites and mobile apps to meet the harmonized standard. Second, businesses covered by the European Accessibility Act (e-commerce, banking, e-books, transport, telecoms, and covered products), since EN 301 549 is the technical benchmark regulators and buyers use, and V4.1.1 is due to become the EAA's harmonised standard once it is cited in the Official Journal. Third, vendors selling ICT to European public-sector buyers, who are routinely asked for EN 301 549 conformance evidence in procurement (the VPAT EU edition exists exactly for this). Non-EU companies serving EU customers in covered sectors are included.

Is EN 301 549 a law?▾
No. It is a technical standard, not legislation. Its legal force comes from the laws that reference it: the Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102) for public-sector websites and apps, and the European Accessibility Act (2019/882) for private-sector products and services. When a version of the standard is cited in the Official Journal of the EU as a harmonized standard, conforming to it creates a presumption of conformity with the corresponding law. You can also comply with those laws by other means, but you then carry the burden of demonstrating the requirements are met without the standard's safe harbor.

What do chapters 9, 10, and 11 cover?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
These are the three chapters most digital teams work with. Chapter 9 (Web) applies WCAG 2.1 A and AA success criteria to web pages. Chapter 10 (Non-web documents) applies adapted WCAG criteria to documents that are not web pages (PDFs, Office files, e-books), whether distributed on the web or elsewhere. Chapter 11 (Software) applies adapted criteria to non-web software, including native mobile and desktop apps, and adds requirements like interoperability with assistive technology and accessible authoring tools. The adaptations mostly replace web-specific wording; the substance of the criteria stays the same.

How do I test and document EN 301 549 conformance?▾
For web content, test against WCAG 2.1 AA (or 2.2 AA for headroom) using a combination of automated scanning, manual expert review, and assistive-technology testing; chapter 9 is satisfied by WCAG conformance. For apps and documents, apply the adapted criteria of chapters 11 and 10 respectively. Document the results in an accessibility statement (mandatory for public-sector bodies under the Web Accessibility Directive, and expected under the EAA's service-information requirements) or, for procurement, in an ACR using the VPAT EU edition, which mirrors the standard's clause structure.

chunks.heading: Web Accessibility Law in India: the RPwD Act and IS 17802
chunks.text:
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated October 2026

India already names a technical standard for digital accessibility. Since May 2023, rule 15 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules has required websites, apps and other ICT to comply with IS 17802, the Indian adoption of EN 301 549 with WCAG 2.1 AA inside. What has been missing is enforcement. The Supreme Court said so in November 2024, and the government's answer, the draft 2026 rules, would add deadlines by turnover, publicly disclosed conformance reports and fines, and would reach any business offering into India, wherever it is based.

chunks.heading: What the Law Says Today: RPwD Act 2016, Sections 40 to 46
chunks.text:
The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (Act 49 of 2016) is India's implementation of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Chapter VIII puts accessibility duties on the state and on establishments, and five sections carry the weight for digital products:
Section 40, Accessibility. The Central Government shall, in consultation with the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, formulate rules laying down standards of accessibility for the physical environment, transportation, information and communications, including appropriate technologies and systems, and other facilities and services provided to the public. The word is “shall”: the standards are a duty, not an option.
Section 42, Access to information and communication technology. The appropriate Government must take measures so that content in audio, print and electronic media is in accessible formats, that electronic media is accessible through audio description, sign language interpretation and closed captioning, and that everyday electronic goods are universally designed.
Sections 44 and 45. New buildings cannot get permission or a completion certificate without meeting the accessibility rules, and existing public buildings had five years from the notification of the rules. These are the physical-world consequences the Court later pointed to as the model for enforcement.

chunks.heading: What the Law Says Today: RPwD Act 2016, Sections 40 to 46
chunks.text:
Section 46, Time limit for accessibility by service providers. Service providers, whether Government or private, shall provide services in accordance with the section 40 rules within two years from the date those rules are notified. The Central Government may extend the period for categories of services.
Section 89, Punishment for contravention. Any contravention of the Act or of a rule made under it is punishable with a fine of up to ten thousand rupees for a first contravention and, for any subsequent contravention, a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees and up to five lakh rupees.

“Establishment” is defined widely in section 2: it includes Government establishments and private establishments, and a private establishment means a company, firm, cooperative or other society, association, trust, agency, institution, organisation, union, factory or any other establishment the appropriate Government notifies. There is no small-business carve-out in the Act.

chunks.heading: What the Law Says Today: RPwD Act 2016, Sections 40 to 46
chunks.text: The section 40 rules are rule 15 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules, 2017 (G.S.R. 591(E), 15 June 2017). As notified, rule 15(1) said every establishment shall comply with the listed standards, and for ICT clause (c) pointed at the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites as the website standard and required documents on websites to be in ePUB or OCR-based PDF. The section 46 two-year window from that notification ran out in June 2019, a point the Supreme Court made in 2024.

chunks.heading: What Changed: the 2023 IS 17802 Mandate and the 2024 Judgment
chunks.text: May 2023: IS 17802 enters rule 15. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Amendment) Rules, 2023 (G.S.R. 359(E), signed 10 May 2023, published 11 May 2023, in force on publication) inserted item (iii) into rule 15(1)(c). Websites, apps, ICT-based public facilities and services, electronic goods and equipment for everyday use, and ICT-based consumer products and accessories “shall comply with” IS 17802 (Part 1): 2021 and IS 17802 (Part 2): 2022, as amended from time to time. From that day India had a named, mandatory ICT standard. What it did not have was a deadline, a reporting duty or an enforcement route for ICT.

chunks.heading: What Changed: the 2023 IS 17802 Mandate and the 2024 Judgment
chunks.text: 8 November 2024: Rajive Raturi v. Union of India. A bench of Chief Justice D. Y. Chandrachud and Justices J. B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra decided a public interest petition filed in 2005 (2024 INSC 858). Relying on a nationwide audit by the court-appointed Centre for Disability Studies at NALSAR University of Law, the Court compared the Act's mandatory scheme in sections 40, 44, 45, 46 and 89 with the content of rule 15. Rule 15(1) uses “shall”, so its clauses are mandatory in form, but most of the documents it points to are ministry guidelines that describe themselves as illustrative, broad or to be achieved over time. The Court held that rule 15 “does not provide for non-negotiable compulsory standards, but only persuasive guidelines”, that a ceiling without a floor is hardly a sturdy structure, and that rule 15(1) is therefore ultra vires the Act (paragraphs 74 and 75).

chunks.heading: What Changed: the 2023 IS 17802 Mandate and the 2024 Judgment
chunks.text:
The directions in paragraphs 76 to 78 shape everything that followed. The Union was directed to delineate mandatory rules under section 40 within three months, by segregating the non-negotiable rules from the expansive guidelines already in rule 15, in consultation with all stakeholders and with NALSAR-CDS involved. Progressive compliance with the existing standards was to continue, but a baseline of non-negotiable rules had to be prescribed. Once those rules exist, the Union, States and Union Territories must implement the consequences in sections 44, 45, 46 and 89, including fines. Among the principles the Court listed for the exercise was mandating the integration of assistive technologies such as screen readers, audio descriptions and accessible digital interfaces across public and private platforms.
The three-month deadline fell in February 2025. The ICT draft arrived twenty months after the judgment, and at a hearing on 29 July 2026 Justices Pardiwala and K. V. Viswanathan asked the Additional Solicitor General to consider the suggestions of experts and litigants before the draft is finalised and published in the Gazette, so that no deficiencies are left behind, and listed the matter for January 2027 with compliance affidavits due. For a broader view of how India sits next to other regimes, see the accessibility laws tracker.

chunks.heading: The Draft 2026 Rules: What They Require and When
chunks.text:
The Draft Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Amendment) Rules, 2026 were signed on 16 July 2026 as notification S.O. 3962(E) by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (Divyangjan) in the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, and issued in the Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II Section 3(ii), on 20 July 2026. Objections and suggestions were invited for thirty days from the date the Gazette was made available to the public. The notification recites the Supreme Court's direction as its reason for being, and its explanatory note describes the aim as “a mandatory accessibility floor” for ICT products and services.
Rather than adding another item, the draft replaces clause (c) of rule 15(1) wholesale with a self-contained code in ten parts: definitions, scope, applicable standards, the Accessibility Conformance Report, non-negotiable standards and timelines, enforcement, quality control orders, grievance redressal, a National Accessibility ICT Committee, and a three-yearly review. The timelines are the part most businesses need first. Every one of them is counted from the date the final rules are published, so none has started.
Compliance timelines in the draft Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Amendment) Rules, 2026, all counted from publication of the final rules
Who Must do what Within

chunks.text: Turnover is read from the immediately preceding financial year and, for applicability, includes the consolidated turnover of the establishment together with any entity that controls it, is controlled by it or is under common control, where those entities make covered items available to persons in India, including through platforms or intermediaries. The only exemption is archived content, clearly identified as such and not intended for active public use or update.

chunks.heading: Schedule I for the web is WCAG 2.1 Level A
chunks.text:
Schedule I lists the non-negotiable clauses of IS 17802 (Part 1) for websites, documents and software. Its web column names thirty clauses of clause 9, and they are exactly the thirty WCAG 2.1 Level A success criteria, from 9.1.1.1 Non-text content to 9.4.1.2 Name, role, value. The document column (clause 10) and the two software columns (clause 11, open and closed functionality) list the same criteria as adapted for non-web content. The Level AA criteria, including contrast, reflow, resize text, focus visible and consistent navigation, arrive with the full-compliance duty at two years. The Schedule also says references follow the latest BIS version of the standard, so a future revision of IS 17802 would flow through automatically.
