chunks.heading: Web Accessibility Glossary
chunks.text: Plain-language definitions of 100+ terms you will meet in accessibility work — standards like WCAG and EN 301 549, technologies like ARIA and screen readers, and legal concepts like the ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act. Jump to a letter below or scroll through the full list.

chunks.heading: Accessibility Overlay
chunks.text: A third-party widget or script that claims to make a website accessible automatically by injecting JavaScript fixes at page load. Overlays cannot repair the underlying code, frequently interfere with screen readers and keyboard navigation, and sites using them are still regularly named in accessibility lawsuits. Read our guide to accessibility overlays before considering one.

chunks.heading: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text: A public page that describes an organization's commitment to accessibility, the standard it targets (usually WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA), any known limitations, and how users can report barriers. Many laws, including the European Accessibility Act and the EU Web Accessibility Directive, require one. You can create one in minutes with our accessibility statement generator.

chunks.heading: Accessibility Tree
chunks.text: A simplified, parallel version of the DOM that the browser builds and exposes to assistive technology. Each node carries an element's name, role, state, and properties — a screen reader reads this tree, not your raw HTML. Semantic markup and correct ARIA usage are what keep the accessibility tree accurate.

chunks.heading: Accessible Name
chunks.text: The text label that assistive technology announces for an element, such as "Search" for a magnifying-glass button. It is computed from sources like element content, the alt attribute, an associated <label>, aria-labelledby, or aria-label, following the accessible name computation algorithm. Every interactive element needs one; see our ARIA reference for how the naming attributes work.

chunks.heading: ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act)
chunks.text: The landmark 1990 US civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against people with disabilities. Courts have widely applied Title III (public accommodations) to websites and apps, making the ADA the legal basis for most US digital accessibility lawsuits. A 2024 Department of Justice rule also requires state and local governments to meet WCAG 2.1 AA under Title II.

chunks.heading: Alt Text (Alternative Text)
chunks.text: A short text description of an image, supplied through the alt attribute, that screen readers announce in place of the image and that displays if the image fails to load. Good alt text conveys the image's purpose in context; purely decorative images should get an empty alt="" so they are skipped. Try our alt text generator to write better descriptions faster.

chunks.heading: APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm)
chunks.text: A modern contrast model, developed as a candidate method for WCAG 3, that scores text contrast on a perceptual lightness scale (Lc) instead of WCAG 2's simple luminance ratio. APCA accounts for font size, weight, and polarity (light-on-dark vs dark-on-light), so it better matches how people actually perceive readability. It is not yet a normative requirement — WCAG 2 ratios still govern conformance, which you can test with our contrast checker.

chunks.heading: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)
chunks.text: A W3C specification (formally WAI-ARIA) of roles, states, and properties that supplement HTML so custom widgets and dynamic content make sense to assistive technology. ARIA only changes what screen readers perceive — it adds no keyboard behavior — so the first rule of ARIA is to prefer native HTML elements when they exist. Explore every role and attribute in our interactive ARIA reference.

chunks.heading: Assistive Technology (AT)
chunks.text: Any hardware or software that people with disabilities use to operate computers and browse the web. Examples include screen readers, screen magnifiers, refreshable braille displays, switch devices, eye trackers, and voice control software. Accessible websites work because they expose structure and semantics that assistive technology can interpret.

chunks.heading: ATAG (Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines)
chunks.text: W3C guidelines for the tools people use to create web content — CMSs, page builders, WYSIWYG editors, and code editors. ATAG 2.0 has two parts: the authoring tool's own interface must be accessible, and the tool should help authors produce accessible content, for example by prompting for alt text.

chunks.heading: Audio Description
chunks.text: Additional narration added to video that describes important visual information — actions, on-screen text, scene changes — for people who are blind or have low vision. WCAG Success Criterion 1.2.5 (Level AA) requires audio description for prerecorded video content. Descriptions are usually timed to fit natural pauses in dialogue.

chunks.heading: Accessible Description
chunks.text: The supplementary text assistive technology can read after an element's name, computed from aria-describedby, aria-description or the title attribute. A password field named "Password" with a description of "At least twelve characters" announces both. It is optional where the accessible name is not.

chunks.heading: Accessible Name Computation (accname)
chunks.text: The W3C algorithm that decides what text names an element, in a fixed order: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native sources such as a label element, alt text or the control's own text, then title. Browsers, screen readers, testing libraries and AI agents all rely on it. Try it with the accessible name previewer.

chunks.heading: Agentic Browser (Browser-Use Agent)
chunks.text: An AI system that operates a website on a person's behalf by reading the page's accessibility tree and issuing clicks and keystrokes. Anthropic's browser-use tool, OpenAI's computer-using agent and Google's Mariner all work this way, so a control without an accessible name is as invisible to them as it is to a screen reader.

chunks.heading: Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR)
chunks.text: The completed document produced from a VPAT template, stating criterion by criterion whether a product supports, partially supports or does not support each requirement of WCAG, Section 508 or EN 301 549. Buyers ask for it in procurement; it is a claim, not a certification. See the VPAT guide.

chunks.heading: Automated Accessibility Testing
chunks.text: Software that inspects markup or a rendered page for machine-detectable failures such as missing alt text, empty links, unlabelled fields and low contrast. Tools such as axe, WAVE, Lighthouse and IBM Equal Access find a minority of WCAG issues and cannot judge whether a name is meaningful or a task is completable. See automated vs manual testing.

chunks.heading: Auxiliary Aids and Services
chunks.text: The ADA's term for the means of making communication accessible: interpreters, captioning, braille, and, in the Justice Department's view, accessible electronic technology. A public accommodation must provide them unless doing so would be an undue burden or fundamentally alter the service.

chunks.heading: Braille Display
chunks.text: A hardware device with a row of refreshable cells that raise and lower pins to show, in braille, the text a screen reader is reading. Used by deafblind people and by many blind professionals for reading precision. It can only render what the page exposes as text.

chunks.heading: Captions (Open vs Closed)
chunks.text: Text versions of the spoken audio and important sounds in video, displayed in sync with playback, primarily for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. Closed captions can be turned on and off by the viewer, while open captions are permanently burned into the video image. WCAG Success Criterion 1.2.2 (Level A) requires captions for prerecorded video with audio.

chunks.heading: Cognitive Accessibility
chunks.text: Designing content so it works for people with cognitive and learning disabilities, including memory, attention, reading, and executive-function differences. Practical techniques include plain language, consistent navigation, generous time limits, clear error messages, and avoiding unnecessary complexity. The W3C's COGA task force publishes detailed guidance in "Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities."

chunks.heading: Color Contrast Ratio
chunks.text: A measure of the luminance difference between foreground text and its background, expressed on a scale from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white). WCAG 2 Level AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; user interface components and graphics need 3:1. Measure any color pair instantly with our color contrast checker.

chunks.heading: Conformance Level (A / AA / AAA)
chunks.text: WCAG's three tiers of conformance. Level A covers the most basic barriers, Level AA is the standard referenced by virtually every law and contract worldwide, and Level AAA is the strictest tier, which even the W3C says may not be achievable for all content. Conformance is cumulative — meeting AA means meeting every A and AA success criterion. See how the levels fit together in our WCAG hub.

chunks.heading: CAPTCHA
chunks.text: A challenge intended to tell people from bots. Visual CAPTCHAs are unsolvable for blind users, and audio alternatives are often unusable; screen reader users rank CAPTCHA as the single most problematic item on the web in WebAIM's surveys. WCAG 1.1.1 requires alternatives in more than one modality.

chunks.heading: Colour Vision Deficiency
chunks.text: Reduced ability to distinguish certain colours, affecting about 8% of men and 0.5% of women, most commonly red and green. WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color requires that colour is never the only means of conveying information, which is why error states need an icon or text as well as a red outline.

chunks.heading: Certiorari
chunks.text: The Supreme Court's discretionary decision to review a lower court's ruling. A denial of certiorari, as in Domino's Pizza v. Robles in October 2019, means the Court declined to hear the case; it decides nothing and creates no precedent, despite being widely reported as a ruling.

chunks.heading: Decorative Image
chunks.text: An image that adds nothing a user needs, such as a divider or a stock photo beside text that already says everything. It should carry an empty alt attribute (alt="") so screen readers skip it. An image that carries information is an informative image and needs real alt text under WCAG 1.1.1.

chunks.heading: Disclosure Widget
chunks.text: A button that shows or hides a section of content, such as an FAQ answer or an accordion panel. The button must expose aria-expanded so the state is announced, and must control the content programmatically via aria-controls. See the accordion guide.

chunks.heading: Dynamic Content
chunks.text: Page content that changes after load without a full page refresh, such as search results, notifications or a loading spinner. Screen readers only learn of changes that are exposed through focus management or live regions; otherwise the change is silent. See notifications and focus management.

chunks.heading: EAA (European Accessibility Act)
chunks.text: An EU directive (2019/882) that requires a wide range of private-sector products and services — e-commerce, banking, e-books, transport, telecoms, and more — to be accessible. Its obligations have applied to new products and services since June 28, 2025. For websites and apps, conformance is demonstrated against EN 301 549, which incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA.

chunks.heading: EN 301 549
chunks.text: The European standard for accessibility of information and communication technology, covering websites, apps, documents, hardware, and support services. Its web requirements incorporate WCAG 2.1 Level AA. It is the harmonized standard used to show compliance with both the EU Web Accessibility Directive and the European Accessibility Act.

chunks.heading: Effective Communication
chunks.text: The ADA regulation (28 CFR 36.303) requiring public accommodations to provide auxiliary aids and services so that communication with disabled people is as effective as with others. It was central to the dissent in Gil v. Winn-Dixie, which argued a website is a means of communication and so is covered.

chunks.heading: Error Identification
chunks.text: WCAG 3.3.1: when an input error is detected automatically, the field in error must be identified and the error described in text. A red border alone fails; "Email address: enter an address in the form name@example.com" passes. Related to form validation.

chunks.heading: Focus Indicator
chunks.text: The visible outline, ring, or highlight that shows which element currently has keyboard focus. WCAG Success Criterion 2.4.7 requires a visible focus indicator, and WCAG 2.2 adds minimum size and contrast expectations in 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured) and the AAA-level 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance). Never remove the outline without providing a clearly visible replacement — see our keyboard accessibility guide for patterns.

chunks.heading: Focus Order
chunks.text: The sequence in which interactive elements receive keyboard focus as a user presses Tab. WCAG Success Criterion 2.4.3 requires that this order preserve meaning and operability — focus should move in a way that matches the logical reading order, which usually means keeping DOM order aligned with visual order.

chunks.heading: Focus Trap (Keyboard Trap)
chunks.text: A situation where keyboard focus enters a component and cannot leave using the keyboard alone, which violates WCAG Success Criterion 2.1.2. The one intentional exception is a modal dialog, which deliberately contains focus while open but must always be dismissible with Escape and return focus to the triggering element on close.

chunks.heading: Focus Visible
chunks.text: WCAG 2.4.7: the element that has keyboard focus must have a visible indicator. Removing the browser's outline without replacing it is one of the most common keyboard barriers, and GDS lists lack of visible focus among the top issues found in UK public sector monitoring. WCAG 2.2 adds 2.4.11 on the indicator's minimum size and contrast.

chunks.heading: Form Label
chunks.text: The visible text programmatically associated with a form field, normally a label element linked by for and id. It gives the field its accessible name, gives sighted users a larger click target, and is required by WCAG 3.3.2 and 1.3.1. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears on input and is not reliably announced.

chunks.heading: Heading Structure
chunks.text: The hierarchical outline created by h1–h6 elements. Screen reader users routinely navigate by jumping between headings, so a page should have one h1, use lower levels to nest subtopics, and avoid skipping levels (such as jumping from h2 to h4). Headings must be real heading elements, not just bold text.

chunks.heading: High Contrast Mode (Forced Colors)
chunks.text: An operating-system feature — most notably Windows Contrast Themes — that replaces a site's colors with a limited, user-chosen palette to improve readability. Browsers expose it to CSS through the forced-colors media query and system color keywords. Designs should not rely on background images or subtle color differences alone, because forced-colors mode strips many of them away.

chunks.heading: Hidden Content
chunks.text: Content removed from the accessibility tree with aria-hidden="true", display: none or the hidden attribute, or hidden visually only, as with a visually-hidden or sr-only class that keeps it for screen readers. Hiding a focusable element from assistive technology while leaving it in the tab order is a common failure.

chunks.heading: Inclusive Design
chunks.text: A design methodology that considers the full range of human diversity — ability, language, culture, age, and circumstance — from the start of a project rather than retrofitting fixes later. It overlaps with accessibility but is broader: solving for permanent disabilities (one arm) also helps temporary (arm injury) and situational (holding a baby) limitations.

chunks.heading: Image Map
chunks.text: An image with clickable regions defined by area elements. Each area needs its own alt text or it is an unnamed link. The 2006 Target case pleaded inaccessible image maps; the site's home page at filing had 85 areas, none with alt text.

chunks.heading: Keyboard Accessibility
chunks.text: The principle that every piece of functionality must be operable with a keyboard alone, without requiring a mouse or specific timing (WCAG Success Criterion 2.1.1). It is foundational because screen readers, switch devices, and many other assistive technologies all drive the page through keyboard-style input. Our complete keyboard accessibility guide covers testing and common fixes.

chunks.heading: Keyboard Trap
chunks.text: A state in which keyboard focus enters a component and cannot leave it with the keyboard, failing WCAG 2.1.2. Distinct from a deliberate focus trap inside an open modal, which must release focus when the modal closes.

chunks.heading: Landmark Regions
chunks.text: Major page areas — banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo, search — that assistive technology users can jump between directly. HTML5 elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, and <footer> create landmarks automatically. Every page should have exactly one main landmark, and repeated landmarks (like multiple navs) should be given distinguishing labels; see the landmark roles in our ARIA reference.

chunks.heading: Live Region
chunks.text: A page area marked with aria-live (or a role like status or alert) whose content changes are announced automatically by screen readers, even when focus is elsewhere. Use aria-live="polite" for non-urgent updates such as search-result counts, and assertive (or role="alert") only for critical messages, because assertive announcements interrupt whatever the user is doing.

chunks.heading: Label in Name
chunks.text: WCAG 2.5.3: where a control has a visible text label, its accessible name must contain that text. A button that shows "Search" but has aria-label="Submit query" fails, because a voice control user who says "click Search" gets nothing.

chunks.heading: Language of Page
chunks.text: WCAG 3.1.1: the default human language of a page must be programmatically determined, normally with the lang attribute on the html element. Without it screen readers may pronounce the page with the wrong voice and rules. Pages with no lang attribute are still common, including on large retail sites.

chunks.heading: Link Purpose
chunks.text: WCAG 2.4.4: the purpose of each link must be determinable from its text alone or with its surrounding context. "Read more" repeated five times is the classic failure; screen reader users often navigate by pulling up a list of links out of context.

chunks.heading: Motion Actuation
chunks.text: WCAG 2.5.4: functions triggered by moving or tilting the device, such as shake to undo, must also be available through the interface and must be switchable off, because tremor and mounted devices trigger them accidentally.

chunks.heading: Name, Role, Value
chunks.text: The requirement (WCAG Success Criterion 4.1.2) that every user interface component exposes its accessible name, its role (button, checkbox, tab), and its current states and values to assistive technology. Native HTML elements do this for free; custom widgets built from divs must supply all three through ARIA and keep them updated as state changes.

chunks.heading: Nexus Test
chunks.text: The rule, first applied to websites in NFB v. Target in 2006, that Title III of the ADA reaches a website only where its inaccessibility impedes the goods and services of a physical place of public accommodation. Applied by the Ninth Circuit in Robles v. Domino's. See the case law reference.

chunks.heading: Non-text Content
chunks.text: WCAG 1.1.1: all images, icons, charts and other non-text content must have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except decorative content, which is marked so that it is ignored. Missing alternative text was found on 53.1% of the top million home pages in 2026.

chunks.heading: Orientation
chunks.text: WCAG 1.3.4: content must not be locked to portrait or landscape unless the orientation is essential, because people with mounted devices, such as wheelchair users, cannot rotate them.

chunks.heading: PDF/UA
chunks.text: The ISO 14289 standard for universally accessible PDF documents. A conforming PDF is fully tagged with a logical structure tree, includes alternative text for images, marks the document language, and sets a correct reading order so screen readers can navigate it like a web page. Check your documents with our PDF accessibility checker.

chunks.heading: POUR
chunks.text: The four principles that organize all of WCAG: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust. Content must be perceivable through more than one sense, operable by keyboard and other inputs, understandable in language and behavior, and robust enough to work with current and future assistive technologies. Every WCAG success criterion lives under one of these four principles.

chunks.heading: prefers-reduced-motion
chunks.text: A CSS media query that detects when a user has asked their operating system to minimize animation, often because motion triggers vestibular disorders, migraines, or nausea. Sites should use it to disable or tone down parallax effects, auto-playing animation, and large transitions. It complements WCAG 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions).

chunks.heading: Programmatically Determined
chunks.text: A phrase used throughout WCAG meaning that information can be reliably extracted by software — including assistive technology — from the markup itself, rather than existing only visually. A label is programmatically determined when it is linked with a <label> element or ARIA attribute; a heading is programmatically determined when it uses an actual heading tag rather than large bold text.

chunks.heading: Pause, Stop, Hide
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2.2: any moving, blinking or auto-updating content that starts automatically and lasts more than five seconds must have a control to pause, stop or hide it. Carousels and tickers are the usual failures. See the carousel patterns.

chunks.heading: Place of Public Accommodation
chunks.text: The ADA's term for private businesses open to the public, listed in twelve categories in 42 U.S.C. 12181(7), all of them physical. Whether a website is one, or is a service of one, is the question every US website case turns on. The case law reference tracks each circuit's answer.

chunks.heading: Pointer Gestures
chunks.text: WCAG 2.5.1: functions that use multipoint or path-based gestures, such as pinch to zoom or swipe to delete, must also work with a single pointer without a path, because switch, head-pointer and tremor users cannot perform them.

chunks.heading: Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations (PSBAR)
chunks.text: The UK regulations (2018) implementing the EU Web Accessibility Directive, requiring public sector websites and apps to meet the accessibility requirement (in practice WCAG 2.2 AA) and publish a compliant accessibility statement. Monitored by GDS, which found only 39 of 593 statements fully compliant in its first round. See the statement checker.

chunks.heading: Parsing (WCAG 4.1.1)
chunks.text: A WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 criterion about valid markup, removed in WCAG 2.2 because modern browsers repair broken HTML consistently. Duplicate ids and unclosed elements are still worth fixing because they break label associations and aria references.

chunks.heading: Query Fan-out
chunks.text: The way AI answer engines decompose a question into many sub-queries, retrieving a passage for each before synthesising an answer. It is why a page is cited for a single self-contained passage that answers a sub-question, and why every figure on the statistics page is written to stand alone.

chunks.heading: Reading Level
chunks.text: WCAG 3.1.5 (AAA): where text requires more than lower secondary education reading ability, a simpler version or summary should be available. Plain language benefits people with cognitive disabilities, the largest disability group in US data at 13.9% of adults. See the cognitive accessibility guide.

chunks.heading: Redundant Entry
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2's 3.3.7: information a user has already entered in the same process must be auto-populated or selectable, not typed again, unless re-entry is essential such as confirming a password.

chunks.heading: Remediation
chunks.text: The work of fixing accessibility failures in code, content or design after they are found. Distinct from an audit, which finds them, and from an overlay, which claims to mask them. The only remediation estimate ever given in evidence at a web accessibility trial was $37,000 or less, in Gil v. Winn-Dixie.

chunks.heading: Screen Magnifier
chunks.text: Software that enlarges a portion of the screen, used by people with low vision. Examples include ZoomText, Windows Magnifier, and macOS Zoom. Because magnifier users see only a small slice of the page at a time, placing error messages or updates far from the user's point of focus can make them easy to miss entirely.

chunks.heading: Screen Reader
chunks.text: Software that converts on-screen content into synthesized speech or braille output, used primarily by people who are blind or have low vision. Major screen readers include JAWS and NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on Apple platforms, and TalkBack on Android. They navigate via the accessibility tree, so semantics matter more than visuals — learn how to test in our screen reader testing guide.

chunks.heading: Section 508
chunks.text: A US federal law (part of the Rehabilitation Act) requiring federal agencies to make their electronic and information technology accessible, which in practice extends to vendors selling to the government. The 2017 "refresh" of the Section 508 standards incorporates WCAG 2.0 Level AA as the technical benchmark for web content.

chunks.heading: Semantic HTML
chunks.text: Using HTML elements for their intended meaning — <button> for buttons, <nav> for navigation, <table> for tabular data — instead of generic <div> and <span> containers styled to look the part. Semantic elements come with built-in roles, keyboard behavior, and accessibility tree entries for free. Our accessible component patterns show semantic-first implementations of common UI.

chunks.heading: Skip Link
chunks.text: A link, usually the first focusable element on a page, that lets keyboard users jump straight to the main content instead of tabbing through the entire header and navigation on every page. It is typically visually hidden until it receives focus. Skip links are the classic technique for WCAG Success Criterion 2.4.1 (Bypass Blocks).

chunks.heading: Success Criterion
chunks.text: A single testable requirement in WCAG, identified by number and name — for example, 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum). Each success criterion is assigned a conformance level (A, AA, or AAA) and is written so that testers can objectively determine pass or fail. WCAG 2.2 contains 86 success criteria in total; browse them all in our WCAG reference.

chunks.heading: Switch Access
chunks.text: An input method for people with significant motor disabilities that uses one or more physical switches — pressed by hand, head, foot, or breath — instead of a keyboard or mouse. Software scans through interface options and the user activates a switch to select. Switch access depends entirely on content being keyboard-operable, since switches map to keyboard-style focus and activation.

chunks.heading: Sensory Characteristics
chunks.text: WCAG 1.3.3: instructions must not rely solely on shape, colour, size, position or sound. "Click the round button on the right" fails for a screen reader user; "click Submit" passes.

chunks.heading: Serial Plaintiff
chunks.text: A plaintiff who files many similar accessibility lawsuits. Courts have sanctioned abusive schemes, and disability organisations including the NFB have criticised high-volume filing, while noting that the barriers pleaded are usually real. 46% of 2025 federal website cases named a defendant that had been sued before.

chunks.heading: Statutory Damages
chunks.text: A fixed sum a statute awards per violation without proof of loss. Title III of the ADA has none; California's Unruh Act awards a minimum of $4,000 per violation, which is why the money in Domino's and Target came from California law.

chunks.heading: Status Message
chunks.text: WCAG 4.1.3: a message that reports a result or progress without taking focus, such as "3 items in your basket" or "Search returned 12 results", must be exposed to assistive technology, normally with a live region, so screen reader users hear it without moving.

chunks.heading: Structured Negotiation
chunks.text: A method of resolving accessibility claims through a collaborative process with a written agreement instead of a lawsuit, associated with the lawyer Lainey Feingold. Safeway's 2013 commitment to WCAG 2.0 AA for its grocery site came from a structured negotiation with nine blind customers.

chunks.heading: Tab Order
chunks.text: The order in which focus moves through interactive elements when the user presses the Tab key. By default it follows DOM source order, which is why placing elements visually with CSS while leaving the DOM in a different order creates confusing navigation. Tab order should always match the expected visual and logical reading order.

chunks.heading: tabindex
chunks.text: An HTML attribute that controls whether and how an element participates in keyboard focus. tabindex="0" adds an element to the natural tab order, tabindex="-1" makes it focusable only via script (useful for moving focus to headings or dialogs), and positive values like tabindex="5" override natural order and are strongly discouraged because they create unpredictable jumps.

chunks.heading: Text Spacing
chunks.text: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.12 requires that content lose nothing when users override typography to at least: line height 1.5× the font size, paragraph spacing 2×, letter spacing 0.12×, and word spacing 0.16×. People with dyslexia and low vision often apply these overrides, so layouts must not clip or overlap text when spacing grows.

chunks.heading: Touch Target
chunks.text: The tappable area of an interactive control on a touch screen. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires targets to be at least 24×24 CSS pixels or have equivalent spacing, while the AAA-level 2.5.5 recommends 44×44. Small, tightly packed targets are a major barrier for people with tremors or limited dexterity — our WCAG 2.2 checklist covers the new criteria.

chunks.heading: Transcript
chunks.text: A full text version of the spoken and important non-speech audio in a recording. Transcripts are the only way audio-only content (like podcasts) reaches deaf users, they help deafblind users via braille, and they make media searchable and skimmable for everyone. WCAG 1.2.1 requires a text alternative for prerecorded audio-only content.

chunks.heading: Target Size
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2's 2.5.8 (AA): pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels or have that much spacing, with exceptions for inline links and essential cases. The AAA criterion 2.5.5 asks for 44 by 44. Small tap targets are among the mobile issues most often found. See 2.5.8.

chunks.heading: Timing Adjustable
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2.1: where content has a time limit, users must be able to turn it off, adjust it or extend it, with limited exceptions. Session timeouts on checkout and banking flows are the common case; a warning with a way to extend passes.

chunks.heading: Title Attribute
chunks.text: An HTML attribute that shows a tooltip on hover. It is the last resort in the accessible name computation, is not shown to keyboard or touch users, and is unreliable in screen readers, so it should never be the only label for a control. It is required on iframes, where it names the frame.

chunks.heading: Unruh Act
chunks.text: California's civil rights act, which prohibits discrimination by businesses and treats any ADA violation as an Unruh violation. Because it allows statutory damages of at least $4,000 per violation plus attorney's fees, it is a primary reason such a large share of US web accessibility lawsuits are filed in California courts.

chunks.heading: User Agent
chunks.text: Any software that retrieves and presents web content on behalf of a user — browsers, media players, and even assistive technologies acting alongside them. The W3C's User Agent Accessibility Guidelines (UAAG) cover this layer, complementing WCAG (content) and ATAG (authoring tools).

chunks.heading: Undue Burden
chunks.text: The ADA defence that providing an auxiliary aid would involve significant difficulty or expense, judged against the resources of the whole organisation. It must be pleaded and proved. Neither Domino's nor Winn-Dixie argued it in court; Winn-Dixie's own witness testified the work was feasible.

chunks.heading: Voice Control
chunks.text: Assistive technology that lets people operate a device by speaking commands, such as Dragon NaturallySpeaking, Apple Voice Control, or Android Voice Access. Users typically say the visible label of a control ("click Submit"), which is why WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name) requires an element's accessible name to contain its visible text.

chunks.heading: VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template)
chunks.text: A standardized template, published by the Information Technology Industry Council, that vendors fill out to report how well their product meets accessibility standards. The completed document is called an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR). Editions exist for WCAG, US Section 508, EU EN 301 549, and a combined international version, and procurement teams routinely request one before purchase.

chunks.heading: Vacated Opinion
chunks.text: A court decision that the court has withdrawn, so it has no precedential effect. The Eleventh Circuit's 2021 opinion that websites are not public accommodations was vacated as moot in December 2021 and binds nobody, though it is still widely cited as law. See Gil v. Winn-Dixie.

chunks.heading: WAI (Web Accessibility Initiative)
chunks.text: The group within the W3C that develops web accessibility standards and resources. WAI produces WCAG for content, ATAG for authoring tools, UAAG for browsers, and the WAI-ARIA specification for rich applications, along with widely used educational material and the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide.

chunks.heading: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines)
chunks.text: The international standard for accessible web content, published by the W3C. WCAG 2.2 (2023) is the current version, organized under the four POUR principles into testable success criteria at levels A, AA, and AAA; WCAG 2.1 AA remains the benchmark cited by most laws. Browse every criterion in our WCAG reference or work through the WCAG 2.2 checklist.

chunks.heading: Web Accessibility Audit
chunks.text: A systematic evaluation of a website or app against an accessibility standard, usually WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA. A thorough audit combines automated scanning (which finds roughly a third of issues) with manual keyboard testing and screen reader testing, and produces a prioritized report of failures with remediation guidance.

chunks.heading: WCAG-EM
chunks.text: The W3C's Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology, which sets out how to scope, sample and report an audit of a website against WCAG. Version 2.0, published in 2026, extends it beyond websites. Used to decide how many pages an audit should cover.

chunks.heading: WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)
chunks.text: The W3C's collection of design patterns showing how to build common widgets such as tabs, menus, comboboxes and dialogs with the correct roles, states and keyboard behaviour. The source most of this site's component guides are built from.

chunks.heading: Web Accessibility Directive (EU)
chunks.text: Directive (EU) 2016/2102, requiring public sector websites and apps across the EU to meet EN 301 549 and publish accessibility statements, with national monitoring. The UK's PSBAR implemented it; the European Accessibility Act extends similar duties to private sector products and services.

chunks.heading: Zoom and Reflow
chunks.text: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.10 requires that content reflow — rewrap into a single column without two-dimensional scrolling — when zoomed to 400% on a 1280px-wide screen (equivalent to a 320px viewport). Responsive design generally achieves this, but fixed-width layouts, data tables, and text in images commonly break it, forcing low-vision users to scroll horizontally for every line.

chunks.heading: Put the vocabulary to work
chunks.text: Now that you know the terms, dig into the details: browse every success criterion in the WCAG reference, learn accessible component patterns in Learn, or test your site with our free accessibility tools.

This guide sets out the price figures that are actually published, with sources, and the structural factors that make one audit cost five times another.

Updated August 2026

chunks.heading: The Honest Answer: What Audits Actually Cost
chunks.text:
There is no standard price for a web accessibility audit, and any page that gives you a single confident number without a source is guessing. What we can do is tell you what is actually published, who published it, and what our own audits cost.
Published US figures. US vendors such as AudioEye and DigitalA11Y publish ranges of roughly $1,500 to $5,500 for small business sites, per-page rates around $100 to $250, and $50,000 or more for large enterprise engagements. These are US market figures from vendor-published content, not quotes, and your site may sit anywhere on or off those ranges depending on scope.
The one published UK data point we know of. Independent UK consultant Jim Byrne publishes audit prices from 2,500 GBP. Beyond that, published UK and Irish pricing is genuinely scarce: most agencies and consultancies quote on request only, which makes it hard for buyers to compare offers or even sanity-check a quote. We would rather say that plainly than invent a UK market rate that does not exist in print.
Our pricing. We publish ours: fixed-price WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility audits from $950, including manual testing, assistive technology checks, a full report, and verification retests, with each tier and what it covers listed on the service page.

chunks.heading: The Honest Answer: What Audits Actually Cost
chunks.text:
Published audit prices, checked 3 September 2026. Only providers that print a price are listed; a blank in this market is the norm, not the exception.
Provider What is priced Published price Standard Source date
Accessible.org (US) Fully manual audit, per page or screen $100 to $250 per page; $25 to $100 for light pages; typical project $1,250 to $2,750 WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA 25 July 2026

The spread between those numbers is not vendors being greedy or cheap. It reflects genuinely different products sold under the same word, which is why the next section matters more than any headline figure.

chunks.heading: What Drives the Price
chunks.text:
Audit effort, and therefore cost, scales on a handful of structural factors. When you request quotes, these are the variables each vendor is silently estimating:
Unique templates and page types, not raw page count. A 10,000-page site built from 12 templates is a smaller job than a 40-page site where every page is bespoke. Auditors test representative instances of each template, so template count is the real unit of work.
User flows. Checkout, signup, login, account management, and search each need end-to-end testing with keyboard and screen reader, because a flow can fail even when every individual page in it passes.
Depth of testing. An automated scan, a manual audit with screen reader testing, and a full assistive-technology matrix across multiple screen readers, browsers, and magnification tools are three different price brackets.
Platforms. Web only is the baseline. Adding iOS and Android apps or a library of PDFs adds testers, tooling, and time.
Deliverables. A raw defect list is cheaper than a full report with remediation guidance, which is cheaper than also producing a VPAT or Accessibility Conformance Report for procurement.
Retesting rounds. Verifying fixes is real work. Check whether a retest is included or billed separately; a quote without one is not comparable to a quote with one.

chunks.heading: What Drives the Price
chunks.text:
Day rates. Much of the market prices audits as consultancy days, so the same scope costs different amounts at different firms simply because their day rates differ.

This is also why per-page pricing can mislead: two vendors quoting the same per-page rate can produce wildly different totals depending on how they count pages, templates, and flow states.

chunks.heading: Automated vs Manual: Why the Cheap Number Is Not the Same Product
chunks.text:
The cheapest audits on the market are automated scans dressed up as audits. Automated testing is cheap or free for a reason: it can only detect a subset of WCAG failures, the ones a machine can judge without context. It can tell you an image has no alt attribute; it cannot tell you the alt text that is there is wrong. It can find a form field with no label; it cannot tell you the checkout is impossible to complete with a keyboard.
Manual testing, with a human working through your site using a keyboard and screen reader, is where both the cost and the value of a professional audit live. That is the part you are actually paying for, and the part a scan-only product quietly omits while using the same word.
The smart move is to use both, in order. Run our free URL accessibility auditor and contrast checker to establish a baseline before paying anyone. Fix what they find, then spend your audit budget on the manual testing that machines cannot do.

chunks.heading: What a Proper Audit Should Include
chunks.text:
Whatever you pay, the deliverable should contain the same core elements. Use this as a checklist when comparing quotes:
A written scope: which templates, pages, and user flows were tested, on which browsers and assistive technologies.
Testing against WCAG 2.2 Level AA, the current version of the standard, with each finding mapped to a specific success criterion.
Manual and assistive technology testing, including screen reader and keyboard-only passes, not just scanner output.
A usable report: severity ratings, evidence, and plain-language remediation guidance a developer can act on without an accessibility background.
A verification retest after fixes, so you end with evidence that issues were resolved rather than a list of things that were once wrong.

Never buy a report sight unseen. We publish a sample audit report so you can see exactly what the deliverable looks like; ask any vendor you are considering for the same.

chunks.heading: How to Keep the Cost Down Without Buying Junk
chunks.text:
Arrive with a template inventory. List your unique page types and key user flows before requesting quotes. Vendors who do not have to guess at scope quote tighter, and you can compare offers on an identical scope.
Clear the free findings first. Run automated tools yourself and fix what they surface. Paying a consultant day rate to be told about missing alt attributes is the most expensive possible way to learn something a free scan reports in seconds.
Scope by flow, not by everything. If budget is tight, audit the flows where users and legal risk concentrate first (home, search, product, checkout, signup) and phase the rest.
Do not spend the budget on an overlay instead. Overlay widgets do not make a site conform to WCAG and do not remove the need for an audit; our overlay guide explains why. Money spent there is money you will spend again on real remediation.
Buy the retest. Skipping verification to save money means you cannot prove anything was fixed, which undermines the point of paying for the audit at all.

chunks.heading: UK and Ireland Specifics
chunks.text:
For UK and Irish organisations, the question behind the price question is legal exposure, and the drivers on this side of the Atlantic are different from the US lawsuit machine:
The Equality Act 2010 (UK). Service providers owe an anticipatory duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, meaning you are expected to have addressed barriers before a disabled customer encounters them, not after a complaint. Our UK compliance guide covers how this applies to websites.
The European Accessibility Act. In force since June 2025 for in-scope products and services, with enforcement that in Ireland includes criminal penalties. Our EAA Ireland guide explains who is in scope and what is required.

Weigh the audit price against the cost of not knowing where you stand. For the US picture, where an inaccessible site can turn directly into legal spend, see our ADA website lawsuit cost guide. And an audit is not only risk avoidance: accessible sites reach more customers, and our accessibility ROI calculator lets you put your own numbers on that.
One practical note on the quote-on-request culture: because so few UK and Irish firms publish prices, the burden of making quotes comparable falls on you. Send every vendor the same written scope, insist on an itemised quote against it, and ask for a sample report. That is the closest thing this market offers to price transparency.

chunks.heading: How much does a WCAG audit cost for a small business website?
chunks.text: There is no single market rate, and most UK and Irish agencies do not publish prices at all. US vendors such as AudioEye and DigitalA11Y publish ranges of roughly $1,500 to $5,500 for small business sites, with per-page rates around $100 to $250. In the UK, independent consultant Jim Byrne publishes audit prices from 2,500 GBP. Our own fixed-price WCAG 2.2 AA audits start at $950, including manual testing, assistive technology checks, a full report, and a verification retest. Whatever you pay, get the scope itemised in writing so you can compare quotes like with like.

chunks.heading: Why do audit prices vary so much?
chunks.text: Because an audit is not one product. The main cost drivers are structural: how many unique templates and page types your site has (not the raw page count), how many user flows need testing (checkout, signup, account management), the depth of testing (automated scan versus manual and screen reader testing versus a full assistive technology matrix), the platforms covered (web only, or also iOS and Android apps and PDFs), the deliverables (a defect list, a full report with remediation guidance, or VPAT and ACR production), the number of retest rounds, and the day rates of the consultants doing the work. Two quotes that differ by thousands are usually describing two different products.

chunks.heading: Is a free automated scan enough?
chunks.text: No. Automated scanners are genuinely useful and worth running first, but they detect only a subset of WCAG failures. They cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful, whether a keyboard user can complete your checkout, or whether a screen reader announces form errors sensibly. Those judgments require a human tester working with assistive technology, and that manual work is where both the cost and the value of a professional audit live. Use free tools to establish a baseline and clear the obvious defects, then pay for manual testing on what remains.

chunks.heading: How long does an accessibility audit take?
chunks.text: It depends on scope, and be wary of anyone quoting a fixed duration before seeing your site. As a general shape: a small site with a handful of templates is typically a matter of days of testing and reporting, while a large engagement covering many flows, native apps, and documents runs to weeks. The same structural factors that drive cost (template count, flow count, testing depth, and platforms) drive duration in the same way.

chunks.heading: What should an accessibility audit report include?
chunks.text: A written scope stating which pages, templates, flows, browsers, and assistive technologies were tested; findings mapped to specific WCAG 2.2 success criteria; severity ratings; evidence such as screenshots or code references; plain-language remediation guidance your developers can act on; and a defined retest to verify fixes. If a quote does not specify the deliverable, ask to see a sample report before you sign. A cheap audit that produces an unusable spreadsheet of scanner output is not a bargain.

chunks.heading: Do UK companies legally need an accessibility audit?
chunks.text: No law mandates an audit as such. What the law requires is accessibility: the Equality Act 2010 places an anticipatory duty on UK service providers to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, and the European Accessibility Act imposes accessibility requirements on in-scope products and services in the EU, with criminal penalties available in Ireland. An audit is not the legal obligation; it is how you find out where you stand against the obligation, and the evidence base for fixing what it finds.

chunks.heading: Is a VPAT or ACR included in an audit?
chunks.text: Usually not by default. A VPAT (the template used to produce an Accessibility Conformance Report, or ACR) is a distinct deliverable that documents your conformance position for procurement teams. Most vendors price it as an add-on to an audit, because it requires the audit evidence plus additional authoring work. If you sell to government, education, or enterprise buyers who ask for an ACR, tell prospective auditors up front so the quote includes it.

chunks.heading: Educational Content, Not a Quote
chunks.text: This page is provided for general educational purposes. Third-party price figures are drawn from the named sources' published content and are indicative only; they are not offers, and actual pricing for any engagement, including ours, depends on scope. Nothing here is legal advice. For obligations under the Equality Act, the European Accessibility Act, or other laws, consult a qualified professional.

chunks.heading: The W3C Accessibility Maturity Model: Dimensions, Levels and Assessment
chunks.text:
WCAG tells you whether a page is accessible. A maturity model asks a harder question: can your organisation keep producing accessible pages, documents, products and services, year after year, without relying on a few determined people? The W3C Accessibility Maturity Model is the free, open framework for that question. This guide explains its status, its seven dimensions and four levels in plain terms, how to run an assessment that rests on evidence rather than opinion, how it relates to other models, the European Accessibility Act, procurement rules and ISO/IEC 30071-1, and how to turn the result into a roadmap.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated October 2026·W3C Accessibility Maturity Model (Group Note)

Free tool: Accessibility Maturity Assessment
Rate all 135 proof points across the seven dimensions as Inactive, Launch, Integrate or Optimize, with notes on your evidence. You get a level for each dimension, a chart, next steps for the weakest areas, and Excel and PDF exports. Your answers stay in your browser.

Start the maturity assessment

chunks.heading: What an Accessibility Maturity Model Is
chunks.text:
A maturity model describes the stages an organisation moves through as a capability becomes part of how it works, and the evidence that shows each stage. For accessibility, the capability is producing accessible products, content and services as a matter of routine. The W3C Note draws the line clearly: conformance testing tells you how accessible one product is at one moment, while maturity modelling looks at whether the organisation can deliver accessible work over the long term.

How a conformance audit and a maturity assessment differ
Aspect Conformance audit Maturity assessment
Question Does this product meet WCAG or EN 301 549 today? Can the organisation keep producing accessible products?
What is examined Pages, screens, documents, components Policies, processes, people, budgets, contracts, support
Evidence Test results against success criteria Proof points: documents, records, results and working processes
Output A list of failures, a conformance report or an ACR A level for each dimension and a corrective action plan
Shelf life Until the next release Until the organisation changes, so reassess regularly

chunks.heading: Who it is for
chunks.text:
The Note is written for executives, for the managers who are responsible for accessibility, and for the people who own policy and business processes. It is meant to work for any kind of organisation, public or private, from a one-person consultancy or a small charity to a government department or a multinational, and it covers internal activity such as HR as well as public-facing products and services.
Its appendix of sample use cases shows the situations it is built for: a software company answering a tender that asks it to prove it can keep its ACRs accurate and current, a government agency putting that question into its own tender, an employer facing complaints about disability inclusion in its hiring, a consultancy showing its own maturity, an organisation looking at a supplier of content or of tools and code libraries, and a multinational assessing a single business unit.

chunks.heading: Status: A W3C Group Note, Not a Standard
chunks.text:
The Accessibility Maturity Model was published as a W3C Group Note on 4 November 2025 by the Accessible Platform Architectures (APA) Working Group, which developed it through a dedicated task force. That status matters, and it is often misreported:
It is not a W3C Recommendation. WCAG is a W3C Recommendation, the end point of the W3C’s standards track. A Group Note is endorsed by the working group that wrote it, not by W3C and its Members as a whole.
There is nothing to conform to. No organisation can be “certified” against it, and any level you report is your own judgement unless someone independent has checked the evidence.
It does not replace WCAG, EN 301 549 or the law. It describes the organisation that produces accessible work; those standards and laws describe the work itself.
You may adapt it. The Note allows organisations to omit, rename or reword proof points, provided the dimensions, levels and progression stay the same and the changes are recorded.

The Note links to an assessment spreadsheet with one sheet per dimension, which its editors describe as an experimental prototype, with a more robust tool planned. Feedback goes to the W3C through issues on its GitHub repository. Our accessibility maturity assessment is an independent tool built on the 4 November 2025 version, with every proof point paraphrased in our own words.

chunks.heading: The Seven Dimensions
chunks.text: The model divides an organisation into seven dimensions, the areas where better maturity leads to better conformance with accessibility standards and regulations. Each dimension has proof points: concrete deliverables, such as a policy, a template, a training record or a signed contract, that show which level it has reached. Each dimension also has its own goals and metrics, and almost every one includes a proof point for training that keeps the relevant skills current. The descriptions and examples below are our own summaries of the Note.

chunks.heading: Communications
chunks.text:
Section 3.1 of the Note
Everything the organisation tells people, inside and outside, formal or informal, whether staff or contractors produce it. The question is whether all of it can be used by as many people as possible and meets accessibility standards.
Example proof points
Accessible templates for documents, slides, marketing material and Accessibility Conformance Reports (ACRs)
Captions, transcripts and audio description for video and audio where needed
Accessible meeting, webinar and chat tools
An accessibility statement where one is needed, and a way to send accessibility questions or complaints

Usually owned by: Communications, marketing, legal and document owners

chunks.heading: ICT Development Lifecycle
chunks.text:
Section 3.2 of the Note
Whether accessibility is part of every stage of a digital product's life: research, design, development, testing, conformance reporting, maintenance and retirement.
Example proof points
Disabled people take part in user research, with the adjustments they need
Design reviews, accessible design system components and annotated handoffs to developers
An accessibility category in the bug tracker and a defined way to triage defects
Automated tests plus documented manual checks with assistive technology, and releases that cannot ship without passing them

Usually owned by: Product, design, engineering and quality assurance

chunks.heading: Knowledge and Skills
chunks.text:
Section 3.3 of the Note
Whether people at every level know enough about accessibility for their role and see how their work supports the organisation's goals. Skills that belong to a particular dimension are assessed in that dimension.
Example proof points
Skills surveys that find the gaps
Role-based training plans, tracked in the learning system
Accessibility training for every new starter
Accessibility responsibilities in job descriptions, and specialists placed around the organisation to coach colleagues

Usually owned by: Learning and development, HR and the accessibility lead

chunks.heading: Oversight and Culture
chunks.text:
Section 3.4 of the Note
Whether leadership, values, policy and governance make disability inclusion part of how the organisation runs, rather than a side project.
Example proof points
A named executive sponsor and a public commitment from executives
A financial plan for raising maturity, with money formally committed
Accessibility written into strategy, values, the code of conduct and staff objectives
A written exception process for any inaccessible asset, needing a reason, a time limit and executive approval

Usually owned by: The executive team, governance and finance

chunks.heading: Personnel
chunks.text:
Section 3.5 of the Note
Whether qualified disabled people work at every level and in every part of the organisation, so that lived experience informs its decisions.
Example proof points
Goals and initiatives for recruiting disabled employees
Hiring tools, job boards, the careers site and the application process audited for accessibility
A disabled staff network with an executive sponsor that helps shape accessibility work
Disabled employees in product focus groups, and a mentoring programme

Usually owned by: HR, talent acquisition and inclusion teams

chunks.heading: Procurement
chunks.text:
Section 3.6 of the Note
Whether accessibility is part of how the organisation finds, chooses and contracts for products and services. Most technology arrives this way, so this is where accessibility is often won or lost.
Example proof points
A published procurement policy for digital accessibility
Standard accessibility wording in tenders, bid templates and contracts
A written method for evaluating and scoring bids for accessibility
Vendors supply testing evidence, warranties and remediation plans, and complaints involving a vendor have a defined route

Usually owned by: Procurement, legal and vendor management

chunks.heading: Support
chunks.text:
Section 3.7 of the Note
Whether disabled employees and customers get the help they need with the organisation's digital products, from workplace adjustments to customer support.
Example proof points
Accessibility help topics, and support and IT staff trained in assistive technology and disability etiquette
A written policy for how employees request and receive adjustments to digital tools
Accessible support channels in plain language
Accessibility feedback that is collected, triaged and used to improve products

Usually owned by: Customer support, the IT helpdesk and HR

chunks.heading: The Four Maturity Levels
chunks.text:
Every dimension is judged on the same four levels. The middle column is our summary of what each level means across the model; the right-hand column shows how it plays out in one dimension, Procurement.
The four levels of the W3C Accessibility Maturity Model, what each means, and an example from the Procurement dimension
Level What it means In Procurement, for example
Inactive Little or no awareness that accessibility is needed, and almost nothing being done. Tenders and contracts do not mention accessibility, apart from the odd one-off.
Launch The need is recognised and planning has started, but the work is not yet organised. Work has begun on adding accessibility to tenders, and some procurement training is planned.
Integrate A roadmap exists and the approach is defined and organised. Contract wording is complete and reviewed, vendors must supply accessibility documentation, accessibility is monitored through the contract, and training has started.
Optimize Accessibility is part of how the whole organisation works, is checked consistently, and the results drive action. The processes and wording are used across all purchasing and refined over time, and training is required and measured.

chunks.heading: The rules that sit behind the levels
chunks.text:
The levels are cumulative. A dimension can only reach a level by meeting the ones below it first.
Optimize means complete. Proof points can be partly done at Launch and Integrate, but must be fully in place for Optimize.
Not applicable is allowed. If something does not apply, such as a policy clause about native apps for an organisation that has none, mark it N/A rather than forcing a rating.
Each dimension has its own level. An organisation can be at Integrate in Communications and Inactive in Personnel. The Note defines no overall score and no way of combining the seven.
The names are borrowed. The four level names come from the Policy Driven Adoption for Accessibility (PDAA) model of NASCIO, the US National Association of State Chief Information Officers, which some US state and local agencies already use.

chunks.heading: How to Run an Accessibility Maturity Assessment
chunks.text: The Note’s own advice comes down to a short sequence: form a cross-functional team, gather current evidence, validate the findings with experts and disabled people, write a corrective action plan, and reassess regularly. Here is how to put that into practice.

chunks.heading: 1. Decide the scope
chunks.text: The model covers the whole organisation, but you can apply it to one business unit, region or product line. If you do, the Note asks you to say so plainly in any report you give to a third party, such as a customer answering a tender. A first assessment of one unit is often a sensible pilot.

chunks.heading: 2. Assemble the team
chunks.text: No single person sees procurement, engineering, HR and customer support at once, so the Note recommends a cross-functional review team. Its appendix maps roles to dimensions: some, such as a chief accessibility officer, employees with disabilities and an accessibility consultant, contribute to all seven, while others touch only a few. It also suggests naming a lead for each dimension who has taken at least basic accessibility training. In practice that means one coordinator, seven dimension owners, and disabled colleagues involved from the start rather than consulted at the end.

chunks.heading: 3. Gather evidence, not intentions
chunks.text:
The Note is explicit that evidence should describe what exists now, not what is planned. Useful evidence includes policies, procedures and templates; training plans and completion records; goals and metrics; ACRs; contract clauses and signed contracts; test and audit results; and feedback and tracking systems. Keep a simple log for each proof point so the next assessment can see exactly what you saw:

Dimension: Procurement
Proof point: Contracts for custom development include accessibility checkpoints
Rating: Launch
Evidence: 2 of the 9 development contracts signed this year include
a WCAG 2.2 AA clause (links to both contracts)
Gap: No clause in the standard contract template; no acceptance testing
Owner: Head of Procurement
Next step: Add the clause and an acceptance test to the template by March
Checked on: 2026-10-28

chunks.heading: 4. Rate the proof points, then the dimension
chunks.text: For each dimension the Note describes three steps: pick the proof points that apply, list the documentation that supports them, and decide which level that evidence supports. Because it defines no formula, the judgement is yours. Our assessment tool adds a transparent rule to help: a dimension sits at the level that at least half of its rated proof points have reached, it reaches Optimize only when every rated proof point is at Optimize, and a summary that rests on fewer than half of a dimension’s proof points is marked provisional.

chunks.heading: 5. Validate the findings
chunks.text: Before anything goes in a report, check the ratings with accessibility specialists and with disabled people, as the Note advises. Self-assessment tends to be generous: a policy can exist without being followed, and a training course can be available without anyone taking it.

chunks.heading: 6. Record any customisation
chunks.text: If a proof point does not fit your sector, you may drop, rename or reword it, but keep the seven dimensions, the four levels and the way they build on each other, and write down every change so a third party can map your results back to the Note.

chunks.heading: 7. Reassess on a cycle
chunks.text:
The Note asks for regular reassessment to track progress and spot regressions, without fixing an interval. Once a year, timed to your planning and budget cycle, works for most organisations, plus a check after any major change such as a reorganisation, a new platform or a new legal duty. Keep every assessment so you can compare them.

Free tool: Accessibility Maturity Assessment
Work through the seven dimensions one at a time, record the evidence for each rating in the notes, and export to Excel or PDF to share with dimension owners and compare next year.

Start the maturity assessment

chunks.heading: Turning Results into a Roadmap
chunks.text:
The Note asks for a corrective action plan with goals, milestones, owners and timelines, managed inside the systems you already use. A few principles make that plan realistic:
Aim for the next level, not Optimize. Moving one dimension up a single level is a solid goal for a year; trying to reach the top everywhere at once is how roadmaps stall.
Start with the dimensions that unlock the rest. An executive sponsor, a policy and a budget (Oversight and Culture) make every other dimension easier. Procurement clauses stop new barriers arriving while you fix old ones.
Tie every action to a proof point. If an action does not change a proof point, the next assessment will not see it.
Put it where work is planned. Backlog items, objectives and budget lines get done; a separate spreadsheet does not.

Here is an illustrative first-year roadmap for an organisation whose assessment found most dimensions at Inactive or Launch:

An illustrative first-year accessibility maturity roadmap by quarter, with dimension, target level, actions and the evidence each produces
Quarter Dimension and target Actions Evidence at the end
Q1 Oversight and Culture: Inactive to Launch Name an executive sponsor, approve an accessibility policy, agree a budget line Signed policy, board minutes, budget entry

chunks.heading: Turning Results into a Roadmap
chunks.text:
Q1 Procurement: Inactive to Launch Add a standard accessibility clause to the tender template; ask vendors of new software for an ACR Updated template, first tenders using it
Q2 ICT Development Lifecycle: Launch to Integrate Automated checks in the build pipeline, an accessibility bug label with triage rules, a manual screen reader test script for releases Pipeline configuration, triage document, test records
Q3 Knowledge and Skills: Launch to Integrate Role-based training plans for designers, developers and content authors; track completion Curricula, learning system records
Q4 Communications and Support: Launch to Integrate Accessible document and slide templates, an accessibility statement with a contact route, a process for triaging feedback Templates, statement URL, feedback log
Q4 All seven Reassess, compare with the baseline, plan year two Second assessment export

Useful building blocks for those actions: the guide to writing an accessibility statement and the statement generator, the VPAT and ACR guide for procurement, the website audit guide and automated versus manual testing for the lifecycle, and the accessibility ROI calculator for the budget conversation.

chunks.heading: How It Compares with Other Maturity Models
chunks.text:
The W3C model is not the only one, and its own appendix lists several others. They differ more in who publishes them and how you use them than in what they look at.
Accessibility maturity models and related standards, who publishes them, their structure, and how they are used
Model Published by Structure How it is used
W3C Accessibility Maturity Model W3C APA Working Group, Group Note, 2025 Seven dimensions, four levels, proof points Free and open; self-assessment or independent review
Digital Accessibility Maturity Model (DAMM) Level Access, an accessibility software and services company Seven dimensions, five levels: Initial, Repeatable, Defined, Managed, Optimizing A free short Quick Check, plus a programme-building tool and expert-led assessments as services
Accessibility Maturity Model (BDF) Business Disability Forum, a UK membership organisation, through its Technology Taskforce Self-assessment linked to BDF’s Accessible Technology Charter, covering areas such as IT governance and procurement Offered through BDF; check the current version and access terms with BDF
Policy-Driven Adoption for Accessibility (PDAA) NASCIO A high-level, policy-led assessment; the source of the W3C level names Used by some US state and local agencies; can be tuned for procurement

chunks.heading: How It Compares with Other Maturity Models
chunks.text:
Accessibility Capability Maturity Model (CCC ACMM) California Community Colleges Five stages across governance, content creation, procurement and staff development Built for decentralised higher education institutions
ISO/IEC 30071-1:2019 ISO and IEC, international standard A code of practice for accessible ICT, not a maturity scale A paid standard describing the processes to follow

Sources: the W3C Note’s appendix of related models; Level Access’s DAMM overview and DAMM maturity levels; the ILO Global Business and Disability Network’s listing of the BDF Accessibility Maturity Model.
The models overlap heavily: governance, communications, the development lifecycle, procurement, skills and support appear in almost all of them. The practical differences are openness, cost and comparability. The W3C model is free, can be adapted with a record of changes, and gives a shared vocabulary that a customer, a supplier and an auditor can all read. If you already use another model, there is no need to switch; you can map your results onto the W3C dimensions when a partner asks for them.

chunks.heading: The European Accessibility Act
chunks.text:
The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882), which has applied since 28 June 2025, sets accessibility requirements for the products and services in its scope. It never mentions maturity models and does not require one. But several of its duties are about process, and those are exactly what the maturity model measures:
Article 13(3): service providers must have procedures that keep their services conformant, taking account of changes to the service, to the requirements and to the standards. Article 7(4) asks the same of manufacturers for series production. That is the ICT Development Lifecycle dimension: release gates, regression testing and checks on changes between releases.
Article 13(2) and Annex V: service providers must publish, in accessible formats, information explaining how their services meet the requirements, and keep it for as long as the service runs. That sits in Communications and Support.
Article 13(4): when a service does not conform, the provider must correct it and inform the national authorities. Defect triage and feedback handling are proof points in the lifecycle and Support dimensions.

chunks.heading: The European Accessibility Act
chunks.text:
Article 14: businesses relying on the disproportionate burden exception must document their assessment (microenterprises dealing in products are excused from the paperwork), and service providers must renew it when the service changes, when an authority asks, and in any case at least every five years. That needs the governance and record-keeping of Oversight and Culture.

A maturity assessment is not evidence that anything conforms. Conformance is about the products and services themselves, tested against the Act’s requirements and the standards that support them, such as EN 301 549. Use the EAA readiness checklist for the obligations themselves and the maturity model for the organisation that has to keep meeting them.

chunks.heading: Public procurement
chunks.text:
In the EU, Article 42(1) of the public procurement Directive 2014/24/EU says that technical specifications for anything people will use must, except in justified cases, take accessibility into account, and must refer to any mandatory accessibility requirements set by EU law. Article 24(1) of the EAA makes its Annex I requirements those mandatory requirements for the products and services it covers. In the United States, Section 508 requires federal agencies to make the technology they develop, buy, maintain or use accessible, and suppliers usually answer with an Accessibility Conformance Report, often built on the VPAT template.
The maturity model helps on both sides of a tender. For buyers, the Procurement dimension is a checklist for their own process: policy, standard clauses, evaluation and scoring, contract remedies and monitoring. For suppliers, an ACR describes a product on the day it was tested, and two of the Note’s sample use cases revolve around tenders that ask suppliers to show they can keep their ACRs accurate and current. Evidence from the ICT Development Lifecycle, Knowledge and Skills and Personnel dimensions is a credible answer.

chunks.heading: ISO/IEC 30071-1
chunks.text:
ISO/IEC 30071-1:2019, a code of practice for creating accessible ICT products and services, grew out of the UK standard BS 8878. It is about process rather than technical criteria: it asks organisations to adopt an accessibility policy, consider accessibility at every stage of a system’s life, document and justify their decisions, and publish an accessibility statement when a system launches, and it applies to any organisation and to technologies from websites and apps to connected devices. The W3C Note lists it among related models.
The two fit together well. ISO/IEC 30071-1 describes the processes to follow; the maturity model measures how far those processes have taken root. An organisational accessibility policy shows up in Oversight and Culture, lifecycle decisions and their justification in the ICT Development Lifecycle, procurement in Procurement, and the accessibility statement in Communications and Support.

chunks.heading: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
chunks.text:
Common accessibility maturity assessment pitfalls, why they hurt, and what to do instead
Pitfall Why it hurts Do this instead
Treating the result as a compliance certificate. The Note separates maturity from conformance. A mature programme can still ship an inaccessible page. Pair the assessment with audits and testing, and report both.
Rating plans as if they were practice. Aspirational evidence inflates the levels and hides the gaps you most need to see. Rate only what exists today, and record the evidence for each rating.
One person fills it in alone. Nobody sees procurement, HR, engineering and support at once, so whole dimensions get guessed. Use a cross-functional team with an owner for each dimension.
Averaging everything into one score. The Note defines no overall score, and an average hides the dimension that is holding you back. Report a level per dimension, with the spread of ratings behind it.
Aiming for Optimize everywhere at once. A roadmap that tries to jump several levels in every dimension stalls in the first quarter. Move each dimension up one level, in an order that follows dependencies.
Leaving disabled people out. Personnel is a whole dimension, and the Note asks for findings to be validated with disabled people. Involve disabled employees and users in rating, validation and planning.

chunks.heading: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
chunks.text:
Skipping procurement. If you keep buying inaccessible tools, new barriers arrive faster than you remove the old ones. Add standard clauses and a scoring method early; they are cheap and fast.
Editing the model quietly. Partners, customers and auditors cannot compare or map results they do not know were changed. Record every omission and rewording, and state the scope in any report you share.
Assessing once and filing it. Maturity slips when people, priorities and platforms change. Reassess on a set cycle and keep each export for comparison.

chunks.heading: Accessibility Maturity Assessment Checklist
chunks.text:
Scope agreed. Whole organisation or a named unit, written down, and stated in anything you share outside.
Team assembled. A cross-functional group with an owner for each of the seven dimensions, including disabled colleagues.
Evidence gathered. Current documents, records and results for each proof point, not plans or intentions.
Every proof point rated. Inactive, Launch, Integrate or Optimize, with Not applicable where it genuinely does not apply.
A level per dimension. Judged from the evidence, with no overall average; Optimize only where every proof point is complete.
Findings validated. Checked with accessibility specialists and with disabled employees or users.
Customisations recorded. Any omitted, renamed or reworded proof points listed, with the dimensions and levels unchanged.
Corrective action plan written. Goals, milestones, owners and dates, each tied to a proof point, inside your normal planning tools.
Conformance tested separately. Products and content still audited against WCAG 2.2 and, where it applies, EN 301 549.
Next assessment booked. A date in the planning cycle, and this assessment exported so the next one can be compared.

chunks.text:
