chunks.heading: Accessible Video & Media Players
chunks.text:
A single video can fail three different groups at once — deaf viewers who cannot hear it, blind viewers who cannot see it, and keyboard users who cannot operate the player. Accessible media is a stack of parallel alternatives delivered through a second channel: captions, a transcript, audio description, and a player everyone can drive. This guide covers which ones your media owes, how to build each one properly, the HTML <video> and <track> elements, embedded YouTube and Vimeo players, and React — mapped to WCAG 2.2.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated August 2026

chunks.heading: Why Media Is Where So Many Sites Fail
chunks.text:
Text has one channel and it is easy to make accessible. Media has two channels running at once — a picture and a sound — and each one excludes a different group when it is the only way to get the information. The audio is unavailable to a deaf viewer. The picture is unavailable to a blind viewer. The controls are unavailable to anyone who cannot use a mouse. A video is, in effect, three accessibility problems wearing one costume, which is exactly why media is one of the most consistently failed areas of WCAG.
The way to keep it straight is to stop thinking about “the video” and start thinking about the information inside it, and the channels it travels through. Every piece of meaning in a video arrives as either sound or picture. Accessibility is the practice of making sure each of those pieces also arrives through a second channel for whoever cannot use the first: the audio becomes text (captions and transcripts), the essential picture becomes audio (audio description), and everything becomes text for people who use neither (a descriptive transcript).

chunks.heading: Why Media Is Where So Many Sites Fail
chunks.text: This guide is framework-agnostic and works whether you drop in a native <video>, embed a YouTube player, or ship a React component. The requirements cluster around WCAG's 1.2 Time-based Media guideline, plus 1.4.2 Audio Control, 2.1.1 Keyboard, and 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide for the player. We will start where you should always start: deciding what this particular piece of media actually owes.

chunks.heading: The WCAG 2.2 Criteria Your Media Must Satisfy
chunks.text:
WCAG 2.2 success criteria that accessible video and audio media must satisfy and what each requires
Criterion Level What your media must do
1.2.1 Audio-only & Video-only A Provide a text transcript for prerecorded audio-only content, and an audio track or transcript for prerecorded video-only content.
1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) A Synchronized captions for all prerecorded audio in video — dialogue, speaker identification, and meaningful non-speech sounds.
1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative A Either audio description of the essential visuals, or a full text alternative that conveys the whole video.
1.2.4 Captions (Live) AA Real-time captions for live audio in synchronized media — live webinars, streams, and broadcasts.
1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) AA Audio description for prerecorded video; at AA the text-alternative escape allowed by 1.2.3 no longer applies.
1.4.2 Audio Control A Any audio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds can be paused or stopped, or has a volume control independent of the system.
2.1.1 Keyboard A Every player control — play, pause, seek, volume, captions, fullscreen — is fully operable by keyboard.
2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide A Auto-playing video that lasts more than 5 seconds — including a muted, looping background video — can be paused, stopped, or hidden.

chunks.heading: The WCAG 2.2 Criteria Your Media Must Satisfy
chunks.text:
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value A Custom player controls expose a name, a role, and their current state (playing or paused, muted, captions on or off) to assistive technology.

The AAA tier goes further. Beyond AA, WCAG adds 1.2.6 Sign Language (a sign-language interpretation track), 1.2.7 Extended Audio Description (pausing the video to fit description when the gaps are too short), 1.2.8 Media Alternative (a full text alternative for all prerecorded media), and 1.2.9 Audio-only (Live). Most teams target AA, but a descriptive transcript — covered below — quietly gets you most of 1.2.8 for free.

Two criteria are failed far more than the rest. Captions (1.2.2) are the most often attempted but wrong — an auto-generated track left uncorrected — and audio description (1.2.5) is the most often skipped entirely, because teams do not realise their video carries information only the eyes can reach. This guide spends most of its length on those two.

chunks.heading: 1. Decide What This Media Owes
chunks.text: Before you write a caption or record a description, work out which alternatives this specific piece of media actually needs. The obligations are not one-size-fits-all — they fall out of two questions, and answering them turns a vague “make the video accessible” into a concrete checklist.

chunks.heading: Question 1: Prerecorded or live?
chunks.text: Prerecorded media can be captioned, transcribed, and described in advance — so it owes the most. Live media can only realistically be captioned in real time (1.2.4); live audio description is not required at any level because it is so hard to produce on the fly.

chunks.heading: Question 2: Where is the information?
chunks.text:
Information in the audio needs a text equivalent (captions, transcript). Information in the picture that is not spoken needs an audio equivalent (audio description). Most videos carry some of both — so most videos owe both.

Run those two questions against what kind of media you have, and the requirements are mechanical:
Which accessibility alternatives each type of media owes at WCAG level A and AA
Media type Example What it owes (A / AA)
Audio-only (prerecorded) Podcast, audio interview A full text transcript (1.2.1). No captions and no description apply.
Video-only (prerecorded) Silent animation, screen recording with no narration A transcript or an audio track describing it (1.2.1).
Synchronized media (prerecorded) A normal video with sound Captions (1.2.2) + audio description (1.2.3 at A, 1.2.5 at AA). A transcript is strongly recommended.
Live synchronized media Live webinar, streamed talk Real-time captions (1.2.4 at AA). Live audio description is not required.

chunks.heading: Question 2: Where is the information?
chunks.text: The audio-description escape hatch — use it honestly. If a video carries no essential information visually that is not already in the soundtrack — a talking head who says everything they show — then no audio description is needed, and you have satisfied 1.2.3 and 1.2.5 with nothing to add. The test is: close your eyes and listen. If you can still follow everything that matters, you are done. Do not gold-plate a description onto a video that does not need one — but be ruthlessly honest about “essential.” On-screen text, charts, and silent demonstrations almost always count.

chunks.heading: 2. Captions: More Than the Words
chunks.text: Captions are the synchronized text of everything the soundtrack carries, shown in time with the video for someone who cannot hear it. The single most important thing to understand about captions is what separates them from subtitles.

chunks.heading: Subtitles
chunks.text: Assume you can hear, and translate the dialogue into another language. Speech only. A same-language subtitle file is not captions and does not satisfy 1.2.2.

chunks.heading: Captions
chunks.text:
Assume you cannot hear, and carry everything the audio does: dialogue, who is speaking, and meaningful non-speech sounds — [phone rings], [ominous music]. This is what WCAG requires.

Good captions are verbatim, synchronized to the audio, identify the speaker when it is not obvious on screen, and describe the sounds that carry meaning — a knock at the door the characters react to, the sarcasm in a tone, the music that sets the mood. They are also paced to be readable: broken into short lines that stay on screen long enough to read.

chunks.heading: Closed vs open captions
chunks.text: Closed captions are a separate track the viewer can turn on and off — the modern default, delivered as a WebVTT file via the <track> element or through a hosting platform. Open captions are burned permanently into the video pixels; they always show and cannot be styled or turned off, but they survive any player that lacks caption support. Prefer closed captions for the control they give the viewer; reach for open captions only when you cannot rely on the player to render a track.

chunks.heading: The caption file: WebVTT
chunks.text:
Closed captions are usually a WebVTT (.vtt) file — a plain-text list of time-stamped cues. It is readable and hand-editable, which is exactly how you fix an auto-generated draft.
WEBVTT

00:00:01.000 --> 00:00:04.000
[upbeat music]

00:00:04.500 --> 00:00:08.000
<v Dana>Welcome back. Today we're fixing
the checkout flow.</v>

00:00:08.500 --> 00:00:11.000
[keyboard clicking]

00:00:11.500 --> 00:00:14.000
<v Dana>Notice the error appears here —
right under the field.</v>
The <v Speaker> voice tag identifies who is talking; square-bracket cues carry the non-speech sounds. This is the difference between a caption track and a subtitle track written out in a file.
Auto-captions are a draft, not compliance. Automatic speech recognition mishears names and technical terms, drops punctuation that changes meaning, never adds speaker labels or sound descriptions, and often drifts out of sync. WCAG 1.2.2 asks for captions that are accurate and complete. Use the machine track to save typing, then review every line, add the speaker IDs and the sounds, fix the timing, and upload the corrected file. Live captions (1.2.4) usually need a human real-time captioner (CART) for the same reason.

chunks.heading: 3. Transcripts: The Underrated Hero
chunks.text:
Captions get the attention, but the transcript is the alternative that serves the most people for the least effort — and for audio-only content it is the requirement, not an extra. A transcript is a single block of text on the page containing everything the media conveys, readable without pressing play.
Look at who a transcript reaches that a caption track does not:
Deafblind users who cannot see captions or hear audio, and read the transcript through a Braille display — the only channel that reaches them.
People who cannot play media — on a locked-down work network, a slow connection, or a quiet room where sound is not an option.
Skimmers and searchers who want to scan for one fact, quote a line, or Ctrl+F the content rather than scrub through a timeline.
Search engines, which cannot watch a video but happily index a transcript — so the accessible choice is also the discoverable one.

chunks.heading: 3. Transcripts: The Underrated Hero
chunks.text:
The descriptive transcript is the one artifact that covers everything. A plain transcript captures the words; a descriptive transcript also writes out the essential visual information — the on-screen chart, the demonstration, the reaction. That single document serves as the transcript (1.2.1), as the full text alternative that satisfies audio description at level A (1.2.3), and as the media alternative at AAA (1.2.8). For a short explainer video, writing one good descriptive transcript is often less work than producing a separate audio description track.

Put the transcript on the page — visible, or one click away in a <details> disclosure right beside the player — not buried in a downloadable PDF or hosted off-site. It should carry speaker labels and, for a descriptive transcript, the visual notes clearly marked. The disclosure pattern is the same one the accordion & disclosure guide covers if you want it collapsible.

chunks.heading: 4. Audio Description: The Picture as Sound
chunks.text:
Audio description is the mirror image of captions. Where captions turn the sound into text for people who cannot hear, audio description turns the essential picture into sound for people who cannot see. It is a narration, slotted into the natural pauses between dialogue, that describes the visual information the soundtrack leaves out — a graph that appears, a facial reaction, a caption on screen that no one reads aloud, a click that is shown but not narrated.
The trigger for needing it is the test from §1, restated: is there information in the picture that is not in the audio? A cooking video where the host narrates every step needs little or none; the same video where they silently add an unnamed ingredient needs a description of what went in. On-screen text, data, and demonstrations are the usual culprits.

chunks.heading: 1.2.3 at level A gives you a choice; 1.2.5 at AA takes it away
chunks.text: This is the part teams miss. 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (level A) lets you satisfy the requirement either by adding audio description or by providing a full text alternative — a descriptive transcript — for the whole video. But 1.2.5 Audio Description (level AA) removes the text-alternative escape: at AA, actual audio description is required. So if your target is AA — as most legal frameworks and procurement requirements demand — a descriptive transcript alone is not enough for a video with essential visuals; you owe a real described version.

chunks.heading: Standard vs extended description
chunks.text: Standard audio description fits inside the existing gaps between dialogue. Sometimes the gaps are too short to describe everything that matters — a fast, visually dense sequence. That is what 1.2.7 Extended Audio Description (AAA) addresses: the video pauses to let a longer description play, then resumes. You rarely need extended description if you plan the content to leave room for it — which is the real lesson.

chunks.heading: How to deliver it in practice
chunks.text:
Script it into the production. The cheapest, most robust option: write the narration so the presenter says what they show (“I'm clicking the blue Save button in the top right”). Now the main soundtrack is the description and no extra track is needed.
Offer a described version. Produce a second copy of the video with description mixed into the audio, and let the user choose it — a separate source, a toggle, or a second player.
Add a descriptions track — with eyes open. A <track kind="descriptions"> WebVTT file is the standards-based route, but support for browsers and screen readers actually speaking it is still unreliable, and browsers will not pause the video for an over-long cue. Include it, but do not rely on it as your only delivery — verify in real assistive technology.

chunks.heading: 5. The Player: Keyboard, Autoplay, and Controls
chunks.text: Alternatives get the information out of the media; the player is how everyone operates it. The single best decision you can make here is to start with the native controls. A plain <video controls> gives you a play/pause button, a seek bar, volume, a captions menu, and fullscreen — all keyboard operable, all labelled, all maintained by the browser. You throw that away the moment you hide the native controls to build your own, and then you owe every piece of it back by hand.

chunks.heading: If you build a custom player, you owe all of this
chunks.text:
Real buttons with accessible names. Every control is a <button> with a text name — an icon alone is not a name. “Play”, “Mute”, “Captions”, “Fullscreen” (4.1.2).
Full keyboard operation. Every control is reachable by Tab and operable with Enter/Space; the seek bar is a real slider with arrow-key support. Nothing is mouse-only, and focus is never trapped (2.1.1).
Visible focus. A clear focus indicator on each control, including over the video where contrast is unpredictable — see the focus management guide.
State exposed, not just drawn. The play button announces whether it is playing or paused — swap the accessible name (“Play” ↔ “Pause”) or use aria-pressed; the mute and captions toggles do the same. A colour or icon change alone is invisible to a screen reader (4.1.2, 1.4.1).
A captions toggle. If you replace the native controls, you also replace the native captions menu — so the player must offer its own way to turn captions on and off.

The keyboard mechanics — roving focus, a slider seek bar, managing focus as menus open — are the same disciplines covered in the keyboard accessibility and accessible slider guides. A custom player is one of the most control-heavy widgets you can build, which is the best argument for keeping the native one.

chunks.heading: 1.4.2 Audio Control
chunks.text: If audio plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, the user must be able to pause/stop it or control its volume independently. Autoplaying sound with no off switch is a failure — and it talks over screen readers.

chunks.heading: 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide
chunks.text:
Auto-playing, moving content over 5 seconds — including a muted looping background video — must be pausable, stoppable, or hideable, because motion alone is a barrier for some users.

The simplest way to pass both: don't autoplay. Start paused and let the user press play. If a decorative background video must autoplay, mute it and give it a visible, keyboard-reachable pause control. Respect prefers-reduced-motion and don't autoplay for users who have asked the system to reduce motion.

chunks.heading: 6. The <video> Element in Practice
chunks.text:
Here is a self-hosted video wired up the accessible way: native controls, a caption track, a descriptions track, no autoplay, and a transcript one click away.
Read the transcript

chunks.heading: 6. The <video> Element in Practice
chunks.text: A few details earn their place. controls hands you the accessible native player. preload="metadata" and no autoplay keep the page quiet until the user acts. poster gives a still frame before play. The fallback content between the tags is a real text alternative for the rare browser that cannot play the video at all.

chunks.heading: The <track> kinds
chunks.text:
The kind values of the HTML track element and what each is for
kind What it carries Notes
captions Dialogue + speaker IDs + non-speech sounds, same language. What 1.2.2 requires. For people who cannot hear.
subtitles Dialogue translated to another language. Assumes the viewer can hear; not a substitute for captions.
descriptions Text of the audio description, meant to be spoken by AT. Standards-based but unreliably supported — verify; don't rely on it alone.
chapters Named sections for navigating the timeline. Helpful for orientation and long videos.
metadata Data for scripts, not shown to users. Not an accessibility feature by itself.

Get the kind right — captions, not subtitles, for same-language text that includes the sounds — and set label and srclang so the player's menu names each track. The default attribute turns a track on by default; use it thoughtfully.

chunks.heading: 7. Embedded Players: YouTube, Vimeo, and Friends
chunks.text:
Most teams do not host their own video — they embed a YouTube or Vimeo <iframe>. You do not control the platform's player chrome, but you are still responsible for the alternatives. Three things are squarely on you.
Title the iframe. Give the embedding <iframe> a descriptive title — “Video: fixing the checkout error flow” — so a screen reader user hears what the frame contains instead of “video player, frame”.
Upload your own captions. Do not trust the platform's automatic captions. Upload a reviewed caption file to the video so the captions are accurate and complete — the platform will happily serve your file instead of the machine one.
Put the transcript on your page. The platform will not add a transcript to your page, and it is the alternative that serves the most people. Place a descriptive transcript near the embed.

<iframe
src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
title="Video: fixing the checkout error flow"
allow="fullscreen"
loading="lazy"
></iframe>
Beyond that, the player's own keyboard support is out of your hands, so test it: Tab into the embed and confirm play, volume, captions, and fullscreen are reachable and operable. If a platform's player is badly broken for keyboard or screen-reader users, the honest fallback is to self-host with a native <video> element you can fully control.

chunks.heading: 8. Accessible Media in React
8. Accessible Media in React
chunks.text: Two rules keep a React media component honest. First, do not mount the controls-less player and try to recreate the browser's work unless you truly must — and if you must, reach for a maintained accessible player (Vidstack, Plyr, or a wrapper around the native element) and still verify it. Second, keep the caption file and the transcript authored from the same reviewed source so they never disagree. The broader framework patterns are in the React, Vue, and Angular accessibility guides.

chunks.heading: How to Test Accessible Media
chunks.text:
A scanner can tell you a <track> element exists; it cannot tell you whether the captions are accurate or whether a blind user could follow the video. These hands-on checks are what actually matter, and each takes only a couple of minutes.
Turn the sound off and watch. Read only the captions. Do they carry the dialogue, tell you who is speaking, and describe the meaningful sounds — or are they just the words, out of sync, with obvious errors? (1.2.2)
Close your eyes and listen. Can you follow everything that matters from the soundtrack alone? If a visual moment leaves you lost, that is a missing audio description (1.2.5).
Find the transcript. Is there one, on the page, near the player — and for a podcast or audio-only file, is it complete? (1.2.1)
Put the mouse away. Tab to the player and operate every control — play, pause, seek, volume, captions, fullscreen — with the keyboard alone, with a visible focus indicator throughout (2.1.1).
Run a screen reader over the controls. Each control should announce a name and its state — “Pause, button” when playing, “Captions on” when enabled — not “button” with no label. Use the NVDA or VoiceOver guides (4.1.2).
Load the page and wait. Confirm nothing autoplays with sound, and any auto-playing motion can be paused (1.4.2, 2.2.2).

chunks.heading: How to Test Accessible Media
chunks.text: Layer automated checks on top for the mechanical issues — a missing iframe title, an unlabelled control — see automated vs manual testing, and scan the live page with the URL accessibility auditor. But the caption-quality and audio-description checks above are human judgement calls no tool can make for you.

chunks.heading: Common Media Accessibility Mistakes & How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
Common video and audio accessibility anti-patterns, why they fail, and the fix
Anti-pattern Why it fails The fix
Auto-generated captions are left on as the caption solution. Machine captions mishear words, omit speaker IDs and sound effects, and drift out of sync — they are not accurate or complete captions (1.2.2). Treat auto-captions as a draft: review every line, add speaker labels and non-speech sounds, fix timing, and upload the corrected file.
A same-language subtitle file is offered and labelled "captions". Subtitles carry only dialogue; a deaf viewer misses the [door slams] and [tense music] that hearing viewers rely on to follow the scene (1.2.2). Write true captions — dialogue plus speaker identification plus meaningful non-speech sounds — using kind="captions", not kind="subtitles".
The video autoplays with sound, or a background video loops with no pause control. Autoplaying audio talks over screen readers and has no off switch (1.4.2); a moving background over five seconds cannot be paused (2.2.2). Start paused. If a decorative background video must autoplay, mute it and provide a visible, keyboard-reachable pause control.

chunks.heading: Common Media Accessibility Mistakes & How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
Custom player controls are icon-only <div>s with onclick handlers. They have no accessible name, no role, no state, and cannot be reached or operated by keyboard (2.1.1, 4.1.2). Use real <button> elements with text accessible names, keyboard operation, visible focus, and state exposed (playing/paused, muted, captions on).
A video with essential on-screen-only information ships with no audio description. A blind viewer cannot access the chart, the silent demonstration, or the on-screen text that the soundtrack never mentions (1.2.3, 1.2.5). Add audio description of the essential visuals — scripted into the soundtrack or as a described version — or, at level A only, a full text alternative.
A podcast or audio-only recording is published with no transcript. Deaf and deafblind users, skimmers, and search engines get nothing; audio-only content has no captions to fall back on (1.2.1). Publish a full text transcript on the page, with speaker labels, near the audio player — not only as an off-site or downloadable file.

chunks.heading: Accessible Media Checklist
chunks.text:
Alternatives scoped. You have decided what this media owes from its type (prerecorded/live) and where its information lives (audio/picture).
Captions, done right. Prerecorded video has accurate, synchronized captions with speaker IDs and non-speech sounds — not raw auto-captions, not same-language subtitles (1.2.2).
Transcript on the page. A text transcript is available near the media; audio-only content has one as its primary alternative (1.2.1).
Audio description where needed. Video with essential on-screen-only information has audio description; at AA that means a real described version, not just a text alternative (1.2.5).
Live media captioned. Live audio in synchronized media has real-time captions, planned before the event (1.2.4).
Keyboard-operable player. Every control works by keyboard with visible focus; custom controls expose a name and state (2.1.1, 4.1.2).
No hostile autoplay. Nothing autoplays with sound; any auto-playing motion over five seconds can be paused (1.4.2, 2.2.2).
Embeds titled and tested. Any <iframe> has a descriptive title, uses your own reviewed captions, and its keyboard support has been checked.

Work through the full WCAG 2.2 checklist to see media alongside every other requirement, and the keyboard accessibility guide for the player controls in depth.

chunks.heading: Check Your Media on a Live Page
chunks.text:
Scan any page with our free axe-core-powered auditor to catch an untitled video iframe, an unlabelled player control, or a <video> with no caption track — then run the sound-off and eyes-closed tests above for the things no scanner can judge.
Scan a Page NowWCAG 1.2.2 Captions

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is the difference between captions and subtitles?▾
They look similar and are often confused, but they solve different problems for different people. Subtitles assume you can hear the audio and only need the dialogue in another language — they translate speech and nothing else. Captions assume you cannot hear the audio at all, so they carry everything the soundtrack does: the dialogue in the same language, who is speaking when it is not obvious, and the non-speech sounds that carry meaning — [phone rings], [ominous music], [laughter]. WCAG 1.2.2 requires captions, not subtitles. A common failure is shipping a same-language subtitle file, calling it captions, and leaving a deaf viewer to wonder why the tense scene has no explanation — because the [footsteps approaching] that a hearing viewer relies on was never written down. If your file only contains spoken words, it is subtitles; captions also describe the sounds.

Do auto-generated (YouTube) captions meet WCAG?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Not on their own. Automatic speech recognition has improved enormously, but WCAG 1.2.2 requires captions that are accurate and complete, and auto-captions routinely mishear technical terms, names, and homophones, drop punctuation that changes meaning, omit speaker identification entirely, and never transcribe the non-speech sounds captions are supposed to include. They are also often out of sync. Treat auto-captions as a first draft that saves you typing, not as a compliant caption track: review every line, fix the errors, add speaker labels and sound descriptions, and correct the timing. The nickname the disability community gives uncorrected machine captions — 'craptions' — exists for a reason. Upload your corrected file rather than leaving the automatic track live.

What is audio description and when do I actually need it?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Audio description is a narration, inserted into the natural pauses between dialogue, that describes the essential visual information a blind or low-vision viewer would otherwise miss — an on-screen chart, a character's reaction, text that appears without being read aloud, a demonstration that is shown but not narrated. You need it whenever the video conveys information visually that is not already in the soundtrack. The test is simple: close your eyes and listen. If you can still follow everything that matters, you do not need audio description for that video. If you find yourself thinking 'wait, what just happened?' at any point, that gap is exactly what audio description fills. A talking-head interview where everything important is spoken usually needs no description; a software demo where the presenter says 'and then you click here' while clicking silently absolutely does.

Do I need both captions and a transcript?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
For a video with sound, captions are required (1.2.2) and a transcript is strongly recommended; for audio-only content like a podcast, a transcript is the requirement (1.2.1) and there are no captions to add. They serve overlapping but different audiences. Captions are synchronized with the video, so they work for someone watching in real time who cannot hear. A transcript is a single block of text on the page, which serves people who are deafblind and read it in Braille, people who want to skim or search the content, people on a slow connection or in a sound-off environment, and search engines — none of whom are served by a caption track locked inside the player. The most powerful single artifact is a descriptive transcript: the dialogue plus the important visual information, written out as text. That one document can satisfy the transcript need, act as the text alternative for audio description under 1.2.3, and give you SEO-friendly content for free.

Is the HTML <track kind="descriptions"> element enough for audio description?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
It is the standards-based mechanism, but in practice its support is not yet dependable enough to rely on alone. The idea is elegant — a WebVTT file marked kind="descriptions" whose cues a screen reader speaks in the gaps — but browser and screen-reader support for actually announcing that track has historically been patchy and inconsistent, and browsers do not pause the video to fit a description that is too long for the gap. So while you can and should include a descriptions track, the reliable ways to deliver audio description today are to script the description into the production so it is part of the main soundtrack, or to offer a separate described version of the video (an alternate source or a second player) that the user can choose. Whichever you use, verify it in your target screen readers rather than assuming the track is read.

Does WCAG allow autoplaying video?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
It allows it only under tight conditions, and the safest answer is: do not autoplay with sound, ever. Two criteria apply. WCAG 1.4.2 Audio Control says that if any audio plays automatically for more than three seconds, the user must be able to pause or stop it or control its volume independently of the system volume — autoplaying sound with no off switch is a straight failure. WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide says that auto-playing, moving content lasting more than five seconds — which includes a silently looping background video — must be pausable, stoppable, or hideable. Autoplaying audio is also simply hostile: it talks over screen readers, startles people, and competes with whatever else the user is listening to. Start paused, let the user press play, and if you must autoplay a decorative background video, mute it and give it a visible pause control.

How do I make an embedded YouTube or Vimeo video accessible?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
You are responsible for the alternatives even though you do not control the player. Three things are on you. First, give the embedding <iframe> a descriptive title attribute so screen reader users know what the frame contains rather than hearing 'video player, frame'. Second, do not trust the platform's automatic captions — upload your own reviewed caption file to the video so the captions are accurate and complete. Third, put a transcript on your own page near the embed, because the platform will not, and a transcript is the alternative that serves the most people. Beyond that, the platform's player controls and their keyboard support are outside your control, so test them: tab through the player, confirm play, volume, captions, and fullscreen are reachable and operable, and if the player is badly broken, consider hosting the video yourself with a native <video> element you can make accessible.

Are captions required for live video?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: Yes. WCAG 1.2.4 Captions (Live) is a level AA requirement that live audio in synchronized media — a live webinar, a streamed conference talk, a town-hall broadcast — must be captioned in real time. In practice this is usually delivered by CART (Communication Access Real-time Translation), where a trained human captioner types or re-speaks the audio into a live caption stream, because automatic speech recognition rarely reaches the accuracy WCAG requires, especially with multiple speakers, cross-talk, accents, or specialist vocabulary. Live audio description is not required at any WCAG level, which is a deliberate acknowledgement of how hard it is to produce in real time. Plan live captioning before the event, not after — you cannot retrofit real-time captions once the stream has ended, though you should also publish a corrected transcript or captioned recording afterward.

chunks.heading: How to Make a Word Document Accessible
chunks.text:
Most inaccessible PDFs, policies and reports start as Word documents, and nearly every problem is cheaper to fix there. This guide walks through each step in Microsoft 365 for Windows and Mac, with the web version where it differs: a title, the language, heading styles, real lists, alt text, simple tables, clear links, contrast and layout. It ends with what Word's own checker misses, how to export a tagged PDF, and a checklist you can print.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated October 2026

Check your document as you go
The free Word and PowerPoint Accessibility Checker opens a .docx file in your browser and lists missing alt text, headings, table header rows, link text, language and more, with the fix for each. The file is never uploaded.

Check a Word file free

chunks.heading: Why Word Accessibility Matters
chunks.text:
A Word document is not just text on a page. Under the surface it records which paragraphs are headings, which are list items, which row of a table holds the column names and what each picture shows. A screen reader uses that structure to let someone jump from heading to heading, hear how many items a list has, and know which column a number belongs to. When the structure is missing, the document still looks fine but turns into one long, flat stream of words for anyone who cannot see it.
The same structure helps far more people than screen reader users. Someone with low vision who zooms in or switches to high contrast needs real text in the main body, not text boxes and pictures of text. People with dyslexia or cognitive disabilities rely on clear headings, short sections and good spacing. Everyone gets a working Navigation Pane, an automatic table of contents and PDF bookmarks.

chunks.heading: WCAG applies to documents too
chunks.text:
WCAG was written for web pages, but the W3C's WCAG2ICT guidance explains how its success criteria apply to non-web documents: a .docx file is treated much like a page, its title is the page title and its default language is the page language. The laws and standards that matter in practice build on that:
EN 301 549, clause 10. The European ICT accessibility standard applies adapted WCAG criteria to non-web documents such as Office files and PDFs. V3.2.1, the edition cited under the Web Accessibility Directive, uses WCAG 2.1 Level AA, and V4.1.1 moves to WCAG 2.2. See EN 301 549 explained, what changed for documents in EN 301 549 v4.1.1, and the EN 301 549 checklist, which can be filtered to the documents chapter.
European Accessibility Act. Beyond websites and apps, covered services have to think about the electronic documents they give customers, such as invoices and e-tickets. The EAA readiness checklist covers what that means.
Section 508. The Revised 508 Standards apply WCAG 2.0 Level AA to electronic documents, not just web pages, so US federal agencies and their suppliers need accessible Word files. See Section 508 compliance.

chunks.heading: WCAG applies to documents too
chunks.text:
ADA Title II. The Department of Justice rule for state and local governments sets WCAG 2.1 Level AA for web content, and it names word processing, presentation, PDF and spreadsheet files as covered conventional electronic documents. Documents posted before the compliance date are generally exempt, unless they are later updated or are still used to apply for or take part in a service. The compliance dates are now 26 April 2027 and 26 April 2028; our Title II deadline guide explains the change.
UK public sector. Under the public sector accessibility regulations, documents on public sector websites must be accessible. GOV.UK's accessibility requirements guidance says documents published before 23 September 2018 are exempt unless people need them to use a service.

The success criteria you will meet most often in a Word file are 1.1.1 Non-text Content, 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence, 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), 2.4.2 Page Titled, 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), 2.4.6 Headings and Labels and 3.1.1 Language of Page. Each step below says which one it serves.

chunks.heading: Step by Step: Make a Word Document Accessible
chunks.text: Menu paths are for Word in Microsoft 365. Where Word for Mac or Word for the web works differently, the step says so. Older versions such as Word 2019 use slightly different names for a few commands; those are noted too.

chunks.heading: 1. Give the document a title
chunks.text:
The title in a document's properties is what a screen reader announces when the file opens, what a browser tab shows when the file is opened online, and what the window title of an exported PDF shows. Without one, people hear the file name, such as “FINAL_v3_JB_edits.docx”. This is 2.4.2 Page Titled.
Windows: select File > Info. Under Properties on the right, click the Title box and type a title that describes the content, then save. For the full set of fields, choose Properties > Advanced Properties > Summary.
Mac: select File > Properties, open the Summary tab, fill in Title and select OK.
Web: Microsoft documents the title property for the desktop apps, so open the file in the desktop app to set it if you cannot find it online.

A good title is the document's real name: “Parking permit application guide 2026”, not “Document1”, “Title” or the file name. Word sometimes fills the field from the first line of text, so check it rather than assume.

chunks.heading: 2. Set the document language
chunks.text:
Screen readers switch pronunciation rules based on the language stored with the text. If it is missing or wrong, a French screen reader may read English text with French sounds, which is close to unintelligible. The default language is 3.1.1 Language of Page, and a passage in another language is 3.1.2 Language of Parts.
Windows: press Ctrl+A to select all the text, then choose Review > Language > Set Proofing Language. Pick the language and select OK. Selecting Set As Default in the same dialog makes new documents use it too.
Mac: press Cmd+A, then select Review > Language, choose the language and select OK.
Web: select the text, then Review > Editor > Set Proofing Language.

For a quotation or section in another language, select just that text and set its language the same way. The Language dialog on Windows also has a Detect language automatically option; it helps spelling, but check what it chose, because it can guess wrong on short passages.

chunks.heading: 3. Build the structure with heading styles
chunks.text:
Headings are the single most important structure in a long document. Screen reader users pull up a list of headings to skim, and jump between them the way sighted readers scan bold titles. Word only knows a paragraph is a heading if it uses a Heading style. Making text bigger and bold changes how it looks but not what it is. This is 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, and 2.4.6 Headings and Labels asks that the headings describe what follows.
Click in the heading text and choose Heading 1, Heading 2 or Heading 3 from the Styles gallery on the Home tab. On Windows, Ctrl+Alt+1 to Ctrl+Alt+3 apply them from the keyboard; on a Mac, use Cmd+Option+1 to Cmd+Option+3.
Use the Title style, or one Heading 1, for the document's own title, then work down one level at a time. A Heading 3 belongs under a Heading 2, never straight under a Heading 1.
To change how a heading looks, change the style, not the paragraph: right-click the style in the gallery and choose Modify, or format one heading the way you want and choose Update Heading 1 to Match Selection. Every heading of that level updates at once.

chunks.heading: 3. Build the structure with heading styles
chunks.text:
Check the outline in the Navigation Pane: on Windows, select View > Navigation Pane or press Ctrl+F, then the Headings tab. Microsoft notes the pane does not show headings inside tables, text boxes, headers or footers, so a heading missing from the list is a sign it sits somewhere a screen reader may not treat as part of the outline.

Good: one level at a time, every heading a style

Heading 1 Annual Report 2026
Heading 2 Summary
Heading 2 Our services
Heading 3 Housing
Heading 3 Waste and recycling
Heading 2 Finances

Bad: bold Normal text and a skipped level

Normal, bold, 16 pt Annual Report 2026 <- not a heading
Heading 3 Summary <- skips 1 and 2
Normal, bold Our services <- not a heading

Keep headings short and specific. “Section 2” tells nobody anything; “How to apply” does. Do not apply a Heading style to an empty paragraph to create space, because it is announced as a blank heading. The cognitive accessibility guide covers writing headings and sections people can scan.

chunks.heading: 4. Use real lists
chunks.text:
A list made with Home > Bullets or Home > Numbering is announced as a list with a number of items, so a listener knows how much is coming and when it ends. Typing a hyphen, an asterisk or “1.” at the start of each line produces ordinary paragraphs that only look like a list (1.3.1 Info and Relationships). Word often converts typed bullets automatically; if it did not, select the paragraphs, delete the typed characters and apply Bullets or Numbering.
Microsoft also advises against dropping a plain, unbulleted paragraph into the middle of a list, because screen readers may then miscount the items or announce that the list has ended. Use Numbering for steps that must happen in order, and Bullets for everything else.

chunks.heading: 5. Add alt text, or mark images as decorative
chunks.text:
Every picture, chart, SmartArt graphic, shape, icon and embedded object that carries meaning needs a text alternative (1.1.1 Non-text Content). Anything that is only decoration should be marked as decorative so screen readers skip it; when you export to PDF, Microsoft tags decorative objects as artifacts, which screen readers ignore.
Windows, Microsoft 365: right-click the object and choose View Alt Text, or select it and choose Alt Text on its format tab (for example Picture Format). In Word 2019 to 2024 the command is Edit Alt Text.
Mac: Control-click the object and choose View Alt Text, or choose Alt Text on its Format tab.
Decorative: in the Alt Text pane, tick Mark as decorative (called Decorative in Word 2019 to 2024). The description box greys out.
Charts and SmartArt: click the outer border of the whole object before opening alt text, so the description applies to the graphic, not one shape inside it.
Groups: if several pictures form one idea, group them and describe the group. If they are grouped only for positioning, ungroup them and describe each.

chunks.heading: 5. Add alt text, or mark images as decorative
chunks.text:
Say what the image means in this document, in a sentence or two. Do not start with “image of” or “picture of”, because the screen reader already says it is a graphic, and do not repeat a caption or the sentence next to it. For a chart, give the main finding, and put the numbers in the text or a table where everyone can use them. For examples covering every kind of image, see how to write alt text.
Examples of weak and better alt text for images in a Word document
Image Weak alt text Better
Photo in a staff newsletter of the new reception area “image of office” The new ground-floor reception, with the visitor desk just inside the main doors.
Bar chart of quarterly enquiries “chart” Bar chart: enquiries rose in every quarter, from 410 in Q1 to 690 in Q4. Full figures are in Table 2.
Screenshot in a how-to guide “screenshot.png” Word Options dialog with Accessibility selected in the left-hand list.
Logo beside the organisation's name in the header “logo” Mark as decorative, because the name is already in the text next to it.
Decorative divider line between sections “line” Mark as decorative.

chunks.heading: 5. Add alt text, or mark images as decorative
chunks.text: Generated alt text needs a person. Recent Microsoft 365 builds write a description with AI when you ask for one in the Alt Text pane, and Copilot+ PCs can do it automatically when you insert a picture. On Windows the setting is under File > Options > Accessibility (Enable the option to generate alt text using AI). Older builds added captions ending “Description automatically generated” when a picture was inserted. Either way, read and rewrite the text before you share the file: a description of what is in a photo is not the same as what the photo is there to say. Avoid pictures of text altogether where you can (1.4.5 Images of Text); if a scanned page or a screenshot of text is unavoidable, put the text itself in the document.

chunks.heading: 6. Keep tables simple, with a real header row
chunks.text:
A screen reader reads a table cell by cell, announcing the column header as you move across, but only if Word knows which row holds the headers (1.3.1 Info and Relationships). Use tables for data, not to position things on the page.
Insert the table with Insert > Table and type the column headings in the first row.
Click in the first row and select Table Layout > Repeat Header Rows (in the Data group; the tab is called Layout in some versions). Or right-click the row, choose Table Properties > Row and tick Repeat as header row at the top of each page. The row must be the first row of the table.
Keep Table Design > Header Row ticked in the Table Style Options group too. Microsoft's accessibility instructions use this option, but Word ticks it on every new table and it mainly controls formatting. Repeat Header Rows is what marks the row as a header in the file, which is why the free checker on this site looks for it. Setting both covers each way the header is read.
Avoid merged and split cells, tables inside tables, and empty rows, columns or cells added for spacing. Each one makes it harder to tell which row and column a cell belongs to. If a table needs merged cells to make sense, split it into two simpler tables.

chunks.heading: 6. Keep tables simple, with a real header row
chunks.text:
Introduce the table with a sentence or a caption (References > Insert Caption) that says what it shows, and avoid fixed-width tables that do not reflow on small screens.

Repeated headers only show in Print Layout and when printing, and Word will not repeat them across a manual page break inside the table. For a deeper look at table structure, see accessible data tables.

chunks.heading: 7. Write link text that makes sense on its own
chunks.text:
Screen reader users often list every link in a document and choose from that list, where “click here” and “read more” say nothing, and a pasted address is read out character by character. Link text should name the destination (2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context)).
Right-click the link and choose Edit Hyperlink (Edit Link in some versions), or select it and press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac). Change Text to display to words that describe the destination.
Bad: “For the fees, click here.” Better: “See the 2026 planning fees.”
A ScreenTip (the button in the same dialog) shows on hover, but it is not a substitute for clear link text.
If the document will be printed, keep the readable link text and add a short address in brackets or a references list, rather than making the long address the link text.

chunks.heading: 8. Check colour and contrast
chunks.text:
Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, and large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold) at least 3:1 (1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)). Colour must never be the only way you show something, such as red for overdue items or a coloured row for the recommended option (1.4.1 Use of Color): add a word, a symbol or a pattern. Lines and bars in charts need 3:1 against their background (1.4.11 Non-text Contrast).
Use the Automatic font colour for body text where you can. Microsoft recommends it because it adapts when someone uses a high contrast mode.
Pale grey text, coloured text on coloured table shading and text over pictures are the usual failures. Test any colour pair with the contrast checker.
In Word for Windows, the Accessibility Assistant flags low-contrast text and offers a font colour picker with a High-contrast only switch.
Underline links so they stand out without relying on colour.

chunks.heading: 9. Choose readable fonts and spacing
chunks.text:
WCAG does not set a minimum font size for documents, but readable text is part of making a document usable. Microsoft suggests familiar sans serif fonts such as Arial or Calibri, and advises against all capitals and heavy use of italics or underlining.
Use a comfortable body size (11 to 12 pt is common for print) and left-aligned text. WCAG's Level AAA 1.4.8 Visual Presentation criterion asks for text that is not justified, because the uneven gaps between words make it harder to read, especially for many people with dyslexia.
Add space with paragraph settings, not blank lines: set Spacing Before and After on the Layout tab, and line spacing in the Paragraph dialog. Turn on Home > Show/Hide to see empty paragraphs as pilcrow marks and delete them.
Start a new page with Insert > Page Break (Ctrl+Enter on Windows), not a run of empty lines that shifts whenever text changes.
Set your font choices in the Normal and Heading styles so the whole document stays consistent. The accessible typography guide goes further on size, line length and spacing.

chunks.heading: 10. Avoid text boxes and floating objects
chunks.text:
Text boxes, shapes with text and pictures set to float with text wrapping sit outside the normal flow of the document. Screen readers may read them out of order or not at all, their headings do not appear in the Navigation Pane, and they often lose their place or structure when the document is saved as a PDF (1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence).
Move text out of text boxes into the main body and format it with a style. A pull quote or callout can be a shaded paragraph instead of a text box; Microsoft suggests shaded paragraphs as an alternative to tables for this kind of banner.
Set pictures and charts to sit in the text: on Windows, select the picture, open the Layout Options button and choose In Line with Text, or use Picture Format > Wrap Text > In Line with Text. On a Mac, use Picture Format > Arrange > Wrap Text > In Line with Text. Then place the picture next to the paragraph it belongs with.
Keep important information out of headers and footers, which Microsoft lists among its best practices: some screen readers do not read them as part of the main text.

chunks.heading: 11. Check the file before you share it
chunks.text:
Properties: confirm the Title in File > Info (step 1), and that the Author and other fields say what you want them to say.
Restricted access: Microsoft's checker treats restricted access (Information Rights Management) as an error, because it can stop screen readers reading the file. Use permissions on the storage location rather than in the file where you can.
Tracked changes and comments: accept or reject changes and delete comments before you publish, so nobody hears the draft history.
Format: save as .docx, the current format. Saving as the old .doc format puts Word into Compatibility Mode, which turns off some newer features, and the checker on this site cannot read .doc files.
Forms: if the document uses content controls for people to fill in, give each control a title in its Properties; Microsoft's checker flags controls without one.

chunks.heading: Start From an Accessible Template
chunks.text:
The cheapest accessible document is one built on a template that already does the right thing, so authors get headings, lists and table styles by default instead of by memory.
Microsoft's templates: select File > New and search the online templates for “accessible”. Microsoft publishes a set designed with accessibility in mind. Still run the checks in this guide on them, because your content can undo their good structure.
Your own house template: set the Normal style's font, size and spacing; style Heading 1 to 3 in your brand fonts; choose theme colours whose text combinations pass 4.5:1; create a table style with a distinct header row; set the default language. Then select File > Save As and choose Word Template (.dotx).
Make the right thing easy: add a short instruction page or placeholder text that tells authors to use the Styles gallery and the Alt Text pane, and remove styles nobody should use.

Keep the template under version control like any other shared asset. When you change it, check one real document built from it with the free checker before rolling it out.

chunks.heading: Word's Check Accessibility, and What It Misses
chunks.text:
Word has a built-in checker on every platform. Select Review > Check Accessibility in Word for Windows, Mac or the web. If you do not see the button on Windows, use File > Info > Check for Issues > Check Accessibility.
Windows: in current Word for Windows, Check Accessibility opens the Accessibility Assistant. It runs in the background, highlights an Accessibility indicator in the status bar when it finds issues, and groups them under Color and Contrast, Media and Illustrations, Tables, Document Structure and Document Access, with suggested fixes.
Mac: the Accessibility pane lists Errors, Warnings and Tips.
Web: the pane adds an Intelligent Services group, which suggests alt text for review, and a Recheck button.

Run it on every document. But it is a structural check, and Microsoft's published rules for the Accessibility Checker cover a short list of issues. For Word, the errors are missing alt text, tables without column header information, restricted document access and content controls without titles; the warnings are tables without a simple structure and low text contrast; the one tip is to use heading styles; and an Intelligent Services rule suggests alt text for you to review. Microsoft updates the rules over time, so your version may flag more, but several common problems are not on the list at all.

chunks.heading: Word's Check Accessibility, and What It Misses
chunks.text:
Which Word accessibility issues Microsoft's published checker rules cover, which the free checker on this site covers, and what needs a manual check
Issue Microsoft's published rules Free checker on this site Still check by hand
Alt text on pictures, charts and SmartArt Yes (error) Yes, and flags generated text, file names and "image of" Is the description accurate and useful here?
Table header information Yes (error) Yes, looks for a header row marked to repeat Do the headers describe each column?
Merged cells, nested tables Yes, as "simple structure" (warning) Yes Could the data be simpler, or not a table at all?
Text contrast Yes (warning) Text with a fixed colour only Theme colours, text on images, charts
Heading styles used Yes (tip) Yes Do the headings describe their sections?
Skipped heading levels Not listed Yes Covered by the checks
Text formatted to look like a heading Not listed Yes Covered by the checks
Document title in properties Not listed Yes Does the title describe the document?
Document language Not listed Yes Are passages in other languages marked?
Link text Not listed Yes: web addresses, "click here", empty links Does each link make sense on its own?
Typed bullets, blank paragraphs Not listed Yes Covered by the checks
Text boxes and floating objects Not listed Yes Does the reading order make sense?

chunks.heading: Word's Check Accessibility, and What It Misses
chunks.text:
Restricted access (rights management) Yes (error) Password-protected files cannot be opened Covered by the checks
Colour used as the only signal Not listed No Yes, by reading the document
Text inside pictures Not listed No Yes, by looking at every image

Neither checker can tell whether your alt text is right, whether the headings describe their sections, or whether the order makes sense when read aloud. That part needs a person, and the testing section below shows a quick way to do it.

chunks.heading: Export to an Accessible PDF
chunks.text:
Many Word documents end up as PDFs. Word turns headings, lists, tables, alt text and the title into PDF tags only if you export with tags switched on; printing to PDF throws them away. Microsoft's accessible PDF instructions also recommend running the Accessibility Checker first.
Windows: select File > Save As or Save a Copy, choose PDF (*.pdf) as the file type and select More options, then Options. Make sure Document structure tags for accessibility is ticked. Also tick Document properties, and Create bookmarks using Headings so the PDF gets bookmarks from your headings. Select OK, then Save.
Mac: select File > Save As, choose PDF as the File Format, and select Best for electronic distribution and accessibility (uses Microsoft online service). Microsoft says this option is what makes the PDF tagged. It sends the file to a Microsoft conversion service, which Microsoft says does not keep it; bear that in mind for confidential files.
Web: select File > Save As > Download as PDF.

chunks.heading: Export to an Accessible PDF
chunks.text:
Avoid any Print to PDF option, such as the Microsoft Print to PDF printer on Windows: it produces a PDF with no tags at all. After exporting, open the PDF and check that headings appear as bookmarks, the title shows in the window bar, and tables have header cells. Problems such as text boxes and floating pictures that read in the wrong order are easier to fix in Word and export again than to repair in the PDF.
To check the result, run it through the PDF accessibility checker, and read the guide to accessible PDFs for tags, reading order and PDF/UA.

chunks.heading: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
Common Word accessibility mistakes, why they fail, and the fix
Mistake Why it fails The fix
Bold, larger text instead of Heading styles Screen reader users cannot move by heading, the Navigation Pane is empty and the PDF gets no heading tags (1.3.1). Apply Heading 1, 2 and 3 from Home > Styles, and change the style's look if you want a different font.
Typing a hyphen or number to start each list item It is read as ordinary paragraphs, so nobody hears that a list starts or how long it is (1.3.1). Use Home > Bullets or Home > Numbering.
Pressing Enter several times to add space Each empty paragraph is announced as blank, and the layout breaks when fonts or page sizes change. Set Spacing Before and After on the Layout tab; use Ctrl+Enter for a page break.
A table used to lay out a form or a page Screen readers announce rows and columns that mean nothing and may read cells in an odd order (1.3.2). Use styles, tabs and paragraph spacing for layout; keep tables for data.
Key information in a text box or floating shape Text boxes may be read out of order or skipped, and their headings do not appear in the Navigation Pane. Move the text into the main body; set pictures to In Line with Text.

chunks.heading: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
"Click here" or a pasted web address as link text Listed out of context, the link says nothing about where it goes, or reads out a long address (2.4.4). Use the destination's name as the link text, through Edit Hyperlink > Text to display.
Red text as the only sign that something is overdue People who cannot tell red apart, or who use high contrast, miss the meaning (1.4.1). Add a word or symbol as well as the colour.

chunks.heading: Word Accessibility Checklist
chunks.text: Tick the boxes as you work, or print this page (Ctrl+P or Cmd+P) and use it on paper. Nothing you tick is saved or sent anywhere.

chunks.heading: Set-up
chunks.text:
The file is a .docx, built on an accessible template.
Title set in File > Info > Properties, and it describes the document.
Document language set; passages in other languages marked.

chunks.heading: Structure
chunks.text:
Every heading uses a Heading style; none is just bold text.
Heading levels go down one step at a time, and the Navigation Pane shows a sensible outline.
Lists use Bullets or Numbering, not typed characters.
No empty paragraphs for spacing; page breaks used for new pages.

chunks.heading: Images and tables
chunks.text:
Every meaningful picture, chart and SmartArt graphic has alt text that says what it means.
Decorative images are marked as decorative.
Generated alt text has been reviewed and rewritten.
No pictures of text, or the text is also in the document.
Tables hold data only, with a header row set to repeat.
No merged cells, nested tables or blank cells for layout.

chunks.heading: Text, links and layout
chunks.text:
Link text names the destination; no “click here” or bare web addresses.
Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).
Colour is never the only way information is shown.
Readable sans serif font, left-aligned, no long runs of capitals or italics.
No content in text boxes or floating objects; pictures in line with text.
Nothing important only in headers or footers.

chunks.heading: Before you share
chunks.text:
Review > Check Accessibility shows no errors, and its warnings have been reviewed.
The free Word and PowerPoint checker shows no errors.
Tracked changes resolved, comments removed, no restricted access.
Read through with a screen reader or Read Aloud, start to finish.
PDF exported with Document structure tags for accessibility, and the PDF checked.

chunks.heading: Test the Document With the Free Checker
chunks.text:
Word and PowerPoint Accessibility Checker
Drop in a .docx file to see errors, warnings and tips for each check, located by page and paragraph, with the Microsoft 365 fix. Download the list as CSV or Excel to share it. Your file stays on your device.

Check a Word file free
Save a .docx copy. The checker reads .docx files, the format Word has used since 2007. If you have an old .doc file, use File > Save As and choose Word Document (.docx). Remove any password from a copy first, since encrypted files cannot be read. For a Google Doc, choose File > Download > Microsoft Word (.docx).
Open it in the checker. Drop the file on the Word and PowerPoint Accessibility Checker. It checks the title, language, headings and heading order, text that only looks like a heading, alt text and its quality, table header rows, merged and nested tables, link text, typed lists, blank paragraphs, text boxes and floating objects, and the contrast of text with a fixed colour.
Fix errors first, then warnings. Errors are clear failures such as a picture with no alt text. Warnings need a judgement, such as a skipped heading level. Tips are good practice, such as removing blank paragraphs.
Run Word's own checker too. It sees the document as Word lays it out, including some contrast problems the free checker cannot measure, such as theme colours.

chunks.heading: Test the Document With the Free Checker
chunks.text:
Listen to it. Open the Navigation Pane and read the outline as if it were a contents page. Then use View > Immersive Reader and Read Aloud, or a screen reader such as Narrator, NVDA or VoiceOver, to hear the document in order. Anything read in a strange place, or not at all, is a structure problem.
Check the PDF. If you publish a PDF, export it with tags and check that file as well.

For hands-on screen reader testing, see the screen reader testing guide and the NVDA guide. Presentations have their own pitfalls, covered in how to make PowerPoint accessible.

chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
How do I make a Word document accessible?▾
Give the file a title in File > Info > Properties, set the document language, and build the structure with Word's built-in Heading styles and real bulleted or numbered lists. Add alt text to every meaningful picture, chart and SmartArt graphic, and mark purely decorative ones as decorative. Keep tables simple, with a header row set to repeat and no merged or empty layout cells. Write link text that says where the link goes, keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or more, and keep content in the main text rather than in floating text boxes. Then run Review > Check Accessibility, check what it does not cover, and export to PDF with document structure tags turned on.

Does Word have an accessibility checker?▾
Yes. Select Review > Check Accessibility in Word for Windows, Mac or the web. On Windows it opens the Accessibility Assistant pane, which groups issues under Color and Contrast, Media and Illustrations, Tables, Document Structure and Document Access, and a status bar reminder appears when it finds problems. It is worth running on every file, but Microsoft's published rule list does not include a missing document title, the document language, vague link text, skipped heading levels or text that is only formatted to look like a heading, so check those separately. The free Word and PowerPoint Accessibility Checker on this site looks for them.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Do Word documents have to meet WCAG?▾
In many settings, yes. The W3C's WCAG2ICT guidance explains how WCAG applies to non-web documents, and the rules that matter in practice follow it. EN 301 549 applies adapted WCAG criteria to non-web documents in clause 10, which is how documents come into scope in the EU. The US Section 508 standards apply WCAG 2.0 Level AA to electronic documents, and the ADA Title II rule for state and local governments covers word processing files posted online, with an exception for older documents that are not updated or still needed to use a service. UK public sector bodies must make documents published on their websites since 23 September 2018 accessible, with similar exceptions.

How do I add alt text to a picture in Word?▾
In Word for Microsoft 365, right-click the picture and choose View Alt Text, or select it and choose Alt Text on the Picture Format tab. In Word 2019 to 2024 the command is called Edit Alt Text. On a Mac, Control-click the picture and choose View Alt Text. Type a sentence or two that says what the picture shows and why it is there, without starting with "image of". If the picture adds nothing, tick Mark as decorative instead. For a chart or SmartArt graphic, select its outer border first so the alt text applies to the whole object.

How do I make a table accessible in Word?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Use Insert > Table for real data only, never for layout. Put column headings in the first row, then mark that row as a header: click in it and select Table Layout > Repeat Header Rows, or right-click, choose Table Properties and tick Repeat as header row at the top of each page on the Row tab. Also keep Header Row ticked on the Table Design tab. Avoid merged and split cells, tables inside tables, and empty rows or columns used for spacing, and give the table a caption or a sentence before it that says what it shows.

How do I save an accessible PDF from Word?▾
On Windows, select File > Save As or Save a Copy, choose PDF as the file type, select More options and then Options, and make sure Document structure tags for accessibility is ticked. Ticking Create bookmarks using Headings adds bookmarks too. On a Mac, choose PDF as the file format and select Best for electronic distribution and accessibility, which Microsoft notes uses its online conversion service. In Word for the web, select File > Save As > Download as PDF. Do not use a Print to PDF printer, which produces an untagged file, and check the PDF itself afterwards.

If the accessibility checker finds no issues, is my document accessible?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: Not necessarily. Automated checks find structural problems such as missing alt text or a table with no header row. They cannot judge whether alt text is accurate, whether headings describe their sections, whether colour carries meaning on its own, or whether the reading order makes sense. Treat a clean result as the start of the review: scan the headings in the Navigation Pane, read the document with a screen reader or Read Aloud, and check the exported PDF.

chunks.heading: How Much Does an ADA Website Lawsuit Actually Cost?
chunks.text:
The honest answer: anywhere from a $1,000 demand letter to a multimillion-dollar class-action settlement, such as Fashion Nova's $5.15 million. Most single-plaintiff cases land around $30,000 once legal fees are counted. Below is the full range by resolution type, what actually drives the number up or down, and why the cheapest option is almost always to fix the site first.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated October 2026

chunks.heading: Cost by resolution type (2026)
chunks.text:
Resolution type Average Typical range
Demand Letter Settlement $5K $1K – $25K
Out-of-Court Settlement $30K $5K – $150K
Court Judgment $85K $10K – $500K
Class Action Settlement $400K $50K – $6.00M
Legal Defense (No Damages) $30K $5K – $125K

Source: Accessibility.build Lawsuit Tracker, from public court records and legal-industry reports. Figures are indicative ranges, not legal advice.

chunks.heading: The counter-intuitive part: the ADA has no damages
chunks.text:
Here is what surprises most business owners. Under federal ADA Title III, a private plaintiff cannot win money damages — the statute only lets a court order you to fix the website and pay the plaintiff's attorney's fees. So where does the money in a “settlement” come from? Two places:
Attorney's fees. The plaintiff's lawyer is entitled to reasonable fees, and a negotiated payment to resolve those fees is the bulk of most settlements.
State statutory damages. This is the real multiplier. California's Unruh Civil Rights Act treats an ADA violation as an automatic state violation carrying $4,000 minimum per violation, with no need to prove actual harm. New York and a handful of other states have their own damages regimes. This is why a case tied to California or New York routinely costs several times more than the same barriers would in a state without such a law.

chunks.heading: What pushes your number up
chunks.text:
A statutory-damages state. California (Unruh) and New York are the most expensive jurisdictions. Most 2025 filings clustered in New York, Florida, and Illinois federal courts, with California pushed into state court.
Class-action structure. A single plaintiff is capped by their own fees and one $4,000 increment. A class multiplies statutory damages across everyone affected — the mechanism behind the $5.15M Fashion Nova settlement.
Company size. In 2025, 36% of sued companies had revenue over $25 million, and larger firms settle for more because they can — and because they are more visible targets.
A prior lawsuit on record. Repeat defendants made up 46% of 2025's federal cases. Being sued once marks you as a proven, un-remediated target.
Egregious, well-documented barriers. A broken checkout or an inaccessible core flow is worth more to a plaintiff than a cosmetic issue on a rarely visited page.

chunks.heading: What brings it down
chunks.text:
A visible, in-progress accessibility program. Audit records, a remediation backlog, and a published accessibility statement signal good faith and weaken a plaintiff's leverage.
Fast engagement. Responding quickly and credibly, with a remediation timeline, often resolves a case before fees balloon.
Actually fixing the site. The single most effective cost control, because it removes the basis for the next claim.

The math almost always favors remediation
A single out-of-court settlement averages ~$30,000 and does not fix your site. A professional WCAG 2.2 AA audit and remediation program often costs the same or less, permanently removes the exposure, and improves SEO, conversion, and reach to the ~27% of U.S. adults with a disability. When 46% of federal cases are repeat defendants, paying to settle without remediating is paying twice.

chunks.heading: Don't forget the overlay trap
chunks.text: Businesses often buy an accessibility overlay widget expecting it to cap this risk. It does not. Overlays are named in hundreds of suits a year, and in 2025 the FTC settled with a major overlay provider over misleading compliance claims. Budgeting for a subscription widget instead of real remediation usually means paying for the widget and the lawsuit. See why overlays fail.

chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
What is the average cost of an ADA website lawsuit?▾
Most single-plaintiff web accessibility cases settle out of court for roughly $5,000 to $50,000, with an average around $30,000 once legal fees are included. Demand letters that never reach court typically resolve for $1,000 to $25,000. The figure rises steeply for class actions: in 2025, Fashion Nova settled a web accessibility class action for $5.15 million. Even winning costs money — defending a case with no damages award still runs $5,000 to $125,000 in legal fees.

Do I have to pay damages under the ADA?▾
Under federal ADA Title III, private plaintiffs cannot recover money damages — only injunctive relief (an order to fix the site) plus their attorney's fees and costs. The money in most settlements is really the plaintiff's legal fees and a negotiated payment to make the case go away. Damages enter the picture through state laws: California's Unruh Act ($4,000 minimum per violation), New York's laws, and similar statutes let plaintiffs recover statutory damages, which is why California- and New York-linked cases cost more.

How much does it cost to just defend and win?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Even a meritless case is expensive to fight. Retaining counsel, responding to the complaint, and negotiating typically costs $5,000 to $125,000 depending on how far the case goes. Because that defense cost often exceeds a quick settlement, many defendants settle even when they believe they would win — which is exactly what plaintiff's firms count on. The only durable way out is to remediate the site so future plaintiffs have nothing to allege.

Is it cheaper to fix my site or risk a lawsuit?▾
For almost every business, remediation is cheaper. A professional WCAG 2.2 AA audit and remediation program is a one-time or annual cost that also improves SEO, conversion, and reach — while a lawsuit is a pure loss that does not even guarantee you have fixed the underlying problem. And because 46% of 2025's federal cases targeted repeat defendants, paying a settlement without remediating often just invites the next filing.

What drives the price of a settlement up or down?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text: Key factors: whether a statutory-damages state law (California, New York) applies; whether it is a single plaintiff or a class action; the size and revenue of the business (36% of 2025 defendants had over $25M in revenue, and larger companies pay more); whether you have a prior lawsuit on record; how egregious and well-documented the barriers are; and how quickly you engage counsel and signal a remediation plan. Demonstrating a good-faith, in-progress accessibility program is one of the few things that reliably lowers exposure.
