chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
What is a website accessibility audit?▾
A website accessibility audit is a structured evaluation of a website against an accessibility standard — most commonly WCAG 2.2 Level AA. It identifies barriers that prevent people with disabilities from perceiving, operating, or understanding the site, and documents each issue with severity, the WCAG criterion it fails, the user impact, and a recommended fix. A complete audit combines automated scanning, manual keyboard and screen reader testing, and code-level review.

How long does an accessibility audit take?▾
For a single template-driven marketing site of under 20 unique page types, a thorough WCAG 2.2 AA audit typically takes 20–40 hours of expert time. Large applications with authenticated flows, complex forms, dashboards, and dynamic widgets can take 80–200+ hours. Automated tools can scan thousands of pages in minutes but only catch 30–40% of real WCAG issues, so manual review is always required for a defensible audit.

What WCAG version should I audit against in 2026?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Audit against WCAG 2.2 Level AA. WCAG 2.2 was published as a W3C Recommendation in October 2023 and is the version referenced by current U.S. Department of Justice Title II rulemaking, the EU European Accessibility Act, and most procurement requirements as of 2026. WCAG 2.2 is fully backward compatible with 2.1 and 2.0, so meeting 2.2 means you also meet the earlier versions.

Can I audit a website for accessibility using only automated tools?▾
No. Automated tools like axe-core, Lighthouse, and WAVE catch roughly 30–40% of WCAG failures — primarily missing alt text, color contrast, missing labels, and obvious ARIA misuse. They cannot reliably evaluate whether alt text is meaningful, whether the keyboard tab order is logical, whether focus is managed correctly in dynamic widgets, or whether screen reader announcements make sense. A defensible audit always combines automated scanning with manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing.

What's the difference between an accessibility audit and a VPAT?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
An accessibility audit is the testing and analysis activity itself, producing a list of issues to fix. A VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) is a standardized vendor document, published as an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR), that describes how a product conforms to accessibility standards on a criterion-by-criterion basis. You perform an audit, then use the findings to fill out the VPAT. A VPAT without an underlying audit is essentially unsupported.

How often should I re-audit my website?▾
At minimum, run a full WCAG audit once per year and after any major redesign or platform migration. In addition, integrate automated accessibility scanning into your CI pipeline so every pull request is checked, and spot-check newly built components manually before they ship. High-risk sectors (government, healthcare, financial services, education) often require quarterly audits and re-audits after every release.

What does an accessibility audit report include?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
A complete audit report includes: an executive summary with overall conformance status, a per-issue breakdown listing the WCAG criterion failed, severity (critical / high / medium / low), the affected pages or components, a description of the user impact, reproduction steps, screenshots or code snippets, and a recommended remediation. Strong reports also link each issue to the relevant WCAG technique (e.g., H44, ARIA14) and include a prioritized remediation roadmap.

How much does an accessibility audit cost?▾
Expert-led WCAG 2.2 AA audits typically cost $5,000–$15,000 for a small marketing site, $15,000–$40,000 for a mid-size application, and $50,000+ for large enterprise platforms with authenticated workflows. AI-assisted tooling can dramatically lower this by handling the triage and remediation drafting, leaving accessibility specialists to focus on judgment calls and assistive-technology verification.

chunks.heading: How to Write Alt Text, with Examples for Every Kind of Image
chunks.text:
Alt text is what a screen reader says in place of an image, and what a browser shows when the image fails to load. Good alt text is not a description of pixels. It says what the image is doing on that page, in as few words as that takes. This guide gives you a decision process for every kind of image, worked examples of good and bad alt text, the markup, and how to add alt text on social media.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated October 2026·W3C Images Tutorial

Free tool: Alt Text Checker
Enter a page address and every image a visitor can see is checked for missing alt, image links with no name, file names, placeholders and alt that repeats the caption. An optional AI review looks at up to eight images in context and suggests better text.

Check a page's alt text

chunks.heading: What Alt Text Is For
chunks.text:
The alt attribute gives an image a text alternative. Screen readers speak it, braille displays show it, and browsers display it when the image does not load because of a slow connection, a blocked request or a broken link. Search engines read it too: Google's image SEO guidance says it combines alt text with computer vision and the page's content to work out what an image shows.
The requirement comes from WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content: every image that conveys something needs a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, and every image that is pure decoration must be marked so assistive technology can ignore it. Purpose is the word that matters. The alt does the image's job, which is not always the same as describing what the image looks like.

WCAG success criteria that apply to alt text, their level, and what each asks
Criterion Level What it means for images
1.1.1 Non-text Content A Informative images get a text alternative with the same purpose; decorative images get alt="" so they are skipped.
2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) A When an image is the only content of a link, its alt is the link text, so it must say where the link goes.
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value A Image buttons and icon-only controls need an accessible name that says what they do.

chunks.heading: What Alt Text Is For
chunks.text:
1.4.5 Images of Text AA Use real text instead of text baked into images, except for logos and where a particular look is essential.

So does every image need alt text? Every img needs an alt attribute. Whether that attribute holds words or is left empty depends on what the image is for, which is the next decision.

chunks.heading: Decide What the Image Is For First
chunks.text:
The same photo can need a full sentence on one page and nothing at all on another. A picture of a red bicycle on a product page is the product, so it needs a description. The same picture inside a link that already says “Shop bikes” adds nothing, so it gets alt="". Before you write a word, work through these questions in order. They follow the logic of the W3C alt decision tree, in our own words.

Does the image contain text? If the same words appear as real text next to it, or the lettering is only there for visual effect, use alt="". If the text has a function, as on an icon, say what the function is. Otherwise put the words from the image in the alt, and consider replacing the image with real text (1.4.5).
Is it in a link or a button? If the control's purpose would be unclear without it, the alt says where the link goes or what the button does, not what the picture shows.
Does it add meaning to the page? If it is a simple photo or illustration, write a short alt that carries that meaning. If it is a chart, diagram or map, write a short alt and give the full information in text elsewhere on the page. If it only repeats nearby text, use alt="".
Is it decoration, or not meant to be seen? Borders, flourishes, mood photos, spacers and tracking pixels get alt="".
Still unsure? The full W3C Images Tutorial covers the edge cases, including image maps.

chunks.heading: What to write for each kind of image
chunks.text:
Kinds of image by purpose, what the alt text should contain, and an example
Purpose What the alt should do Example
Informative Give the information or impression the image adds, in a phrase or a sentence. Volunteers planting trees along the canal towpath
Functional (links and buttons) Say where the link goes or what the button does. Acme home; Search; Print this page
Decorative Nothing. Use alt="" so screen readers skip it. A wave divider; a mood photo; an icon next to text that says the same
Image of text Repeat the words in the image, unless they are already real text nearby. Summer sale: 30% off all lamps
Complex (charts, diagrams, maps) Name it and give the main point; put the full detail in text on the page. Bar chart: sales doubled between 2023 and 2025. Data in the table below.
Group of images Let one image carry the alt for the whole group; give the rest alt="". Five star icons: first gets "Rated 4 out of 5", the others alt=""

Informative or decorative is a decision the author makes, based on why the image is on the page. Nobody else can make it for you, which is why automated tools can find missing alt but cannot tell you whether the alt you wrote is right.

chunks.heading: Alt Text Examples: Good and Bad
chunks.text: Eleven common images, each with the context that decides its alt text, a good version, versions to avoid, and the reasoning. Change the context and the right answer changes with it.

chunks.heading: Product photo
chunks.text:
The main image on a product page for a coat. The product name and price are in the text beside it.
Good
alt="Navy wool overcoat, knee length, with notch lapels and two flap pockets"

Avoid
alt="coat"
alt="mens-coat-navy-01.jpg"
alt="best wool coat mens winter coat navy coat sale"

Why
Describe what a shopper would look at: colour, cut, material, details. The name is already on the page, so spend the words on what the photo adds. In a product grid where the image and the product name sit inside one link, use alt="" so the name is not read twice.

chunks.heading: Logo on its own
chunks.text:
A partner's logo in a row of client logos. It is not a link.
Good
alt="Northwind Bank"

Avoid
alt="logo"
alt="northwind_logo_rgb.png"

Why
A logo is an image of text, so the alt is the words in it. Add "logo" only when the fact that it is a logo matters, for example on a brand guidelines page.

chunks.heading: Logo as a home link
chunks.text:
The site logo in the header, linking to the home page, with no other text in the link.
Good
alt="Acme home"

Avoid
alt=""
alt="Acme logo, click here to go to the home page"

Why
The alt becomes the link's name, so it should say where the link goes. An empty alt leaves the link with no name at all. If the link also contains the visible word "Acme", give the image alt="" instead.

chunks.heading: Icon button
chunks.text:
A magnifying glass button that opens site search. There is no visible text.
Good
aria-label="Search" on the button, with the SVG inside it hidden
alt="Search" on an image button

Avoid
alt="magnifying glass"
alt="icon"
alt="search-icon.svg"

Why
For controls, describe the action, not the picture. A printer icon is "Print this page", a cross is "Close", an arrow in a carousel is "Next slide". A visible text label is better still.

chunks.heading: Chart or graph
chunks.text:
A line chart in a quarterly report. The figures are in a table under the chart.
Good
alt="Line chart: website visits grew every quarter in 2025, from 40,000 to 95,000. Full figures in the table below."

Avoid
alt="chart"
alt="graph showing data"
a 300-word alt that reads out every data point

Why
The alt gives the point the chart makes and says where the detail is. The table gives the data in a form people can navigate. Without the table, the chart fails anyone who cannot see it.

chunks.heading: Image of a data table
chunks.text:
A screenshot of a delivery price table pasted into a blog post.
Good
A real HTML table instead of the image
If the image must stay: alt="Delivery prices by zone, also listed in the table below"

Avoid
alt="table"
every cell of the table typed into the alt

Why
An image of a table cannot be navigated cell by cell, resized, searched or translated. Screen reader users move through real tables with the row and column headers announced, which no alt text can match.

chunks.heading: Photo of a person in a news story
chunks.text:
A news photo with the caption: Council leader Maria Lopez after Tuesday's budget vote.
Good
alt="Lopez at the podium, holding up a copy of the flood defence plan"

Avoid
alt="Woman smiling"
alt that repeats the caption word for word

Why
The caption already names her, so the alt says what the photo shows that matters to the story. Mention appearance, such as age or ethnicity, only when it is relevant and you know it to be true.

chunks.heading: Artwork
chunks.text:
A painting on an art history page about the painter.
Good
alt="The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh, 1889: swirling blue sky with glowing stars and a crescent moon over a sleeping village, a dark cypress in the foreground"

Avoid
alt="painting"
alt="A beautiful masterpiece"

Why
Art is a sensory experience, so WCAG only asks you to identify it at minimum. On a page that is about the art, describe the subject, composition, colour and style. Put longer interpretation in visible text where everyone can read it.

chunks.heading: Screenshot
chunks.text:
A step in a help article showing where a setting lives.
Good
alt="Settings page with the Accessibility tab open and the Reduce motion switch turned on"

Avoid
alt="Screenshot"
alt="Screen Shot 2026-03-14 at 10.42.17.png"

Why
Say what the reader should see to confirm the step, not everything on the screen. The written steps should still work without the picture.

chunks.heading: CAPTCHA
chunks.text:
An image CAPTCHA on a sign-up form.
Good
alt="CAPTCHA: type the letters shown in this image. An audio version is available below."

Avoid
alt that contains the answer
alt="captcha"

Why
WCAG 1.1.1 asks the alt to say what the CAPTCHA is and what it is for, and requires another version in a different sense, such as audio. Better still, avoid image CAPTCHAs: at login, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication rules out a transcription test as the only way in.

chunks.heading: Decorative flourish
chunks.text:
A swirl divider between two sections of an article.
Good
alt=""
or a CSS background image

Avoid
alt="decorative swirl"
alt="divider"
no alt attribute at all

Why
An empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image. Describing it only adds noise, and leaving the attribute out can get the file name read aloud.

For charts, the accessible charts guide covers the data table and description patterns in depth, and the accessible data tables guide shows how to build the table that replaces an image of one. Maps have their own accessible maps guide.

chunks.heading: How Long Should Alt Text Be?
chunks.text: You will see “keep alt text under 125 characters” repeated as a rule. It is not one. WCAG sets no limit, and neither does the W3C Images Tutorial.

chunks.heading: Where the 125-character figure comes from
chunks.text: The number traces back to an old test in which JAWS 6, a screen reader release from around twenty years ago, read long alt text in chunks of roughly 125 characters. People who saw the break took it for a cut-off, and the figure spread from there, but the same testing found no screen reader that cut long alt text off. The history is laid out in a W3C WCAG discussion on alt text length and in accessibility consultant Eric Eggert's 2022 post There is no character limit for alt text.

chunks.heading: What actually matters
chunks.text:
Purpose sets the length. A home link needs two words. A product photo needs a sentence. A painting on a page about the painting may need two.
Lead with what matters. Screen reader users hear alt text read straight through and cannot skim it the way they skim a page, so put the key information first.
Say it once. No “image of”, no repeating the caption or the heading above, no list of keywords.
Long means move it. Alt text is invisible to sighted users. If a description needs more than a couple of sentences, the detail probably helps everyone, so put it in visible text: a caption, the body copy, or a long description linked to the image. Keep the alt short and say where the detail is.

As a working signal, our Alt Text Checker flags alt over 150 characters for a person to review rather than failing it. Some platforms set their own caps: X allows up to 1,000 characters per image description.

chunks.heading: Common Alt Text Mistakes and How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
Common alt text mistakes, why each one fails, and the fix
Mistake Why it fails The fix
Starting with "image of" or "picture of" Screen readers already announce that it is an image, so the user hears it twice. Start with the content. Name the medium only when it matters: "Oil painting of", "Screenshot of", "Pencil sketch of".
File names as alt (IMG_2041.jpg, hero-final-v3.png) They say nothing about the image, and they tend to appear when alt is filled in automatically rather than written. Write the alt by hand, and check whether your CMS, theme or upload tool fills it in for you.
Keyword stuffing A list of keywords is useless to someone listening. Google's image guidance warns that it is a poor experience and can look like spam. Describe the image. If it is relevant to the page, the right words appear naturally.
Repeating the caption A screen reader reads both, so the user hears the same sentence twice. Let the alt say what the picture shows and the caption give context, credit or date. If nearby text already describes the picture fully, alt="" is fine.
Empty alt on a linked image When the image is the only content of a link, the link has no name. Screen readers fall back to the URL or file name. W3C lists this as failure F89 of 2.4.4 and 4.1.2. Give the image alt text that says where the link goes.

chunks.heading: Common Alt Text Mistakes and How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
A title attribute instead of alt The title is only a fallback for the accessible name and only appears as a mouse tooltip, so keyboard and touch users never see it. Put the text in alt. Drop the title, or keep it only if it adds something the alt does not.
CMS placeholders ("image", "photo", "untitled", "alt text here") Placeholder words pass a check for an alt attribute while telling the user nothing. Ask for alt on every upload, with an explicit "decorative" option and help text that explains the decision process above.
No alt attribute at all Assistive technology cannot tell whether the image matters. Some screen readers read out the file name. Every img gets an alt attribute: descriptive text, or empty for decoration.

Auto-generated alt text deserves the same scepticism. Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn can add descriptions from object recognition, and AI tools write fluent drafts, but neither knows why the image is on your page. Treat them as a first draft to correct, never as the finished text.

chunks.heading: The alt attribute and alt=""
chunks.text: An empty alt is a deliberate signal that says “skip this”. A missing alt is an unanswered question, and some screen readers answer it by reading the file name. Acme

chunks.heading: SVG icons and images
chunks.text:
Inline SVG has no alt attribute. Give an informative SVG role="img" and a name, either with aria-label or with a title element referenced by aria-labelledby. Hide decorative SVGs, and SVG icons inside a button that already has a name, with aria-hidden="true". An SVG used through an img element takes a normal alt.
<!-- Informative inline SVG -->
<svg role="img" aria-label="Warning" viewBox="0 0 24 24">...</svg>

<!-- Or name it with a title element -->
<svg role="img" aria-labelledby="growth-title" viewBox="0 0 400 200">
<title id="growth-title">Visits doubled between 2024 and 2025</title>
...
</svg>

<!-- Icon button: name the button, hide the icon -->
<button type="button" aria-label="Search">
<svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24">...</svg>
</button>

<!-- Better still: a visible label -->
<button type="button">
<svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24">...</svg>
Search
</button>

The guide to using ARIA explains how aria-label, aria-labelledby and aria-hidden combine into the accessible name.

chunks.heading: figure and figcaption
chunks.text: A figcaption is visible to everyone and labels the figure, but it does not replace the image's alt. Let the two divide the work: the alt says what the picture shows, the caption adds the context, credit or date.

chunks.heading: Long descriptions for complex images
chunks.text:
For a chart or diagram, keep the alt short and put the full description in the page. The most robust pattern is a figure that contains the image, a caption and the data table. For a description that is plain text with no headings or tables, aria-describedby links it to the image; screen readers read the referenced text as one continuous paragraph, so keep it simple.

Customers request a label, post the item, and get a refund within five working days of it arriving.

chunks.heading: Groups of images and CSS backgrounds
chunks.text: When several images form one piece of information, such as a star rating, give one image the alt for the whole group and the rest alt="". Images set with CSS background-image have no alt at all, so use them only for decoration; anything informative belongs in an img element.

chunks.heading: How to Add Alt Text on Instagram, X, LinkedIn and Facebook
chunks.text: The same rules apply on social media: say what the image adds to the post, and if it contains text, such as a quote card or an event flyer, include the words. Menu names change often; these steps match each platform's help pages as of October 2026.

chunks.heading: Instagram
chunks.text:
New post in the app: after editing the photo, tap Next, then More options, then Write alt text. Type it and tap Done.
Existing post in the app: open it, tap the Options menu, tap Edit, then Edit alt text in the bottom right.
On a computer: choose Accessibility while editing the post, or for a shared post, Options, Edit, then Accessibility.

Instagram fills in automatic alt text if you write none. Replace it. Instagram help: edit alt text

chunks.heading: X
chunks.text:
In the apps: after adding the image to a post, tap +ALT on the image, type the description and tap Done.
On the web: select Add description under the image, type it and select Save.
An ALT badge then shows on the image. Each description can be up to 1,000 characters.

X's help covers adding it while you write the post, so do it before posting. X help: add image descriptions

chunks.heading: LinkedIn
chunks.text:
On desktop: after uploading the image, click the Alt text option below it, write the description and click Save.
On mobile: tap ALT below the image, write the description and tap Done.

LinkedIn may add alt text automatically to images that have none, and on mobile it does not tell you, so check before posting. LinkedIn help: alternative text

chunks.heading: Facebook
chunks.text:
Before posting, on a computer: hover over the photo, click Edit, choose Alternative text, then Custom alt text. Write it and click Save.
After posting: open the photo, choose Options, then Change alt text on a computer or Edit alt text in the iPhone and Android apps.

The apps only let you change alt text after posting; the automatic text starts with “Image may contain”. Facebook help: alternative text

chunks.heading: How to Test Your Alt Text
chunks.text:
Testing alt text has two halves. A tool can find alt that is missing or malformed on every image in seconds. Only a person can judge whether the alt that is there is right, so finish with a short screen reader pass.
Step 1: run the Alt Text Checker
Check one page of each template: home, article, product, listing. Fix the Failures first (missing alt, image links and buttons with no name, file names, placeholders), then work through Needs review. The optional AI review suggests alt for up to eight images; treat its suggestions as drafts.

Check a page's alt text
Draft what is missing. For a single image, the AI Alt Text Generator writes a first draft from an upload or an image address, with optional context about where the image is used. Edit it with the page in front of you.
Jump through the images with a screen reader. In NVDA (browse mode) and JAWS (virtual cursor), press G to move from graphic to graphic. In VoiceOver on a Mac, press VO+Command+G. Then read the page from the top, because alt only makes sense in context.
Ask four questions of each image. Would I understand this part of the page without seeing it? Does each linked image say where it goes? Are decorative images silent? Do I hear anything twice?

chunks.heading: How to Test Your Alt Text
chunks.text:
Check controls and the reading order. The screen reader simulator lists every image and control a screen reader meets on a page, and the accessible name previewer shows the name each button and link exposes.

New to screen readers? Start with the screen reader testing guide, then the NVDA or VoiceOver walkthrough.

chunks.heading: Alt Text Checklist
chunks.text:
Every img has an alt attribute. Words for images that convey something, empty for decoration, never missing.
Purpose decided first. Informative, functional, decorative, text, complex or group, before any words are written.
Links and buttons say what they do. No image-only link or button is left without a name (2.4.4, 4.1.2).
Text in images is repeated. And replaced with real text wherever possible, logos excepted (1.4.5).
Complex images have a long description. A short alt plus the full information in visible text or a table.
Key information first. Concise, no “image of”, no file names, no keyword lists.
No duplication. Alt does not repeat the caption, the link text or the heading beside it.
SVGs are named or hidden. role="img" with a name for informative SVGs, aria-hidden for decorative ones.
No placeholders shipped. CMS defaults, automatic captions and AI drafts reviewed by a person.
Tested. The Alt Text Checker is clean and a screen reader pass makes sense in context.

Then verify the rest of the page against the WCAG 2.2 checklist.

chunks.heading: Find Every Image That Needs Better Alt Text
chunks.text:
Audit a whole page in one pass, then draft the alt text that is missing and review it in context.
Open the Alt Text CheckerDraft alt text with AI

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
How do you write good alt text?▾
Start with what the image is doing on that page, not what it looks like. If it is a link or a button, say where it goes or what it does. If it shows information, write the information in a short phrase or sentence, leading with what matters most. If it repeats nearby text or is only decoration, use an empty alt attribute (alt="") so screen readers skip it. If it is a chart, diagram or map, write a short alt that gives the main point and put the full detail in text on the page. Leave out "image of", file names and keywords, and read it back in context to check it makes sense without the picture.

What is an example of good alt text?▾
For a product photo of a coat, "Navy wool overcoat, knee length, with notch lapels and two flap pockets" is good, while "coat" is too vague and "best mens wool coat winter sale" is keyword stuffing. For a logo that links to the home page, "Acme home" is good because it names the destination. For a magnifying glass search button, "Search" is good and "magnifying glass icon" is not. For a chart, "Line chart: visits grew every quarter in 2025, from 40,000 to 95,000. Full figures in the table below" gives the point and says where the data is.

How long should alt text be?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
As long as it needs to be to do the image's job, and no longer. WCAG sets no character limit. The often repeated 125-character rule traces back to an old version of the JAWS screen reader that read long alt text in pieces of about 125 characters, which some people mistook for a cut-off. Most informative images need a phrase or one or two sentences. Screen reader users hear alt text in one go and cannot skim it, so lead with what matters. If you need more than a couple of sentences, the image is probably complex: keep the alt short and put the full description in visible text.

When should alt text be empty?▾
Use an empty alt attribute (alt="") when the image adds nothing a screen reader user needs: decorative flourishes, dividers, background-style photos, and images whose meaning is already in the text right next to them, such as an icon beside a link that already says the same thing. Keep the attribute and leave the value empty. Never leave the attribute out, because some screen readers then read the file name. And never use an empty alt on an image that is the only content of a link or button, because the control is then left with no name.

What alt text should a logo have?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
A logo is an image of text, so its alt text is usually the words in the logo: the organisation's name, such as "Acme". When the logo is a link to the home page, the alt becomes the link's name, so say where it goes, such as "Acme home". If the link also contains the visible name as text, give the logo alt="" so the name is not read twice. Add the word "logo" only when the fact that it is a logo matters, for example on a page about brand guidelines.

How do you write alt text for a chart or graph?▾
Give the chart a short alt that names the type of chart and states its main point, for example "Bar chart: sales doubled between 2023 and 2025", and say where the detail is. Then put the full data on the page as text, ideally as a real HTML table next to the chart or in a figure with a caption. Do not cram every data point into the alt attribute: screen reader users cannot navigate it the way they can navigate a table, and sighted users who would benefit from the numbers never see it.

How do I add alt text on Instagram?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: In the Instagram app, when you create a post, tap Next after editing the photo, tap More options, then Write alt text, type your description and tap Done. To change the alt text of a post you have already shared, open it, tap the Options menu, tap Edit, then Edit alt text in the bottom right. On a computer, choose Accessibility while editing the post and write the alt text there. Instagram adds automatic alt text from object recognition if you write none, and your own description is almost always better.

chunks.heading: How to Write an Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
Three different legal regimes ask for three different documents, and most guides blur them together. This one keeps the UK's PSBAR model statement, the EU Web Accessibility Directive's model statement, and the EAA's Annex V information duty separate, then shows you exactly what to write and how to avoid publishing a statement that makes things worse.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated August 2026

Legal Regimes
3
PSBAR, WAD, and EAA all differ

EAA Legal Hook
Annex V
An information duty, not a template

Report Against
WCAG 2.2 AA
The standard behind your status

Our Tool
Free Generator
Builds a statement interactively

chunks.heading: What an Accessibility Statement Is, and Which Law Requires One
chunks.text:
An accessibility statement is a public page that tells users which accessibility standard your website targets, how far it actually meets that standard, what the known gaps are, and how to reach you when something does not work. Whether the law requires you to publish one depends entirely on which of three distinct regimes you fall under, and the single most common error on this topic is treating them as one:
UK public sector: PSBAR. The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 require public sector bodies to publish an accessibility statement in the government's model format. The content is prescribed, and GDS monitors published statements. Our UK compliance guide covers the wider context.
EU public sector: the Web Accessibility Directive. Directive (EU) 2016/2102 requires public sector bodies in EU member states to publish statements following the model in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1523. This is where the official EU model statement lives. It applies to the public sector, not to private companies under the EAA.
EU private sector: the European Accessibility Act. The EAA, which has applied since 28 June 2025, mandates no statement template at all. Instead it imposes an information requirement, explained in detail below.

chunks.heading: What an Accessibility Statement Is, and Which Law Requires One
chunks.text:
Everywhere else: voluntary. No law requires a private US website to publish a statement. A voluntary one still demonstrates good faith, gives users a working contact route, and is commonly requested in procurement. The W3C publishes guidance and a free generator, and our own accessibility statement generator produces one interactively.

Many competitor pages tell private companies to follow “the official EU accessibility statement template” for EAA compliance. There is no such thing: the model statement belongs to the public sector directive, and the EAA asks for something different. Getting this distinction right is the point of this guide.

chunks.heading: The UK Public Sector Statement Under PSBAR
chunks.text:
If you are a UK public sector body, the statement is not optional and its structure is not up to you. PSBAR requires a statement in the government's model format, containing:
Compliance status: fully compliant, partially compliant, or not compliant with WCAG at level AA.
Non-accessible content, with reasons: each item listed as a non-compliance with the regulations, a claim of disproportionate burden, or content that is out of scope of the regulations.
Accessible formats: how users can request content in an accessible format.
Reporting route: how users can report accessibility problems with the site.
Enforcement procedure: in Great Britain, EASS (the Equality Advisory and Support Service) and the EHRC; in Northern Ireland, the ECNI.
Dates: when the statement was prepared and when it was last reviewed.

GDS reviews statements as part of its PSBAR monitoring programme, and that monitoring now tests against WCAG 2.2 AA, so the status you declare should be measured against the current standard. Our WCAG 2.2 checklist and UK compliance guide cover what that testing looks for.

chunks.heading: The EAA and Private Companies: An Information Duty, Not a Template
chunks.text:
The European Accessibility Act has applied to in-scope products and services since 28 June 2025, and it takes a different approach from the public sector directive. There is no single mandated statement template. What service providers must do is provide information, in their general terms and conditions or an equivalent document, explaining how the service meets the accessibility requirements. That duty comes from the Directive's Annex V, and it breaks down into three parts:
Describe the service in a general way, so it is clear what the information covers.
Explain how it meets the accessibility requirements that apply to it. In practice, conformance is assessed against EN 301 549, the European standard that incorporates WCAG for web content.
Make the information available in accessible form to the public, including for persons with disabilities.

A public accessibility statement is the practical way most businesses satisfy this: one well-structured page can describe the service, state its conformance status against EN 301 549 and WCAG, list known limitations, and be accessible itself. That is good practice and we recommend it. But be precise about the legal position: the hook is the Annex V information requirement, not a statement template, and copying the public sector model statement does not automatically discharge it.

chunks.heading: The EAA and Private Companies: An Information Duty, Not a Template
chunks.text: Enforcement is national, and it has teeth. Ireland, for example, enforces the EAA with criminal penalties; see our EAA Ireland guide for the details, and the EAA overview for who is in scope.

chunks.heading: What Every Good Statement Contains
chunks.text:
Across all three regimes, and for voluntary statements too, the same core elements separate a useful statement from filler:
The standard you target. Name the version and level, normally WCAG 2.2 Level AA. Our WCAG 2.2 AA requirements guide explains what that commitment covers.
Your actual conformance status, told honestly. Fully compliant, partially compliant, or not compliant. Most live sites are partially compliant, and saying so is a strength, not a confession.
Known limitations, listed specifically. “Some older PDFs are not tagged” and “the store locator map has no keyboard alternative” are useful; “some content may not be fully accessible” is not.
A real contact channel with a response commitment. An email address or form that reaches someone empowered to act, and a stated timeframe for replying.
Dates. When the statement was prepared and when it was last reviewed.
How the site was evaluated. Say whether the status rests on self-evaluation or a third-party accessibility audit, and when. Our auditing guide walks through both approaches.

chunks.heading: Statement Mistakes That Create Risk
chunks.text:
A bad statement is worse than no statement. The failure patterns are consistent:
If a statement is already published, the accessibility statement checker will read it and report which of the required elements are actually present. When GDS monitored 593 UK public sector sites, only about 7 percent had a fully compliant statement, while 83 percent had published one that was missing mandatory information.
Overclaiming. Declaring “fully compliant” while the homepage fails basic automated checks contradicts what users experience, and in a dispute the statement becomes evidence that you knew accessibility was an obligation and misstated your position. A statement is a claim about your site, so it should follow testing, not precede it.
Vagueness. A page of “we care about accessibility” sentiment with no conformance status, no contact route, and no date commits you to nothing and helps no one. It reads as decoration because it is.
Stale dates. A statement last reviewed years ago tells users, monitors, and procurement teams that nothing behind it is being maintained either.
No contact route. The contact channel is the most practically valuable part of the whole document: it lets a blocked user reach you instead of an enforcement body or a law firm. Omitting it wastes the statement's best feature.

chunks.heading: Statement Mistakes That Create Risk
chunks.text: And keep expectations realistic: a statement is not a legal shield. It does not immunize you against Equality Act claims, ADA lawsuits, or EAA enforcement. It is transparency plus a communication channel, and its value depends entirely on being accurate.

chunks.heading: Write Yours Now
chunks.text:
Draft it with the generator. Our free accessibility statement generator walks you through the elements above interactively: the standard you target, your conformance status, known limitations, evaluation method, contact details, and dates, and produces a statement you can publish.
Validate every claim before you publish. Run your key pages through the URL accessibility auditor for an automated baseline, and remember that automated tools catch only part of WCAG. For a conformance status you can stand behind, commission a professional audit with manual and screen reader testing; our sample audit report shows what that evidence looks like.
Publish it where users look. Link the statement from your site footer on every page, and make sure the statement page itself meets the standard it describes.
Keep it current. Update the statement after each remediation round or audit, review it at least annually, and refresh the review date so readers can see it is maintained.

chunks.heading: Do I legally need an accessibility statement?
chunks.text: It depends on who you are and where you operate. UK public sector bodies must publish one under PSBAR, in the government's model format. Public sector bodies in EU member states must publish one under the Web Accessibility Directive, following the model statement in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1523. Private companies covered by the European Accessibility Act are not handed a statement template at all: since 28 June 2025 they must provide information, in their general terms and conditions or an equivalent document, explaining how the service meets the accessibility requirements, and most meet that duty with a public statement. For private US websites, no law requires a statement, but a voluntary one demonstrates good faith, gives users a working contact route, and is commonly requested in procurement.

chunks.heading: What must a PSBAR accessibility statement include?
chunks.text: PSBAR statements must follow the UK government's model format and state the compliance status (fully compliant, partially compliant, or not compliant with WCAG at level AA), list non-accessible content with the reason for each item (non-compliance with the regulations, a disproportionate burden claim, or content out of scope), explain how to request content in accessible formats, explain how to report accessibility problems, describe the enforcement procedure (EASS, the Equality Advisory and Support Service, and the EHRC in Great Britain; the ECNI in Northern Ireland), and give the date the statement was prepared and the date it was last reviewed. GDS checks statements as part of its PSBAR monitoring, which now tests against WCAG 2.2 AA.

chunks.heading: Does the EAA require an accessibility statement?
chunks.text: Not in the way many pages claim. There is no single mandated EAA statement template; the official EU model statement belongs to the Web Accessibility Directive for the public sector, not to the EAA. What the EAA actually requires of service providers is an information duty: under the Directive's Annex V, they must describe the service, explain how it meets the applicable accessibility requirements, and make that information available to the public in written and oral format, in a way accessible to persons with disabilities, in their general terms and conditions or an equivalent document. A public accessibility statement is the most practical way to satisfy that duty, and good practice besides, but the legal hook is the information requirement, not a template.

chunks.heading: Can I write an accessibility statement before testing my site?
chunks.text: You can, but you should not. A statement is a factual claim about the current state of your site, so it should follow testing, not precede it. A statement written before any evaluation is guesswork, and if it guesses optimistically it becomes a liability: claiming full compliance while your homepage fails basic checks contradicts user experience, destroys trust, and can be cited in a dispute as evidence that you knew accessibility mattered and misrepresented your status anyway. Run at least an automated scan, and ideally a manual audit, before you publish a conformance claim.

chunks.heading: What does "partially compliant" mean in an accessibility statement?
chunks.text: Partially compliant means the site meets most of the target standard, typically WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 at level AA, but has known exceptions, and the statement lists them. It is the honest status for the majority of real websites. Fully compliant means every applicable success criterion passes, a claim you should only make after thorough testing. Not compliant means the site has not been evaluated against the standard or fails it broadly. Choosing partially compliant and itemizing the gaps, with plans to fix them, is far more credible than an unsupported claim of full compliance.

chunks.heading: Does an accessibility statement protect me from being sued?
chunks.text: No. A statement is not a legal shield: it does not immunize you against Equality Act claims in the UK, ADA lawsuits in the US, or EAA enforcement in the EU. What it does is provide transparency about where your site stands and a communication channel that lets users report problems to you before they escalate elsewhere. That can reduce friction and demonstrate good faith, but the underlying obligation is an accessible service, not a published document. An inaccurate statement can even make things worse by showing awareness without action.

chunks.heading: How often should I review my accessibility statement?
chunks.text: Review it at least annually, and update it whenever the site changes significantly or after each audit or remediation round. PSBAR statements must carry both a preparation date and a last review date, and GDS monitoring checks that statements are kept current. Even for voluntary statements, a review date from several years ago signals that the commitments inside are stale, and users and procurement teams read it exactly that way. Put the review on a calendar, and tie it to your regular testing cycle so the status you publish always reflects a recent evaluation.

chunks.heading: Educational Content, Not Legal Advice
chunks.text: This page is provided for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Accessibility statement obligations differ by jurisdiction and sector, and enforcement practice under PSBAR, the Web Accessibility Directive, and the European Accessibility Act continues to develop. For advice about your specific obligations, consult a lawyer experienced in accessibility law in the relevant jurisdiction.

chunks.heading: JAWS Screen Reader Testing: The Complete Guide
chunks.text:
JAWS is the screen reader your enterprise and government users are most likely running — and you can test with it today without buying a license. This guide covers the JAWS key, the Virtual Cursor and Forms Mode, quick navigation keys, and a repeatable testing workflow, with full command cheat sheets mapped to WCAG 2.2 AA.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated July 2026

chunks.heading: Why Test with JAWS
chunks.text:
A screen reader turns the visual interface into speech and braille. It reads out headings, links, buttons, form labels, and status messages, and lets the user navigate by those structures instead of by sight. If your markup is wrong — a button with no name, a table with no headers, an update that never announces — the screen reader has nothing meaningful to say, and the feature is unusable no matter how good it looks.
JAWS (Job Access With Speech), from Freedom Scientific, is the longest-established Windows screen reader and has consistently been among the most used in WebAIM’s screen reader user surveys. It is especially entrenched in the environments where accessibility is legally required — government, higher education, banking, healthcare, and large enterprises, where it is often the standard-issue assistive technology. If your audience includes those users, testing with NVDA alone does not cover them. In WebAIM’s 2026 survey JAWS was the primary desktop screen reader for 55.0% of respondents, up from 40.5% in 2024, and 72.5% in North America; the screen reader survey 2026 analysis has the full regional split.

chunks.heading: Why Test with JAWS
chunks.text: JAWS also has a testing personality worth knowing about: it is aggressive about inference. It works hard to guess what an author meant, which is wonderful for its users and slightly dangerous for you — JAWS can quietly paper over sloppy markup that NVDA or VoiceOver read literally and get wrong. That cuts both ways. Something that fails in JAWS is almost certainly broken; something that passes in JAWS is not automatically fine elsewhere. Automated scanners like axe and WAVE catch roughly a third of issues; the rest needs a human listening. This guide is the JAWS-specific companion to our VoiceOver testing guide, our TalkBack testing guide for Android, and our broader screen reader testing guide.

chunks.heading: 1. Install JAWS & Configure It for Testing
chunks.text: JAWS is commercial software, but you do not need a license to test with it — and that surprises a lot of teams into skipping JAWS entirely.

chunks.heading: Getting a copy
chunks.text:
Download JAWS from Freedom Scientific. It is Windows only.
Unlicensed, it runs in 40-minute demo mode — fully functional, then restart Windows for another 40 minutes. That is enough for a testing pass.
A Home Annual License covers personal, non-commercial use cheaply; organizations need a professional license.
No Windows machine? Use a VM or a cloud Windows desktop.

chunks.heading: Configure before you test
chunks.text:
Pick your keyboard layout: Desktop (JAWS key = Insert) or Laptop (JAWS key = CapsLock). Laptops have no Insert key or numpad — choose Laptop.
Test in Chrome, the most common JAWS pairing. Edge behaves nearly identically.
Slow the speech rate down at first (JAWS+V Quick Settings) — default JAWS speech is fast.
Press Ctrl anytime to silence speech.

One practical tip: turn on Speech History (JAWS+Space, then H) early. It shows you a transcript of what JAWS just spoke, which is invaluable when a live region fires once and you are not sure whether you actually heard it.

chunks.heading: 2. The JAWS Key, the Virtual Cursor, and Forms Mode
chunks.text: Two concepts explain most of how JAWS works. Get these right and the rest of the commands fall into place — and one of them is the source of the most common JAWS-only bug you will find.

chunks.heading: The JAWS key
chunks.text:
Most commands start with the JAWS key, which depends on your layout setting:
Desktop layout: Insert
Laptop layout: CapsLock

So JAWS+F6 means Insert+F6 or CapsLock+F6. If cheat sheet commands are not working, a mismatched layout is almost always why.

chunks.heading: Virtual Cursor vs Forms Mode
chunks.text:
Virtual Cursor — reading mode. Arrow keys and single-letter quick nav keys (H, B, F) move you through a virtual copy of the page.
Forms Mode — interaction mode. Keystrokes pass through to the control so you can type.

JAWS enters Forms Mode automatically on a text field, or on Enter. Leave it with Numpad Plus or Escape.

Here is why this matters more than any other JAWS concept. In the Virtual Cursor, pressing B jumps to the next button — it does not type the letter B. So if you build a custom text input or combo box that JAWS does not recognize as a form control, JAWS never switches to Forms Mode, and every letter the user types teleports them somewhere else on the page instead of entering text. The widget looks fine, passes an automated scan, works with a mouse — and is completely unusable. That failure mode is the single best reason to test with JAWS specifically, and it comes down to giving controls a role JAWS understands. See the ARIA roles & attributes reference and the focus management guide.

chunks.heading: 3. Quick Navigation Keys (Cheat Sheet)
chunks.text:
Single letters that jump between element types. These work when the Virtual Cursor is active — not in Forms Mode. Add Shift to go backwards. This is how a JAWS user actually moves around a page, so it is also the fastest way to audit whether your structure exists at all.
JAWS quick navigation keys for moving between element types on a web page
Key What it does
H / Shift+H Next / previous heading
1 – 6 Next heading at that level (Shift for previous)
R / Shift+R Next / previous region (landmark)
K / Shift+K Next / previous link
B / Shift+B Next / previous button
F / Shift+F Next / previous form field
E / Shift+E Next / previous edit box
X / Shift+X Next / previous checkbox
C / Shift+C Next / previous combo box
T / Shift+T Next / previous table
L / Shift+L Next / previous list
G / Shift+G Next / previous graphic

If H finds no headings, R finds no regions, or B skips a control that looks like a button, you have found a real structural defect — not a JAWS quirk.

chunks.heading: 4. Essential JAWS Commands (Cheat Sheet)
chunks.text:
JAWS below means the JAWS key — Insert in the Desktop layout, CapsLock in the Laptop layout. These commands cover almost everything you need to test a web page.
Essential JAWS keyboard commands and what each one does
Command What it does
JAWS+Down Arrow Say All — read continuously from the cursor
Ctrl Stop speech immediately
Tab / Shift+Tab Move to the next / previous focusable control
JAWS+Tab Say the currently focused control (name, role, state)
Enter Activate the control, or enter Forms Mode on a field
Numpad Plus Leave Forms Mode, return to the Virtual Cursor
JAWS+Z Toggle the Virtual Cursor on or off
JAWS+F6 Headings List — the page outline
JAWS+F7 Links List
JAWS+F5 Form Fields List
JAWS+F9 Frames List
JAWS+F3 Virtual HTML Features — every element list in one dialog
JAWS+T Read the page title
JAWS+B Read the active window or dialog from top to bottom
JAWS+F1 Screen-sensitive help for the current control
JAWS+Space, then H Open Speech History — re-read what JAWS just said
JAWS+V Quick Settings for the current application
JAWS+F12 Toggle verbosity / speech on many builds — check Quick Settings

To learn what any key does without triggering it, turn on keyboard help with JAWS+1 and press keys freely; press JAWS+1 again to leave. Command sets do shift slightly between JAWS releases — the authoritative list is always in the JAWS Help menu on the version you have installed.

chunks.heading: 5. Audit Structure with the JAWS Lists
chunks.text:
JAWS can dump every element of a given type into a dialog. Open each list and read it as if it were the page’s table of contents — this is exactly how a JAWS user surveys an unfamiliar page, and it takes about ninety seconds.
Headings List (JAWS+F6). Confirm there is exactly one <h1>, that levels do not skip, and that the outline alone tells you what the page is about. Maps to 1.3.1 Info and Relationships.
Links List (JAWS+F7). Read out of context, every link should still make sense — no wall of “click here” or “read more” (2.4.x link purpose). This list is the single most damning view of lazy link text.
Form Fields List (JAWS+F5). Every field should show a real label, not “edit.” Cross-check with the accessible forms guide.
Virtual HTML Features (JAWS+F3). One dialog with every element type — regions, lists, tables, buttons, graphics. Check that banner, navigation, main, and contentinfo regions all exist.

chunks.heading: 6. A Repeatable JAWS Testing Workflow
chunks.text:
Run this pass on every key page or flow. It fits comfortably inside one 40-minute demo session.
Check the page title. Press JAWS+T. It should be unique and describe the page, not just the site name.
Survey the structure. Open the Headings List (JAWS+F6), then Links (JAWS+F7), then regions via JAWS+F3.
Read it all. Press JAWS+Down Arrow to Say All from the top. Note anything that sounds wrong — an image reading its file name, a button that says only “button,” content in the wrong order.
Walk it with quick nav keys. Press H repeatedly, then B, then F. Every heading, button, and field should announce a name and a role.
Tab through it. Now use Tab only. The order should be logical, and JAWS+Tab should announce a sensible name, role, and state for each stop.
Operate each widget — and watch Forms Mode. Open menus, toggle disclosures, type into custom inputs. If typing jumps you around the page, JAWS never entered Forms Mode and the widget is broken.
Trigger dynamic changes. Submit a form with an error, add to cart, filter a list. JAWS should announce the change without you moving focus — that is 4.1.3 Status Messages. Verify in Speech History if unsure.
Check modals and focus. When a dialog opens, JAWS+B should read it; focus should move into it, stay trapped, and return to the trigger on close.

chunks.heading: Common JAWS Findings & How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
These are the problems JAWS surfaces most often. Each one is a real WCAG failure that automated tools frequently miss or can only partially detect.
Common problems found when testing with JAWS, why they fail, and the fix
What you hear Why it fails The fix
A <div onclick> that JAWS skips entirely with the B quick nav key. It has no button role and is not focusable, so it is invisible to a screen reader (WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2). Use a real <button>. If you cannot, add role="button", tabIndex, and key handlers.
A custom widget where typing does nothing — letters jump you around the page instead. JAWS never entered Forms Mode, so quick nav keys consumed the keystrokes (WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2). Give the widget a role that triggers Forms Mode (textbox, combobox, listbox) and manage focus into it.
A field JAWS announces as just "edit" with no label. Unlabeled input — the user does not know what to type (WCAG 1.3.1, 4.1.2). Associate a <label> with for/id, or use aria-label / aria-labelledby.
An error appears on submit but JAWS says nothing. The update is not in a live region (WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages). Render errors into an aria-live="assertive" or role="alert" container, or move focus to the summary.

chunks.heading: Common JAWS Findings & How to Fix Them
chunks.text:
A data table where JAWS reads cell values with no column context. Missing header association, so relationships are lost (WCAG 1.3.1). Use <th scope="col">/<th scope="row">, and a <caption> naming the table.
The Headings List (JAWS+F6) is empty or shows one flat level. Styled <div>s instead of real headings — no structure to navigate (WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.6). Use <h1>–<h6> in a logical, non-skipping order.

Fixing most of these comes down to correct roles, names, and states — verify them programmatically under 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value. When you report a JAWS bug, always name the JAWS version and the browser: behavior is a product of both working together, and a report without them is often unreproducible.

chunks.heading: What JAWS Testing Verifies in WCAG 2.2
chunks.text:
WCAG 2.2 success criteria you can verify by testing with JAWS
Criterion Level What JAWS reveals
1.1.1 Non-text Content A Graphics announce meaningful alt text, not file names.
1.3.1 Info and Relationships A Headings, lists, and table headers appear in the JAWS lists.
2.1.1 Keyboard A Every control is reachable and operable — including in Forms Mode.
2.4.3 Focus Order A Tabbing follows a logical, meaningful order.
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value A Controls announce a name, role, and current state via JAWS+Tab.
4.1.3 Status Messages AA Dynamic updates are announced without moving focus.

See the full picture in the WCAG 2.2 Level AA requirements and track your coverage with the WCAG 2.2 checklist.

chunks.heading: JAWS vs NVDA in brief
chunks.text:
Both are Windows-only. JAWS is paid (40-min demo); NVDA is free.
JAWS key is Insert/CapsLock; NVDA key is Insert/CapsLock too — but commands differ.
JAWS “Virtual Cursor / Forms Mode” ≈ NVDA “browse / focus mode.”
JAWS infers more from imperfect markup; NVDA is more literal. Test both.
JAWS dominates enterprise and government; NVDA is common everywhere else.

See the NVDA testing guide for the free alternative.

chunks.heading: Test the keyboard first
chunks.text:
A screen reader relies on the keyboard working.
If Tab cannot reach a control, JAWS will struggle too.
Fix keyboard operability before chasing speech bugs.

Start with the keyboard accessibility guide.

chunks.heading: JAWS Testing Checklist
chunks.text:
Setup. JAWS installed (demo mode is fine), keyboard layout matches your hardware, testing in Chrome, Speech History available.
Title & structure. Unique page title; one <h1>; heading levels do not skip; regions present in JAWS+F3.
Names & roles. Every link, button, and field announces a clear name and role — no bare “button” or “edit.”
Quick nav. H, B, F, and R all find what they should — nothing structural is missing.
Forms Mode. Every text input and custom widget lets you actually type; no keystroke ever teleports you across the page.
Tables. Data tables announce column and row headers with each cell.
Dynamic updates. Errors, cart counts, and filter results are announced — confirmed in Speech History.
Dialogs. Focus moves into modals, is trapped, and returns to the trigger on close.
Cross-check. Anything that passes only in JAWS re-verified in NVDA or VoiceOver, since JAWS is the most forgiving of the three.

chunks.heading: Scan Before You Listen
chunks.text:
Automated scanning clears the obvious issues so your 40-minute JAWS session is spent on the problems only a human can hear. Run a free axe-core scan first, then work through the JAWS pass above.
Scan a Page NowScreen Reader Testing Guide

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is JAWS free, and how can I test with it without buying a license?▾
JAWS is commercial software from Freedom Scientific and is not free, but you do not need to buy a license to test with it. JAWS runs in a 40-minute demo mode: install it, use it fully for 40 minutes, then restart Windows to get another 40 minutes. That is enough for most testing passes, and it is how many teams do their JAWS verification. Freedom Scientific also offers a Home Annual License for personal, non-commercial use at a much lower cost than a professional license. If you are testing on behalf of an organization, the professional license is the correct route, and many enterprises and government agencies already own one.

Why test with JAWS if NVDA is free?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Because your users are on JAWS. In WebAIM's screen reader user surveys, JAWS has consistently been among the most used screen readers, and it is dominant in exactly the environments where accessibility is legally required — government agencies, universities, banks, healthcare, and large enterprises where it is the standard-issue assistive technology. More importantly, JAWS and NVDA do not behave identically: they differ in how they interpret certain ARIA patterns, how aggressively they switch into Forms Mode, and how they announce tables, live regions, and custom widgets. A pattern that sounds perfect in NVDA can be silent or confusing in JAWS. If your audience includes enterprise or government users, NVDA testing alone does not cover them.

What is the JAWS key?▾
The JAWS key is the modifier that starts most JAWS commands. Which key it is depends on your keyboard layout setting. In the Desktop layout — the default on machines with a full keyboard — the JAWS key is Insert. In the Laptop layout, it is Caps Lock, which matters because most laptops have no Insert key and no numeric keypad. So a command written as JAWS+F6 means Insert+F6 on a desktop and Caps Lock+F6 on a laptop. You can set the layout during installation or afterwards in JAWS Settings Center. If commands in a cheat sheet are not working for you, a mismatched keyboard layout is the most likely cause.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is the difference between the Virtual Cursor and Forms Mode in JAWS?▾
The Virtual Cursor (also called the PC Cursor in virtual documents) is JAWS's reading mode for web pages. It builds a virtual copy of the page you can move through with arrow keys and quick navigation keys — press H for the next heading, B for the next button, and so on. Forms Mode is JAWS's interaction mode: your keystrokes pass straight through to the control so you can actually type in a field. JAWS switches to Forms Mode automatically when focus lands on a text input, and you can force it with Enter. To leave Forms Mode and get back to the Virtual Cursor, press Numpad Plus (Desktop layout) or Escape. This is the single most important JAWS concept for testers, because the classic bug it exposes is a custom widget that JAWS never enters Forms Mode for — meaning quick nav keys steal the keystrokes and the widget cannot be operated at all.

Which browser should I use for JAWS testing?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Chrome is the best default. Freedom Scientific officially supports Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and Chrome is both the most-used browser among JAWS users and the pairing that receives the most attention from Freedom Scientific. Edge, being Chromium-based, behaves very similarly and is a reasonable choice in enterprises standardized on it. Whichever you pick, be consistent — reporting a bug as "fails in JAWS" without naming the browser makes it hard to reproduce, since screen reader behavior is genuinely a function of the screen reader and browser working together.

Does passing JAWS testing mean my site is accessible?▾
No. JAWS testing proves your content works with one screen reader on one platform. It does not cover NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, or TalkBack on Android — all of which interpret ARIA and announce content differently — and it says nothing about low vision, cognitive, or motor needs. JAWS is also, in one specific way, a deceptively forgiving tester: it is aggressive about guessing what an author meant, so it can paper over sloppy markup that other screen readers read literally and get wrong. Treat JAWS as one layer alongside keyboard-only testing, an automated scan, color contrast checks, and at least one other screen reader. Meeting WCAG 2.2 AA is the standard; JAWS is one of the tools you use to verify you have met it.

chunks.heading: Keyboard Accessibility
chunks.text:
Every feature on a page has to be reachable and operable with a keyboard alone, and that one requirement decides how you build focus order, skip links, custom widgets, and modals. This guide covers focus management, roving tabindex, keyboard traps, and focus trapping, with interactive demos and copy-ready code mapped to WCAG 2.2.
Reviewed by Khushwant Parihar, CPACC
Updated March 2026

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
Keyboard accessibility ensures that every feature on your website can be reached and operated using only a keyboard -- no mouse or touch input required. According to the CDC, approximately 26% of adults in the United States have some form of disability, and roughly 7.5% have a motor disability that affects their ability to use a pointing device. These numbers represent tens of millions of people who may depend entirely on keyboard navigation to interact with the web.
The reach of keyboard accessibility extends far beyond users with permanent disabilities. Power users prefer keyboard shortcuts for speed and efficiency. Screen reader users rely on the keyboard as their primary navigation interface since screen readers are inherently keyboard-driven tools. People with temporary injuries -- a broken arm, recovering from surgery, or dealing with repetitive strain injury -- also depend on keyboard access. By building keyboard-accessible interfaces, you serve all of these groups simultaneously.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text:
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) encode these requirements into specific, testable success criteria. The four most directly relevant are: 2.1.1 Keyboard (all functionality must be operable via keyboard), 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (focus can always be moved away from any component), 2.4.3 Focus Order (navigation sequence must be logical and meaningful), and 2.4.7 Focus Visible (the keyboard focus indicator must always be clearly visible). This guide covers all four in depth, with interactive demos and production-ready code examples.

Level A
2.1.1
Keyboard

Level A
2.1.2
No Keyboard Trap

Level A
2.4.3
Focus Order

Level AA
2.4.7
Focus Visible

chunks.heading: Tab Order
chunks.text:
When a user presses the Tab key, the browser moves focus to the next focusable element in the DOM order -- the order elements appear in your HTML source. This is why your source order should match your visual layout. Using CSS to visually rearrange elements (via flexbox order, grid positioning, or absolute positioning) without matching the DOM order creates a disorienting experience for keyboard users.
The tabindex attribute controls how elements participate in the tab sequence. Use tabindex="0" to add a non-interactive element to the natural tab order. Use tabindex="-1" to make an element focusable via JavaScript but not via Tab. Never use positive values like tabindex="5" -- they override the natural DOM order and create an unpredictable, maintenance-nightmare tab sequence.
Never use positive tabindex values. They override the natural tab order and make maintenance extremely difficult. Stick to 0 and -1.

chunks.heading: Native vs Custom Elements
chunks.text: Semantic HTML elements like <button>, <a href>, and <input> are keyboard-accessible by default. A button can be activated with Enter or Space. A link can be followed with Enter. Form inputs accept keyboard input naturally. When you use a <div> or <span> as an interactive element, you lose all built-in behavior and must manually add tabindex, role, onKeyDown, and onClick handlers. Always prefer native elements when a suitable one exists.

chunks.heading: Focus Indicators
Skip Links
chunks.text:
Skip navigation links are anchor links placed at the very beginning of a page. They are visually hidden until they receive keyboard focus, at which point they slide into view. When activated, they move focus directly to the main content area, allowing keyboard users to bypass the header, navigation menus, and other repetitive blocks that appear on every page. Without skip links, a keyboard user visiting your site must press Tab through every single navigation link on every page load before reaching the content.
WCAG Success Criterion 2.4.1 (Bypass Blocks) requires a mechanism for skipping repeated content. Skip links are the simplest, most universally supported approach. They are typically implemented as the very first element inside the <body> tag, styled off-screen by default, and animated into view on focus.

Interactive Demo

Press Tab to focus into this demo. The skip link will appear at the top-left. Press Enter to jump past the nav links directly to the main content area.
Skip to main contentLogo

chunks.heading: Main Content Area
Focus Management
chunks.text: In static HTML pages, focus management happens naturally -- the user tabs through elements in sequence. But modern web applications are dynamic: content loads asynchronously, pages change without full reloads, and elements appear and disappear in response to user actions. In these situations, you must programmatically move focus to keep keyboard users oriented.

chunks.heading: When to Manage Focus
When to Manage Focus
Roving Tabindex
Roving Tabindex
Keyboard Traps
chunks.text:
A keyboard trap occurs when a keyboard user navigates into a component and cannot navigate out using the keyboard alone. The Tab key and Shift+Tab either do nothing or cycle within the same component indefinitely. Common causes include custom widgets that intercept Tab key events without allowing escape, embedded third-party iframes (ads, chat widgets, video players), JavaScript event listeners that call e.preventDefault() on all keydown events, and auto-focus loops where a blur handler immediately refocuses the same element.
WCAG 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap): If keyboard focus can be moved to a component using a keyboard interface, then focus must be movable away from that component using only a keyboard. If it requires more than standard keys (Tab, Shift+Tab, Arrow keys), the user must be advised of the method.

Interactive Demo

Switch between the "Bad" and "Good" tabs to compare. In the Bad tab, activating the trap prevents Tab from working. Press Escape to exit the trap.
Bad: Keyboard TrapGood: No Trap

chunks.heading: Custom Widget (Trap Demo)
Modal Focus Trapping
chunks.text: Modal dialogs are the single exception to the "no keyboard trap" rule. When a modal is open, focus should be trapped inside it because the background content is inert and not visible to the user. Without focus trapping, a keyboard user could Tab behind the modal into content they cannot see, which is even more disorienting than the trap itself.

chunks.heading: Requirements for Accessible Modals
Requirements for Accessible Modals
Custom Widgets
chunks.text:
When building custom interactive widgets -- dropdown menus, tab panels, tree views, sliders, comboboxes -- you must implement the keyboard patterns that users expect based on the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide. These conventions are what assistive technology users learn and rely on. Deviating from them means your widget will be unpredictable and unusable for keyboard-only users.
The table below summarizes the expected keyboard interactions for common widget types. When building any custom widget, always consult the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide for the full specification.

Widget Keys Behavior
Button Enter Space Activate
Link Enter Navigate
Checkbox Space Toggle
Radio Group Arrow keys Select option
Tab Panel Arrow keys Switch tabs
Menu Arrow keys Enter Escape Navigate, select, close
Dialog Tab Escape Cycle focus, close
Combobox Arrow keys Enter Escape Navigate, select, close
Slider Arrow keys Adjust value

chunks.heading: Testing Checklist
chunks.text:
Use this checklist every time you build or audit a page. Disconnect your mouse, put it in a drawer, and navigate the entire page using only your keyboard. Mark each item as you verify it. You can download a PDF copy of this checklist using the button below.
1. Can you Tab to all interactive elements?
2. Is the tab order logical and follows visual layout?
3. Are focus indicators clearly visible?
4. Can you activate all controls with Enter/Space?
5. Can you navigate custom widgets with arrow keys?
6. Are there any keyboard traps?
7. Do modals trap and return focus correctly?
8. Do skip navigation links work?
9. Can you access all content without a mouse?
10. Does focus move correctly for dynamic content?
