chunks.heading: Why an agent and a screen reader fail on the same page
chunks.text:
Anthropic's browser-use tool, generally available since 19 August 2026, operates a page “through its structure: the accessibility tree, elements, forms, and tabs”. OpenAI's computer-using agent and Google's Mariner ground their actions in the same tree plus a screenshot. The tree is what a screen reader has always read: for each control, a role and a name. When the name is missing, a screen reader announces “button” and an agent receives - button. Neither can tell it from the next one.
Google now tells site owners the same thing. Its guide to optimizing for generative AI features in Google Search says browser agents may gather what they need from a site by “analyzing visual renderings (like screenshots), inspecting the DOM structure, and interpreting the accessibility tree”. A control with no name is a gap in that last view.
This is not a new class of defect. It is WCAG 4.1.2, the criterion pleaded in Robles v. Domino's, and it is what WebAIM found on 30.6% of the top million home pages (empty buttons) and 46.3% (empty links) in 2026. What has changed is who is affected. Agentic traffic passed half of all internet traffic in June 2026, and an agent acting for a sighted customer fails on the same nameless button a blind customer does.

chunks.heading: Method
chunks.text:
Two samples, both reproducible from Wikidata queries: companies in the FTSE 100 index on the measurement date that the query found with an official website (76 of the 100, with membership checked against FTSE Russell's record of index changes), scored on one home page per company (its main corporate site), and UK local authorities (unitary, district, county and London borough councils) with an official website. Each home page was loaded once on 2026-09-02 in headless Chromium through Playwright at 1280 by 900, waited 2.5 seconds after DOM ready, and its ARIA snapshot was taken.
In the snapshot every control is a line such as - button "Search" or, when the accessible name computation yields nothing, - button. We counted both for buttons, links, text boxes, checkboxes, radios, comboboxes, menu items, tabs, switches, sliders and search boxes. Separately, in the DOM, we counted images with no alt attribute, form fields with no label by any mechanism, the language attribute, h1 count, skip links, a main landmark, untitled iframes and markers of known accessibility overlays.
Sites that returned an HTTP error, blocked automated browsers, or produced a tree of fewer than twenty lines were excluded rather than scored, and the number excluded is reported for each group. A site can be excluded and still be inaccessible; we simply could not measure it.

chunks.heading: Method
chunks.text: Correction, 22 October 2026: The FTSE 100 group now counts one home page per company, for companies in the index on 2 September 2026, the measurement date. The Wikidata query used to draw the sample had two faults. Some companies have several official websites, so secondary sites were counted as separate companies: five JD Sports retail sites, a second site each for Aviva, Barclays and St. James's Place, a second RELX entry, and a Direct Line Group entry whose website resolves to aviva.com. Index membership also has no end date, so 29 measured companies were not in the FTSE 100 in September, among them Shire (measured as takeda.com), Micro Focus (opentext.com), Inmarsat, Avast and WPP, which rejoined on 1 October. Membership was checked against the London Stock Exchange's FTSE 100 constituent list and FTSE Russell's record of FTSE 100 additions and deletions. The group is now 60 companies measured of 76 sampled, 16 excluded (it was 99 home pages of 127, 28 excluded); the query found 76 of the 100 constituents. Every FTSE and combined figure was recomputed from the remaining rows, and the removed rows are kept in the dataset as secondarySites and nonConstituentSites. The FTSE role table could not be split the same way, because some removed sites no longer serve the pages measured in September, so it still covers all 97 home pages measured.

chunks.heading: What to take from it
chunks.text:
The public sector, which has had a legal duty since 2020, does markedly better. Councils expose a nameless control on 11.7% of measured home pages against 31.7% for FTSE 100 companies, and their nameless share of all controls is 0.4% against 1.4%. The duty, the monitoring and the mandatory statement appear to have worked on the defect class an agent meets first.
The defects are few per site and easy to find. Most sites with a problem have one to five nameless controls, usually icon buttons and image links in the header or a carousel. Any of the four checkers in our tools benchmark reports them, and the accessible name previewer shows exactly what the agent receives for any snippet.
This is a floor, not a verdict. A home page with every control named can still hide an unusable checkout, and the measurement says nothing about keyboard traps, focus visibility, timing or content. It measures the one thing an agent cannot work around: a control it cannot name.

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Why does an AI agent care whether a button has a name?
Browser-use agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google act on a page through its accessibility tree, where every control is a role plus a name. A button with no name reaches the agent as 'button' and nothing else, so the agent cannot reliably choose it, describe it, or report what it did. It is the same failure a screen reader user hits, which is why the fix is the same: an accessible name.

How was the agent's view measured?
Each home page was loaded in headless Chromium with Playwright, and the ARIA snapshot of the page body was taken: a text rendering of the accessibility tree, one line per node, in which a control either carries a quoted name or does not. Controls counted are buttons, links, text boxes, checkboxes, radios, comboboxes, menu items, tabs, switches, sliders and search boxes. Sites that returned an error, blocked automation or produced a near-empty tree were excluded and the count of exclusions is reported.

Is this a WCAG audit?

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
No. It is one automated measurement of the home page, taken once, of the defects an agent hits first. It says nothing about checkout, forms beyond the home page, keyboard traps, focus visibility or content. A site with zero unnamed controls here can still be unusable; a site with several may be fine everywhere else. Treat it as a screening measure with the method published so it can be repeated.

Why FTSE 100 companies and UK councils?
Both are public, defined lists that anyone can reproduce from Wikidata, and they represent two different obligations: councils have had a legal duty to meet WCAG since 2020 under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations, while listed companies have only the general duty of the Equality Act and, where they sell into the EU, the European Accessibility Act.

chunks.heading: US Disability Prevalence
chunks.text:
How many adults report a disability, which types are most common, and how that has shifted since 2016. The numbers most accessibility business cases are built on, with the caveats that usually get dropped.

Download dataMethodologyPrimary dataset
Headline finding
28.7% of United States adults report a disability, about 73.4 million people. Cognitive disability is now the largest category at 13.9%, having overtaken mobility and grown faster than any other type.
Source: CDC Disability and Health Data System (DHDS). Age-adjusted prevalence from BRFSS. Disability types overlap and must not be summed.

Executive summary

chunks.heading: The audience is larger and different than assumed
chunks.text:
More than one in four United States adults reports a disability. The composition is the part that tends to surprise teams: cognitive disability is the largest single category and the fastest growing, while vision, where most accessibility effort concentrates, is the smallest of the major types.
This is public domain federal data, pulled directly from the CDC data API rather than transcribed from a secondary source.

01

chunks.heading: More than 1 in 4 adults
chunks.text:
28.7% report a disability, an estimated 73,434,428 people, up from 24.6% in 2016.

02

chunks.heading: Cognitive is now the largest type
chunks.text:
13.9% in 2022, up from 10.8% in 2016. It overtook mobility, which stayed roughly flat.

03

chunks.heading: Do not add the categories up
chunks.text: People report multiple disability types, so the individual figures overlap. Only the any-disability number is a valid total.

chunks.heading: Prevalence by disability type, 2022
chunks.text:
Age-adjusted prevalence among United States adults aged 18 and over. Categories overlap, because a person can report more than one type.
Cognitive disability is now the most commonly reported type at 13.9%, ahead of mobility. That ordering matters for the web: cognitive and learning disabilities are the least well served by the checklist-driven approach most teams take, and the hardest to catch with automated testing.

chunks.heading: Seven years of change
chunks.text:
Age-adjusted prevalence by disability type, 2016 to 2022.
Reported disability rose from 24.6% to 28.7% of United States adults over this period, and cognitive disability drove most of it, climbing from 10.8% to 13.9%. Mobility, by contrast, is roughly flat. The 2020 dip across every series is a survey artifact, not a real fall.

Read 2020 with care. Every series dips in 2020 and recovers in 2021. That reflects a pandemic-related change in how the BRFSS survey was collected, not a year in which fewer Americans had disabilities. The shaded band on the chart marks it.

Source: CDC Disability and Health Data System (DHDS)
View data tableDownload CSV

Interpretation

chunks.heading: What this means for the web
chunks.text: Accessibility work still skews heavily toward screen reader support. The prevalence data does not.

chunks.heading: Cognitive is the largest category
chunks.text: 13.9% of adults, roughly 33 million people, and the fastest growing. Yet cognitive accessibility is the area with the fewest testable success criteria and almost no automated coverage. Plain language, consistent navigation, generous timeouts, and forgiving forms matter more than any ARIA attribute here.

chunks.heading: Vision is the smallest of the big five
chunks.text: At 5.5% it is real and it matters, but it is smaller than cognitive, mobility, independent living, and hearing. Most people in this group have low vision rather than blindness, so contrast, text resizing, and reflow do more good than screen reader support alone.

chunks.heading: These categories overlap
chunks.text:
The type percentages sum to more than 28.7% because a person can report several. Never add them together to produce a total, and be careful with any source that does.

For the criteria that serve these groups, see 1.4.3 Contrast and 1.4.10 Reflow for low vision, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry and 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation for cognitive load, captions and transcripts for hearing, and keyboard accessibility for motor disabilities.

chunks.heading: Data Sources
chunks.text:
CDC Disability and Health Data System (DHDS)Age-adjusted prevalence of disability among US adults aged 18 and over, from BRFSS survey data published through the CDC Disability and Health Data System.

Sample Size
BRFSS survey responses; 132,827 unweighted respondents for the any-disability estimate in 2022

Date Range

2016 to 2022

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
Figures are age-adjusted prevalence, which standardises for the age structure of the population so years can be compared. They are not raw counts of people, and they will not match crude prevalence figures from other sources.
BRFSS is a self-report telephone survey of non-institutionalised adults aged 18 and over. People in nursing homes, prisons, and other institutions are not represented, and children are excluded entirely.
Disability types overlap. A person can report several, so the type percentages must never be summed into a total.
The 2020 estimates reflect a pandemic-related change in survey data collection and should not be read as a real decline in disability prevalence.
The latest available data year is 2022, even though the dataset and CDC pages have been reviewed more recently. Check for a newer year before quoting these as current.
Geography is United States, DC and Territories. Individual state estimates are available in the source dataset but are not reproduced here.

Last updated: 2026-08-27

Use the research

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
How to quote these figures without misrepresenting them.

What percentage of adults have a disability?▾
28.7% of United States adults aged 18 and over reported a disability in 2022, which is roughly 1 in 4 and an estimated 73.4 million people. That is the age-adjusted prevalence from the CDC Disability and Health Data System, based on the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System survey. The 95% confidence interval is 28.4% to 29.0%.

What is the most common type of disability?▾
Cognitive disability is now the most commonly reported type among US adults at 13.9%, an estimated 33.2 million people. Mobility follows at 12.2%, then independent living at 7.7%, hearing at 6.2%, vision at 5.5%, and self-care at 3.6%. Cognitive disability overtook mobility during this period and has grown faster than any other category.

Can I add the disability type percentages together?▾
No. The categories overlap because a person can report more than one type of disability, so the individual percentages sum to well over the 28.7% who report any disability. Adding them produces a badly inflated number. If you need a total, use the any-disability figure of 28.7%. Be sceptical of any source that presents a summed total.

Why does disability prevalence dip in 2020?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
The 2020 dip appears across every disability type and reverses in 2021, which is the signature of a data collection artifact rather than a real change. The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System changed how it collected data during the pandemic year. Treat 2020 as a break in the series rather than as evidence that fewer people had disabilities that year.

What does age-adjusted prevalence mean?▾
Age adjustment standardises the figures against a reference age distribution so that different years and different places can be compared without the result being driven by one population simply being older. Because disability becomes more common with age, an unadjusted figure for an older population would look higher even if nothing else differed. Age-adjusted figures will not match crude prevalence numbers from other sources, so do not mix the two in the same comparison.

How should accessibility teams use this data?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text: Mainly as a corrective to where effort usually goes. Accessibility work tends to concentrate on screen reader support, but vision is the smallest of the major categories at 5.5%, while cognitive disability is the largest at 13.9% and growing. That argues for investing in plain language, consistent navigation, generous timeouts, forgiving forms, and reduced cognitive load alongside the ARIA work, since those serve the largest and fastest-growing group and are poorly covered by automated testing.

chunks.heading: How to read this register
chunks.text:
A maximum penalty belongs to a route, not to a country. The same state can use different regulators, different acts and very different amounts for products, e-commerce, banking and telecoms. A maximum in the law also says nothing about what anyone has actually been fined.
Verified: we read the provision and any act it relies on, at a source named in the row.
Partly verified: we read part of it. The note says what is missing, or that the figure rests on a legal reading.
Not verified: we could not read it, so we give no figure.

chunks.heading: Method and limits
chunks.text:
Figures come from legal texts we downloaded or opened on or around 31 October 2026. Each quotation was checked word for word against the downloaded text. Vendor pages were never used as evidence.
Amounts stay in the original currency. France's EUR 7,500 and EUR 15,000 are our arithmetic from the articles, as the row says.
Later amendments were not checked for every act. The notes say where this matters.
Estonia, Lithuania, Romania: the official sites blocked automated access or did not connect, so we give no figure.
Competent authorities are listed only as far as we read them. Check the national law for your sector.
A community sanctions table helped us find some laws, and ComplyLoft keeps a separate tracker. Neither was used to verify a figure here.
Found an error? Tell us through the contact page. See also our corrections policy.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is the maximum fine under the European Accessibility Act?▾
The Directive sets no fine. Article 30 leaves penalties to each Member State, so the maximum depends on the country and often on the sector and enforcement route. In the texts we read, Germany's BFSG goes up to EUR 100,000 for the listed breaches, Sweden's act up to SEK 10,000,000 and Spain's fallback regime up to EUR 1,000,000.

Has anyone been fined under the EAA?▾
As of 31 October 2026 we found no fine issued by a national regulator under an EAA transposition law. That means none was found, not that none exists. A French court did order Carrefour France to pay two associations EUR 10,000 in provisional damages and EUR 3,000 in costs, but those are not regulatory fines.

Why do sites give different fine amounts for the same country?▾
Often because one country has several routes. In the Netherlands, some routes use the fifth fine category, which rose from EUR 103,000 to EUR 110,000 on 1 January 2026, while others appear to reach EUR 900,000 or 1% of turnover. A single figure can only ever describe one route, and it can go out of date.

Is this legal advice?▾
No. This page records published legal texts for information. It may be incomplete, translations are ours and unofficial, and no lawyer has reviewed it. Check the linked text and take advice for your own situation.

Executive summary

chunks.heading: The law landed. The evidence has not.
chunks.text:
The European Accessibility Act has applied since June 2025 and every Member State has notified national measures. What does not exist, and will not for years, is any official picture of whether it is working. That gap is being filled by vendor marketing, so this page states plainly what is documented and what is not.
Every date below is quoted from the Directive on EUR-Lex, article by article.

01

chunks.heading: Applying since 28 June 2025
chunks.text:
Article 31(2). The transposition deadline three years earlier, 28 June 2022, is a different date and is often confused with it.

02

chunks.heading: All 27 have notified measures
chunks.text:
380 instruments in total, from 59 in Germany to one each in Ireland, Cyprus and Malta. The spread reflects drafting style, not diligence.

03

chunks.heading: 3 obligations still ahead
chunks.text:
Article 4(8) may be deferred to 2027, and transitional cover for existing products, contracts and self-service terminals runs to 2030 and beyond.

The statutory timeline

chunks.heading: Every date that is actually in the Directive
chunks.text:
Quoted from the text of Directive (EU) 2019/882 rather than paraphrased, because the dates circulating in vendor marketing are frequently wrong or missing their conditions.

28 June 2022
Article 31(1)In effect
Transposition deadline
Member States shall adopt and publish, by 28 June 2022, the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive.

28 June 2025
Article 31(2)In effect

They shall apply those measures from 28 June 2025.
This is the date the obligations began to bite for in-scope products and services.

Article 31(3)Upcoming

Member States may decide to apply the measures regarding the obligations set out in Article 4(8) at the latest from 28 June 2027.

28 June 2030
Article 32(1)Upcoming

Member States shall provide for a transitional period ending on 28 June 2030 during which service providers may continue to provide their services using products which were lawfully used by them to provide similar services before that date.

By 28 June 2030, and every five years thereafter, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament, to the Council, to the European Economic and Social Committee and to the Committee of the Regions a report on the application of this Directive.

chunks.heading: Every date that is actually in the Directive
chunks.text: This is why no official EU-wide compliance or enforcement dataset exists yet.

chunks.heading: Two transitional rules people miss
chunks.text:
Article 32(1): Service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may continue without alteration until they expire, but no longer than five years from that date.
Article 32(2): Self-service terminals lawfully used to provide services before 28 June 2025 may continue to be used until the end of their economically useful life, but no longer than 20 years after their entry into use.

chunks.heading: There is no EU-wide EAA enforcement dataset, and there will not be one until 2030
chunks.text: There is no official EU-wide compliance or enforcement dataset for the European Accessibility Act, and there will not be one before 2030. Article 33(1) sets the first Commission report on the application of the Directive at 28 June 2030. Some national regulators now publish figures, but each covers one country or one sector, and many enforcement claims in vendor content could not be traced to a regulator or court. Anything on this subject should be sourced to a named national regulator or court, one country at a time. Traced to primary sources as of 31 October 2026: on 4 June 2026 the Tribunal judiciaire de Caen, in an interim first-instance order in a case brought by the associations ApiDV and Droit Pluriel, ordered Carrefour France to comply, under a penalty of 500 euros per day that starts six months after the order (about 4 December 2026). It also ordered Carrefour France to pay the associations 10,000 euros in provisional damages and 3,000 euros in costs, and said the site cannot be only slightly accessible. On 5 May 2026 the Tribunal judiciaire de Lille refused interim relief in a similar case against Auchan E-Commerce France; that was not a ruling on the merits, and the associations say they will appeal.

chunks.heading: There is no EU-wide EAA enforcement dataset, and there will not be one until 2030
chunks.text:
On 24 March 2026 the Dutch regulator ACM, which tested about 100 of the largest Dutch online stores plus the largest telecom and energy providers, reported that 61% of the largest online stores are not digitally accessible, and warned that companies that fail to improve risk enforcement action. Dutch broadcaster NOS reported in June 2026 that ACM had visited ten large webshops and planned a new test three months later. On 11 March 2026 the European Commission sent additional reasoned opinions to Germany and Croatia over remaining transposition gaps. We found no monetary fine issued by a national regulator under an EAA transposition law as of 31 October 2026. That means none was found, not that none exists. The Caen payments go to the associations and are not a regulatory fine.
We looked for an EU-wide dataset and did not find one. Rather than fill the gap with vendor claims, we are telling you the gap exists. If you need enforcement intelligence for a specific market, go to that country's named market surveillance authority. For penalties and the actions we traced, see EAA fines and penalties by country.

chunks.heading: National transposition measures by Member State
chunks.text:
Instruments each Member State has communicated to the Commission, as recorded by EUR-Lex on 28 October 2026.
All 27 Member States have now communicated transposition measures, 380 in total. The spread from 59 to 1 says almost nothing about effort or quality: it reflects whether a country transposed through one consolidated act or amended dozens of existing laws.

A count is not a score. These counts are the number of national instruments each Member State has communicated to the Commission, not a measure of implementation quality or completeness. A state with one consolidated act is not behind a state with fifty amendments; it reflects legislative drafting style. EUR-Lex states that Member States bear sole responsibility for this information and that it does not prejudge Commission verification of completeness and correctness.Latest change. Since the previous count on 14 October 2026, France notified Décret n° 2026-883 of 23 September 2026 (Journal officiel, 24 September 2026). It adds the directive's definitions of economic operators to the Consumer Code and requires market surveillance authorities to give consumers, on request and in an accessible format, the conformity information supplied by manufacturers, importers and distributors.

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
Measure counts are the number of national instruments communicated, not a measure of implementation quality, completeness, or enforcement activity.
EUR-Lex states that Member States bear sole responsibility for this information and that it does not prejudge the Commission's verification of the completeness and correctness of transposition.
A Member State that transposed through one consolidated act will show a low count next to one that amended many existing laws. The counts are not comparable as effort or compliance.
No official EU-wide compliance or enforcement dataset exists. Article 33(1) sets the first Commission report on application of the Directive at 28 June 2030.
National enforcement claims appear on this page only where we traced them to a court, regulator or official release, or where the source is named as press. Untraced vendor claims are excluded.
This tracker covers the Directive itself. Individual Member State implementing laws may impose additional or earlier obligations that are not reflected in these counts.

Last updated: 2026-10-31

Use the research

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Answered from the Directive text and the EUR-Lex record.

When did the European Accessibility Act come into force?▾
Article 31(2) of Directive (EU) 2019/882 states that Member States shall apply their implementing measures from 28 June 2025. That is the date the obligations began to apply to in-scope products and services. The separate transposition deadline, by which Member States had to adopt and publish their national laws, was 28 June 2022 under Article 31(1). The Directive itself was adopted on 17 April 2019 and published in OJ L 151 on 7 June 2019.

Have all EU Member States transposed the EAA?▾
All 27 Member States have communicated national transposition measures to the European Commission, 380 instruments in total as recorded by EUR-Lex. That confirms each country has notified something, but it is not evidence that transposition is complete or correct. On 11 March 2026 the Commission sent additional reasoned opinions to Germany and Croatia because transposition gaps remain. EUR-Lex states explicitly that Member States bear sole responsibility for this information and that it does not prejudge the Commission's verification of completeness and correctness.

Which country has done the most to implement the EAA?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
You cannot tell that from measure counts, and it would be a mistake to try. Germany has communicated 59 instruments while Ireland, Cyprus, and Malta have each communicated one. That difference reflects legislative drafting style rather than effort: a country that transposes through a single consolidated act shows one measure, while a country that amends dozens of existing sectoral laws shows dozens. Treat the counts as a record of notification, not a league table.

How many companies are complying with the EAA?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Nobody knows, and no official source can tell you. There is no EU-wide compliance or enforcement dataset for the European Accessibility Act. Article 33(1) requires the Commission to report on the application of the Directive by 28 June 2030 and every five years after that, so the first authoritative picture is about four years away. National figures exist for individual countries, and these developments trace to primary sources as of our 31 October 2026 review: an interim June 2026 order of the Tribunal judiciaire de Caen against Carrefour France, with a conditional daily penalty, 10,000 euros in provisional damages and 3,000 euros in costs payable to the two associations that sued; and a March 2026 report by the Dutch regulator ACM finding 61% of the largest Dutch online stores not digitally accessible. We found no fine issued by a national regulator under an EAA transposition law, which means none was found, not that none exists.

What are the remaining EAA deadlines?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Three dates are still ahead. Under Article 31(3), Member States may defer the obligations in Article 4(8) until 28 June 2027 at the latest. Under Article 32(1), a transitional period runs until 28 June 2030 during which service providers may continue using products they lawfully used before the application date, and service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may run unaltered until they expire but no longer than five years. Under Article 32(2), self-service terminals lawfully in use before 28 June 2025 may continue until the end of their economically useful life, capped at 20 years from entry into use.

Does the EAA apply to companies outside the EU?▾
The Directive applies to products placed on the EU market and services provided to consumers in the EU, regardless of where the provider is established. A United States or United Kingdom company selling to EU consumers can therefore be in scope. For the detail on scope, the microenterprise exemption, and the technical route to compliance through EN 301 549, see our European Accessibility Act compliance guide, which covers requirements rather than the legislative tracking on this page.

chunks.heading: Screen Reader Survey 2026: JAWS, NVDA and AI Use
chunks.text:
Research report
Survey #11: July to August 2026
1,780 responses
Reviewed: Oct 14, 2026

chunks.heading: Screen Reader Survey 2026: What Changed Since 2024
chunks.text:
WebAIM's eleventh Screen Reader User Survey (1,780 valid responses, July to August 2026) set against the tenth (1,539 responses, December 2023 to January 2024). Both values for every question asked twice, the percentage-point change, and the new questions on AI and documents.

Download dataMethodologyPrimary dataset
Headline finding
JAWS is back on top: 55.0% of respondents now use it as their primary desktop screen reader, up 14.5 points from 40.5% in 2024, while NVDA fell to 32.9% and VoiceOver to 6.5%.
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11. Self-selected sample, not a market share. © WebAIM, reproduced with attribution.

JAWS primary (2024)
55.0% (40.5%)

NVDA primary (2024)
32.9% (37.7%)

Headings first (2024)
67.8% (71.6%)

Use AI for alt text
60.1%

Executive summary

chunks.heading: Two years, one big swing, and a new question about AI
chunks.text:
In 2024 JAWS and NVDA were nearly level as primary screen readers, and more respondents used NVDA than JAWS overall. In 2026 JAWS leads on both measures. Headings are still how most people find their way around a page, but slightly fewer start there, and more respondents feel the web got worse over the past year.
All survey figures are © WebAIM and come from Survey #11 and Survey #10. The only number we add is the percentage-point difference between them.

01

chunks.heading: JAWS overtook NVDA on every measure
chunks.text:
Primary use 40.5% to 55.0% for JAWS, 37.7% to 32.9% for NVDA. Commonly used: JAWS 60.5% to 69.2%, NVDA 65.6% to 59.3%.

02

chunks.heading: Geography still decides the answer
chunks.text:
JAWS is primary for 72.5% in North America, NVDA for 77.4% in Asia and 83.0% in Africa and the Middle East. More North American respondents answered this time, which WebAIM says does not alone explain the shift.

03

chunks.heading: AI is now part of how people read the web
chunks.text: 60.1% use AI for image descriptions or alt text, and only 8.2% use none of the listed AI tools. 85.6% expect PDFs to cause accessibility problems.

chunks.heading: This is a survey of volunteers, not a market share
chunks.text:
WebAIM states plainly that the sample was not controlled and may not represent all screen reader users. People choose to answer, and the ones who do are more engaged with the accessibility community than average. Neither survey measures sales, licences or installations.
The mix of respondents also moved. North America rose from 47.2% to 54.1% of the sample and Europe fell from 30.7% to 27.7%. JAWS is far more common in North America, so some of its rise is who answered. WebAIM’s own note: “This survey had a slightly higher number of respondents from North America where JAWS is more frequently used, but this alone does not account for the notable increase in overall JAWS usage.”

chunks.text:

JAWS: 40.5% to 55.0% (+14.5 pp). NVDA: 37.7% to 32.9% (−4.8 pp). VoiceOver: 9.7% to 6.5% (−3.2 pp). Beyond JAWS, NVDA and VoiceOver, all other primary screen readers totalled 5.5% (down from 12.2% in 2024).

chunks.text:
"When trying to find information on a lengthy web page, which of the following are you most likely to do first?"
Headings remain the first move for 67.8%, against 71.6% in 2024 (−3.8 pp). Reading through the page (+3.3 pp) and following links (+1.9 pp) picked up the difference. Frequent use of landmarks/regions (whenever available or often) decreased to 28.3% in 2026 from 31.8% in 2024.

88.3% find heading levels very or somewhat useful (88.8% in Survey #10). Advanced screen reader users are much more likely to use headings first (72.1%) than beginners (41.4%). chunks.text:

22.9% now say the web became less accessible, up from 18.6%, while "more accessible" fell from 34.6% to 32.2%. Asked what would have the bigger impact, 83.9% still chose better web sites over better assistive technology (85.9% in 2024).

chunks.heading: What Survey #11 did not ask
chunks.text:
Survey #10 asked respondents to rank their most problematic items. WebAIM published the order (weighted scores, not percentages). Survey #11 did not ask this question, so there is no 2026 ranking. Anyone quoting “CAPTCHA is the top problem in 2026” is quoting the 2024 survey. The Survey #10 order, most problematic first:
CAPTCHA - images presenting text used to verify that you are a human user
Interactive elements like menus, tabs, and dialogs do not behave as expected
Links or buttons that do not make sense
Screens or parts of screens that change unexpectedly
Lack of keyboard accessibility
Images with missing or improper descriptions (alt text)
Complex or difficult forms
Missing or improper headings
Too many links or navigation items
Complex data tables
Inaccessible or missing search functionality
Lack of "skip to main content" or "skip navigation" links

Also asked in 2024 only: age; different screen reader at work or school than at home; braille output; contacting website owners about barriers; accessibility of social media sites; describing appearance in virtual meetings. chunks.heading: What this means for testing
chunks.text: Test with JAWS and NVDA on Windows, plus VoiceOver on iOS for mobile. Which desktop reader matters most depends on your audience’s region, and most users run more than one. Start with the screen reader testing guide, then the JAWS and NVDA walkthroughs. For the wider numbers, see web accessibility statistics.

chunks.heading: Data Sources
chunks.text:
WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #111,780 valid responses collected July to August 2026. Page last updated by WebAIM 2026-09-29. © WebAIM.

WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #101,539 valid responses collected December 2023 to January 2024. Page last updated by WebAIM 2024-02-22. © WebAIM.

Sample Size
1,780 (2026) and 1,539 (2024) valid responses

Date Range

December 2023 to January 2024 and July to August 2026

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
Every table was parsed from the raw HTML of both WebAIM results pages, not retyped. Regional JAWS and NVDA shares, and figures such as the PDF and AI totals, come from WebAIM's published commentary and are labelled as such in the dataset.
WebAIM states that the sample was not controlled and may not represent all screen reader users. Respondents self-select, so these are shares of survey respondents, not market share, sales or installations.
The regional mix changed: North America went from 47.2% to 54.1% of respondents. Shifts in overall shares partly reflect who answered. WebAIM says this alone does not account for the rise in JAWS.
The only figure we calculate is the percentage-point change (2026 minus 2024). We do not re-weight, combine or estimate anything, and where an answer appears in only one year's table we show it as Not listed rather than zero.
Survey #11 dropped several 2024 questions, including the problematic items ranking that placed CAPTCHA first, and added questions on AI, skip links and documents. Single-survey questions are shown separately.
Totals may not equal 100% because of rounding, and not every respondent answered every question, so the base for each percentage differs slightly.

Last updated: 2026-10-14

Use the research

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
What the two surveys support, and what they do not.

What is the most popular screen reader in 2026?▾
JAWS. In WebAIM's Screen Reader User Survey #11 (July to August 2026, 1,780 valid responses), JAWS was the primary desktop or laptop screen reader for 55.0% of respondents, NVDA for 32.9% and VoiceOver for 6.5%. JAWS also led on screen readers commonly used, at 69.2% against 59.3% for NVDA. These are shares of a self-selected survey sample, not sales or installation figures, so treat them as a picture of engaged screen reader users rather than a market share.

Did JAWS gain users between 2024 and 2026?▾
Among survey respondents, yes: JAWS primary use rose from 40.5% in Survey #10 to 55.0% in Survey #11, while NVDA fell from 37.7% to 32.9% and VoiceOver from 9.7% to 6.5%. Part of this is who answered. North American respondents rose from 47.2% to 54.1% of the sample, and JAWS is far more common there. WebAIM says the larger North American sample alone does not account for the increase, and JAWS also gained inside North America, from 55.5% to 72.5%.

Should I test with JAWS or NVDA?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Both, if you can. Which one dominates depends on where your users are. In 2026 JAWS led NVDA in North America (72.5% against 15.6%), the two were level in Europe (42.8% against 42.3%), and NVDA led in Asia (77.4%), Africa and the Middle East (83.0%) and South America (67.2%). 70.3% of respondents use more than one desktop screen reader, so a site that only works in one will fail real users.

How do screen reader users use AI?▾
Survey #11 asked this for the first time. 60.1% of respondents commonly use AI to generate image descriptions or alternative text, 49.7% for in-depth descriptions of complex images, 40.6% for guidance through an online task and 37.1% for summaries of pages or documents. Only 8.2% reported none of the listed uses. Users working around missing alt text with AI is not a reason to skip writing it: the description they get is a guess, not the author's intent.

Do screen reader users still navigate by headings?▾
Yes, by a wide margin, though slightly less than before. 67.8% said headings are the first thing they use to find information on a lengthy page, down from 71.6% in 2024. Landmarks were the first choice of only 3.4%. 88.3% find heading levels very or somewhat useful. A correct heading outline remains the single most useful structural fix for screen reader users.

Do screen reader users think the web is getting more accessible?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Fewer than in 2024. In Survey #11, 32.2% said web content had become more accessible over the previous year, 44.9% said it had not changed and 22.9% said it had become less accessible. In Survey #10 the figures were 34.6%, 46.8% and 18.6%. WebAIM describes perception as decreasing slightly from 2021 to 2024 and again from 2024 to 2026.

Is CAPTCHA still the biggest problem for screen reader users?▾
Survey #11 did not ask the problematic items question, so there is no 2026 ranking. The most recent answer is Survey #10 (December 2023 to January 2024), where CAPTCHA was the most problematic item by a notable margin, ahead of interactive elements that do not behave as expected, links or buttons that do not make sense, and screens that change unexpectedly. Survey #11 did ask about documents: 85.6% said PDFs are very or somewhat likely to pose accessibility issues, up from 75.1% in 2019.

How reliable is the WebAIM screen reader survey?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text: It is the largest recurring public survey of screen reader users, but WebAIM states that the sample was not controlled and may not represent all screen reader users. Respondents choose to take part, so it over-represents people engaged with the accessibility community. The regional mix also moved between surveys: North America went from 47.2% to 54.1% of respondents and Europe from 30.7% to 27.7%. Compare the two surveys as two snapshots of similar communities, not as a measured trend in the whole population.

Accessibility maturity across all 60 United States federal agencies, from the FY2025 governmentwide Section 508 assessment.

Download dataMethodologyPrimary dataset
Headline finding
58.3% of federal agencies rated Low or Very Low on whether their technology is actually accessible. On testing and remediation, the weakest factor in the assessment, 61.7% rated that low.

Executive summary

chunks.heading: A programme on paper, not in practice
chunks.text:
Section 508 has been law since 1998. Nearly three decades later, most federal agencies report having the policies, governance, and contract language in place, and most also report that their technology still is not accessible. The assessment measures both, and the distance between them is the story.
Every percentage on this page is computed from the government's own published response file, so you can reproduce it from the source CSV.

01

chunks.heading: Conformance lags implementation badly
chunks.text:
26.7% of agencies rated Low or Very Low on having a programme, but 58.3% rated that low on whether the technology is accessible.

02

chunks.heading: Testing is where it breaks
chunks.text:
61.7% of agencies rated Low or Very Low on testing and remediation, the weakest factor measured.

03

chunks.heading: Buying is the easy part
chunks.text: 61.7% rated High or Very High on acquisition. Writing the requirement into a contract is fully within an agency's control; verifying the result is not.

chunks.heading: These scores are self-reported
chunks.text: Agencies answer the assessment themselves. Nobody independently audits their websites, documents, or internal software to produce these ratings. That cuts in an uncomfortable direction: if anything, self-assessment tends to flatter, so the real picture is unlikely to be better than what agencies reported about themselves.

chunks.heading: How agencies scored on each factor
chunks.text:

The two index scores tell different stories. 58.3% of agencies rated Low or Very Low on the Accessibility Conformance Index, which measures whether their ICT is actually accessible, while only 26.7% rated that low on Implementation, which measures whether they have a programme in place. Having a programme is not the same as having accessible technology.

Interpretation

chunks.heading: Good at buying it, bad at checking it
chunks.text: The factor scores form a clear shape. Agencies have largely succeeded at writing accessibility into policy and contracts. They have largely failed at verifying that what they bought and built actually works.

chunks.heading: Acquisition is the strongest factor
chunks.text: 61.7% of agencies rated High or Very High on Acquisition, the best result of any factor. Putting Section 508 language into a solicitation is a paperwork exercise an agency controls completely, and it shows.

chunks.heading: Testing is the weakest
chunks.text: 61.7% of agencies rated Low or Very Low on Testing and Remediation, the worst factor in the assessment. Testing requires trained staff, assistive technology, and time against real user journeys. That is where the effort collapses.

chunks.heading: A VPAT is not a test result
chunks.text:
Strong acquisition scores alongside weak testing scores suggest agencies are accepting vendor conformance claims without verifying them. A supplier's accessibility conformance report is a starting point for evaluation, not evidence of conformance.

If you are on the buying side of this, our accessible procurement guidance covers how to evaluate a conformance report, and the audit guide covers what real verification involves. For the standard itself, see Section 508.

chunks.heading: Data Sources
chunks.text:
Governmentwide Section 508 Assessment, FY2025Annual assessment of federal agency Section 508 programmes, mandated by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023. Responses from 60 federal agencies, published as open data by GSA.

Sample Size
60 federal agencies

Date Range

FY2025, published 2026-03-02

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
Agencies self-report. No independent audit of agency websites, documents, or internal software produces these ratings.
The Accessibility Conformance Index and Accessibility Implementation Index are maturity ratings on a five-point scale, not counts of WCAG failures. A Very High rating does not mean an agency's ICT is conformant.
The percentages on this page are our own computation from the published agency response data file, not figures quoted from the GSA narrative report.
Agency size and mission vary enormously across the 60 respondents, and the assessment does not weight by the number of people an agency serves.
A correction issued on 30 July 2026 added missing data from five agencies. This page uses the corrected file.
The assessment covers United States federal agencies only. It says nothing about state or local government, which fall under ADA Title II rather than Section 508.

Last updated: 2026-08-27

Use the research

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
What the assessment measures, and what it does not.

What is the governmentwide Section 508 assessment?▾
It is an annual assessment of how well United States federal agencies are meeting their Section 508 obligations, mandated by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 and run by the General Services Administration. Agencies answer a structured questionnaire covering policy, acquisition, testing, and remediation, and their responses are scored into two indexes: the Accessibility Implementation Index, which measures whether the programme exists, and the Accessibility Conformance Index, which measures whether the technology is actually accessible. GSA publishes the agency response data as open government data.

How many federal agencies are failing on accessibility?▾
In the FY2025 assessment, 35 of 60 agencies, or 58.3%, rated Low or Very Low on the Accessibility Conformance Index. Only 14 agencies, 23.3%, rated High or Very High. Those percentages are our own computation from the published agency response data file rather than figures quoted from the GSA narrative, so they can be reproduced directly from the source CSV.

What are federal agencies worst at?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Testing and remediation. 37 of 60 agencies, or 61.7%, rated Low or Very Low on that factor, making it the weakest area in the entire assessment. By contrast, Acquisition was the strongest factor, with 46.7% of agencies rating Very High. The pattern is that agencies are comparatively good at writing accessibility requirements into policy and contracts, and comparatively bad at verifying that what they bought and built actually works for disabled users.

Does a high Implementation Index score mean an agency is accessible?▾
No, and the gap between the two indexes is the most revealing thing in the data. Only 26.7% of agencies rated Low or Very Low on Implementation, which measures whether the programme, policies, and staffing exist, while 58.3% rated that low on Conformance, which measures whether the technology is accessible. Having a governance structure is not the same as having accessible websites, documents, and software.

Is this data independently verified?▾
No. Agencies self-report their answers, and no independent audit of agency websites, documents, or internal systems produces these ratings. That matters for how you read the results: self-assessment generally flatters, so the real state of federal ICT accessibility is unlikely to be better than what agencies reported about themselves and may well be worse.

Does Section 508 apply to state and local government?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text: No. Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act applies to United States federal agencies and to the ICT they develop, procure, maintain, or use. State and local government are covered instead by Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, which has its own rulemaking and deadlines. This assessment therefore says nothing about the accessibility of a state DMV site or a city services portal.

chunks.heading: State of Web Accessibility 2026
chunks.text:
An independent synthesis of public accessibility research, centered on WebAIM's evaluation of one million homepages and supported by HTTP Archive context.

Download reportMethodologyPrimary dataset
Headline finding
95.9% of the one million homepages evaluated had automatically detectable WCAG failures, with 56.1 detected errors per homepage on average. Both figures are worse than 2025, reversing six consecutive years of gradual improvement.
Source: WebAIM Million 2026. Automated results do not establish full WCAG conformance.

Primary sample
1,000,000 homepages

Evaluation type
Automated detection

Primary period
February 2026

Executive summary

chunks.heading: In 2026 the web moved backwards
chunks.text:
For six straight years the share of homepages with detectable failures inched downward. In February 2026 it rose instead, from 94.8% to 95.9%, while the average number of detected errors per homepage climbed 10.1%. Two years of measured progress were erased in a single cycle, putting the web back at roughly its 2024 position.
This report keeps measurements from different studies separate and distinguishes automated signals from complete accessibility evaluation.

01

chunks.heading: The same six failures, for a seventh year
chunks.text:
Six categories account for 96% of the automatically detected errors in WebAIM's sample, and the list has not changed in seven years. Four of the six became more common in 2026.

02

chunks.heading: Complexity is outrunning remediation
chunks.text:
The average homepage contained 1,437 elements in February 2026, a 22.5% jump in a single year and nearly double the 2019 figure. ARIA attributes grew 27% in the same period.

03

chunks.heading: Automated results are incomplete
chunks.text:
These findings identify repeatable code-level failures, not full WCAG conformance or the lived usability of a website.

At a glance

chunks.heading: Homepages analyzed
chunks.text:
A homepage-level sample, not one million complete websites.

95.9%

chunks.text:

Low contrast remains the most widespread detected issue and grew sharply, from 79.1% to 83.9% of homepages. Four of the six categories became more common in 2026; only missing alternative text and missing document language improved. Together these six account for 96% of all errors WebAIM detected, and the list has been unchanged for seven years.

Interpretation

chunks.heading: What the numbers do and do not show
chunks.text: Automated measurements are useful for tracking recurring code-level barriers. They are not a substitute for manual review or testing with disabled people.

chunks.heading: Pages are getting more complex
chunks.text: WebAIM found an average of 1,437 elements per homepage, up 22.5% in a single year and nearly double the 2019 figure. More markup means more places for a barrier to appear.

chunks.heading: ARIA is not a shortcut
chunks.text: 82.7% of homepages used ARIA, and homepages now carry 133 ARIA attributes on average, up 27% in one year. Pages with ARIA averaged 59.1 detected errors versus 42 without it, an association that also reflects greater page complexity.

chunks.heading: A score is not conformance
chunks.text:
The HTTP Archive Web Almanac reported a median Lighthouse accessibility score above 85 in 2025, improving 1% year over year even as WebAIM's error counts rose. Lighthouse tests only part of WCAG, so even a perfect automated score cannot establish accessibility.

What changed

chunks.heading: Why 2026 moved backwards
chunks.text:
WebAIM attributes the reversal primarily to two things that grew faster than remediation did: page complexity and ARIA. Homepages gained 22.5% more elements in a single year and 27% more ARIA attributes. In WebAIM's own reading, this likely reflects heavier reliance on third-party frameworks and libraries alongside automated and AI-assisted coding practices. Their conclusion is that accessibility at scale will need both better practices and simpler systems.
The underlying structural measures below show where that complexity lands. They are drawn from the same February 2026 sample and are useful as a benchmark when auditing your own pages.

Structural accessibility measures across one million homepages in February 2026, and why each one matters
Measure Homepages Why it matters
Had at least one landmark region 84.3% Landmarks let screen reader users jump straight to a section instead of reading linearly.
Had a main element or main landmark 46.1% Fewer than half of homepages mark their primary content, so most offer no reliable jump target.
Had a skip link 17.1% One in ten of those skip links was broken: hidden inaccessibly, or pointing at a target that was not there.
Had skipped heading levels 41.8% Headings are the primary way screen reader users navigate; skipped levels misrepresent the document outline.

chunks.heading: Why 2026 moved backwards
chunks.text:
Had more than one h1 18.1% Up from 16.3% in 2025. Multiple top-level headings obscure what the page is actually about.
Had ambiguous link text 15.2% Links such as “click here” or “more” carry no meaning when read out of context in a links list.
Used an ARIA menu role 5.7% 22% of those menus introduced barriers through missing menu markup or interactions.

Each of these maps onto a fixable pattern. For the contrast failures that top the list, see 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) and the contrast checker. For unlabeled inputs, which were 33.1% of all form inputs in the sample, see the accessible forms guide. For broken skip links, see 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks. And for the ARIA menus that introduced barriers on a fifth of the pages using them, the accessible menu & menu button guide explains why most navigation dropdowns should not use role="menu" at all.
The same February 2026 sample can be cut two other ways. See how the error count varies by technology stack across content management systems, frameworks and libraries, or by industry across 29 sectors.

chunks.text:
WebAIM Million 2026Automated evaluation of the home pages for the top one million websites in February 2026, published 30 March 2026.

HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025Accessibility analysis based on HTTP Archive data and Lighthouse audits from the 2025 dataset, published January 2026.

Sample Size
1,000,000 homepages in the primary WebAIM dataset

Date Range

February 2026 primary sample; 2025 HTTP Archive context

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
Automated tests evaluate only a subset of WCAG requirements and cannot establish conformance.
The primary WebAIM sample covers homepages, not every template or user journey on each website.
HTTP Archive findings are presented as separate context and are not merged into the WebAIM sample. The two sources use different engines (WAVE versus Lighthouse and axe-core) and can move in different directions in the same period.
Observed associations, including the relationship between ARIA usage and detected errors, do not prove causation. WebAIM notes that pages using more ARIA were also more complex.
Year-over-year comparisons reflect a changing sample: the underlying one-million-site list is rebuilt from Tranco rankings each year, so some movement reflects which sites were measured.

Last updated: 2026-08-27

Use the research

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Definitions and limitations that are important when quoting these findings.

What percentage of homepages have detectable accessibility failures?▾
WebAIM found automatically detectable WCAG 2 failures on 95.9% of the one million homepages evaluated in February 2026, up from 94.8% in 2025. This is a homepage-level automated result, not a full-site conformance assessment. Because only automatically detectable failures were counted, the rate of full WCAG 2 A/AA conformance is certainly lower than the remaining 4.1%.

Did web accessibility get better or worse in 2026?▾
Worse, by both of WebAIM's headline measures. The share of homepages with detected WCAG failures rose from 94.8% to 95.9%, and the average number of detected errors per homepage rose 10.1%, from 51 to 56.1. WebAIM describes this as reversing a trend of small improvements in each of the previous six years, returning the web to roughly its 2024 position. WebAIM attributes the reversal primarily to rapidly increasing page complexity and ARIA usage, and suggests it reflects broader shifts in web development including heavier reliance on third-party frameworks and libraries and automated or AI-assisted coding practices.

What is the most common detected accessibility failure?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
Low contrast text was again the most common failure reported by WebAIM in 2026, appearing on 83.9% of the homepages evaluated, a sharp increase from 79.1% in 2025. Homepages averaged 34 distinct instances of low-contrast text, up 15% year over year. The same six failure types have topped the list for seven consecutive years and account for 96% of all detected errors.

How many accessibility errors were found on an average homepage?▾
The WebAIM Million 2026 study detected 56,114,377 distinct errors across the sample, an average of 56.1 automatically detected errors per homepage, a 10.1% increase over the 51 errors per page found in 2025. The number does not include barriers that require manual review or user testing.

Does an automated accessibility score prove WCAG conformance?▾
No. Automated tools evaluate only a subset of WCAG requirements. WebAIM is explicit that the absence of detected errors does not indicate that a page is accessible or conformant. Manual testing, assistive-technology testing, and evaluation of real user journeys remain necessary.

Where does this report's data come from?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text: The primary measurements come from WebAIM Million 2026, published 30 March 2026 and based on a February 2026 crawl evaluated with the WAVE engine against WCAG 2.2 A/AA. The HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025 accessibility chapter, published in January 2026 and based on Lighthouse and axe-core, provides separate supporting context; the two datasets are not merged into a single sample.

chunks.text:

Each one is written to stand on its own, with what it measures, who measured it and when, and links to the source. Where a number is a projection or a survey, it says so. Nothing here is estimated by us.
