chunks.heading: How many people have a disability
chunks.text:
Prevalence figures from national statistical agencies and the WHO. Definitions differ between them, so the figures are not directly comparable with each other; each is comparable with itself over time.
1.3 billion

chunks.heading: About 1.3 billion people, 16% of the world's population, live with a significant disability.
chunks.text:
Source: World Health Organization, disability fact sheet, 7 March 2023

28.7%

chunks.heading: 28.7% of adults in the United States, about 73.4 million people, report a disability.
chunks.text:
Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, 2022 data; the highest figure the CDC has recorded.
Source: CDC Disability and Health Data System, 16 July 2024 · Full dataset

13.9%

chunks.heading: Cognitive disability is the most common type among US adults, at 13.9% (33.2 million), ahead of mobility at 12.2%.
chunks.text:
Cognitive rose from 10.8% in 2016 to 13.9% in 2022, the fastest-growing category and not where most accessibility effort goes.
Source: CDC BRFSS via DHDS, 16 July 2024 · Full dataset

5.5%

chunks.heading: 5.5% of US adults, about 14.4 million, report serious difficulty seeing even with glasses; 6.2% (17.7 million) report serious difficulty hearing.
chunks.text:
Source: CDC BRFSS via DHDS, 16 July 2024 · Full dataset

23.9%

chunks.heading: 23.9% of people aged 16 or over in the EU, about 90 million, reported a disability (activity limitation) in 2024, ranging from 12.7% in Bulgaria to 41.2% in Latvia.
chunks.text:
Source: Eurostat, population with disability, 3 December 2025

16.1 million

chunks.heading: 16.1 million people in the UK, 24% of the population, had a disability in 2022/23.
chunks.text: Source: House of Commons Library, from the DWP Family Resources Survey, 7 October 2024

chunks.heading: How accessible the web is
chunks.text:
WebAIM's annual automated evaluation of the home pages of the top one million websites is the largest consistent series. It detects the machine-detectable subset of WCAG failures, so every figure here is a floor, not a measure of usability.
95.9%

chunks.heading: 95.9% of the top one million home pages had at least one detectable WCAG 2 failure in February 2026, up from 94.8% in 2025, reversing six years of gradual improvement.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

56.1

chunks.heading: Home pages averaged 56.1 detectable errors each in 2026, up 10.1% from 51 in 2025; 56,114,377 errors were detected across the sample.
chunks.text:
One error for every 26 page elements on average.
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

83.9%

chunks.heading: Low-contrast text appeared on 83.9% of home pages in 2026, the most common failure, up from 79.1% in 2025.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

53.1%

chunks.heading: 53.1% of home pages had images with missing alternative text, 51.0% had form inputs without labels, 46.3% had empty links and 30.6% had empty buttons.
chunks.text:
The same six failure types account for 96% of all detected errors, every year since the series began.
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

59.1 vs 42

chunks.heading: Home pages that use ARIA averaged 59.1 errors; pages without ARIA averaged 42. ARIA was present on 82.7% of pages, at 133 attributes per page.
chunks.text:
Correlation, not cause: heavier pages use more ARIA and have more of everything.
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

17.1%

chunks.heading: Only 17.1% of home pages had a skip link, 46.1% had a main landmark, 41.8% skipped heading levels and 18.1% had more than one h1.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

42.4 vs 71.4

chunks.heading: Government sites averaged the fewest detected errors of any category (42.4 per page) and sports sites the most (71.4); shopping sites averaged 71.0.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, category analysis, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

85

chunks.heading: The median Lighthouse accessibility score across the sample was 85 out of 100, on pages where 95.9% had detectable failures.
chunks.text:
A high automated score and a failing page are not contradictory; the score weights a small set of checks.
Source: WebAIM Million 2026, 30 March 2026 · Full dataset

chunks.heading: Screen reader users
chunks.text:
WebAIM's eleventh screen reader user survey, 1,780 valid responses collected in July and August 2026, is the most recent large sample of how blind and low-vision people actually use the web.
55.0%

chunks.heading: JAWS is the primary desktop screen reader for 55.0% of respondents, NVDA for 32.9%, VoiceOver for 6.5% and Narrator for 0.4%. JAWS gained sharply on the 2024 survey, while NVDA and VoiceOver declined.
chunks.text:
Primary use varies by region: JAWS leads in North America (72.5%) while NVDA leads in Asia, Africa and South America.
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

70.3%

chunks.heading: 70.3% of screen reader users use more than one desktop screen reader; JAWS is used by 69.2% of respondents and NVDA by 59.3%.
chunks.text:
Testing with one screen reader covers the primary tool of only about half of users.
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

91.8%

chunks.heading: 91.8% of screen reader users also use a screen reader on a mobile device; VoiceOver is commonly used by 72.2% of respondents and TalkBack by 29.5%.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

31.2%

chunks.heading: JAWS with Chrome is the single most common screen reader and browser combination at 31.2%; Chrome is the primary browser for 52.3% of respondents.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

67.8%

chunks.heading: 67.8% of screen reader users navigate a lengthy page by its headings first, down from 71.6% in 2024 but still far ahead of any other method, which is why heading structure ranks with alternative text as a first-order requirement.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

22.9%

chunks.heading: 22.9% of screen reader users said web content had become less accessible over the previous year, 44.9% said it was unchanged and 32.2% said it had improved, a more negative balance than in 2024.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

85.6%

chunks.heading: 85.6% of screen reader users say PDF documents are very or somewhat likely to pose accessibility problems, up from 75.1% in 2019.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

60.1%

chunks.heading: 60.1% of screen reader users commonly use AI to generate image descriptions or alternative text; only 8.2% reported none of the AI uses the survey listed.
chunks.text:
Users working around missing alt text with AI is not a reason to skip writing it: the description they get is a guess, not the author's intent.
Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #11, 29 September 2026 · Full dataset

#1

chunks.heading: In WebAIM's 2024 survey, CAPTCHA was the most problematic item screen reader users reported, ahead of interactive elements behaving unexpectedly, nonsensical link and button text, unexpected screen changes and missing keyboard access. The 2026 survey did not repeat this question.
chunks.text: Source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10, 22 February 2024 · Full dataset

chunks.heading: PDF documents
chunks.text:
Dual Lab, the main developers of the open-source veraPDF validator, analysed the 20,578,394 PDFs in the June 2026 Common Crawl, dating each file by its modification date. A tag tree is a precondition for an accessible PDF, not proof of one.
50%

chunks.heading: More than half of web PDFs dated from July 2025 onward contain a structure tag tree, and the tagged share is rising by about 1.5 percentage points a year.
chunks.text:
At that rate Dual Lab expects it to take more than ten years before 70% of PDFs are tagged. About 2% of files have a tag tree that is empty.
Source: Dual Lab, PDF Trends 2026: structure, tagging and conformance, 5 October 2026 · Full dataset

Under 1%

chunks.heading: Fewer than 1% of web PDFs claim PDF/UA conformance, against roughly half that are tagged; of the PDF/UA files found, 99.3% declare PDF/UA-1 and 0.3% PDF/UA-2.
chunks.text:
A conformance claim is metadata the author sets. It says what the file asserts, not what a validator found.
Source: Dual Lab, PDF Trends 2026: structure, tagging and conformance, 5 October 2026 · Full dataset

chunks.heading: Lawsuits
chunks.text:
Two series are commonly mixed. Seyfarth Shaw counts federal-court website cases by manual review; UsableNet counts federal and state filings together and runs much higher. Both are given here, labelled.
3,117

chunks.heading: 3,117 website accessibility lawsuits were filed in US federal courts in 2025, up 27% on 2024 and the highest annual total in the series.
chunks.text:
Website cases were 36% of all 8,667 ADA Title III federal filings in 2025.
Source: Seyfarth Shaw, federal filing series, 1 March 2026 · Full dataset

21,550

chunks.heading: UsableNet projects about 6,176 digital accessibility lawsuits across federal and state courts in 2026, a record and nearly 20% above 2025, based on filings to 14 June 2026.
chunks.text:
A projection, and a different series from the federal count above.
Source: UsableNet 2026 midyear report, 30 June 2026 · Full dataset

80%

chunks.heading: About 80% of digital accessibility lawsuits are brought against e-commerce companies.
chunks.text:
Source: UsableNet 2026 midyear report, 30 June 2026 · Full dataset

1,021

chunks.heading: 46% of federal website cases in 2025 were filed against a company that had already been sued at least once before; 1,427 defendants were repeat defendants.
chunks.text:
Source: Industry litigation reports compiled in the lawsuit tracker, 27 August 2026

$0

chunks.heading: Title III of the ADA provides no damages to a private plaintiff; the remedy is an injunction and legal fees. Every dollar awarded in the landmark cases came from state law, mainly California's Unruh Act at $4,000 per violation.
chunks.text:
Source: 42 U.S.C. 12188; the three case studies, 2 September 2026

$37,000

chunks.heading: The only remediation estimate ever given in evidence at a web accessibility trial was $37,000 or less, against a $250,000 budget the defendant had set aside; the judge found the difference of no moment.
chunks.text:
Source: Gil v. Winn-Dixie, trial verdict, 12 June 2017

500+

chunks.heading: In February 2026 the Justice Department recorded that one class counsel had filed substantially the same website lawsuit more than 500 times between 2019 and 2023, in a statement opposing a $2.52 million fee award.
chunks.text: Source: US Department of Justice, statement of interest in Alcazar v. Fashion Nova, 2 February 2026 · Full dataset

chunks.heading: Public sector and regulation
chunks.text:
Where a regulator publishes its own monitoring, the numbers are usually worse than the sector's statements claim.
1,203

chunks.heading: The UK Government Digital Service monitored 1,203 public sector websites and 21 mobile apps between January 2022 and September 2024; 85% had published an accessibility statement, and 16,482 issues were fixed as a direct result of monitoring.
chunks.text:
Source: GDS accessibility monitoring report, December 2024, 17 December 2024 · Full dataset

39 of 593

chunks.heading: In GDS's first monitoring round, only 39 of 593 UK public sector accessibility statements examined between February 2020 and November 2021 were fully compliant with the regulations.
chunks.text:
The statement is a legal document with mandatory content; most failures were missing required information, not tone.
Source: GDS accessibility monitoring, first report, 1 January 2022 · Full dataset

26 Apr 2027

chunks.heading: US state and local governments serving 50,000 or more people must meet WCAG 2.1 AA under ADA Title II by 26 April 2027, and smaller entities by 26 April 2028, after a Justice Department interim final rule of 20 April 2026 extended each deadline by a year.
chunks.text:
Source: US Department of Justice, Title II web rule and 2026 interim final rule, 20 April 2026 · Full dataset

28 Jun 2025

chunks.heading: The European Accessibility Act has applied to in-scope products and services since 28 June 2025; all 27 member states have notified transposing measures, 380 national instruments in total.
chunks.text:
Source: Directive (EU) 2019/882, Article 31; Commission transposition register, 28 October 2026

60

chunks.heading: The Section 508 assessment covers 60 US federal agencies for fiscal year 2025, rating each on conformance and implementation maturity.
chunks.text:
Source: GSA and OMB, Section 508 assessment, 27 August 2026 · Full dataset

0

chunks.heading: There is still no federal technical accessibility regulation for private business websites under ADA Title III; the 2024 rule that adopted WCAG 2.1 AA binds state and local government only.
chunks.text:
Source: US Department of Justice, Title II rule, 24 April 2024 · Full dataset

28 Aug 2026

chunks.heading: Missouri's SB 907 safe harbour, operative 28 August 2026, creates a rebuttable presumption against abusive litigation where a defendant takes substantial good-faith steps to fix a noticed violation within 90 days; it does not change the federal duty.
chunks.text: Source: Missouri Senate Bill 907, 28 August 2026 · Full dataset

chunks.heading: Inside organisations
chunks.text:
Self-reported survey figures from accessibility and technology professionals. They describe what practitioners say about their organisations, not measured outcomes, and the sample leans to large companies.
83%

chunks.heading: 83% of organisations require documented proof of accessibility before buying digital products, up from 75% a year earlier, and 42% require it every time.
chunks.text:
Sapio Research surveyed 2,530 professionals in June and July 2026; 97% work at organisations with 1,000 or more employees, 52% are in the US and 43% in the UK and Europe.
Source: Level Access with IAAP and G3ict, Eighth Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 16 September 2026 · Full dataset

80%

chunks.heading: 80% of professionals use AI for digital accessibility work, but no single use case was adopted by more than 31% of respondents; the most common was developers finding and fixing issues in their code editor.
chunks.text:
35% of organisations now address accessibility at the planning stage, up from 28% in 2025.
Source: Level Access with IAAP and G3ict, Eighth Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 16 September 2026

chunks.heading: What it costs and what it pays
chunks.text:
Published prices, dated. Most providers do not publish; these are the ones that do, and our own page on audit pricing explains what drives the differences.
$100 to $250

chunks.heading: A fully manual WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA audit is priced at $100 to $250 per page or screen, with $25 to $100 for light pages, and typical projects at $1,250 to $2,750.
chunks.text:
Source: Accessible.org published pricing, 25 July 2026 · Full dataset

£4,950

chunks.heading: AbilityNet's fixed-price Digital Accessibility Review, covering up to ten pages, components or features with screen reader testing against WCAG 2.2, is £4,950 plus VAT.
chunks.text:
Source: AbilityNet published pricing, 3 September 2026 · Full dataset

$1,500 to $5,000

chunks.heading: DigitalA11Y prices web accessibility audits at $1,500 to $5,000, each including a screen reader user tester.
chunks.text:
Source: DigitalA11Y audit cost guide, 5 February 2026 · Full dataset

$350 to $950

chunks.heading: A VPAT or accessibility conformance report is priced at $350 (WCAG edition), $550 (Section 508), $650 (EN 301 549) or $950 (international), on top of the audit.
chunks.text:
Source: Accessible.org published pricing, 25 July 2026 · Full dataset

$101,688

chunks.heading: The average salary of digital accessibility professionals worldwide was $101,688 in early 2026, with a median of $94,394, across 300 respondents in 23 countries.
chunks.text:
Down from $109,542 the year before, which WebAIM attributes to fewer very senior respondents rather than falling rates.
Source: WebAIM Global Digital Accessibility Salary Survey #2, 1 February 2026 · Full dataset

35.9%

chunks.heading: Accessibility professionals with more experience earn 35.9% more on average than those with less, the largest single pay gap in the survey.
chunks.text:
Source: WebAIM Global Digital Accessibility Salary Survey #2, 1 February 2026 · Full dataset

$3,738,864.96

chunks.heading: The fee award in the first web accessibility class action, NFB v. Target, was $3,738,864.96, on top of a $6 million damages fund for California claimants.
chunks.text: Source: NFB v. Target, fee order of 3 August 2009, 3 August 2009

chunks.heading: AI, agents and the accessibility tree
chunks.text:
The newest numbers, and the reason accessibility is becoming a machine-readability problem as well as a human one.
50%

chunks.heading: Automated agent and crawler traffic passed half of all internet traffic for the first time in June 2026.
chunks.text:
Source: Cloudflare, reported by Ahrefs, 30 June 2026

19 Aug 2026

chunks.heading: Anthropic's browser-use tool, generally available from 19 August 2026, operates web pages through their accessibility tree: the same names, roles and states a screen reader uses.
chunks.text:
A control with no accessible name is invisible to both.
Source: Anthropic release, August 2026, 19 August 2026 · Full dataset

97%

chunks.heading: 97% of llms.txt files across 137,000 domains were never requested by any crawler in May 2026; Google has said it does not read the file.
chunks.text:
Robots.txt is honoured by every major crawler; llms.txt by almost none.
Source: Ahrefs server-log study, 30 June 2026

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
What percentage of websites are accessible?
No large-scale study measures full accessibility. The closest proxy is WebAIM's automated evaluation of the top one million home pages: in February 2026, 95.9% had at least one detectable WCAG 2 failure, so at most 4.1% passed the automated checks, and true conformance is lower because automation finds only a subset of failures.

How many accessibility lawsuits were filed in 2025?
3,117 website accessibility lawsuits were filed in US federal courts in 2025 according to Seyfarth Shaw's manually reviewed series, up 27% on 2024. Counts that include state courts run higher: UsableNet counted 4,928 for 2025 and projects about 6,176 for 2026. The two series should not be mixed.

What is the most common web accessibility failure?
Low-contrast text, found on 83.9% of the top one million home pages in 2026, followed by missing alternative text on images (53.1%), missing form labels (51.0%), empty links (46.3%) and empty buttons (30.6%). The same six failure types account for 96% of all detected errors.

Which screen reader is most used?
JAWS, by a clear margin. In WebAIM's 2026 survey JAWS is the primary desktop screen reader for 55.0% of users and NVDA for 32.9%, and JAWS is also used at all by more people (69.2% against 59.3%). 70.3% of users use more than one. On mobile, VoiceOver is used by 72.2% and TalkBack by 29.5%.

chunks.heading: Frequently asked questions
chunks.text:
How much does an accessibility audit cost?
Published prices in 2026 range from $100 to $250 per page for a fully manual audit (Accessible.org), $1,500 to $5,000 per audit (DigitalA11Y) and £4,950 plus VAT for a fixed ten-page review (AbilityNet). Most providers do not publish prices; our audit cost guide explains what drives them.

chunks.heading: How this page is maintained
chunks.text:
Every figure links to its source and carries the date of that source. Figures from our own datasets link to the dataset page, where the numbers can be downloaded as CSV or JSON. Series that measure different things (federal filings against federal plus state filings; automated home-page checks against full audits) are labelled so they are not added together.
The page is reviewed monthly. Last review: 28 October 2026. Corrections go through the corrections policy. To cite this page: Accessibility.build, Web Accessibility Statistics 2026, accessibility.build/research/web-accessibility-statistics, with the individual source for any figure you reuse.

chunks.heading: Northstar Checkout Accessibility Audit
chunks.text:
This is the structure every audit follows; the delivery format is agreed before work begins. Northstar Checkout is a fictional product, so the findings are illustrative. Each finding is written so a developer can reproduce it without asking a follow-up question: what the defect is, exactly how to trigger it, what happens, what should happen instead, who it affects, and what to change.

Version
1.0

Issued
July 12, 2026

Target
WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA

Auditor
Khushwant Parihar (CPACC, DHS Trusted Tester)

chunks.heading: Demonstration disclosure
chunks.text: Northstar Checkout is a fictional product created solely to demonstrate the structure and evidence quality of an Accessibility.build audit report. It is not a client, an endorsement, or a conformance claim, and the findings below describe a product that does not exist.

chunks.heading: Scope
chunks.text:
Checkout entry page
Delivery address form
Payment method step
Order review dialog
Confirmation state

chunks.heading: Test environments
chunks.text:
Chrome 128 with NVDA 2025.1 on Windows 11
Safari 18 with VoiceOver on macOS 15
Keyboard-only interaction across all five states
Browser zoom to 400 percent and reflow at 320 CSS pixels
axe-core 4.10 used as supporting evidence only

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
This sample covers five representative states, not every possible checkout configuration.
No usability testing with disabled participants is represented in this fictional sample.
Conformance cannot be claimed from a sample. A conformance claim requires every page in scope to be evaluated.

Methodology. Manual testing against WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA, carried out by a CPACC-certified auditor, with automated checks used only to surface candidates for manual review. Every finding below was reproduced by hand.

chunks.heading: Who Needs Accessibility Audits?
chunks.text:
Accessibility audits are essential for organizations that want to ensure their digital products are usable by everyone, including people with disabilities. They're particularly valuable for:
Businesses and organizations seeking to reach a wider audience and avoid legal risks related to accessibility
Government agencies required to comply with accessibility regulations like Section 508
Educational institutions ensuring equal access to learning materials and platforms
Healthcare providers making critical health information and services accessible to all
E-commerce businesses ensuring all customers can browse and purchase products

chunks.heading: Benefits of an Accessibility Audit
chunks.text:
Expanded Audience Reach
Make your digital products usable by the estimated 16 percent of the global population, about 1.3 billion people, who live with a significant disability (WHO fact sheet).

Regulatory Context
Findings are mapped to WCAG 2.2 AA, which goes beyond the WCAG 2.1 AA in the ADA Title II rule and the WCAG 2.0 AA in Section 508, giving you documented evidence toward conformance. This is regulatory context, not legal advice.

Improved User Experience
Accessibility improvements benefit all users, not just those with disabilities.

Enhanced SEO
Many accessibility improvements also boost search engine optimization.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Find answers to common questions about our services.

How long does an accessibility audit take?▾
The Essential Audit is delivered in 7-10 business days, the Product Audit in 2-3 weeks, and the Complex Product Audit in 4-5 weeks. Timelines begin after access, test accounts, and the representative sample are confirmed.

What accessibility standards do you test against?▾
I test against WCAG 2.2 at the AA level, the most widely recognized standard and the one referenced in most accessibility regulations worldwide. AAA criteria or specific country regulations can be added to the scope on request. Regulatory mapping is provided as context, not legal advice.

Will the audit disrupt our website or application?▾
No. The audit is non-invasive: I only observe and test your digital product without making any changes to it. There is no downtime or disruption to your users.

What deliverables will we receive?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
You'll receive a comprehensive report detailing all identified issues, categorized by severity and WCAG criteria. The report includes screenshots, code examples, and specific recommendations for remediation. The Product Audit adds an executive brief and a prioritized remediation backlog; the Complex Product Audit adds a leadership summary, a procurement-ready evidence package, and a remediation planning workshop. The Essential Audit includes a severity-ranked issue register and a findings walkthrough.

Do you provide remediation services after the audit?▾
Yes. Remediation support is a separate service that ranges from guidance for your development team to hands-on implementation. It can be scoped alongside the audit so the findings flow straight into fixes.

How often should we conduct accessibility audits?▾
I recommend a full audit annually and smaller spot-checks after major updates or releases. That keeps your evidence toward WCAG 2.2 AA current as your digital product evolves and the standard is updated.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Find answers to common questions about our services.

What is an accessibility statement and why do I need one?▾
An accessibility statement is a public-facing document that communicates your commitment to accessibility, the current state of your digital product's accessibility, known limitations, and how users can provide feedback. It's increasingly required by regulations like the EU Web Accessibility Directive and is considered a best practice globally. A well-crafted statement demonstrates transparency and commitment to all users.

What is the difference between a VPAT and an ACR?▾
A VPAT is the reporting template. The completed, evidence-based document is an Accessibility Conformance Report, or ACR. Procurement teams often request an ACR when evaluating software for government, education, healthcare, and enterprise use. Our WCAG ACR package requires current audit evidence so every conformance statement can be supported.

How often should accessibility documentation be updated?▾
Accessibility documentation should be reviewed and updated whenever significant changes are made to your digital product, when new features are added, or at least annually. For rapidly evolving products, more frequent updates may be necessary. Outdated documentation can create legal risk if it no longer accurately reflects your product's accessibility status.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Can you help with documentation for legal defense?▾
Yes. I can help document your good-faith accessibility efforts: your accessibility policy, ongoing work, remediation plans, and user feedback mechanisms. chunks.heading: Why PDFs Fail
chunks.text:
A PDF that looks finished on screen is usually the least accessible thing an organisation publishes. The visual layout carries the meaning, and none of it is written into the file, so assistive technology gets a wall of undifferentiated text. The most common failures are:
No tag tree at all, so there are no headings to navigate by and the document is one continuous block
Reading order that follows the layout rather than the meaning, so a two-column page is read straight across and the sentences interleave
Tables without header associations, so a figure is announced with no indication of which row and column it belongs to
Scanned pages that are images of text, invisible to a screen reader and unsearchable
Form fields with no labels, so the person filling it in cannot tell what any box is asking for

chunks.heading: Why It Is Worth Fixing
chunks.text:
Documents Are In Scope
The European Accessibility Act and Section 508 both cover published documents, not just web pages. A compliant site with inaccessible PDFs is still exposed.

Auditors Look Here First
Annual reports, policies, and application forms are the documents complaints and procurement reviews tend to cite, because they are the ones people actually need.

Searchable and Reusable
Tagging and OCR make a document searchable, indexable, and easier to convert to other formats, which benefits every reader.

Fixed Price Before You Commit
Pages are banded from the real files, so you approve a total up front rather than an hourly estimate that moves.

chunks.text:
Find answers to common questions about our services.

How much does PDF remediation cost per page?▾
Standard text-led pages are $3 per page, structured pages with tables or multi-column layouts are $7 per page, and complex pages with forms, charts, or scanned content are $12 per page. Pages are banded individually inside a document, so you are not charged the highest rate for the whole file. A minimum order of $150 applies per project.

How do you decide which band a page falls into?▾
By what has to be built in the tag tree, not by how the page looks. A page with running text, headings, and links is standard. Once meaning depends on a data table, multiple columns, or footnote relationships, it is structured. When a page needs labelled form fields, a described chart, or OCR to recover text from an image, it is complex. I band every page from the real document and show you the split before you commit.

What standard do you remediate to?▾
PDF/UA (ISO 14289-1) together with the applicable WCAG 2.2 Level AA criteria. That combination is what the European Accessibility Act, Section 508, and most procurement rules expect for documents. If you need a specific profile such as PDF/UA-2 or a Section 508 attestation, say so at quoting and I will confirm it in scope.

Can you fix the source file so future exports are accessible?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Yes, and for documents you republish regularly it is usually the cheaper path. The Source file rebuild add-on is $18 per page and repairs the styles, alt text, and table structure in the InDesign or Word original, so every future export starts accessible instead of needing remediation again. For a quarterly report, that pays for itself within a year.

Do you handle confidential or regulated documents?▾
Yes. Financial statements, patient materials, and HR documents are routine. Files containing personal or regulated data are handled under a signed agreement covering transfer, storage, and deletion before anything is sent. Documents are processed on encrypted storage and removed on request once the work is accepted.

How long does remediation take?▾
Standard pages are typically returned in 3-5 business days, structured pages in 5-8 business days, and complex pages in 8-12 business days, measured from the point the final files are confirmed. Large sets are delivered in batches so you can publish the first documents while the rest are still in progress. The Accessibility rush add-on roughly halves the window.

Who participates in your user testing?▾
Participants are people with disabilities who use different assistive technologies: screen reader users, keyboard-only users, magnification users, voice recognition users, and people with cognitive disabilities. Profiles are matched to your product and testing objectives. Participants are recruited per engagement rather than from a standing panel; the recruitment route (your own users, partner organizations, or paid panels) and participant compensation are agreed in the statement of work.

When should we conduct accessibility user testing?▾
Ideally, testing should occur at multiple stages: early with prototypes to catch fundamental issues, during development to validate specific features, and before launch for final validation. However, testing at any stage provides valuable insights, even with existing products.

How is accessibility testing different from regular user testing?▾
Accessibility testing specifically focuses on the experience of people with disabilities using assistive technologies. It evaluates both technical compliance and real-world usability for these users, identifying barriers that standard testing might miss.

Do you test remotely or in-person?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
The published packages cover moderated remote testing, which supports broader participant recruitment and lets people use their own assistive technology setup. In-person studies are scoped separately because venue, travel, equipment, and participant location materially change the project cost.

What deliverables will we receive?▾
Every package includes a research plan, moderated sessions, barrier analysis, actionable recommendations, and a stakeholder readout. Product and Extended studies add deeper task analysis and prioritization. A consent-based, captioned highlight reel is available for a fixed $500.

How do you measure success in accessibility testing?▾
Success is measured through task completion rates, time-on-task metrics, error rates, and participant satisfaction scores, alongside qualitative feedback about the experience and the specific barriers that prevented successful interaction.

chunks.heading: Which accessibility tool do you actually need?
chunks.text:
Most accessibility work splits into four jobs, and the tool you want depends on which one you are doing. Automated checkers are excellent at the mechanical layer and cannot judge meaning, so treat any clean report as a starting point rather than proof of conformance. The automated versus manual testing guide explains where that line falls.
WordPress site owners
The completely free Build with Accessibility plugin helps you monitor detectable changes, review native content repairs, and record manual testing. Repeat scans can help catch regressions on an already accessible site; they cannot guarantee continued accessibility or replace manual evaluation.

Developers shipping a fix
Start with the URL accessibility auditor for a page-level scan, the contrast checker for WCAG 2.2 and APCA ratios, and the heading analyzer to catch a broken document outline.

Designers building a system
The accessible colour palette generator produces WCAG-aware palettes and previews them in real UI states, so contrast is settled before handoff rather than caught in review.

QA and audit teams
Track findings against every criterion with the interactive WCAG 2.2 checklist, then turn them into a shareable document with the accessibility report generator.

Compliance and procurement

chunks.heading: Which accessibility tool do you actually need?
chunks.text: Publish where you stand with the accessibility statement generator, and check a vendor’s claims against the overlay detector if they rely on an accessibility widget.

chunks.heading: What these tools cannot tell you
chunks.text: No scanner can tell you whether alt text describes the right thing, whether focus order preserves meaning, whether an error message helps someone recover, or whether a custom widget works with a screen reader. Those need a keyboard, a screen reader, and a person. Use these tools to clear the mechanical failures fast, then spend the time you saved on the screen reader testing and keyboard accessibility passes that actually decide whether the product is usable.

chunks.heading: What the Audit Helper Does
chunks.text:
The audit helper turns a described accessibility problem into a structured write-up. You give it a description of the issue, an optional code snippet, and the technology and component involved; a hosted language model returns a bug-ticket style analysis with a title, a severity, the current and expected behaviour, the effect on users, the WCAG success criteria involved, a recommended fix with example code, ordered implementation steps, a testing checklist, and links to further reading.
The response streams in as it is written, so you see the sections complete one by one, and it falls back to a single request if streaming fails. The server checks that every required section is present and that the severity is one of critical, high, medium, or low before returning it; a missing severity defaults to medium.

chunks.heading: How to Use It
chunks.text:
Describe the issue as a user experienced it. “Screen reader users hear ‘button’ for every icon in the toolbar” gives the model the symptom, the audience, and the component in one sentence.
Paste the relevant code. With a snippet, the model reviews your actual markup and returns a corrected version. Without one, it explains the pattern from semantic HTML up to the ARIA needed and offers more than one approach.
Choose the stack and component type. Both are optional but they shape the example code, so a React team gets JSX and a WordPress team gets PHP templates and plain HTML.
Run the analysis and verify it. Read the WCAG section against the linked criterion pages, apply the fix, then work through the testing checklist before you close the ticket.

chunks.heading: What the Analysis Covers and Its WCAG 2.2 References
chunks.text:
The model is prompted to name each criterion by number and title, state its level, and explain why it applies to your issue, and to write the testing checklist around the things automated tools miss: screen reader behaviour, keyboard operation, 200 percent zoom, voice control, and mobile screen readers. The criteria that come up most often for the component types in the form are:
Navigation, buttons, dropdowns, tabs, and accordions: 2.1.1 Keyboard, 2.4.3 Focus Order, 2.4.7 Focus Visible, and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.
Forms: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, 3.3.1 Error Identification, 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions, 3.3.3 Error Suggestion, and 4.1.3 Status Messages.
Modals and dialogs: 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap alongside the focus criteria above.
Images and videos: 1.1.1 Non-text Content, 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded), and 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded).
Carousels: 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide; tables: 1.3.1 again, for header and cell relationships.

WCAG 2.2 has 86 success criteria, and the model can reference any of them. The site's criterion pages give you the normative text to check its reasoning against.

chunks.heading: What It Cannot Do
chunks.text:
The helper never sees your page. It cannot confirm that the issue you describe actually exists, cannot find issues you did not mention, and cannot test the fix it proposes. Its severity rating is the model's reading of your description, not a measurement, so two differently worded reports of the same bug can come back with different severities. Its links are constructed from the criterion and pattern names it chooses, and occasionally point at a slug that does not exist.
An analysis is not an audit finding until a person has confirmed it
Reproduce the issue with the assistive technology named in the report, apply the fix, and run the testing checklist yourself. If the write-up is going into a formal report or an accessibility statement, cross-check each criterion against the WCAG 2.2 checklist and follow the audit methodology guide for the parts of the page the helper never looked at.

chunks.heading: Reading the Output
chunks.text:
The first card is the ticket: a plain title, a severity badge, the user impact as a subtitle, and side-by-side Current Problem and Expected Solution boxes you can paste into an issue tracker. WCAG Criteria and Review Requirements lists each criterion with its level and the reason it applies. Review Recommendations is the narrative fix, and Code Solution, when present, is the corrected markup with a copy button.
Implementation Steps is an ordered list you can hand to a developer, and Testing Checklist is the acceptance criteria: use it to decide when the fix is done, not just whether it was attempted. Related Resources closes with the external reading the model chose. Your remaining credit balance and, for guests, your remaining trial uses are shown above the form once an analysis completes.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
How is this different from the URL Accessibility Auditor?▾
The URL auditor loads a live page and runs axe-core against it, so it finds issues you did not know about but only the ones an automated rule can detect. The audit helper starts from an issue you already know about, described in words and optionally code, and explains it: which criteria apply, who it affects, how to fix it, and how to test the fix. Use the auditor to find, and the helper to understand and resolve.

What should I put in the issue description?▾
Describe what a user tried to do, what happened, and what you expected. Name the assistive technology if you know it, for example NVDA with Firefox or VoiceOver on iOS. Paste the smallest code snippet that reproduces the problem rather than a whole page, and pick the tech stack and component type so the fix comes back in the right idiom. Vague descriptions produce generic answers.

Are the WCAG references and links reliable?▾
Mostly, but verify them. The model is asked to cite criteria in the form '1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)' with a level, and to link to the W3C Understanding documents and ARIA Authoring Practices patterns, but it fills in those slugs itself. Check every criterion number against the site's WCAG pages and follow each link before quoting it in a report.

Can it audit my whole site or a URL?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
No. It never fetches a page. It reasons only from the text and code you paste, which is what makes it useful for issues on pages behind a login or in components that are not deployed yet, and useless for discovering issues you have not described.

How much does an analysis cost?▾
One credit per analysis for signed-in users. Guests get a small number of free analyses from the shared daily allowance before they need to sign in. Unlimited access accounts are not charged and can choose which model runs the analysis.

chunks.heading: What the Code Generator Does
chunks.text:
You describe a UI component, choose a framework and a WCAG target, and a hosted large language model drafts the component for you. The prompt it receives is not a generic coding request: it names the WCAG version and conformance level you picked, spells out which success criteria that version adds, and demands a fixed JSON structure with the code, an explanation of the accessibility decisions, usage examples, and lists of the criteria addressed, tests to run, mistakes to avoid, and follow-up improvements.
The response streams back as it is written, and the server parses it as JSON before handing it over; a reply that is not valid JSON becomes an error message rather than a broken page. The contents of each section are not verified. What you see has the right shape, but it has not passed an accessibility test; that part is yours.

chunks.heading: How to Use It
chunks.text:
Pick the component type and framework. The type steers which interaction pattern the model follows, so choose Combobox rather than Dropdown if the user can type, and Modal rather than Alert if the user must respond before continuing.
Set the WCAG version and level. The defaults, WCAG 2.2 at Level AA, are right for almost every project. Level AAA asks the model for 7:1 contrast tokens and extra cognitive support; Level A drops the AA criteria.
Describe the behaviour, not the look. Say what the component does, what states it has, and what happens on error. “A date picker that opens on click, supports arrow keys between days, and returns focus to the input on close” produces a far better draft than “a nice date picker”.
Generate, then review the sections in order. Read the code, then the testing guide, and run those tests before you read the WCAG compliance list. The list describes what the model intended, and the tests tell you whether it succeeded.

chunks.heading: The WCAG 2.2 Criteria It Targets
chunks.text:
Interactive components fail a predictable cluster of success criteria, and the prompt is built around them. Expect the draft and its compliance list to address:
2.1.1 Keyboard and 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A): every action reachable by keyboard, and focus able to leave.
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): native elements or correct ARIA roles, accessible names, and state attributes such as aria-expanded and aria-selected.
1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A): labels associated with fields, groups, headings, and list structure expressed in markup.
2.4.3 Focus Order and 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level A and AA): focus moved deliberately in dialogs and menus, and never hidden by CSS.
3.3.1 Error Identification and 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A) for forms, with 4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA) for anything announced through a live region.
The criteria new in WCAG 2.2 that the prompt calls out by number when you choose 2.2: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum).

The compliance list in the output pairs each criterion number with a one-line justification. Check the numbers against the criterion pages linked above; models occasionally cite a plausible-sounding number that does not match the requirement they describe.

chunks.heading: What It Cannot Do
chunks.text:
The generator never executes, renders, or tests the code. It cannot see your design system, your existing focus styles, or the page the component will live in, so it cannot know whether the contrast tokens it suggests actually meet 1.4.3 in your theme or whether its focus ring will be visible on your background. It cannot verify its own WCAG claims. And like any language model it can produce ARIA that is syntactically valid and semantically wrong, such as a role that conflicts with the native element or a live region that fires on every keystroke.
Every draft needs a manual review before it ships
At minimum: operate the whole component with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, and the arrow keys; listen to it with a screen reader; check contrast and focus visibility in your real theme; and run an automated checker on the rendered result. The keyboard accessibility guide covers what to expect from each key, and the interactive pattern demos show working modal, table, search, pagination, and carousel behaviour to compare against.

chunks.heading: Reading the Output
chunks.text:
The result opens with the component code and a quick-actions bar for copying or downloading it with the right file extension for your framework. Detailed Code Analysis explains the choices in three tabs: a walkthrough of the code, the accessibility context behind it, and a real-world scenario. Implementation Examples shows basic usage, an advanced configuration, and a fuller integration.
The four summary cards are the review aids. Accessibility Features lists what the code claims to implement, WCAG Compliance lists the criteria and why, Testing Guide gives two to six concrete checks, and Best Practices records the conventions applied. Common Mistakes to Avoid and Enhancement Suggestions follow, and the Implementation Summary closes with ordered integration steps and your credit balance. If several cards read “No items provided”, the model padded a thin response; regenerate with more detail rather than trusting the code alone.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is the generated code production ready?▾
Treat it as a reviewed first draft, not a finished component. The model is instructed to produce runnable code with keyboard handling and ARIA, and the server checks that the response has the right shape, but nothing runs or tests the code before you see it. Wire it into your project, tab through it, try it with a screen reader, and run an automated checker before shipping.

How much does a generation cost?▾
Two credits per generation for signed-in users. Guests can try the tool a limited number of times from the shared daily allowance before signing in. Unlimited access accounts are not charged.

Which frameworks and component types are supported?▾
Ten targets: plain HTML and CSS, React, React with TypeScript, Vue, Vue 3 with TypeScript, Angular, Svelte, Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. Eighteen component types are offered, from buttons, forms, and modals through tabs, carousels, accordions, dropdowns, tooltips, data tables, skip links, breadcrumbs, search, pagination, alerts, toggles, progress bars, and comboboxes.

Why do some result cards say no items were provided?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
The model is required to return every section, but it is told to pad a list with empty entries rather than invent content when it has nothing substantive to say, and the interface shows an empty list as 'No items provided'. If several cards are empty, or the code block itself is blank, the request was too vague or too long for a useful answer. Try again with a shorter, more specific description of the behaviour you need.

Should I pick WCAG 2.2 or an earlier version?▾
Pick 2.2 unless a contract or policy names an earlier version. WCAG 2.2 is backwards compatible with 2.1 and 2.0 apart from removing 4.1.1 Parsing, and it adds criteria that matter for components, including 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, and 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum). Level AA is the target referenced by most laws and procurement rules.

chunks.heading: How mature is your accessibility programme?
chunks.text:
Rate your organisation against the W3C Accessibility Maturity Model, one dimension at a time. You get a level for each of the seven dimensions, a chart and table of where you stand, and next steps for the weakest areas. Answers stay in your browser, and you can download them as Excel or PDF.

chunks.heading: How the assessment works
chunks.text:
The model looks at seven dimensions of how an organisation works. For each one you rate its proof points, the evidence the model looks for, against four levels. Choose “Not sure” when you don't know and “Does not apply” when a proof point doesn't fit your organisation. The W3C suggests doing this with people from across the organisation rather than alone.
Answers are saved in this browser as you go, so you can stop and come back. Nothing is sent to us.

chunks.heading: The four levels
chunks.text:
Inactive
Little or no awareness that accessibility is needed, and almost nothing being done about it.

Launch
The need is recognised and planning has started, but the work is not yet organised.

Integrate
There is a roadmap, and the organisation's approach is defined and well organised.

Optimize

chunks.heading: What the W3C model measures
chunks.text:
WCAG tells you whether a page is accessible. The Accessibility Maturity Model asks a different question: does the organisation have what it takes to keep producing accessible products and services? It is a W3C Group Note published on 4 November 2025, and this tool follows that version, checked on 28 October 2026. It looks at seven dimensions:

Communications
Whether everything the organisation communicates, inside and outside, formal and informal, and whether written by staff or by contractors, can be used by as many people as possible and meets accessibility standards.

ICT Development Lifecycle
Whether accessibility is built into every stage of a digital product's life: the first idea, design, development, testing, conformance reporting, user research, maintenance and retirement, with training that keeps the skills current.

Knowledge and Skills
Whether people at every level know enough about accessibility for their role, and understand how their work supports the organisation's accessibility goals. Skills that belong to one dimension are assessed in that dimension.

Oversight and Culture
Whether leadership's values, policies and processes make disability inclusion part of how the whole organisation operates, and whether everyone understands what digital accessibility means for their own role.

Personnel

chunks.heading: What the W3C model measures
chunks.text:
Whether qualified disabled people work at every level and in every part of the organisation, so that their own experience informs its decisions.

Procurement
Whether accessibility is part of how the organisation finds, chooses and contracts for goods and services. Most digital products arrive through procurement, so this is where accessible products and services are won or lost.

Support
Whether disabled employees and customers get the help they need with the organisation's digital products, from workplace adjustments for staff to accessibility support for customers.

Each dimension is judged on four levels. Inactive means little or no awareness. Launch means the need is recognised and planning has started. Integrate means there is a roadmap and a defined approach. Optimize means accessibility is part of how the whole organisation works and is checked and improved continually. The levels build on each other, so a dimension reaches one only by meeting the ones below it first. Our W3C Accessibility Maturity Model guide explains the model in full, with example proof points and how to turn results into a roadmap.

chunks.heading: How we summarise your answers
chunks.text:
The Note has no numeric score. Its proof points are evidence, and the evaluator decides which level that evidence supports. To give you something to act on, this tool adds a summary for each dimension, and that summary is ours, not the W3C's.
A dimension sits at the level that at least half of its rated proof points have reached. It reaches Optimize only when every rated proof point is at Optimize, because the Note says proof points must be fully complete at that level. Not sure and Does not apply answers are left out, and a summary resting on fewer than half of a dimension's proof points is marked provisional. The table under the chart shows how many answers sit at each level, so you can see the spread behind the summary.

chunks.heading: What a self-assessment can't tell you
chunks.text:
The result is only as good as the evidence behind each rating. Use the notes to record what you looked at, and ask the owner of each area rather than guessing.
It is not a conformance check. A mature programme can still ship an inaccessible page, so test your products against WCAG as well, for example with an accessibility audit or the WCAG 2.2 checklist.
The proof points are our paraphrase of the Note. Where the wording matters, for a contract or a policy, quote the Note itself.
The Note says its proof point lists are not exhaustive and can be adapted. If a proof point does not fit your organisation, mark it Does not apply rather than forcing a rating.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is the W3C Accessibility Maturity Model?▾
A W3C Group Note, published on 4 November 2025, for judging how well an organisation builds accessibility into the way it works, rather than whether one website passes WCAG. It covers seven dimensions, from communications and procurement to personnel and support, and describes four levels of maturity: Inactive, Launch, Integrate and Optimize. Each dimension lists proof points, the evidence an organisation can show for its level.

Who should fill in the assessment?▾
The Note is written for executives, the managers responsible for accessibility, and the people who own policy and process. It recommends a cross-functional team, because no one person sees procurement, development, HR and customer support at once. A practical approach is for one person to work through it with the owners of each dimension, using the notes field to record the evidence behind each rating.

How is my level for each dimension worked out?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
The Note has no numeric score: an evaluator judges which level the evidence supports. To give a summary, we use our own rule. A dimension sits at the level that at least half of its rated proof points have reached, and reaches Optimize only when every rated proof point is at Optimize, because the Note says proof points must be fully complete at that level. Not sure and Does not apply answers are left out, and a summary based on fewer than half of a dimension's proof points is marked provisional.

Is this an official W3C tool?▾
No. It is our independent self-assessment based on the W3C Note. The dimension and level names are the W3C's, and every proof point is paraphrased in our own words with the same meaning. The Note links to its own assessment spreadsheet, which it describes as experimental and a work in progress.

Where are my answers stored?▾
In your browser's local storage on this device, and nowhere else. Nothing is sent to us. Clearing your browser data, or using a private window, removes them, so download the Excel file to keep a copy or to share it with colleagues. Start over clears the saved answers after asking you to confirm.

How often should we reassess?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: The Note advises reassessing regularly, to track progress and to catch areas that slip back, without setting a frequency. Pick a rhythm that matches your planning cycle, such as once a year, and keep each export so you can compare.

chunks.heading: What a Useful Accessibility Report Contains
chunks.text:
A report gets acted on when a developer can go straight from a finding to a fix without asking follow-up questions. That means every finding carries five things:
Where it is. The page URL and a selector or screenshot precise enough to locate the element without hunting.
What is wrong. The actual failure in plain language, not just the rule ID a scanner emitted.
Which criterion it fails. The specific WCAG success criterion, so the finding is traceable to the standard. Browse the WCAG 2.2 reference for exact wording.
Who it affects and how badly. Severity based on user impact, plus which assistive technology or input method hits the barrier.
What to do about it. A concrete remediation, ideally with the corrected markup.

chunks.heading: Setting Severity by Impact, Not Effort
chunks.text:
The most common way a report goes wrong is ranking findings by how easy they are to fix, which floats cosmetic items to the top and buries the blockers. Rank by what it costs the user instead:
Severity levels for accessibility findings and what each one means for the user
Severity What it means for the user Example
Critical Cannot complete the task at all A keyboard trap in checkout, or an unlabelled submit button
Serious Can finish, but only with significant difficulty Form errors announced nowhere, so the user must guess what failed
Moderate Real friction, workaround available A skipped heading level that makes the page harder to skim
Minor Worth fixing, rarely blocks anyone A redundant ARIA role on a native element

chunks.heading: Audit Report, VPAT, or Conformance Report?
chunks.text:
These three get used interchangeably and they are not the same document. An audit report (what this tool produces) tells your team what is broken and how to fix it. A VPAT is a specific vendor-supplied template, and the filled-in result is called an Accessibility Conformance Report, which walks every applicable criterion and records supports, partially supports, or does not support. Procurement teams normally ask for that one.
The relationship is sequential: you audit, you fix what you can, and the audit evidence is what lets you fill in a conformance report honestly. If you need to publish a user-facing summary of where you stand instead, use the accessibility statement generator. For the end-to-end process behind the findings, see the website accessibility audit guide.
A scanner-only report cannot support a conformance claim
Automated testing catches a portion of WCAG failures and cannot judge meaningful alt text, sensible focus order, or whether an error message helps. State your methodology in the report, and add a manual keyboard and screen reader pass before anyone treats it as evidence of conformance. The automated versus manual testing guide covers what each layer can and cannot find.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What formats can I export accessibility reports in?▾
You can export as PDF for a professional layout to hand to a client or stakeholder, Excel for detailed data across multiple sheets that a team can filter and assign, HTML for publishing on an intranet, or Markdown for a repository or docs site. Every format includes the summary statistics, the detailed violation listings, and the recommendations, so the choice is about who is reading it rather than what it contains.

Can I import violation data from other tools?▾
Yes. The generator accepts violation data from JSON files, including the output formats produced by axe-core, WAVE, and other common testing tools. Importing means you do not retype findings, which is where transcription errors normally creep in. You can also build a report manually if your findings came from a manual audit rather than a scanner, which is usually the case for the more serious issues.

What information is included in the report?▾
Organisation and scope details, summary statistics broken down by severity (critical, serious, moderate, and minor), the detailed violation listing with the WCAG success criterion each one maps to, recommendations, and suggested next steps. Every section is editable, so you can cut what does not apply and expand what matters to your audience.

How should I set severity on each finding?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Severity should reflect user impact, not how hard the fix is. A useful rule: critical means a user cannot complete the task at all (a keyboard trap, an unlabelled checkout button), serious means they can complete it but only with significant difficulty, moderate means real friction with a workaround available, and minor means a defect worth fixing that rarely blocks anyone. Ranking by impact rather than effort keeps the report honest and stops easy-but-cosmetic items crowding out blockers.

Is an automated report enough for a compliance audit?▾
No. Automated testing reliably catches only a portion of WCAG failures and cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order preserves meaning, or whether an error message actually helps someone recover. A report built purely from scanner output should say so plainly in its methodology section. For a report that supports a conformance claim you need a manual pass with a keyboard and a screen reader on a representative sample of pages and flows.

Is this the same as a VPAT or an ACR?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
No, though they are often confused. This produces an audit report: what is broken, how badly, and what to do about it, aimed at the team doing the work. A VPAT is a specific vendor-supplied template, and the completed document is called an Accessibility Conformance Report, which walks every applicable criterion and states supports, partially supports, or does not support. Procurement usually asks for the latter. An audit report like this is normally the evidence you draw on to fill one in accurately.

Who should the report be written for?▾
Decide before you export, because it changes what to include. Developers need the selector, the failing code, and the criterion. Designers need the pattern and the visual rule. Executives and clients need the severity counts, the risk, and the trend, not a list of CSS selectors. The Excel export suits triage and assignment; the PDF suits a summary for someone who will read it once. Producing two exports from the same data is usually better than one document that half-serves both audiences.

Is the report generator free?▾
Yes, the accessibility report generator is completely free, with no registration or payment required.

chunks.heading: What is accessibility ROI?
chunks.text: Accessibility ROI compares a defined investment with measurable or modeled benefits. Useful inputs can include reduced support effort, improved task completion, avoided rework, a revenue-opportunity scenario, and program maintenance. Results should be presented as scenarios until your organization replaces defaults with its own evidence.

chunks.heading: How much do accessibility lawsuits cost?
chunks.text: Costs vary widely by claim, jurisdiction, defense strategy, remediation scope, and settlement terms. The calculator uses $75,000 only as an editable starting scenario and does not label it an average. Replace it with an internally reviewed amount before using the result in a business case.

chunks.heading: How is the ROI calculated?
chunks.text: The model combines an incident-cost scenario, a revenue-opportunity scenario, one-time remediation, and annual maintenance. The ROI formula is ((modeled annual benefit - remediation cost) / remediation cost) x 100. Audience share, recovery rate, incident cost, and maintenance rate are editable and included in shared links.

chunks.heading: What industries face the highest accessibility lawsuit risk?

chunks.heading: Why check the statement and not just the site
chunks.text:
When the Government Digital Service monitored 593 UK public sector websites between February 2020 and November 2021, it found that only about 7 percent had a fully compliant accessibility statement. Around 83 percent had published one that was missing mandatory information, and only 10 percent had none at all. The common failure is not a missing statement. It is a statement that looks finished and quietly omits the parts a disabled user actually needs, most often the route to escalate a complaint.
That is invisible to a scanner. An automated WCAG test can tell you a button has no accessible name; it has nothing to say about whether your statement names an enforcement body, dates its last review, or claims a level of conformance you cannot evidence. Those are the parts a regulator reads first, and they are cheap to fix once someone points at them: after GDS wrote to the organisations it monitored, statement compliance rose from 7 percent to 80 percent.

chunks.heading: What it checks
chunks.text:
Whether a statement exists at all, including statements linked by wording rather than URL.
The compliance status, in the prescribed fully, partially, or not compliant wording.
The standard claimed against, such as WCAG 2.2 AA or EN 301 549.
A list of non-accessible content, rather than silence about known problems.
A working feedback route, so a person can report a barrier.
The enforcement procedure and the body that handles escalation.
Preparation and review dates, and whether the statement has gone stale past 12 months.
How the assessment was made, by self-assessment or third-party audit.
Overclaiming, such as "100% compliant", and reliance on an overlay widget as the remedy.

chunks.heading: What it deliberately does not do
chunks.text: It does not tell you whether your website is accessible. A statement can pass every check here and still describe a site with serious barriers, and an honest statement often lists more problems than a careless one. For the site itself, use the URL accessibility auditor. To find out whether the EAA applies to you in the first place, use the EAA scope checker.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is an accessibility statement actually a legal requirement?▾
For UK public sector bodies, yes. Regulation 8 of the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 requires one, in a prescribed form. EU public sector bodies have the same duty under the Web Accessibility Directive, with the format set by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1523. Under the European Accessibility Act, private sector providers of in-scope services must publish information under Annex V explaining how the service meets the accessibility requirements.

What is the most common thing missing from an accessibility statement?▾
The enforcement route. A statement typically explains the problems and gives a contact address, then stops, without telling people where to escalate if the response is unsatisfactory. In the UK that means naming the Equality Advisory and Support Service, and the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland where relevant. Missing review dates are a close second.

How many organisations get this wrong?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
When the Government Digital Service monitored 593 UK public sector websites between February 2020 and November 2021, only 39 of them, about 7 percent, had a fully compliant accessibility statement. A further 461, about 83 percent, had published a statement that was missing mandatory information. Only 10 percent had no statement at all, so the dominant failure is an incomplete statement rather than an absent one. After GDS wrote to those organisations, compliance rose to 80 percent, which shows these are cheap fixes once someone points them out.

Does passing every check mean my site is accessible?▾
No, and it is important not to read it that way. This tool grades the document, not the website. A statement can contain every mandatory element while honestly describing a site with serious barriers. In fact a good statement often admits to more problems than a bad one. Use an audit of the pages themselves to judge the site.

How often should a statement be reviewed?▾
At least once a year, and after any significant change to the site. GDS reported in December 2024 that many public sector statements had not been reviewed in the previous 12 months. A statement carrying a review date from several years ago undercuts everything else it says, because it tells a reader the known issues list is probably out of date.

Why does the checker warn about accessibility overlays?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Because naming an overlay widget as your accessibility measure is a documented weak point rather than a remedy. The European Commission has warned that overlay tools may make a website less accessible. A statement that points at a widget instead of describing the underlying fixes tends to attract scrutiny rather than deflect it.

What this checker found at scale
We ran it over every UK local authority and the FTSE 100. The results, per organisation and downloadable, are in State of Accessibility Statements 2026.

chunks.heading: What Goes in an Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
A statement is only useful if a reader can work out three things from it: how accessible this thing actually is, what to do if they hit a barrier, and whether anyone is still maintaining it. Those map onto seven parts, all of which the generator above collects:
Scope. Which sites, subdomains, apps, and documents this statement covers, and anything deliberately excluded.
Standard and level. Normally WCAG 2.2 at Level AA, which is the level referenced by most laws and procurement rules.
Conformance status. Fully, partially, or not conformant. See the wording section below.
Known limitations. Named plainly, with what a user should do instead and, if you have one, a target fix date.
Feedback route. A real email address or form, and the response time someone can expect. This is the part users actually need.
How you assessed it. Self-assessment or third-party audit, which tools, and whether manual testing was involved.
Date last reviewed. A stale date undermines everything above it.

chunks.heading: Getting the Conformance Wording Right
chunks.text:
The EU model statement defines three claims, and the vocabulary is worth borrowing wherever you are: fully conformant (meets the standard completely, no exceptions), partially conformant (most content conforms, some does not), and not conformant (largely does not meet the standard).
Almost every real site is partially conformant, and writing that down is the honest and defensible position. The temptation is to claim full conformance because it reads better, but a claim you cannot support is worse than an honest partial one: it is a statement in your own words, on your own site, that a complainant can quote back to you. Only claim full conformance if you have genuinely tested every page and pattern against every applicable criterion.
An automated scan does not support a full conformance claim
Automated tools catch only a portion of WCAG failures and cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order preserves meaning, or whether an error message helps. If your statement rests on a scan, describe it as a self-assessment using automated testing and avoid a full claim. The automated versus manual testing guide explains where the line falls.

chunks.heading: Common Accessibility Statement Mistakes
chunks.text:
Claiming full conformance on the strength of a scan. The single most common overclaim, and the easiest to disprove.
No contact route, or one nobody monitors. The feedback mechanism is the part with practical value to a user who is stuck. A dead address makes the statement decorative.
No date, or a date years old. Readers use it to judge whether anyone is still paying attention.
An empty limitations section. Every site has known gaps. Listing none reads as not having looked rather than as perfection.
Boilerplate with the standard left vague. “We are committed to accessibility” with no standard, level, or scope communicates nothing and cannot be checked.
A statement page that is itself inaccessible. It is the one page guaranteed to be read by people who will notice. Test it with a keyboard and a screen reader.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is an accessibility statement?▾
An accessibility statement is a public page explaining how accessible your website or app is and what you are doing about the parts that are not. A useful one names the standard you are measuring against (normally WCAG 2.2 at Level AA), states how far you currently conform, lists the known problems, explains how someone can report a barrier and what response they can expect, and records when it was last reviewed. It is a commitment and a contact route, not a compliance badge.

Am I legally required to publish an accessibility statement?▾
It depends entirely on where you operate and what kind of organisation you are, so treat this as orientation rather than legal advice. WCAG itself does not require you to publish a statement; conformance claims are optional under the standard. In the EU, the Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102) does require public sector bodies to publish an accessibility statement, and Commission Implementing Decision 2018/1523 sets out a model for it. The European Accessibility Act extends accessibility obligations to many private sector products and services. In the United States, neither the ADA nor Section 508 requires a public statement in the way the EU directive does, though a statement is common good practice and is often requested during procurement. Check your own jurisdiction and sector.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What should an accessibility statement contain?▾
At minimum: the scope (which sites, apps, or documents it covers), the standard and level you are measuring against, your conformance status, the known limitations written plainly with what a user should do instead, a feedback mechanism with a real contact route and a response time, how the assessment was carried out (self-assessment or third-party audit), and the date it was last reviewed. If your jurisdiction requires an enforcement or escalation route, include that too. The generator on this page collects each of these in turn.

What conformance wording should I use?▾
The EU model statement uses three levels of claim and they are a good vocabulary to borrow even outside the EU. "Fully conformant" means the content meets the standard completely, with no exceptions. "Partially conformant" means most of the content conforms but some parts do not. "Not conformant" means the content largely does not meet the standard. Most real sites are partially conformant, and saying so is the honest and defensible position. Only claim full conformance if you have actually tested every page and pattern against every applicable criterion, because a false claim is worse than an honest partial one.

Can I claim full WCAG conformance based on an automated scan?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
No. Automated tools reliably catch only a portion of WCAG failures, typically around a third, and they cannot judge things like whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order preserves meaning, or whether an error message actually helps. A clean automated report tells you that you have no detectable violations of the rules the tool checks, not that you conform. If your statement rests only on a scan, say so in the assessment section: describe it as a self-assessment using automated testing, and avoid a full conformance claim. Pair the scan with manual keyboard and screen reader testing before making stronger claims.

How often should I update the statement?▾
Review it whenever the site changes materially and on a fixed schedule otherwise, with annually being a common minimum and every six months being better for actively developed products. The review date is part of the statement's credibility: a statement dated three years ago tells a reader that nobody is watching, even if the content happens to still be accurate. If a known limitation gets fixed, remove it and update the date rather than leaving a stale list.

What formats can I export?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
You can export a draft as HTML that is ready to paste into a page, Markdown for a docs site or repository, plain text, or PDF. Whichever you choose, review the wording for accuracy before publishing, because the generator can only structure what you tell it. Then test the published page itself for accessibility: an accessibility statement that fails the standard it describes is a poor first impression, and it is the one page guaranteed to be read by people who will notice.

Is this tool free?▾
Yes, the accessibility statement generator is completely free, with no account or payment required. Nothing you enter is needed for it to work beyond producing your draft.
