chunks.heading: Why the name is the whole thing
chunks.text:
Every control on a page reaches assistive technology as a role and a name. The role says what it is (button, link, checkbox); the name says which one. Sighted users get the name from a label, an icon or its position. Everyone and everything else gets it from the accessibility tree, and if the tree has no name for it, there is nothing to announce and nothing for an agent to target.
This is why missing names are what litigation turns on. The complaint in Robles v. Domino's pleaded buttons with no accessible name; the plaintiff in Gil v. Winn-Dixie testified that nine in ten controls did nothing for his screen reader; the Target site read out file names because its images had no alt text. WebAIM's 2026 evaluation found empty links on 46.3% of the top million home pages and empty buttons on 30.6%.
Browser-use agents changed the audience for this without changing the fix. Anthropic's browser tool, OpenAI's computer-using agent and Google's Mariner all ground their actions in the accessibility tree, the same names and roles a screen reader uses. A site that cannot be used by a blind customer cannot be used by an agent acting for a sighted one.

chunks.heading: How to give a control a name
chunks.text:
Common controls, the failure, and the fix that gives them a name
Control What fails Fix
Icon-only button SVG or icon font with no text Visible text, or aria-label on the button, with the icon aria-hidden
Image link img without alt inside a link alt text that names the destination, not the picture
Form field placeholder used as the label A label element, visible, associated by for and id
Custom control div or span with a click handler A button element, or role plus tabindex plus keyboard handling
Repeated links Several links that all say Read more Make the visible text specific, or add aria-label with the subject
Embedded frame iframe with no title A title attribute that says what the frame contains

The relevant criteria are 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, 1.1.1 Non-text Content, 2.4.4 Link Purpose and 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions, all Level A. For the full rules see the guide to using ARIA.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is an accessible name?▾
The text assistive technology uses to identify an element: what a screen reader announces for a button, link or field, and what an AI agent reads in the accessibility tree. It is computed from the markup by the W3C accessible name algorithm, in a fixed order: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native sources such as a label element, alt text or the control's own text, then the title attribute.

Why does an AI agent care about accessible names?▾
Browser-use agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google operate pages through the accessibility tree rather than the pixels. Each control reaches the agent as a role and a name. A button with no name arrives as just 'button', indistinguishable from every other unnamed button on the page, so the agent cannot reliably act on it. The same failure is why a screen reader user cannot use it.

Which WCAG criteria does this relate to?▾
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value requires that user interface components expose a name and role. 1.1.1 Non-text Content requires text alternatives for images, which become link and button names when an image is the only content. 2.4.4 Link Purpose requires link text that makes the purpose clear. 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions requires labels for form fields. Missing names are among the five most common failures in WebAIM's annual evaluation of a million home pages.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is this the same as what a screen reader says?▾
It is the name part. A screen reader adds the role and state in its own words, for example 'Add to basket, button', and different screen readers phrase things differently. This tool uses dom-accessibility-api, the accname implementation used by Testing Library and jsdom, so the names match what those tools and most browsers compute. Always confirm important flows with a real screen reader.

Why does a div with onclick show as not in the tree?▾
A div has no role, so it is not exposed as a control at all. A screen reader user cannot tab to it and an agent does not see it as something that can be pressed. Use a button element, or add role="button", tabindex="0" and keyboard handling.

chunks.heading: Beyond one-off contrast checks: a complete color-system workspace
chunks.text: Most color tools stop at a contrast ratio between two hex codes. Production design systems need full 50–950 scales that hold up under hover, focus, disabled, and translucent overlay states; that work in light and dark mode; that survive deuteranopia; and that drop straight into Tailwind, Figma, iOS, and Android without hand-tuning. The Accessible Palette Studio builds that system from a single base color in one pass, then compares every pairing with WCAG 2.2 requirements and experimental APCA estimates so teams can make better-informed design decisions.

chunks.heading: For design systems

chunks.heading: For accessibility reviews
chunks.text:
Every state of every interactive token is graded by both contrast models. The report card pinpoints exactly which pairing fails, in which state, under which scoring model — and tells you whether a CVD simulation breaks it further.

Spot-check one pair → Contrast CheckerNeed something simpler? → Color Palette Generator

chunks.heading: OKLCH lightness curve
chunks.text: Each stop targets a perceptually-uniform L* value, with chroma peaking around the 500 stop and tapering at the extremes so 50 stays subtle and 950 stays inky. Every stop is then gamut-mapped into displayable sRGB.

chunks.heading: APCA Lc scoring
chunks.text: APCA computes a signed Lc estimate that respects polarity. The Studio uses configurable target bands to help compare text and interface colors. Treat these bands as experimental design guidance, not WCAG conformance thresholds.

chunks.heading: Machado CVD transforms
chunks.text: Color-blindness simulations use 3×3 matrices from Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes (2009) applied in linear sRGB. The CSS filter is generated from the same matrices via SVG <feColorMatrix>, so every preview pixel — text, borders, charts — re-renders through the simulated lens.

chunks.heading: Best practices
chunks.text:
Don't rely on color alone — pair it with icons, text, or shape
Verify the report card in both light and dark mode
If any state-aware row falls into "Caution" under both WCAG and APCA, fix it
Treat the focus-on-surface row as load-bearing — many sites miss this
Spot-check at least one CVD simulation before shipping

chunks.heading: What is APCA and how does it differ from WCAG 2.2 contrast?
chunks.text: APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) is an experimental perceptual contrast model. It produces a signed Lc estimate that reflects polarity and is interpreted with text size and weight. The Studio shows APCA beside the normative WCAG 2.2 luminance ratio for design exploration; APCA results are not a WCAG conformance claim.

chunks.heading: Why OKLCH instead of HSL?
chunks.text: HSL is mathematically convenient but not perceptually uniform — two HSL colors with the same lightness can look very different in brightness. OKLCH (a perceptual color space) keeps lightness consistent across hues, so an 11-stop scale generated in OKLCH actually steps evenly to the human eye. This is what makes the scales feel coherent across primary, secondary, and accent families.

chunks.heading: Which color-blindness simulations are supported?
chunks.text: Protanopia (no red cones), deuteranopia (no green cones), tritanopia (no blue cones), and achromatopsia (full grayscale). The simulation uses the Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes (2009) transforms applied to linear sRGB, which is the model used by Chrome DevTools' vision deficiency emulator.

chunks.heading: What does state-aware grading check?
chunks.text: Every interactive token (primary, secondary, accent, danger, etc.) is tested in its rest, hover, active, focus, and disabled states. Focus rings are graded against the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 non-text contrast requirement. Disabled states are flagged informationally — WCAG 2.2 exempts them, but APCA still surfaces unreadable combinations.

chunks.heading: Can I export to Tailwind v4 and v3 at the same time?

The Studio generates a Tailwind v4 @theme block and a v3 tailwind.config.ts side-by-side, plus W3C Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) JSON, Tokens Studio JSON for Figma, a Swift UIColor extension for iOS, and a Jetpack Compose Color object for Android. chunks.heading: Body size and resize resilience
chunks.text: WCAG 1.4.4 does not set a minimum font size; it requires text to resize without loss of content or functionality. The Studio uses 16px as a practical starting point and flags smaller sizes for manual readability review.

chunks.heading: Line height & spacing (WCAG 1.4.12)
chunks.text: WCAG 1.4.12 requires content to remain usable when users apply specified spacing values. Toggle the override to test those user styles for clipping, overlap, or lost content; the values are test conditions, not mandatory default styles.

chunks.heading: Line length (WCAG 1.4.8)
chunks.text: WCAG 1.4.8 is a Level AAA criterion that limits blocks of text to no more than 80 characters or glyphs per line. The Studio also shows a narrower comfort band as design guidance and keeps it distinct from conformance.

chunks.heading: Per-role contrast (WCAG 1.4.3 + APCA)
chunks.text: When you paste a palette primary, the report grades each text role's contrast against the derived background — body, small, caption, code, all H tags — using both the normative WCAG 2.2 luminance ratio and an experimental APCA Lc estimate. APCA output is supplemental design guidance, not a conformance result.

chunks.heading: Readability (WCAG 3.1.5)
chunks.text: Flesch Reading Ease ≥ 60 and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level ≤ 8 are the recommended targets for general audiences. The analyzer also flags long-sentence patterns and 3+ syllable word density.

chunks.heading: Accessible Typography Studio FAQ
chunks.text: Modular scales, WCAG 1.4.12, APCA, and design-token exports — answered.

chunks.heading: What makes typography accessible under WCAG 2.2?
chunks.text: Three things matter most: text remains readable when users resize up to 200% (1.4.4), text-spacing overrides (line-height ≥ 1.5, letter-spacing ≥ 0.12em, word-spacing ≥ 0.16em, paragraph-spacing ≥ 2× font size — WCAG 1.4.12) don't break the layout, and body text meets contrast minimums (4.5:1 for body, 3:1 for large text per 1.4.3). The Studio grades all of these automatically.

chunks.heading: What is a modular type scale and why use one?
chunks.text: A modular scale multiplies a base font size by a ratio (1.125, 1.2, 1.25, 1.333, 1.5, 1.618) to derive every other size in the system. The result is a hierarchy that feels mathematically consistent — h1 to h6 read as steps along the same scale rather than arbitrary numbers. The Studio supports eight common ratios and shows the visual feel of each.

chunks.heading: How does fluid clamp() sizing work?
chunks.text: Each font size is wrapped in clamp(min, preferred, max) so it scales smoothly between a small viewport (360px) and a large one (1280px). Body text generally stays constant; headings shrink on small screens to avoid breaking the line at narrow widths. The math is a linear interpolation between viewport sizes — no media queries needed.

chunks.heading: Which accessibility presets are available?
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2 default, Dyslexia-friendly (Atkinson Hyperlegible, looser tracking, ≤ 60ch), Low-vision (20px body, generous spacing), Cognitive load (Lexend, 1.75 line-height), Editorial / long-form (serif at 19px, ≤ 70ch), and Compact UI (14px dense layouts with extra grading rigor).

chunks.heading: What is the WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing override test?
chunks.text: WCAG 1.4.12 requires that pages still work when users apply text-spacing overrides — line-height of 1.5× font size, paragraph spacing of 2× font size, letter-spacing of 0.12em, word-spacing of 0.16em. Toggle 'WCAG 1.4.12 override' in the Studio to simulate these overrides in any specimen and watch for clipped or overlapping text.

chunks.heading: Can I pair this with the Accessible Palette Studio?
chunks.text: Yes — that's the point. Paste a palette's primary hex into the Studio (or share a URL between the two) and the typography report grades each text role's contrast against your real background and surface tokens, using both WCAG 2.2 ratios and APCA Lc.

chunks.heading: What's Flesch Reading Ease?
chunks.text: Flesch Reading Ease (1948) scores text from 0 to ~120 based on average sentence length and average syllables per word. Scores ≥ 60 are recommended for general audiences. The Studio also reports Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (US school grade) and flags overly long sentences or syllable-heavy word patterns.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is ADA compliance risk?▾
Accessibility legal risk depends on jurisdiction, business model, user barriers, and applicable law. This tool organizes planning factors but cannot determine legal compliance or predict a claim.

How is the risk score calculated?▾
The planning score applies documented weights to industry, traffic, geography, known barriers, and program maturity. It is a scenario-comparison aid, not a prediction of whether a claim will be filed or succeed.

What industries have the highest ADA compliance risk?▾
Digital-accessibility filings have been concentrated in e-commerce and food-service businesses, but exposure varies substantially by jurisdiction, business model, user journeys, and current barriers.

How can I reduce my ADA compliance risk?▾
Reduce risk by removing user barriers, testing important journeys with disabled users and assistive technologies, maintaining an accessibility program, documenting remediation, and obtaining legal advice for your jurisdiction.

Turn on the AI review and a vision model looks at up to eight images in context and suggests better text.

The rule checks are always free.

chunks.heading: Good alt text depends on what the image is doing
chunks.text:
The same photo can need a full sentence on one page and nothing at all on another. Before writing alt text, decide what the image does there.
Kinds of image, what their alt text should say, and an example
Kind of image What the alt should say Example
Informative What it shows that matters here, in a phrase or a sentence Volunteers planting trees along the canal towpath
Functional (links and buttons) Where the link goes or what the button does Acme home page; Search; Next photo
Decorative Nothing: alt="", so screen readers skip it A wave divider; a photo beside the same words in the same link
Complex (charts, diagrams, maps) The point it makes, with the detail in nearby text or a linked description Bar chart: sales doubled between 2023 and 2025
Text in images The words shown, when they matter Summer sale: 30% off all lamps

Avoid starting with “image of” or “picture of”: screen readers already say it is an image. Text in images is better as real text where possible, which 1.4.5 Images of Text asks for at Level AA, and logos are the exception. For charts, the accessible charts guide covers the data table that makes the real text alternative. Our guide on how to write alt text shows good alt text for each kind of image, with examples.

chunks.heading: Good alt text depends on what the image is doing
chunks.text: Need a first draft for a single image? The AI alt text generator writes one from an upload or an image address. To see the name every control on a page exposes, not only the images, use the accessible name previewer.

chunks.heading: What the checker looks for
chunks.text:
Failures are problems a rule can be sure of: no alt attribute, a link or button whose only content is an image with no text alternative (including an icon hidden with aria-hidden), a file name such as IMG_2041.jpg used as alt, placeholder text such as “image” or “logo” on its own, and role="img" with no name. These fail 1.1.1 Non-text Content, and for links and buttons 2.4.4 Link Purpose or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value as well.
Needs review covers things that are usually wrong but need a person to confirm: alt over 150 characters, alt that repeats the caption or the link's own text, the same alt on images of different files, “click here” or “link to” in alt, an SVG with no name that is not hidden, and an image named only by its title attribute.
Decorative and fine means alt="" (or an equivalent) on an image that is not the only content of a link or button. The rules accept it; whether the image really is decorative is a judgement, which is one thing the AI review looks at.

chunks.heading: What it cannot tell you
chunks.text:
Whether alt text is accurate. A rule cannot see the picture. The AI review can, but it works from a screenshot and a little nearby text, and it makes mistakes. A person who knows what the page is for decides.
Images it does not reach: CSS background images (counted, not checked), images inside frames, canvas drawings, icon fonts, and images that appear only after a click or a form step.
More than one page at a time, or more than the first 300 images on a page. Some sites block automated browsers, and those cannot be checked at all.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What does the alt text checker check?▾
Every img (including those inside picture), image button, image map area, element with role="img" and inline SVG that a visitor can see. It fails images with no alt attribute, links and buttons whose only content is an image without a text alternative, file names and placeholder words used as alt, and role="img" with no name. It flags for review alt text over 150 characters, alt that repeats the caption or the link's own text, the same alt on different images, "click here" or "link to" in alt, SVGs with no name that are not hidden, and images named only by a title attribute. Hidden images and tracking pixels are skipped.

When should an image have an empty alt attribute?▾
When it adds nothing a screen reader user needs: a decorative flourish, a divider, a background-style photo, or an image whose meaning is already in the text right next to it, such as a product photo beside the product name inside the same link. alt="" tells assistive technology to skip it. Never leave the attribute out instead, because many screen readers then read the file name. And never use alt="" on an image that is the only content of a link or button, because the control is then left with no name.

What should the alt text of a linked image or icon button say?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What the control does, not what the picture looks like. A logo that links to the home page should say something like "Acme home page" or just "Acme"; a magnifying glass button should say "Search". If the link or button already has visible text, give the image alt="" so the name is not read twice. WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value both depend on this.

How long should alt text be?▾
WCAG sets no limit. Most good alt text is a short phrase or sentence, because a screen reader user cannot skim it or jump back a few words. This checker flags anything over 150 characters for review rather than failing it: long descriptions usually belong in a visible caption or nearby text, and complex images such as charts need a short alt plus a fuller description elsewhere on the page.

How does the AI review work, and what does it cost?▾
Tick the AI review box and the checker picks up to eight images, starting with those missing alt, then images that are the only content of a link or button, then large images. Each is captured as a screenshot on its own and sent, with its current alt and nearby text, to a third-party vision model, which judges whether the alt fits and suggests better text. Without an account you get two reviews a day; signed in, a review costs 2 credits. Nothing is charged if the review does not complete. The rule checks are always free.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Does a clean result mean the page meets WCAG 1.1.1?▾
No. Rules can find alt text that is missing or malformed, but not alt text that is wrong: "Two people at a desk" passes every rule even if the photo shows a bridge. The AI review is a second opinion and can be wrong too. Whether each image's text alternative serves the same purpose is a judgement a person has to make, and 1.1.1 also covers CSS background images, canvas, icon fonts, audio and video, which this tool does not check.

chunks.heading: Accessible Color Palette FAQ
chunks.text: Short answers for teams using WCAG color palettes in websites, apps, and design systems.

chunks.heading: What makes a color palette accessible?
chunks.text: An accessible color palette includes foreground and background combinations that meet WCAG contrast requirements, supports visible focus indicators, avoids color-only meaning, and works across light mode, dark mode, hover states, disabled states, and error states.

chunks.heading: What contrast ratio does WCAG 2.2 require?
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2 Level AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Level AAA requires 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text. UI components and graphical objects should have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors.

chunks.heading: Why should I preview colors on buttons, forms, cards, and charts?
chunks.text: A swatch can look good in isolation but fail when used as button text, card borders, form focus rings, alerts, links, or chart colors. Live previews reveal whether the palette works in real interface states before it becomes part of a design system.

chunks.heading: Can one palette be fully WCAG compliant?
chunks.text: A palette itself is not automatically compliant. Compliance depends on specific color pairings, text size, component state, and context. The safest workflow is to generate colors, preview real UI pairings, then verify important combinations with a contrast checker.

chunks.heading: Should accessible palettes include dark mode?
chunks.text: Yes. Dark mode often needs different surface, border, text, focus, and accent choices because colors that pass in light mode can become muddy or too low contrast on dark surfaces.

chunks.heading: What is the minimum contrast ratio for WCAG compliance?
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2 Level AA requires a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold). Level AAA requires 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text. Our contrast checker tests both levels automatically.

chunks.heading: Can I check contrast from hex codes?
chunks.text: Yes. Type or paste a hex code such as #1D4ED8 for the text colour and another for the background. This WCAG colour contrast checker converts both to relative luminance, reports the ratio to two decimal places, and marks AA and AAA as pass or fail for normal or large text. Three-digit shorthand like #FFF works too.

chunks.heading: How do I use the color contrast checker?
chunks.text: Simply input your foreground and background colors using the color pickers or hex codes. The tool instantly calculates the contrast ratio and shows whether it meets WCAG AA or AAA standards. You can adjust colors in real-time to achieve compliance.

chunks.heading: Why is color contrast important for accessibility?
chunks.text: Adequate color contrast ensures text and UI elements are readable for users with visual impairments, including those with low vision or color blindness. It also improves readability in different lighting conditions and on various devices, benefiting all users.

chunks.heading: Does the EAA apply to you?
chunks.text:
The European Accessibility Act has applied since 28 June 2025, and the sanctions are real: Ireland enforces it with criminal penalties. Answer four questions about your customers, sector, and size to see where you likely stand. Nothing you enter leaves your browser.

Step 1 of 4

chunks.heading: Do you offer products or services to consumers in the EU?
chunks.text:
This includes selling online to consumers located in an EU member state, wherever your company is established. Business-to-business sales alone do not count. Ireland is in the EU; Great Britain is not, but GB companies selling into the EU are caught.
Do you offer products or services to consumers in the EU?Yes, we serve consumers in the EUNo, we are B2B only or have no EU customers
Continue

Nothing you enter leaves your browser. No answers are stored or sent.

chunks.heading: How this checker decides
chunks.text:
The questions mirror the structure of Directive (EU) 2019/882 itself. First, the consumer nexus: the Act protects consumers in the EU, wherever the trader is established. Second, the covered categories: the Directive names specific products and services rather than covering every website, but the e-commerce category catches any consumer sales journey. Third, the microenterprise exemption for service providers, which requires both the headcount and the turnover condition.
The result is deliberately phrased as likely or unlikely. Scope edge cases, such as mixed B2B and consumer offerings or the transitional rules for pre-2025 service contracts and terminals, deserve legal advice. For the legislative detail, see our EAA tracker with every statutory date quoted from the Directive, the EAA compliance guide, and the Ireland-specific enforcement picture.

chunks.heading: If you are in scope, what next
chunks.text:
Find out where you stand: a fixed-price WCAG 2.2 AA audit establishes your baseline against the standard the EAA is measured with. See a sample report first.
Understand the technical standard: EN 301 549 explained, and track your work with the EAA readiness checklist (every obligation in the Act, with Excel export) and the WCAG 2.2 checklist.
Publish the required accessibility information: write an accessibility statement or generate one with the free statement generator.
Do not reach for an overlay widget: overlays do not satisfy the EAA.

chunks.heading: Who does the European Accessibility Act apply to?
chunks.text: The EAA applies to businesses that place covered products on the EU market or provide covered services to consumers in the EU, wherever the business itself is established. The named service categories include e-commerce, consumer banking, e-books, passenger transport, electronic communications, and access to audiovisual media services; covered products include computers, smartphones, self-service terminals, and e-readers. The obligations have applied since 28 June 2025.

chunks.heading: Does the EAA apply to companies outside the EU?
chunks.text: Yes. The test is where your consumers are, not where you are. A UK, US, or any other non-EU company selling covered products or services to consumers in the EU is in scope for those products and services. This is why many British and American e-commerce businesses are affected despite the UK and US not being member states.

chunks.heading: What is the EAA microenterprise exemption?
chunks.text: Service-provider microenterprises, meaning fewer than 10 employees and an annual turnover or balance sheet total not exceeding 2 million euro, are exempt from the EAA service requirements. Both conditions must hold. Microenterprises dealing with covered products get lighter documentation duties rather than a full exemption, and any business relying on the exemption should be able to show documentation supporting it.

chunks.heading: Is an ordinary online shop really covered by the EAA?
chunks.text: Usually yes. E-commerce services are a named category, and it is the broadest one: if consumers in the EU can buy from you through a website or app, that sales journey is an e-commerce service under the Act, even if your core trade is not otherwise on the list. Purely informational sites with no consumer transactions are the typical genuinely out-of-scope case.

chunks.heading: What do I have to do if the EAA applies to me?
chunks.text: Meet the accessibility requirements for your product or service, provide the required accessibility information, and be able to demonstrate conformity. The practical technical route is EN 301 549, the harmonised European standard, which incorporates WCAG at Level AA for web content and apps. An audit against WCAG 2.2 AA tells you where you stand today, and an accessibility statement covers the information requirement.

chunks.heading: Does this checker store my answers?
chunks.text: No. The checker runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you select is stored, transmitted, or logged, and there is no account or email gate.

chunks.heading: Educational Tool, Not Legal Advice
chunks.text: This checker gives a structured indication based on the Directive's scope rules. It cannot account for every business model, national transposition detail, or transitional arrangement. For a decision you intend to rely on, consult a lawyer familiar with the European Accessibility Act and the member states you sell into.

chunks.text:
Keyboard users, switch users and many screen reader users move through a page with the Tab key. This checker loads your page in Chrome, presses Tab the way they do, and numbers every stop on a screenshot. It flags stops with no visible focus, focus hidden behind sticky headers and cookie banners, and keyboard traps. A second mode measures every link and button against the 24 pixel minimum in WCAG 2.5.8.

chunks.heading: What it checks
chunks.text:
WCAG success criteria and what the checker does for each
Criterion Level What the checker does
2.1.1 Keyboard A Shows everything Tab reaches. A control that is missing from the list may only work with a mouse; the tool does not press anything, so confirm it by hand.
2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap A Flags focus that stays on one element or cycles through a few, then tries Escape and Shift+Tab to see whether either gets out.
2.4.3 Focus Order A Flags positive tabindex, focus that is dropped to the page mid-way, and big jumps back up the page. Whether the order makes sense is for you to judge from the numbered screenshot.
2.4.7 Focus Visible AA Compares each element focused and unfocused, pixel by pixel. If nothing changes, there is no visible indicator. Also flags focus landing on invisible, zero-size or off-screen elements.
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA Samples points across each focused element to see whether a sticky header, cookie banner or other layer covers it completely. Partly covered is noted against 2.4.12 (AAA).
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA Target size mode measures every link, button and control against 24 by 24 pixels and applies the spacing, inline and browser-default exceptions.

chunks.heading: What automated tabbing cannot tell you
chunks.text:
The checker reports what happens when Tab is pressed. That finds the most common keyboard failures quickly, but it is not a keyboard audit, and a clean result does not mean a page works from the keyboard.
It cannot judge whether the order is logical. It flags likely problems; reading the numbered screenshot against the layout is your job.
It does not press Enter, Space or arrow keys. Menus, tabs, sliders, grids and other widgets that use arrow keys inside a single Tab stop are not tested, and neither are custom keyboard shortcuts or whether controls actually work when activated.
It checks that focus is visible, not that it is clear. Indicator contrast and thickness (2.4.13, AAA) are not measured.
It sees one state of the page. A first visit, on a 1280 by 800 desktop window, with motion reduced. Mobile layouts, signed-in pages and content that opens only after a click are not covered, and focus inside embedded frames is not followed.

Treat the results as a map of where to look, then confirm with a keyboard yourself. Our keyboard accessibility guide covers manual testing step by step.

chunks.heading: How the focus tests work
chunks.text:
Computed styles cannot tell you whether focus is visible: an outline the same colour as the background changes the styles but not the screen, and an indicator drawn on a parent card or a pseudo-element does not show up on the element at all. So the checker looks at pixels. At each stop it captures the element while focused, removes focus, captures again, and restores focus. Chrome keeps the keyboard focus style when focus is restored by script after a key press, so both captures are of the real keyboard state. Transitions and animations are switched off first, so indicators are captured in their final state, and the text cursor is hidden so it cannot pass for an indicator.
When something changed, a third capture checks that the area is not changing on its own, as videos and carousels do. Those stops are marked as unknown rather than passed. To decide whether focus is hidden, the checker asks the browser which element is on top at five points across the focused element, after the browser has scrolled it into view. If something else is on top at every point, focus is entirely hidden.

chunks.heading: Target size and its exceptions
chunks.text:
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) asks for pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. A target can be smaller and still pass in five ways, and the checker handles them as follows.
Spacing: a 24 pixel circle centred on the small target must not touch any other target, or another small target's circle. Measured.
Inline: a link inside a sentence of text. Detected from the surrounding text.
User agent: a native control the browser sizes, such as an unstyled checkbox. Detected by comparing it with the same control on a blank page.
Equivalent: another control on the page does the same thing and is large enough. Not detected; check failures for this.
Essential: the size is essential to the information, as with pins on a map. Not detected; check failures for this.

The enhanced AAA criterion, 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), asks for 44 by 44 pixels. The checker reports against the AA minimum only. To measure targets on a phone screen, where they matter most, use the Target Size Checker, which opens on a 390 pixel phone viewport.

chunks.heading: Fixing what it finds
Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Can an automated tool tell whether my focus order is logical?▾
No. A logical order depends on what the page means, which only a person can judge. The checker records the order Tab actually follows and flags the patterns that usually signal a problem: positive tabindex, focus that jumps far back up the page, focus dropped mid-way, and loops. Use the numbered screenshot to read the order against the visual layout.

How does it decide whether focus is visible?▾
For every stop it captures the element and a small margin around it while focused, removes focus and captures again, then counts the pixels that changed. No meaningful change means no visible indicator, which fails WCAG 2.4.7. If nothing changes in the tight capture it looks again over a wider area, so indicators drawn on a surrounding card are not missed. It records which styles changed as supporting evidence, but the pixels decide, because an outline in the same colour as the background changes the styles and not the screen.

Does it check focus indicator contrast or thickness?▾
No. It checks that an indicator exists and can be seen, which is what 2.4.7 (AA) requires. How strong the indicator is belongs to 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, a AAA criterion, and needs a contrast and area measurement this tool does not make. A faint colour change on link text will pass here and may still be hard to see.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Why did the check stop inside a cookie banner or dialog?▾
A modal dialog is supposed to keep focus inside it until it is closed. When that dialog is a cookie banner, the checker closes it once with its reject button where it has one, and carries on with the page. Other dialogs end the run, with a note on whether Escape released focus. The tool always loads the page as a first-time visitor with no cookies, so you see what a new visitor sees.

What is the WCAG 2.5.8 target size rule?▾
Pointer targets such as links, buttons and checkboxes must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exceptions: a smaller target passes if a 24 pixel circle centred on it does not touch any other target or another small target's circle; links inside a sentence are exempt; controls left at the browser's default size are exempt; and so are targets where another control does the same job at full size, or where the size is essential. The tool applies the first three and tells you to check the last two by hand.

Which pages can it check?▾
Public pages that load without signing in. It uses Chrome at 1280 by 800 pixels, follows up to 80 Tab stops within about 25 seconds, and does not follow focus into embedded frames such as videos and maps. Some sites block automated browsers; when that happens you will see an error rather than a misleading result.

chunks.heading: What the Image Color Picker Does
chunks.text:
This tool reads the colour of individual pixels in an image you supply. Upload a screenshot, a brand asset, or an exported design frame, click any point on it, and the picker reports that pixel's value as HEX, RGB, and HSL. Each pick is added to a running list, and the list can be exported as CSS custom properties, SCSS variables, or JSON.
The typical accessibility use is recovering the real colours from a page or mockup so they can be tested. Designers often know the intended token, but the shipped colour after gradients, overlays, opacity, and image compression can differ. Sampling the rendered pixel tells you what users actually see, which is the value a contrast test needs.

chunks.heading: How to Use It
chunks.text:
Choose an image. Click Choose Image and pick a file. The image dimensions appear as a badge once it loads.
Pick by clicking or by coordinates. Press Pick Color, then click anywhere on the image. If you need a repeatable sample, type an X and Y position into the coordinate fields and press Sample coordinate instead. The coordinates are in the image's own pixels, not the displayed size, so they stay valid at any zoom level.
Copy or export. Each picked colour shows its HEX, RGB, and HSL values with a copy button beside each. Use the Export Palette card to download the whole set, or Save Palette to keep a snapshot while you keep sampling.

chunks.heading: What It Checks, and What It Does Not
chunks.text:
The picker does not evaluate anything against WCAG. It is a measuring instrument: it tells you what colour a pixel is, and it stops there. It does not know which of two colours is the text and which is the background, it does not compute a contrast ratio, and it cannot tell whether a colour is being used to convey information on its own.
The values it produces feed directly into four WCAG 2.2 success criteria, all of which need a manual step after sampling:
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA): text needs a 4.5:1 ratio against its background, or 3:1 for large text. Sample the text colour and the background colour, then test the pair.
1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) (Level AAA): the stricter 7:1 and 4.5:1 thresholds.
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA): a 3:1 ratio for the visible boundaries of controls and for the parts of graphics needed to understand them. Sample the border or icon colour, not the fill behind it.
1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A): knowing the exact colours of, say, a red and a green status dot helps you check that something other than hue also distinguishes them.

chunks.heading: What It Checks, and What It Does Not
chunks.text: For the ratio itself, paste the HEX values into the Contrast Checker. Remember that a sample from a screenshot reflects one rendering on one display; the authoritative test is against the colours in your CSS, and for text on images or gradients you should sample the lightest and darkest points the text sits on and test the worst case.

chunks.heading: Reading the Output
chunks.text:
Every entry in the Picked Colors list carries the same information in three notations. HEX is the six-digit form most CSS uses. RGB gives the red, green, and blue channels from 0 to 255, which is what the canvas returns before any conversion. HSL is derived from the RGB values: hue in degrees, then saturation and lightness as percentages, rounded to whole numbers. The Position line records the X and Y pixel you sampled so you can return to it.
Picking a colour that is already in the list does not add a duplicate; the earlier entry is replaced by the new one, so the list stays unique by HEX value. Exports number the colours in list order: the CSS file declares --color-1, --color-2, and so on inside :root, the SCSS file declares $color-1 onwards, and the JSON file includes the RGB, HSL, and position data for each entry. Rename the variables to something meaningful before you commit them.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is my image uploaded to a server?▾
No. The file is read with the browser's FileReader API, drawn onto a hidden canvas, and sampled locally with getImageData. Nothing is sent over the network, and reloading the page clears the image and every picked color.

Can this tool check color contrast?▾
No. It reports the sampled values and nothing else. Paste the HEX values into the Contrast Checker to test them against WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced), and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast.

Why is the sampled color slightly different from my design file?▾
The picker reads exactly one pixel. Anti-aliased edges, JPEG compression, colour profile conversion when the image was exported, and browser scaling can all shift that pixel by a few values. Sample the middle of a flat area, or type the same coordinates twice to confirm you are reading the same spot, and compare the result with the token in your design system rather than trusting the screenshot.

Which image formats can I upload?▾
Any format the browser can decode and the file input accepts as an image type, which in practice means PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG, and, in browsers that support it, AVIF. Very large images are drawn at their natural size onto the canvas, so a multi-thousand-pixel photograph will work but may take a moment to sample.

Do saved palettes persist between visits?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: No. Save Palette keeps palettes in memory for the current session only; they are gone when you close or reload the tab. Export the palette as CSS, SCSS, or JSON before you leave if you want to keep it.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is an accessibility overlay?▾
An accessibility overlay is a third-party JavaScript widget added to a website that claims to automatically fix accessibility issues. Common overlay vendors include accessiBe, UserWay, AudioEye, and EqualWeb. They typically add a toolbar icon with features like text resizing and contrast changes.

Do accessibility overlays actually work?▾
Most accessibility experts and disability advocacy organizations agree that overlays do not provide meaningful accessibility improvements. Automated tools can only detect 30-40% of WCAG issues, and overlays can fix even fewer. They often introduce new barriers for assistive technology users.

Can an overlay protect me from ADA lawsuits?▾
An overlay does not by itself establish ADA or WCAG conformance. Legal outcomes depend on jurisdiction and facts, while technical conformance requires evidence that users can complete real tasks. Seek qualified legal advice for a specific claim.

How does this detector work?▾
Our tool loads the target URL in a browser, scans for known overlay vendor scripts, DOM patterns, and global JavaScript variables. It then runs a comprehensive WCAG 2.2 AA audit using axe-core to show real accessibility issues that persist despite the overlay.

What should I use instead of an overlay?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Build accessibility into your website from the start. Conduct manual audits, train your development team on WCAG 2.2, integrate automated testing into your CI/CD pipeline, and test with real assistive technology users.

Which overlay vendors can you detect?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What does the PDF Accessibility Checker test?▾
Our tool checks 12 accessibility criteria including: tagged PDF structure, document title, language setting, heading hierarchy, image alt text, bookmarks/navigation, font embedding, Unicode mapping, form field labels, table structure, and readable text content.

What is a tagged PDF?▾
A tagged PDF contains structural markup (tags) that describe the document's logical structure — headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, and images. Screen readers use these tags to navigate and read the document. An untagged PDF is largely inaccessible.

What is PDF/UA?▾
PDF/UA (Universal Accessibility) is the ISO 14289 standard for accessible PDF documents. It defines requirements for tagged structure, alt text, reading order, and metadata. Meeting PDF/UA is considered best practice for PDF accessibility.

How do I make a PDF accessible?▾
Start by creating the source document with proper heading structure and alt text. Use the built-in accessibility features of your authoring tool (Word, InDesign, etc.) to add tags, set the language, and add bookmarks. Run the accessibility checker before exporting. Then validate the exported PDF.

Does this tool check scanned PDFs?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Yes. If a PDF contains only scanned images with no extractable text, our tool will flag it as inaccessible. Scanned PDFs need OCR (Optical Character Recognition) processing to make the text readable by screen readers.

chunks.text:
Paste text or check a web page to get six readability scores, an average school grade and a reading age. Then see exactly which sentences are long or hard, where the passive voice and wordy phrases are, and which abbreviations nobody has explained, highlighted in your text with a plainer alternative where there is one.

Paste textCheck a web page
Text to checkEnglish text, up to 60,000 characters. Put a blank line or a new line between paragraphs and headings. Nothing you paste leaves your browser.
