Plain language helps everyone, but most accessibility failures are in the code: missing labels, low contrast, keyboard traps. Scan the page for those too.
Page to scanScan this page free
One free scan a day, no account. It runs axe-core on the live page and shows your score and the most severe findings.

chunks.heading: What the scores measure
chunks.text:
Every readability formula works from the same two signals: how long the sentences are, and how long the words are. Flesch Reading Ease turns them into a score out of 100, where higher is easier. The other five give a US school grade: Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning Fog from syllables, SMOG from words of three or more syllables, and Coleman-Liau and the Automated Readability Index from letters. The average of the five grades is the single number to watch, and the reading age is that grade plus five or six years.
The formulas were calibrated against how well readers understood test passages, so they are a fair guide to how much effort a text asks for. But they cannot see meaning. “The cat sat on the mat” and a sentence of short, unfamiliar jargon can score the same, and a short sentence can still be confusing. Use the score to find the hard parts, and the findings to fix them.

chunks.heading: What the checker flags
chunks.text:
Each plain-language finding and when the checker raises it
Finding When we flag it What to do
Very long sentence Over 25 words Split it. One idea per sentence.
Hard or very hard sentence 8 words or more scoring grade 10 or more (very hard: 14 or more) on its own Shorten it and use shorter words.
Possible passive voice A form of "be" followed by a past participle Say who does what: "we approved", not "was approved".
Wordy word or phrase On our list of words with a plainer alternative Use the suggestion if it keeps your meaning.
Unexplained abbreviation Capitals with no expansion in brackets and no abbr title Spell it out the first time.
Long paragraph Over 100 words Break it up, or use a list.
Adverb Words ending in -ly (off by default) Cut it if the sentence works without it.

chunks.heading: Reading level and WCAG
chunks.text:
WCAG 3.1.5 Reading Level asks that when text needs reading ability above lower secondary education, after removing proper names and titles, you also provide supplemental content or a simpler version. Lower secondary education ends around nine years into school, so this tool treats an average grade above 9 as the point to act. A plain-language summary at the top of the page, a diagram or an easy read version all meet it.
The same chapter of WCAG covers the words themselves. 3.1.4 Abbreviations asks for a way to find the expanded form of each abbreviation, and 3.1.3 Unusual Words asks for definitions of jargon and idioms. All three are Level AAA, so they go beyond what most laws require. They matter most to people with cognitive and learning disabilities; see the guide to cognitive accessibility.

chunks.heading: What this tool can't tell you
chunks.text:
It is for English. The formulas were made for English, and the syllable count, word list and passive voice check only work in English.
Syllables are counted by a rule of thumb, not a dictionary, so a few words are miscounted and the grades can differ a little from other tools, which count syllables their own way.
Passive voice, abbreviations and adverbs are found by pattern, not by understanding the sentence. Expect some false alarms and some misses.
Headings, list items and labels count as sentences. On a page with many of them the average sentence is short and the scores look easier than the body text really is.
The web page mode reads the HTML the server sends. It does not run JavaScript, log in, or get past bot checks, so some pages come back nearly empty.
No formula knows your readers. Testing a page with people from your audience tells you far more than any score.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is a good readability score?▾
For a general audience, aim for an average grade of about 8 or 9 or lower and a Flesch Reading Ease of 60 or more, the range usually described as plain English. Text written for specialists can score higher, but every extra grade narrows who can read it comfortably. WCAG 3.1.5 uses lower secondary education, roughly grade 9, as the point where a simpler version or a summary is needed.

Why do the formulas give different grades for the same text?▾
Each one measures something slightly different. Flesch-Kincaid uses syllables per word, Gunning Fog and SMOG count words of three or more syllables, and Coleman-Liau and the Automated Readability Index count letters instead of syllables. A text full of short but unusual words scores easier on all of them than it really is. That is why the tool shows all five grades and their average rather than picking one.

Does WCAG require a particular reading level?▾
Only at Level AAA. Success criterion 3.1.5 Reading Level says that when text needs reading ability above lower secondary education, after removing proper names and titles, you provide supplemental content or a version that does not. Most laws and policies cite Level AA, so 3.1.5 is not usually a legal requirement, but plain language helps people with cognitive and learning disabilities most, and also anyone reading on a phone or in a second language.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
How is the reading age worked out?▾
From the average grade. US school grades start at about age six, so a reader in grade 8 is typically 13 or 14 years old. The tool adds five and six years to the rounded average grade and shows the range. Grade 13 and above is shown as 18 or over, university level. Like the grades themselves, it is an estimate from word and sentence length.

Why can't the tool read my web page?▾
The web page mode fetches the page's HTML and reads the text in it. Many sites build their content with JavaScript after the page loads, so the HTML has little or no text, and this tool does not run the page's scripts. When it finds fewer than 50 words it says so. Copy the text from the page in your browser and paste it into the Paste text tab instead.

Is my text stored or sent anywhere?▾
Pasted text never leaves your browser: the scores and findings are worked out on your device. When you check a web page, our server fetches that page for you and sends back its HTML, and we record the site's domain, the page path and whether the check worked, so we can see which sites people check. The text itself is not stored.

chunks.heading: Website scope checker
chunks.text: Discover internal pages, documents, and external references before estimating an accessibility audit.

chunks.heading: Scope Checker for Accessibility
chunks.text:
Crawl a website in scoped mode (max 2 minutes) and capture internal URLs, document links, extra external links, and page titles for accessibility audits.

Website URL
Max Pages
Max Depth
Include Subdomains

Run Scope Check2-minute hard limit

chunks.heading: What the Scope Checker Does
chunks.text:
Before you can audit a website you need to know what is in it. The scope checker builds that inventory. Give it a start URL and it looks for sitemaps, follows internal links breadth-first, and returns every page it reached with the page's title, HTTP status, and the depth at which it was found. Along the way it separates out downloadable documents and links that leave the site, so you can see the PDFs and the third-party services an audit would have to account for.
Each run has a hard two-minute budget on the server. Within that window the crawler fetches up to the page cap you set, reads at most 600 links from any one page, and stops following links once the depth cap is reached. The result is a bounded, repeatable snapshot rather than an exhaustive crawl, which is normally what a scoping conversation needs.

chunks.heading: How to Use It
chunks.text:
Enter the site's public URL. A bare domain is fine; https is assumed when you leave the scheme off. Start from the homepage for a broad inventory, or from a section landing page to scope one part of a large site.
Set the limits. Max Pages (default 200) caps how many HTML pages are recorded. Max Depth (default 3) caps how many link hops from the start URL the crawler will follow. Turn on Include Subdomains if content lives on hosts like docs.example.com that should be in scope.
Run the check and wait. Most small sites finish in well under a minute. The run ends when the queue is empty, the page cap is hit, or the two minutes expire, whichever comes first.
Review the tabs and export. Use Pages to check titles, Documents for PDFs and Office files, Extras for external services, and Issues for anything that could not be fetched. Export CSV gives you a spreadsheet to annotate; Copy JSON gives you the full result for other tools.

chunks.heading: What It Collects, and What It Does Not
chunks.text:
Discovery uses two sources. First it reads robots.txt for Sitemap lines and fetches sitemap.xml and sitemap_index.xml, following nested sitemap indexes up to 25 files. Then it crawls: every HTML page fetched has its anchor links extracted, resolved to absolute URLs, and sorted into same-site pages (queued for crawling), same-site documents (recorded but not fetched), and external links (recorded with the page they were found on). Page titles come from the <title> element, falling back to an og:title or twitter:title meta tag, then the first <h1>, and finally the URL itself.
The tool does not test accessibility. It never opens the documents it lists, does not execute JavaScript, sends no cookies, and cannot see pages that require a login or that are only linked from script-rendered navigation. It also drops query strings and fragments when it deduplicates URLs, so a search results page with filters appears once. Treat the inventory as a starting list to be checked against your own knowledge of the site, not as proof that nothing else exists.

chunks.heading: Where It Fits in a WCAG Audit
chunks.text:
WCAG-EM, the W3C's evaluation methodology, starts with two steps this tool supports directly: defining the scope of the evaluation and selecting a representative sample of pages. The page list, grouped into chunks of 50, is the raw material for that sample. Documents matter because WCAG applies to PDFs and Office files served from a site just as it does to HTML, and they are the part of an estimate most often forgotten.
The output also gives you an early signal on a few success criteria, though every one of them still needs a manual check:
2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A): if a page's title in the results is its own URL, the page has no <title>, no social title, and no <h1>. Identical titles across many pages are also worth flagging, because the criterion asks for titles that describe the page.
3.2.3 Consistent Navigation and 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (Level AA) can only be judged across a set of pages, so your sample needs pages from different templates and depths.
2.4.5 Multiple Ways (Level AA): whether a sitemap was found, and how much of the crawl came from it versus from links, tells you something about the routes users have to reach content.

chunks.heading: Reading the Output
chunks.text:
The four summary cards count discovered URLs (pages plus documents plus external links), pages, documents, and external extras. Below them, Scanned reports how many URLs were actually fetched, which can exceed the page count because redirects to other hosts, failed fetches, and document responses are scanned but not filed as pages. The Timed out badge tells you the two minutes ran out; if it appears, the inventory is a lower bound.
In the Pages tab, Status is the HTTP status after redirects and Depth is the number of hops from the start URL, with sitemap entries assigned depth 1. The From line under documents and extras names the page where the link was found, which is the page to look at when a document needs replacing. The CSV export has five columns: type, url, title, detail, and discoveredFrom.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Why did the crawl stop before finding every page?▾
Three limits can end a run: the page cap you set (10 to 1,000), the depth cap (1 to 6 link hops from the start URL), and the two-minute time budget, which is enforced on the server and shown as a Timed out badge in the results. Each page fetch also has a 12-second timeout and only the first 1.5 MB of HTML is read. Slow servers, deep site structures, and very large sites will hit one of these. Raise the page cap, add the sitemap URL as your start point, or run the tool once per section of a large site.

Does the scope checker execute JavaScript?▾
No. It fetches the raw HTML of each page and extracts anchor href attributes with a parser, without running scripts. Links that are injected by client-side JavaScript, loaded through infinite scroll, or hidden behind a menu that only renders on interaction will not be found unless they also appear in a sitemap. If your site is a single-page application, the sitemap is usually the more complete source.

What counts as a document?▾
A URL is filed as a document when its file extension is one of pdf, doc, docx, xls, xlsx, ppt, pptx, csv, txt, rtf, odt, ods, odp, epub, zip, rar, 7z, gz, tar, xml, or json, or when the server answers with a document content type such as application/pdf. Documents are listed but not opened or tested; use the PDF Accessibility Checker for the PDFs it finds.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Why do URLs with query strings or fragments disappear?▾
Every URL is canonicalised before it is queued: the fragment, query string, credentials, default port, and trailing slash are removed and the host is lowercased. That keeps the inventory to one entry per page instead of one per filter combination, but it means a page whose content genuinely depends on a query parameter appears once, under its bare path. Add those variants to your audit sample by hand.

Does it respect robots.txt, and does it crawl behind a login?▾
It reads robots.txt only to discover Sitemap declarations; it does not act on Disallow rules, so only point it at sites you are authorised to crawl. It sends no cookies or credentials, so anything behind authentication returns the login page or an error and is recorded under Issues. Local, private, and loopback hosts are refused.

Is the scope checker free?▾
Yes. It needs no account and uses no credits. The two-minute cap per run is the only limit.

chunks.heading: Screen reader simulator: what does your page announce?
chunks.text:
Enter a page address and get a transcript of what a screen reader would come across, line by line in reading order, plus the lists of headings, landmarks, links and controls that screen reader users jump around with. Missing names, vague links and skipped headings are flagged.
It is a preview built from Chrome's accessibility tree, the same data screen readers start from. It is not NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver or TalkBack, which phrase things differently and have behaviour of their own. Use it to find problems fast, then test with a real screen reader.

Page addressPreview this page
Any public page. We load it in Chrome, read its accessibility tree and write out what a screen reader would come across, in reading order. The transcript is not saved.

chunks.heading: How the preview is made
chunks.text:
Browsers build an accessibility tree for every page: each element's role (heading, link, button), its accessible name, and its states, such as expanded, checked or required. Screen readers read that tree through the operating system and then decide for themselves how to present it.
This tool loads your page in headless Chrome, waits for it to settle, scrolls it so lazy sections load, and reads the full tree through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. It then walks the tree in reading order and writes one line per stop in plain wording: “heading level 2, Pricing”, “link, Contact us”, “edit, Email, required”, “list, 5 items”, and the start and end of each landmark. Text that a link or button already uses as its name is not read twice, and a label next to the field it names is not repeated.
Reading order is the order of the tree, which follows the page source. Content that CSS moves around visually still reads in source order here, as it does for screen reader users, which is often where a confusing page comes from.
What it cannot tell you is how a particular product will sound, or whether the page works when you use it. The screen reader testing guide covers how to check a page with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack.

chunks.heading: What gets flagged
chunks.text:
The checks run on each list, and the WCAG criteria they relate to
List Flagged WCAG
Headings No level 1 heading, empty headings, and skipped levels such as h2 to h4. More than one h1 is noted but not counted as a problem. 1.3.1, 2.4.6
Landmarks No main landmark, more than one main, and several navigation landmarks with no names to tell them apart. 1.3.1
Links No accessible name, a web address used as the text, vague text such as "click here" or "read more", and the same text going to different places. 2.4.4, 4.1.2
Form fields Fields with no accessible name. 4.1.2
Buttons Buttons with no accessible name. 4.1.2
Images Images with no text alternative that are not marked decorative. An unnamed icon inside a named link or button is not flagged. 1.1.1

The criteria are 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), 2.4.6 Headings and Labels and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, with 1.1.1 Non-text Content for images. A flag is a lead to check, not a verdict: whether a heading describes its section, or a link's context makes its purpose clear, still needs a person.

chunks.heading: Limits worth knowing
chunks.text:
Content inside iframes is not included. Each frame is listed with its title so you can check it separately.
Images, video and audio files are not downloaded. Text alternatives still come through; media players show without their own controls.
The page is read as it loads. Menus, dialogs and tabs that need a click are read in their closed state, and nothing is typed or submitted.
Live region announcements, focus changes and descriptions linked with aria-describedby are not read out.
Pages behind a sign-in, and sites that block automated browsers, cannot be checked.
The transcript stops at about 1,500 lines on very long pages. The lists of headings, landmarks, links and controls still cover the whole page.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is this the same as using NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver or TalkBack?▾
No. It is a preview built from Chrome's accessibility tree, the same data screen readers start from, written out in plain wording. NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack each phrase roles and states their own way, decide for themselves what to read in browse mode, and have their own settings for punctuation, verbosity and tables. VoiceOver usually runs with Safari, whose tree differs from Chrome's in places. Use the preview to find problems quickly, then confirm them with a real screen reader.

Where does the transcript come from?▾
We load the page in headless Chrome, scroll it so lazy sections load, and read the full accessibility tree through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. That tree holds each element's role, accessible name and states, which is what Chrome passes to screen readers through the operating system. The tool walks it in reading order and writes one line per stop, for example 'heading level 2, Pricing' or 'button, Menu, collapsed'.

Why is something I can see on the page missing from the transcript?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Usually because it is hidden from assistive technology, with aria-hidden or a role of presentation, or because it is a CSS background image. Content inside an iframe is not included, and anything that only appears after a click, such as a closed menu or an unopened tab, is read in its closed state. If visible text is missing and it is not in a frame, look for aria-hidden on it or on a parent.

Why does every line of a card start with 'link'?▾
When one link wraps a heading, a summary and a date, screen readers read each part as part of that link, so every line of it is marked as link. The heading still appears in the headings list. A link that only wraps text is announced once, with its name, and the text inside it is not read again.

Does link text such as 'read more' always fail WCAG?▾
Not always. 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), Level A, allows the purpose to come from the sentence, list item, table cell or heading around the link. It is flagged because screen reader users often move through a list of links, where that context is gone and the list reads 'read more, read more, read more'. 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only), Level AAA, needs the link text to make sense on its own.

Will the speech clash with my own screen reader?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: It should not. Speech uses your browser's built-in voices and only starts when you press Play. The transcript is not a live region, so your screen reader does not also read each line as it is spoken. When you move the virtual cursor with the buttons, the new line is announced once. If you already use a screen reader, the buttons are usually the better way through.

chunks.heading: Are your buttons and links big enough to tap?
chunks.text:
Small, crowded targets are hard to hit for people with tremors, limited dexterity or low vision, and for anyone using a phone one-handed. This checker loads a live page in Chrome, on a phone or desktop screen, and measures every link, button and control against the 24 by 24 pixel minimum in WCAG 2.5.8, with the spacing and inline exceptions worked out for you.

Page addressCheck this page
A public page. We load it in Chrome as a 390 by 844 pixel phone with touch, as a first-time visitor with no cookies.
What to checkFocus order and visibilityPresses Tab through the page, up to 80 stops, and checks each one.Target size (WCAG 2.5.8)Measures every link, button and control against 24 by 24 pixels.
Screen sizeDesktop1280 by 800 pixelsPhone390 by 844 pixels, with touch

chunks.heading: Which target size applies
chunks.text:
The figure people quote depends on who they are reading. WCAG sets the requirement you can be held to; the platform guidelines are design advice for touch screens.
Target size minimums from WCAG and platform design guidelines
Source Minimum Status
WCAG 2.2, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing Level AA, the usual legal benchmark
WCAG 2.1 and 2.2, 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) 44 by 44 CSS pixels Level AAA, a stretch goal
Apple Human Interface Guidelines 44 by 44 points Platform design guidance for iOS
Material Design (Android) 48 by 48 density-independent pixels Platform design guidance for Android

Read the criteria in full: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) and 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced).

chunks.heading: The exceptions, and which ones the checker applies
chunks.text:
A target smaller than 24 by 24 pixels is not automatically a failure. 2.5.8 has five exceptions, and most undersized targets on a typical page pass through one of them.
Spacing (measured): a 24 pixel circle centred on the small target does not touch any other target, or another small target's circle.
Inline (detected): the target is a link in a sentence or block of text, where the line height sets its size.
User agent control (detected): the browser decides the size and the author has not changed it, as with an unstyled checkbox.
Equivalent (check by hand): another control on the same page does the same thing and meets the size.
Essential (check by hand): the size is part of the information, as with pins on a map or a legally required presentation.

The results separate targets that pass by spacing from those that fail, so you can see where a redesign that tightens the spacing would tip a page into failure.

chunks.heading: How to fix small targets
Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What is the minimum target size in WCAG?▾
WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, asks for pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. A smaller target still passes if it has enough space around it, if it is a link inside a sentence, if the browser sets its size, if another control does the same job at full size, or if the small size is essential. 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA, asks for 44 by 44 CSS pixels.

Is the WCAG touch target size 44 by 44 or 24 by 24?▾
Both, at different levels. 24 by 24 CSS pixels is the AA minimum added in WCAG 2.2, and AA is what most laws and contracts point to. 44 by 44 is the AAA enhanced level from WCAG 2.1. Apple recommends 44 by 44 points and Material Design 48 by 48 density-independent pixels for touch screens, so on mobile, designing to 44 or 48 and testing against 24 is a sensible approach.

How does the spacing exception work?▾
Imagine a circle 24 pixels across centred on each target that is smaller than 24 by 24. The target passes if its circle does not touch any other target, or the circle of another small target. In practice a row of 16 pixel icons spaced 24 pixels apart, centre to centre, passes; the same icons packed together fail. The checker draws these circles and tests every pair.

Why check on a phone viewport?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Responsive pages often shrink controls, stack them closer together or swap in icon-only buttons on small screens, and touch is less precise than a mouse pointer. A page can pass at desktop width and fail on a phone. The phone option loads the page at 390 by 844 pixels with touch emulation and a mobile user agent, so you see the layout a phone gets.

Does the checker count the clickable area or the visible size?▾
The clickable area: the element's box as the browser lays it out, including padding. An icon that looks 16 pixels wide inside a button with 4 pixels of padding on each side is a 24 pixel target, and passes. A transparent ::before or ::after that extends the hit area past the box counts too, unless it overlaps another target (overlapping area does not count) or a container clips it.

What can it not check?▾
Whether a small target is essential, as with pins on a map, and whether another control on the page does the same thing at full size. Both are exceptions in 2.5.8, so check any failures against them by hand. It also measures one state of the page, as a first-time visitor, so targets that appear only after a click are not included.

chunks.heading: Contrast for text over images, measured at every pixel
chunks.text: A colour picker samples one point of a photo. Text over an image has to pass against all of them. Mark the text in a screenshot and this tool scores it against every background pixel, shows where it fails, and works out the overlay that fixes it. The image is measured in your browser and never uploaded.

chunks.heading: Start with an image
chunks.text:
Choose, drop or paste a screenshot or design export (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF or AVIF, up to 40 MB). It is read in your browser and never uploaded.

Choose an imageTry an example

chunks.heading: Why the worst point decides it
chunks.text:
WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) asks for a ratio between the text and its background: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text. It has no rule for averaging. On a flat colour there is one background, so one number. On a photo or a gradient the background changes under every letter, and the text has to meet the ratio against all of it. The part of the image with the least contrast is the part someone cannot read, so that is the number that passes or fails.
W3C documents this as a named failure, F83: background images that do not give foreground text enough contrast. It is an easy failure to miss: a design can pass a colour check because the text was checked against the image's average colour, or against the part of the image that shows at one screen width.
That is why the tool leads with the worst ratio. The share of the background that passes and the 5th percentile are there to show the size of the problem: a worst point of 2:1 with 98% passing is a small bright spot to cover; a 5th percentile below the threshold means the whole design needs an overlay or a different image.

chunks.heading: How the measurement works
chunks.text:
The marked area is read at the image's own resolution. Areas over 4 megapixels are scaled down to 4 megapixels first, and the results say so. Transparent pixels are treated as white.
The text colour is detected or set by you. Detection splits the area into light and dark groups and takes the most common colour of the group that is shaped like text: thin strokes that stay inside the area. Every pixel within the tolerance of the text colour counts as text.
Background pixels within 2 pixels of the text are skipped, because anti-aliasing blends them with the letters.
Every remaining pixel is scored with the WCAG 2 formula, the same one our contrast checker uses. The tool reports the worst ratio, the 5th percentile, the share that passes each threshold, where the failures are, and the APCA value at the worst point for reference.

chunks.heading: Ways to fix text that fails over an image
chunks.text:
Fixes for text over images and when each one fits
Fix How Good to know
Overlay (scrim) A semi-transparent black or white layer between the image and the text The tool gives the smallest opacity that passes. A gradient scrim that is darkest behind the text keeps more of the photo.
Panel behind the text A solid or semi-opaque background on the text element itself The same opacity as the overlay works, and the rest of the image is untouched.
Halo A wide, dark text-shadow that surrounds every letter Counts as the background only if it surrounds the letters fully. Measure a screenshot.
Move or recrop Place the text over a calm, even part of the image Check every breakpoint: background-size: cover crops differently at each width.
Change the text colour White or near-black text Mid-tone text leaves no room: no overlay can rescue it on a busy image.

The text over images guide sets out each of these fixes with CSS you can copy. The criteria are 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (AA), 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) (AAA) and, for icons and graphics over images, 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA). To see how a page looks with colour vision deficiency or blur, try the website vision simulator.

chunks.heading: What the tool cannot tell you
chunks.text:
It separates text from background by colour. Where the background contains the text colour itself, those pixels count as text and are left out, so the result can be optimistic. Turn on the text tint to check.
Text in more than one colour, gradient text and text with an outline need to be checked one colour at a time: set each colour and mark the letters that use it.
It measures the screenshot you give it. A responsive page shows different parts of the image at different widths, and a carousel or video shows different frames, so check each one that carries text.
Heavy JPEG compression adds noise around letters. Raise the tolerance if the letter edges show as failing, and prefer a PNG screenshot.
Contrast is one requirement among several. Text that is part of the image file also needs to meet 1.4.5 Images of Text and have a text alternative.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Why does the tool report the worst point instead of an average?▾
WCAG 1.4.3 has no averaging rule. Text needs the minimum ratio against the background it sits on, so when the background is a photo or a gradient, the part with the least contrast decides the result. An average can pass while a third of a headline is unreadable over a bright patch of sky. The tool still shows the share of the background that passes and the 5th percentile, which tell you whether a failure is a small spot or most of the area.

Is my image uploaded anywhere?▾
No. The image is read by your browser and measured there. Nothing is sent to our servers, so it is safe to check unreleased designs and screenshots of private pages.

Why are the pixels right next to the letters skipped?▾
Text is drawn with anti-aliasing: the pixels along each letter's edge are a blend of the text colour and the background. They are not background, and counting them would make almost any text look as if it fails. The tool skips background pixels within 2 pixels of a text pixel and measures everything else in the marked area.

How is the overlay opacity worked out?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
The tool composites a black and a white overlay over every distinct background colour in the area, one percent of opacity at a time, exactly as a browser blends a semi-transparent layer, and reports the lowest opacity at which every point passes the threshold you chose. It assumes the words are live text on top of the overlay. If the words are part of the image file, the overlay darkens them too and the figure does not apply.

Does a text-shadow count towards contrast?▾
It can. W3C's guidance on 1.4.3 treats a wide border or halo that surrounds the letters as their background, so a dark halo can supply the contrast. A faint, blurred or offset shadow leaves parts of each letter against the image, which usually still fails. Take a screenshot with the shadow applied and measure it here.

Which ratio should I check against?▾
4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (at least 24 px, or 18.66 px bold) under 1.4.3 at Level AA, and 7:1 and 4.5:1 under 1.4.6 at Level AAA. Icons and other graphics that carry meaning need 3:1 under 1.4.11. Logos and text that is purely decorative are exempt from 1.4.3.

chunks.heading: What the URL Accessibility Auditor Does
chunks.text:
The auditor opens the URL you give it in a headless Chromium browser on our server, waits for the page to load at a 1920 by 1080 desktop viewport, and runs axe-core, the open-source rules engine behind most automated accessibility checkers. Every violation axe reports is stored with its impact level, the WCAG tags axe assigns to the rule, the CSS selector and HTML of the first offending element, and a link to the rule documentation.
Two layers sit on top of the raw scan. A weighted score turns the violation counts into a single number for tracking progress between runs, and a language model writes a short business-oriented summary, with quick wins, from the score, the counts, and the top three findings. Both are conveniences for reading the results; the findings table is the audit.

chunks.heading: How to Use It
chunks.text:
Start without an account, or sign in. One scan a day is free and shows the score and the three most severe findings. Signed in, audits cost five credits, show everything, and are saved to your account. New accounts start with 100 credits.
Enter a full public URL. Include the scheme, for example https://example.com/pricing. Pick the page you actually want to test; the scan does not follow links.
Wait for the three stages. Page load and axe scan, AI summary, then report assembly. Most pages finish in under a minute; the page load itself times out after 30 seconds, so a very slow site fails rather than hanging.
Work the findings table. Sort by impact, open each rule's help link, and locate the element with the selector. Re-run after fixing to confirm the count drops, and use Audit History to compare runs.

chunks.heading: What It Checks and the WCAG 2.2 Criteria It Maps To
chunks.text:
The scan runs the axe-core rules tagged wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa, wcag22aa, and best-practice. Each violation carries the criterion tags axe attaches to the rule, which is where the WCAG mapping in the table comes from. The rules that fire most often on real sites, and the criteria they map to, include:
Missing alternative text on images and inputs: 1.1.1 Non-text Content.
Insufficient text contrast: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum).
Form fields, buttons, and links without an accessible name, and invalid ARIA attributes or roles: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, with link text also mapped to 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context).
Broken list and table structure: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships.
Missing or invalid page language: 3.1.1 Language of Page; missing document title: 2.4.2 Page Titled; no skip link or landmarks: 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks.
Small click targets under the WCAG 2.2 rule set: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum).

Best-practice rules, such as heading order and landmark conventions, appear in the results without a WCAG tag. They are worth fixing but are not conformance failures on their own.

chunks.heading: What It Cannot Check
chunks.text:
Automated rules detect a minority of WCAG failures, and this scan has specific blind spots you should plan around:
Only the initial page state. Nothing is clicked, typed, or scrolled. Menus, modals, form validation, and anything revealed by interaction are not examined, so 3.3.1 Error Identification and dialog focus behaviour are out of reach.
No keyboard or focus testing. 2.1.1 Keyboard, 2.4.3 Focus Order, and 2.4.7 Focus Visible need a person at a keyboard.
Presence, not quality. The scan can tell that an image has alt text, not whether the text is meaningful, and that a video element exists, not whether its captions are accurate.
Desktop viewport only. Reflow at 320 CSS pixels wide (1.4.10 Reflow) and mobile layouts are not exercised.
One page, no login. Cross-page criteria such as 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation and anything behind authentication are outside the scan.
Needs-review results are not shown. axe also returns checks it could not decide, for instance contrast on text over a background image. The report lists only confirmed violations, so those items are silently absent.

A clean scan is the point where manual testing starts, not where it ends. The automated versus manual testing guide explains what each method catches, and the step-by-step audit guide walks through the manual checks.

chunks.heading: Reading the Output
chunks.text:
Impact levels come straight from axe-core: critical and serious findings usually block a task for someone, moderate findings make a task harder, and minor findings are polish. The score subtracts 10, 5, 2, and 1 points respectively per finding from 100 and stops at 0, so a single page with ten critical issues scores zero, and a score of 90 or above is labelled Excellent in the interface. Use the number to compare the same page over time, not to compare different pages, which have different amounts of content to fail.
Each row in the findings table names the axe rule, its description, the WCAG tags, the selector of the first element that failed, and the fix suggestion from the rule's help text. Only the first matching element is stored per rule, so a rule that fired on forty images shows one selector; fix the pattern, not the instance. The AI Intelligence Analysis panel is generated from the score, the counts, and the top three findings only, which makes it a readable narrative for stakeholders rather than a complete plan.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
What does the accessibility score mean?▾
It is a triage number, not a conformance measure. The scan starts at 100 and subtracts 10 for each critical violation, 5 for each serious, 2 for each moderate, and 1 for each minor, with a floor of 0. A 100 means axe-core found no violations among the rules it ran on that page load; it does not mean the page conforms to WCAG, because most success criteria need a person to judge them.

Why does the violation count change between runs of the same URL?▾
Pages are not static. Cookie banners, rotating promotions, A/B tests, lazy-loaded sections, and third-party embeds change what is in the DOM when the scan runs, and contrast checks depend on which fonts and images had loaded. Run the page two or three times and anchor on the findings that appear every time; treat the ones that come and go as leads to confirm by hand.

Can it scan pages behind a login or a whole site?▾
No on both counts. The auditor loads one public URL in a fresh headless browser with no cookies, so anything behind authentication shows the login page instead. It scans only that page in its initial state. Use the Scope Checker to inventory a site, then audit a representative sample of URLs one at a time.

How much does an audit cost?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
One scan a day is free without an account: you get the score, the severity breakdown and the three most severe findings, and can unlock the rest with a work email. Signed in, an audit costs five credits, new accounts start with 100, and completed audits are saved to your history so you can reopen them without paying again. Unlimited access accounts are not charged.

Does it cover WCAG 2.2?▾
The scan runs axe-core rules tagged for WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 at Levels A and AA, the WCAG 2.2 Level AA tags, and axe's best-practice rules. In practice that adds automated coverage for 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum); the other 2.2 criteria, such as 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 3.2.6 Consistent Help, and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication, cannot be judged by an automated rule and need manual review.

chunks.heading: Does your page still make sense without colour or sharp vision?
chunks.text:
Enter a web address or upload a screenshot and see it through simulations of colour vision deficiency, achromatopsia, blurred vision and low contrast sensitivity, next to the original. It is the quickest way to find links, errors and charts that only colour tells apart.

Website addressUpload an image
Page addressSimulate this page
We load the page once in a headless browser, 1280 pixels wide, as a signed-out visitor, and take a screenshot up to 4,000 pixels tall. Pages behind a login can't be loaded: upload a screenshot instead.

chunks.heading: What a simulation can and cannot show
chunks.text:
Colour vision deficiency is common. Colour Blind Awareness estimates it affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women, most often as a reduced ability to tell reds and greens apart. Simulations make that easy to design for: if two states of a control, two lines on a chart or an error and a success message become the same colour in the filter, you have found information carried by colour alone. The colour blind friendly design guide shows how to fix it for links, form errors, status messages and charts.
What a simulation cannot do is show you what a particular person sees. The filters here apply a published model of typical cone loss, an illustrative blur and a flat loss of contrast. Real vision varies with the person, the condition, the screen and the light, and many forms of low vision, such as field loss or sensitivity to glare, cannot be shown on a screenshot at all. Treat a simulation as a way to find problems, never as proof that a design works for someone.
A simulation also cannot measure contrast. If text fades badly under blur or low contrast sensitivity, check the actual ratio with the contrast checker, or for text over photos the text over image contrast checker.

chunks.heading: The WCAG criteria it helps with
chunks.text:
WCAG criteria, what each asks for, and what to look for in a simulation
Criterion What it asks What to look for
1.4.1 Use of Color (A) Colour is not the only way information, actions or responses are shown. Links in text with no underline, red-only errors, required fields marked only in colour, chart series and status badges that differ only by hue.
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (AA) Text has at least 4.5:1 contrast with its background, or 3:1 when large. Grey body text, placeholder text and text over images that fade first under blur and low contrast sensitivity. Then measure them.
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA) Control boundaries, focus indicators and meaningful graphics have at least 3:1 contrast. Pale input borders, icon-only buttons and chart lines that vanish, especially under low contrast sensitivity.

chunks.heading: How the simulations work
chunks.text:
For a web address, our server opens the page in a headless Chrome at 1280 by 800 with reduced motion, scrolls through it so lazy images load, and returns one screenshot up to 4,000 pixels tall. Every filter is then applied in your browser, so switching between them is instant.
Protan, deutan and tritan simulations apply the Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009) matrices in linear light. At 100% they model the full loss of one cone type; lower severities blend the matrix with normal vision, which approximates the anomalous forms rather than reproducing the paper's separate values for each step.
Achromatopsia replaces every colour with a grey of the same relative luminance.
Blurred vision applies a Gaussian blur at three levels, scaled with the screenshot so it stays the same relative to the page. The levels are illustrative and not calibrated to a measure of acuity.
Low contrast sensitivity halves contrast around mid-grey and softens the image slightly.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
How accurate is a colour blindness simulation?▾
It is a model, not a recording of anyone's sight. The colour vision filters use the Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009) model, which is widely used for this, and show a typical result for each type. Two people with the same diagnosis can see differently, and the model does not include things like viewing conditions or how a person has learned to use the cues they have. Use the simulation to spot designs that depend on colour, then fix them so they no longer depend on it.

Which conditions does it simulate?▾
Protan, deutan and tritan colour vision deficiency, each from a mild anomalous form up to the full loss of one cone type (protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia); achromatopsia, shown as lightness only; blurred vision at three illustrative levels; and low contrast sensitivity, shown as halved contrast with slight softening. Low vision covers far more than blur, including field loss and light sensitivity, which a screenshot filter cannot represent.

Does a page that looks fine in every simulation meet WCAG?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Not on its own. WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color asks that colour is never the only way information is conveyed, which a simulation helps you find, but 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 set measured contrast ratios that only a contrast check can confirm. Many other criteria have nothing to do with vision at all. Run an automated scan and check contrast with a contrast checker as well.

Why does the screenshot look different from the page in my browser?▾
Our server loads the page once, 1280 pixels wide, as a new signed-out visitor with reduced motion turned on, so you may see a cookie banner, a different hero image or a paused carousel. The screenshot stops at 4,000 pixels. Some sites block automated browsers altogether; for those, and for pages behind a login, take a screenshot yourself and upload it.

Is my page or image stored?▾
An uploaded image never leaves your browser. For a web address, our server loads the page, sends the screenshot back to your browser and does not keep it. As with our other URL tools, we log the site that was checked and whether the capture worked.

Why not just switch on a colour blindness filter in the operating system?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text: Operating system colour filters are designed to help people with colour vision deficiency tell colours apart, so they shift colours rather than simulate the deficiency. Browser developer tools do include vision deficiency emulation, which is a good way to check a page you are building. This tool works on any public page or image without developer tools, compares the result with the original side by side, and adds severity levels, blur and low contrast sensitivity.

chunks.heading: Check Word and PowerPoint files for accessibility, without uploading them
chunks.text: Choose a .docx or .pptx file and get a list of the problems that stop screen reader users, and anyone else, from using it: missing alt text, headings and slide titles, table header rows, vague link text, a missing document language and more. Each finding says where it is and how to fix it in Microsoft 365. The checks run in your browser, so the file stays on your device.

chunks.heading: Check a document or presentation
chunks.text:
Your file never leaves this device. It is opened and checked by your browser. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere, so it is safe to check confidential documents.

Drop a .docx or .pptx file here, or
Choose a Word or PowerPoint fileWord documents (.docx) and PowerPoint presentations (.pptx), up to 50 MB. Older .doc and .ppt files and password-protected files cannot be read.

No file to hand? Try an example:Sample Word newsletterSample PowerPoint deck

chunks.heading: What it checks
chunks.text:
Each check is tied to the WCAG success criterion it helps you meet. WCAG was written for web pages, but the W3C's guidance on applying it to documents (WCAG2ICT) treats a Word or PowerPoint file as a page, and so do procurement rules such as EN 301 549 and Section 508.
The checks run on Word documents and PowerPoint presentations, and the WCAG criteria they relate to
Check Word PowerPoint WCAG
Title Title in the file's properties, and not a default such as Document1 The same 2.4.2
Language The document's default language Language on the text of every slide 3.1.1
Headings and titles Heading styles used, levels not skipped, text that only looks like a heading Every slide has a title, and titles are different 1.3.1, 2.4.2, 2.4.6
Alt text Pictures, charts, SmartArt and groups have alt text or are marked decorative; generated descriptions and file names flagged The same, plus video and audio 1.1.1
Tables Header row marked to repeat, merged cells, tables inside tables Header Row ticked, merged cells 1.3.1
Links Text that is a web address, "click here" or empty The same, plus linked pictures without alt text 2.4.4
Reading order Text boxes and pictures that float over the text The title is read first; slides crowded with default-named shapes 1.3.2
Lists and spacing Typed bullets and numbers, runs of blank paragraphs Not checked 1.3.1

chunks.heading: What it checks
chunks.text:
Colour contrast Text with a fixed colour against white, the page colour or its shading Not checked 1.4.3
Audio and video Not checked A reminder to check captions and transcripts for each clip 1.2.1, 1.2.2

Errors are clear failures, such as a picture with no alt text. Warnings are likely problems that need a person to decide, such as a skipped heading level. Tips are good practice, such as removing blank paragraphs used for spacing. Our guides on how to make a Word document accessible and how to make PowerPoint presentations accessible walk through each fix step by step.

chunks.heading: Why the file never leaves your device
chunks.text:
Since Office 2007, a .docx or .pptx file has been a zip archive of XML files: one for the text, one for the styles, one per slide, and the pictures alongside. A few lines of code in the page can unzip it and read the XML, so the checker does everything on your device. It opens the archive, reads only the parts that describe text and structure, and never looks at the pictures or media themselves.
Nothing is uploaded, and the page sends nothing about the file anywhere. That matters for the documents people most need to check: contracts, board papers, HR policies and course materials that should not be pasted into an online service.

chunks.heading: What it cannot tell you
chunks.text:
Whether alt text is accurate or useful. It finds missing alt text, file names and unedited automatic descriptions; only a person can judge the rest.
Most colour contrast. It measures text given a fixed colour in Word. Theme colours, colours from table styles, text in shapes and everything in PowerPoint need the contrast checker or Office's own checker.
Whether the reading order makes sense beyond the slide title coming first, or whether headings describe their sections.
Whether a video has captions, or whether the language set on the text is the language it is written in.
Text inside charts, SmartArt and pictures, and footnotes and comments. In headers and footers it checks pictures only.
PDFs exported from the file. Export with tags and check the result with the PDF accessibility checker; the PDF accessibility guide explains what to look for.

Word and PowerPoint include their own checker under Review > Check Accessibility, and it is worth running on every file. It sees the document the way Office lays it out; this tool gives you a list to download and share and looks for a few patterns, such as typed bullets and text formatted to look like a heading, that are easy to miss. Neither replaces reading the file with a screen reader.

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
Is my document uploaded anywhere?▾
No. A .docx or .pptx file is a zip of XML files, and your browser can open it on its own. The page reads the file on your device, unzips only the parts that hold the text and structure (not the pictures or media), runs the checks and shows the results. Nothing about the file is sent to Accessibility.build or anyone else, so it is safe for confidential documents.

Why can it not open my .doc or .ppt file?▾
Files ending .doc and .ppt use the binary formats Office used before 2007, which a browser cannot read without a large converter. Open the file in Word or PowerPoint, select File > Save As, choose Word Document (.docx) or PowerPoint Presentation (.pptx), and check the new copy. Password-protected files are encrypted, so remove the password from a copy first.

How is this different from the Accessibility Checker in Word and PowerPoint?▾
Microsoft's checker, under Review > Check Accessibility, runs inside the app and is worth using on every file. This tool works on a file without opening Office, gives you a list you can download as CSV or Excel and share, and looks for a few patterns that are easy to miss, such as typed bullets, text formatted to look like a heading, skipped heading levels and text with a fixed low-contrast colour. Use both.

Does a clean result mean the document meets WCAG?▾

chunks.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.text:
No. Automated checks find structural problems such as missing alt text or a table with no header row. They cannot tell whether alt text is accurate, whether headings describe their sections, whether colour carries meaning on its own or whether a video's captions are correct. Treat a clean result as a good start, then read the file with a screen reader or have it reviewed.

Can I check a Google Docs or Google Slides file?▾
Yes, once it is downloaded. In Google Docs select File > Download > Microsoft Word (.docx); in Google Slides select File > Download > Microsoft PowerPoint (.pptx). The results describe what Google writes into the file, so a heading made with Google's Heading styles is reported as a heading, and alt text added in Google carries over.

Will my fixes carry over when I save as a PDF?▾
Mostly, if you export with tags. In Word or PowerPoint on Windows, choose PDF as the file type, select Options and make sure Document structure tags for accessibility is ticked. On a Mac, choose Best for electronic distribution and accessibility. Headings, alt text and table headers then become tags in the PDF, and the title is copied into its properties. Check the PDF itself too, because some things, such as text boxes, do not always export cleanly.

chunks.heading: WCAG 3.0: The Next Generation of Accessibility Standards
chunks.text:
The W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 represents a fundamental reimagining of accessibility standards. With 12 guideline categories, six reporting tiers in place of A/AA/AAA, and scope beyond web content — here is everything you need to know.

12 Categories

Working Draft

Broader Than Web

Six Reporting Tiers

Latest draft

chunks.heading: What Changed in the 10 September 2026 Working Draft
chunks.text:
This draft supersedes the one published on 3 March 2026. These are the substantive changes.

1

chunks.heading: Leveling moved out of conformance
chunks.text:
A new Reporting section now carries the idea of levels. The editors write that WCAG 3 “moves the concept of leveling from conformance to reporting”, and use the term “reporting tiers” to keep it distinct from the old “conformance levels”. The previous draft’s Conformance level subsection is gone.

2

chunks.heading: Six reporting tiers, with Bronze, Silver, and Gold above conformance
chunks.text:
The tiers are cumulative: 1 avoid physical harm, 2 foundational access, 3 conformance, 4 Bronze, 5 Silver, 6 Gold. Conformance is tier 3, reached when every core requirement is met. Tiers 4 to 6 add supplemental requirements and assertions, and the exact numbers are still marked TBD.

3

chunks.heading: Core requirements are tagged by severity
chunks.text:
Every core requirement now carries one of four tags describing the worst-case impact of failing it: Physical Harm, Risk, Barrier, or Friction. These tags are what build the reporting tiers. Assertions are separately tagged as being about Content or about the Organization.

4

chunks.heading: Conformance advanced from exploratory to developing
chunks.text:
The Conformance section changed maturity status between the two 2026 drafts. The new Reporting section is still marked exploratory.

5

chunks.heading: Best practices renamed Recommended Practices
chunks.text:
They remain informative and are not needed to conform, but they are now named consistently and can take the form of either a provision or a method.

6

chunks.heading: Images and media split into nine guidelines
chunks.text:
The old Media alternatives guideline was dissolved. Transcripts, Sign language, and Accessible media player are now guidelines in their own right, and Figure captions moved up to 2.1.2. Transcripts, captions, and audio descriptions each gained a full set of requirements covering speakers, sounds, visual information, style guides, and usability testing.

7

chunks.heading: Text appearance gained minimum and enhanced requirements
chunks.text:
Blocks of text readable, text style readable, and text contrast sufficient each now appear in both a minimum and an enhanced form, alongside the existing adjustability requirements.

8

chunks.heading: Requirement type moved from headings into tags
chunks.text: Headings used to read “Core requirement: Images detectable”. They now read “Images detectable”, with the type carried as a tag. Some requirements were also renamed, including No flashing to No flashing over threshold, and No repetitive links to No repetitive adjacent interactive elements.

chunks.heading: The tier model is not settled
chunks.text:
An editor’s note in the Reporting section records an alternative proposal that would use scoring to show progress toward conformance and then award Bronze, Silver, and Gold after it. The Working Group is inviting public comment on which approach to take, so treat the six tiers as the current direction rather than a decided outcome.

Source: W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0, W3C Working Draft 10 September 2026

chunks.heading: The Evolution of Accessibility Standards
chunks.text: WCAG 3.0 builds on over two decades of web accessibility guidelines.

chunks.heading: New Name, Broader Scope
chunks.text: Renamed from "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines" to "W3C Accessibility Guidelines", reflecting expanded scope covering web, native apps, authoring tools, user agents, IoT devices, and virtual/augmented reality.

chunks.heading: Reporting Tiers, Not Levels
chunks.text: No more A/AA/AAA. Conformance is one bar: meet every core requirement. Six cumulative reporting tiers then describe where you are, from avoiding physical harm up through Bronze, Silver, and Gold.

chunks.heading: 12 Guideline Categories
chunks.text: The 4 POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) evolve into 12 functional categories — from Images & Media to Policy & Protection — covering new areas like cognitive accessibility and algorithmic fairness.

chunks.heading: WCAG 3.0 Conceptual Framework
chunks.text: How the new building blocks of WCAG 3.0 connect to form a cohesive accessibility framework.

chunks.heading: Guidelines
chunks.text: Outcome statements that describe what accessible content should achieve, organized into 12 functional categories.

chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text: Testable provisions in two kinds: core requirements, which must all be met to conform, and supplemental requirements, which go beyond conformance.

chunks.heading: Methods
chunks.text: Technology-specific approaches for meeting a requirement or assertion. A method only counts toward conformance if it is accessibility supported.

chunks.heading: Assertions
chunks.text: Documented statements about accessibility practices an organization follows — tagged as being about content or about the organization.

chunks.heading: Reporting tiers
chunks.text: Six cumulative tiers that replace conformance levels, running from avoiding physical harm through conformance to Bronze, Silver, and Gold.

chunks.heading: Functional Needs
chunks.text:
User-need-based groupings that drive the entire framework, replacing disability-category approaches with functional descriptions.

Learn more about each concept

chunks.heading: Important: WCAG 3.0 Is Not Final
chunks.text:
Working Draft status — the specification is subject to significant changes and is not ready for implementation requirements.
Does not deprecate WCAG 2.x — WCAG 2.2 remains the current, stable standard for compliance and legal purposes.
Legal requirements unchanged — ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549, and the European Accessibility Act continue to reference WCAG 2.x.
Several years remaining — the W3C Working Group has confirmed substantial work is still needed before the final Recommendation.

chunks.heading: When will WCAG 3.0 be finalized?
chunks.text: The most recent Working Draft was published on 10 September 2026. The W3C Accessibility Guidelines Working Group states that while the draft has moved closer toward completion, it still has several years of work remaining. There is no firm date for the final Recommendation, but organizations should monitor progress and begin familiarizing themselves with the new framework now.

chunks.heading: Does WCAG 3.0 replace WCAG 2.2?
chunks.text: No, WCAG 3.0 does not deprecate WCAG 2.x. WCAG 2.2 remains the current, stable standard and will continue to be required by laws and regulations in many countries for the foreseeable future. WCAG 3.0 is being developed in parallel and will eventually provide an alternative path to conformance.

chunks.heading: Should I start following WCAG 3.0 now?
chunks.text: Not yet for compliance purposes — WCAG 3.0 is still a Working Draft and subject to significant changes. However, understanding its direction is valuable. The best preparation is ensuring strong WCAG 2.2 AA compliance, as content meeting WCAG 2.2 is expected to satisfy most of WCAG 3.0's minimum conformance level.

chunks.heading: What is the difference between WCAG 2 and WCAG 3?
chunks.text: WCAG 3.0 represents a fundamental redesign. It replaces the 4 POUR principles with 12 guideline categories, expands scope beyond web content to include apps, tools, and devices, and introduces new concepts like assertions and functional needs. The September 2026 draft also moves the idea of levels out of conformance entirely: conformance is a single bar (meet every core requirement), and progress toward and beyond that bar is expressed through six reporting tiers rather than A/AA/AAA.

chunks.heading: Will WCAG 3.0 affect legal compliance requirements?
chunks.text: Not immediately. Current laws (ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549, EAA) reference WCAG 2.x. It will take years after WCAG 3.0 is finalized for regulatory bodies to update their requirements. Organizations should continue meeting WCAG 2.2 AA for legal compliance while monitoring WCAG 3.0 development.

chunks.heading: Is WCAG 3.0 harder to meet than WCAG 2.2?
chunks.text: It is different rather than harder, but it is not a straight swap. The W3C states that content conforming to WCAG 2.2 Level A and Level AA is expected to meet most of the minimum conformance level of the new standard, so existing accessible content largely transfers. It also warns that WCAG 3 adds tests WCAG 2.2 does not have, so additional work will be needed to reach full conformance.

chunks.heading: Conformance Models Compared
chunks.text: The biggest structural change: leveling moves out of conformance and into reporting.

chunks.heading: What Stays the Same
chunks.text: Despite the structural overhaul, much of the foundation remains unchanged.

chunks.heading: WCAG 2.x Not Deprecated
chunks.text: WCAG 2.2 remains a valid, stable W3C Recommendation. It continues to be the required standard for legal compliance worldwide and will not be deprecated when WCAG 3.0 is released.

chunks.heading: Core Principles Transfer
chunks.text: The fundamental accessibility concepts — making content perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust — still apply. WCAG 3.0 reorganizes them into 12 categories but the underlying principles carry forward.

chunks.heading: Existing Knowledge Valuable
chunks.text: Teams with strong WCAG 2.x expertise will find their knowledge directly applicable. Most WCAG 2.2 requirements map to WCAG 3.0 equivalents, and accessible development practices remain the same.

chunks.heading: Legal Continuity
chunks.text: Laws and regulations — including the ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549, and the European Accessibility Act — continue referencing WCAG 2.x. This will not change until years after WCAG 3.0 is finalized.

chunks.heading: What Changes
chunks.text: The key areas where WCAG 3.0 departs from the WCAG 2.x approach.

chunks.heading: New Terminology
chunks.text: WCAG 3.0 introduces new vocabulary: requirements replace success criteria, guidelines are written as outcome statements, methods replace techniques, and assertions represent documented accessibility practices. The entire framework uses updated language.

chunks.heading: Broader Scope
chunks.text: The standard expands beyond web content to cover native applications, authoring tools, user agents, IoT devices, virtual reality, and augmented reality — reflected in the renamed title.

chunks.heading: Levels Move to Reporting
chunks.text: The September 2026 draft moves the concept of leveling out of conformance altogether. Conformance itself is a single bar: meet every core requirement. Progress toward and beyond that bar is expressed through six cumulative reporting tiers instead of A/AA/AAA.

chunks.heading: Regular Updates
chunks.text: WCAG 3.0 is designed as a living standard with regular incremental updates, replacing the static versioned release model that required years between WCAG 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2.

chunks.heading: Will my WCAG 2.2 compliant site need to be re-audited for WCAG 3.0?
chunks.text: Content meeting WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA is expected to satisfy most of WCAG 3.0's minimum conformance level. However, WCAG 3.0 introduces new areas of coverage — such as cognitive accessibility and broader platform scope — so some additional work will likely be needed. A full re-audit is not expected, but a gap analysis against WCAG 3.0's new requirements is recommended once the standard is finalized.

chunks.heading: Can I use WCAG 3.0 for legal compliance today?
chunks.text: No. WCAG 3.0 is currently a Working Draft and is not referenced by any law or regulation. For legal compliance, use WCAG 2.2 Level AA, which is referenced by the ADA, Section 508, EN 301 549, and the European Accessibility Act. It will take years after WCAG 3.0 is finalized for regulatory bodies to update their legal references.

chunks.heading: Is WCAG 3.0 harder to meet than WCAG 2.2?
chunks.text: WCAG 3.0 is different rather than harder. Individual requirements are still pass or fail, but the six reporting tiers give partial progress somewhere to show rather than reporting it as outright failure. Content that already conforms to WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA is expected to meet most of WCAG 3.0's minimum conformance level, so strong WCAG 2.2 compliance is the best preparation. The W3C does caution that WCAG 3 adds tests WCAG 2.2 does not have, so reaching full conformance will take additional work.

chunks.heading: WCAG 3.0 Key Concepts and Terminology
chunks.text:
A reference guide to the new vocabulary and conceptual framework that underpins WCAG 3.0. Understand guidelines, requirements, methods, assertions, functional needs, and outcomes.

6 Core Concepts

New Framework

Reference Guide

chunks.heading: How WCAG 3.0 Concepts Connect
chunks.text: The relationship between the core building blocks of the WCAG 3.0 framework.

chunks.heading: Concept Deep Dive
chunks.text:
Each of the six core concepts explained in detail, with WCAG 2.x comparisons and practical examples.

Evolved

chunks.heading: Guidelines
chunks.text:
Definition
Outcome statements that describe what accessible content should achieve. Rather than abstract organizational groupings, WCAG 3.0 guidelines are actionable outcome descriptions.

WCAG 2.x Equivalent
"Guidelines" existed in WCAG 2.x but were more abstract organizational groupings under the four POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust).

Example
"Users can perceive all non-decorative images through text alternatives" is a WCAG 3.0 guideline outcome — specific, measurable, and user-centered.

Key Insight
Guidelines in WCAG 3.0 are organized into 12 functional categories rather than 4 principles, providing more granular and practical groupings.

Redesigned

chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text:
Definition
WCAG 3 has three types of provisions: core requirements, which must all be met to conform; supplemental requirements, which build on the core set and are not required to conform; and assertions, which are documented statements about accessibility practices an organization follows.

WCAG 2.x Equivalent
"Success Criteria" in WCAG 2.x served a similar role, but WCAG 3.0 requirements are more granular and introduce assertions as an entirely new type.

Example
A core requirement might be: "All non-decorative images have a text alternative that describes the image’s purpose."

Key Insight
These are provision types, not levels. Conformance depends only on the core requirements; supplemental requirements and assertions feed the separate reporting tiers.

Upgraded

chunks.heading: Methods
chunks.text:
Definition
Technology-specific approaches for meeting requirements, with detailed test procedures and expected results. Methods tell you exactly how to test a given requirement for a specific technology.

WCAG 2.x Equivalent
"Techniques" in WCAG 2.x were informative and advisory. WCAG 3.0 ties methods more tightly to conformance: the methods you rely on must be accessibility supported.

Example
An HTML method for image alternatives might include: check for the alt attribute, verify it describes the image purpose, and ensure decorative images use an empty alt.

Key Insight
A method only counts toward conformance if browsers and assistive technologies in general use actually support it. WCAG 3 calls this being accessibility supported, and the accessibility support set must be stated in a conformance claim.

Entirely New

chunks.heading: Assertions
chunks.text:
Definition
Documented organizational commitments requiring evidence. Organizations publicly state what they provide for accessibility and back it up with documentation, training records, and process descriptions.

WCAG 2.x Equivalent
No equivalent exists in WCAG 2.x — this is an entirely new concept introduced in WCAG 3.0.

Example
"We provide accessibility training to all developers" with evidence: training records, certificates, and curriculum documentation.

Key Insight
Assertions acknowledge that real accessibility requires organizational commitment — not just technical fixes. Culture, process, and policy matter.

New Foundation

chunks.heading: Functional Needs
chunks.text:
Definition
User-need-based groupings that drive the entire framework. They describe what users need to successfully use content, regardless of specific disability categories or medical diagnoses.

WCAG 2.x Equivalent
Partially relates to "Understanding" documents, but WCAG 2.x was organized by technical principles (POUR), not user needs.

Example
"Users who cannot see need text alternatives for visual content" describes a functional need that drives multiple guidelines and requirements.

Key Insight
Centering on functional needs rather than disability categories is more inclusive and technology-resilient — it future-proofs the standard.

New in Sept 2026

chunks.heading: Reporting Tiers
chunks.text:
Definition
Six cumulative tiers that describe how far a product has got, each one building on the tiers below it: 1 avoid physical harm, 2 foundational access, 3 conformance, 4 Bronze, 5 Silver, 6 Gold. Conformance itself is tier 3, where every core requirement is met.

WCAG 2.x Equivalent
Closest to WCAG 2.x conformance levels (A / AA / AAA), but the September 2026 draft deliberately separates the two ideas. As the editors put it, WCAG 3 “moves the concept of leveling from conformance to reporting”, and uses the phrase “reporting tiers” to keep them distinct from the old “conformance levels”.

Example
A product that meets every core requirement has conformed, and reports at tier 3. Reaching tier 5 (Silver) additionally requires a number of supplemental requirements and assertions about content.

Key Insight
Conformance is a single bar, not a ladder. The tiers exist to report progress toward it and achievements beyond it. This section is still marked exploratory, and the Working Group is openly asking whether tiers or a scoring model works better.
